The station is found nearby, walked to, or placed from the bag (the AiSmelt station pattern); both inputs go into their exact slots with verified clicks, the server-computed result and level cost are read off the menu, and the result is quick-moved out against an applied revision.

Outcomes that cannot produce a result fail with the reason instead of clicking at a dead slot ({@link #anvilFailure}): incompatible, too-expensive (level cost over 39), or insufficient player levels with the deficit named. A missing input fails with the missing map. Ticks the open interaction may run before the station is reported unusable. Ticks the server computation of result+cost may take after both inputs are in. Ticks the result extraction may wait for its applied server confirmation. The vanilla survival level cap: at or above this the anvil refuses with "Too Expensive!". The open menu id whose slots were verified empty, so foreign contents are never consumed. Inventory count of the result item when its take was dispatched. Chosen stack note for ambiguous same-id picks (result data). Each input must be in the menu already or still in the reachable bag. PICKUP-places one unit of the item from the bag into the exact slot. First bag slot with the item id; the plain-only pass keeps named/enchanted gear out of material roles. Records an ambiguous same-id pick so the result data says exactly which stack was consumed. Player-inventory slot -> anvil menu slot (anvil 0-2, main 3-29, hotbar 30-38). Gets an anvil open: nearby, walked to, or placed from the bag (AiSmelt's station pattern). The nearest anvil block in loaded terrain within a short walk. A FAILED result carrying a machine-readable code, with the same cleanup as done(). Why an anvil state cannot produce a result, or null when it can: an empty result slot is incompatible (the server computed nothing), a cost over the vanilla cap is too-expensive, and a cost above the player's level is insufficient-levels. Pure.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiBlazeFig.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiBlazeFig.notes:
The blaze fight: close quickly, extinguish the kill floor, hit from stable footing and defend actual incoming shots. 26.2's BlazeAttackGoal: a blaze that sees the player hovers where it is and fires three fireballs six ticks apart after a sixty-tick charge, within two blocks it strikes instead, and it hovers about the player's eye height. Twenty health: a diamond axe's crit (13.5) and one more hit end it.

Fire first, then a charged swing from stable footing. Lateral movement only answers an actual uncovered projectile or improves terrain cover between attacks. A critical jump is rolled through the shared physics engine before use; a plain finishing hit goes out immediately. A hovering target gets bounded access, and observed spawners get a small adaptive cap. Horizontal ring held round the target: inside the reach, outside the blaze's two-block strike. Further than this (or out of sight), the approach is a travel. A blaze in sight up to this far is chased on foot with the keys when the straight walk toward it is safe floor. A route search to a blaze in plain view took seconds a time on fortress terrain and was re-planned whenever the blaze drifted three blocks; walked straight at, the same blazes were in reach in about a second. Ticks after our own hit in which the blaze drifting away is expected, not a failed approach. 26.2's knockback sets a blaze's horizontal speed to 0.4 a tick and its air drag keeps 0.91 of it, so a hit carries it about four blocks out (2.7 in the first ten ticks). Counted as "no approach progress", every crit was followed within a second by a route search, and two of those left the blaze at 6.5 health for fifteen seconds while the fight walked to another one. Ticks without approach progress (outside the knockback grace) before the approach becomes a route search. Ticks a fight may go on under its retreat line to land a blow that kills its target (the blow is due within them). Every fight tick's distances, keys and swing gates in the log (with the navigation trace and debug). Ticks before a fireball lands at which the shield goes up (vanilla blocks from the fifth tick of use). Where our hit carries a hovering blaze: 26.2's knockback sets its horizontal speed to 0.4 a tick away from the attacker and air drag keeps 0.91 of it a tick, 0.4 / 0.09 = 4.4 blocks in all, unless a block stops it. A blaze only moves sideways under its own power within two blocks of its target (MoveControl pushes on the ticks its goal sets a wanted position, and in the air that is 0.0046 a tick), so where the hit sends it is where it stays. Ticks one target may spend stepping round to a stance whose hit keeps it over floor, before it is hit from anywhere. Blazes no route reached, until when they are left. Until when a blaze fight is running: the guard layer's projectile dodge stands aside for it. Client-thread native rays; the planner receives only these immutable observed stances. A blaze whose drop would land in lava. Blaze rods are a plain drop: nothing burns them but lava, and the Nether's fortresses stand over a lava sea, so this is the one way a verified kill yields nothing at all. The column under the blaze is read from its own cell down to {@link #LAVA_DROP_COLUMN}, through observed cells only - a chunk the client does not have is not evidence of anything. Lava is tested before the landing test because lava has a collision shape of its own: asking "can the drop rest here" first would call a lava surface a landing. How far under a blaze the drop's landing is looked for before the column is called dry. Pure, for tests: the blaze to fight when the nearest one's rod would be lost and a dry one is in reach. Pure, for tests: the lower the better. Distance first; a blaze out of sight counts six blocks further, the committed one three nearer, a wounded one (one hit from death after a crit) six nearer, and one with no floor under or beside it that a stance could hit it from (knocked out over a fortress's drop) five further. Nearest-only picking left a 6.5-health blaze for a fresh one seventeen blocks away and walked under the fire of both. Whether a standing (or jumping) eye on observed floor within three blocks of the blaze's column reaches its box: the floor a melee kill needs. Reads only the top standable cell of each column, from one over the blaze's feet down six; unloaded cells are no floor. No rays: a ranking signal, the approach goal still proves sight before any walk. Pure, for tests: where a hovering blaze with this box comes to rest when hit along the horizontal direction ({@code dx}, {@code dz}, unit length): {@link #KNOCK_DISTANCE} on, or short of the first block in the way (a wall or a fence stops it, and a blaze stopped against the room's wall stays within reach). Pure, for tests: whether a hit from feet position {@code from} leaves the blaze with floor to hit it from. Pure, for tests: whether a due swing may go out with a fireball on the way. The shield is effective {@code raiseTicks} after it goes up, so a swing now (shield down for it) and the shield back up the same tick still blocks a shot due in {@code raiseTicks + 2} or more. Held for anything within ten ticks, three blazes' volleys kept the shield up so long that a fight swung once in thirty seconds and took the fire anyway. Pure, for tests: a fight under its retreat line keeps going only to land the blow that kills its target - the target in sight and within a step of the reach, its health within one full-charge plain hit, the player above {@code floor}, for at most {@link #FINISH_TICKS}. Disengaged at seven to eleven health beside a 6.5-health blaze, the retreat's cover and heal cost twenty to thirty seconds and the blaze kept shooting. Other blazes that see the player's eye (refreshed every four ticks), and the step out of their sight under way. Of those, the ones charged to shoot (a resting blaze sends nothing for five seconds): what the retreat line counts. Knockback grace after our own hit, ticks spent finishing

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiBrew.jav.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiBrew.jav.notes:
game:brew - one brewing cycle at a brewing stand: fuel, bottles and ingredient are loaded with verified container clicks, the vanilla 400-tick brew is awaited against server-side container changes, and the finished potions are quick-moved out. The station is found nearby, walked to, or placed from the bag (the AiSmelt station pattern).

One call brews ONE cycle (1 ingredient + 1 blaze powder fuel, up to 3 bottles). Blaze powder doubles as the fuel and the ingredient for strength potions - the plan counts both. A stand, bottles, ingredient or fuel shortfall fails up front with the missing map; an ingredient that does not apply to the input fails on the no-progress window instead of silently idling. Ticks the open interaction may run before the station is reported unusable. Ticks without any applied container change before the recipe is declared non-brewable. Consecutive failed quick-moves before the load is declared missing (never spins to the deadline). Ticks the potion collection may wait for its applied server confirmation. Fuel slot / ingredient slot / first bottle slot in the brewing stand menu. The open menu id whose slots were verified empty, so foreign contents are never consumed. True when the ingredient slot was consumed and at least one bottle changed potion type. Quick-moves every transformed bottle out of the stand and describes the yield. A quick-move that keeps finding nothing to move must not spin to the deadline: after MOVE_FAIL_TICKS consecutive failures the op fails with the same missing map checkMissing would have produced. Up-front inventory gate: bottles of the input type, the ingredient, and the fuel (blaze doubles). Quick-moves one matching input bottle from the inventory into the stand. Quick-moves one unit of the item from the inventory into the stand. Player-inventory slot -> brewing menu slot (stand 0-4, main 5-31, hotbar 32-40). Gets a brewing stand open: nearby, walked to, or placed from the bag (AiSmelt's station pattern). The nearest brewing stand block in loaded terrain within a short walk. A FAILED result carrying a machine-readable code, with the same cleanup as done(). The potion-type filter for an input spec: "" or "water_bottle" means plain water bottles, "potion" means any potion, "potion:<path>" or "<path>_potion" or a bare "<path>" means that potion type. Pure. The potion type id carried by a stack's PotionContents component, or "" when it has none.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiBucket.j.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiBucket.j.notes:
game:bucket - fill and empty buckets, verified.

Small capability, large consequences. A water bucket is the cheapest fall-damage answer and the only practical way to make obsidian without a diamond pickaxe; a lava bucket is the furnace fuel that makes a smelting run trivial and half of the no-diamond nether portal. None of that is reachable if the bot cannot reliably point at a fluid and click.

A bucket click is aimed with {@link ClipContext.Fluid#SOURCE_ONLY} because that is what the server re-derives: aiming at flowing water picks up nothing and silently wastes the attempt. The result is verified from the held item changing, never from the click going out. Ticks the sweep may spend before the target fluid or cell is reported unreachable. Ticks to wait for the held stack to change after the click. Nearest SOURCE block of the requested fluid within reach; flowing cells are useless. A free cell within reach with a solid support under it, for emptying. Whether the look ray has arrived at the click the action needs, mirroring how the server resolves it. FILL picks up the fluid block under the crosshair, so the hit cell must BE the source. EMPTY places into the cell adjacent to the hit face (BucketItem places at {@code hit.getBlockPos().relative(hit.getDirection())}), and the OUTLINE ray passes through the air cell and lands on the support below - accepting only {@code equals(target)} would wait forever. Accepting the relative cell covers the support's UP face and any side face. Prove the actual receiving face, including a basin rim that hides the floor's centre. {@code water}: a support that takes water itself (a wall, a slab, a trapdoor) is never the face poured against. Prove a fill ray before turning; a hidden source must not spend 60 ticks aimed at its wall. Registry id of the filled bucket for a fluid name, for callers assembling arguments.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiBuilder..documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiBuilder..notes:
Native blueprint builder: parses and validates a block blueprint, then executes it cell by cell with navigation into reach, shared face-scan support solving, hotbar/inventory item selection and applied-server-revision verification.

The blueprint model, build ordering and material math are pure and package-visible for headless tests. The operation reuses the aim/dispatch/verify mechanics of {@code AiGameOperations.block} (aim at the ray-proven hit, vanilla {@code useItemOn}, then wait for the applied server block revision with a stability window) and a nested {@link AiGoto} for approaches, so per-cell behavior stays consistent with the single-block op.

PER-CELL POLICY: a cell is retried up to {@link #MAX_ATTEMPTS} times (each retry re-approaches through the next candidate standing column and replans the support face), then recorded in the terminal {@code failed} list while the rest of the build continues. The whole operation fails early only when progress is impossible: materials exhausted mid-build (reported with the remaining delta), six consecutive unreachable approaches, low health, or the deadline.

RESUMPTION: the cursor advances monotonically, and every re-issued blueprint re-checks cells against the world first, so already-placed cells are cheap skips. Layer-first ordering with supporters before dependents keeps upper layers reachable by standing on finished lower ones. Placement order and live neighbour state never change the ownership of the requested work. Preserve top-down teardown while spending reachable work before another navigation leg. Schematic/clipboard-backed builds lift the cell cap: preflight is a count and the per-cell machinery already tolerates partial failure. A captured base with its hill (369336 blocks) is a real schematic, so the cap is the decoder's own. Dig-enabled legs out of a room the build closed round the body, per build. Approaches for one cell before it waits for a later pass. Full re-passes over deferred cells after the main order drains. A cell whose approach or placement keeps failing is NOT failed on first exhaustion: the stance it needs often only exists once the cells around it are placed (a bridge support's only face can be a wall block the blueprint itself has not placed yet - FaceScan's honest NOT_A_SUPPORT). Deferral breaks the plan/execute circle: build everything else first, then re-attempt with fresh attempt budgets against the grown structure. Bounded; what still fails is reported failed. How far ahead in the layer the builder looks for a cell it can place without a step. Ticks the humanized sweep may spend reaching one support face before the cell is retried. Standing columns tried in order for each approach, relative to the target cell. The game:build power arguments, parsed once from the op args (pure, headless-tested): rotation (0/90/180/270 clockwise seen from above) and mirror (none/x/z: the named axis's coordinate is negated) applied to every cell and its directional properties at load; an optional blueprint-Y layer slice [layerStart, layerStart+layerHeight) with skipFailed (a failed cell is not retried - one attempt, then failed[] and the build moves on); substitute blocks for material sourcing and verification; and a repeat vector for tunnel-bore/wall builds (count EXTRA copies after the first, -1 = until cancelled or materials out). The schematic's sign text, keyed by blueprint (dx, dy, dz) packed as a BlockPos; typed into each sign's editor. The material candidates for a cell: its own block first, then the listed substitutes. A repeat vector: after each finished copy the origin shifts by (dx,dy,dz); count extra copies (-1 unbounded). Parses the power args shared by game:build and game:paste. Pure validation, no world reads. The substitutes map {"": ["alt1", "alt2"]}: material sourcing may use any listed block (first available wins) and a standing alt counts as correct in verification. Every key and alt must name a real block, an alt must differ from its key, and the lists stay small. Pure validation. Applies mirror (the named axis's coordinate is negated), then rotation (quarter turns clockwise seen from above) to every cell and to the directional block-state properties: facing rotates through the north->east->south->west cycle, axis swaps x/z on odd turns, hinge swaps left/right on a mirror, and half/type (vertical properties) never change. Pure transform, headless-tested. One quarter turn clockwise seen from above: north->east->south->west. Non-cardinal values pass through. A mirror along the named axis: x negates east/west, z negates north/south. Others pass through. Anchors a source blueprint (schematic, clipboard) at its minimum corner: duplicate cells are dropped first-wins (overlapping litematic regions), the whole blueprint shifts so the minimum dx/dy/dz sits at the origin, and offsets beyond +/-MAX_OFFSET or past the cell cap fail the load. Inline blueprints never pass through here - their offsets are deliberate. File builds and previews supply their own bounded spans; inline/clipboard defaults keep MAX_OFFSET. The shared minimum for block, sign, storage, and entity coordinates. The blueprint-Y layer slice [start, start+height): only cells whose dy is inside are kept. Parses and validates the blueprint from operation args. {@code origin} defaults to {@code fallbackOrigin}; {@code blocks} is required. A {@code blueprint} JSON string argument carrying the same object is accepted as the transport for large blueprints. Order of the tests is the contract (reviewer matrix analysis/schematic-20261027/review/special-matrix.md §2):
  1. {@link AiBuilder#derivedCell} (piston head / moving piston) is {@code DERIVED}: the world produces it, it is never a placement request.
  2. A cell the survival normalizer omits (decorative grass, a pitcher crop's upper half) is {@code SKIP} if it ever reaches the site still decoded.
  3. Any fluid cell - a level-0 source and a captured flowing level alike - is {@code FLUID}. A source is bucket work; a flowing cell is an observation of its sources: the site marks it (see {@link AiBuildSite#isObserve}) and reconciles it from the world, it is never clicked. The fixture audit requires a non-source fluid of the same type there.
  4. A cell {@link AiBuilder#survivalGaps} reports an unreproducible fact on is {@code SKIP} (reported, never placed).
  5. A bed head or any {@code half=upper} cell is a {@code PARTNER} (made by its foot/lower half). Only now does {@link AiSchematicActions#special} classify the rest ({@code SPECIAL}: farmland, dirt path, potted plants, filled cauldrons, fed composters); it is not usable before the fluid/partner tests because it is true for every fluid and every upper half.
  6. A double chest's {@code type=left/right} half is {@code INTERACT}: the first half goes down single and the second is sneak-clicked onto its side ({@link #allowedFaces} narrows the click to that side once the first stands; see {@link AiBuildSite#isChestHalf}).

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiBuildSit.notes:
Immutable site model for one schematic build: every required cell with its kind, item, dependency edges and a deterministic sweep priority, plus the runtime bookkeeping the fast engine needs (pending/placed/failed sets, a spatial index, local candidate queries).

One instance per build attempt. All methods run on the client thread; the class may read {@code mc.level} for dependency readiness and world state, but must never write the world, move the body or click. Queries are O(local): no method may scan all cells per tick.

MEMORY CONTRACT (a supplied schematic has 369,336 cells). Everything per cell is a primitive array or a reference into the caller's immutable cell list: no per-cell map and no per-cell list. The one spatial index is a {@code section (16^3) -> int[]} map - one entry per SECTION, never per cell. Construction is O(n log n) (a radix sort on {@code (dy, support depth, class, dz, serpentine dx)}).

ORDER CONTRACT (deterministic, documented in {@link #order(int)}): layer (blueprint Y) ascending, then walkway coverage (a standable source surface with a clear column above ranks before a cell whose column above is not clear, and those rank before a cell that is covered by a required cell above - the human "floor first, then walls under ceilings/roofs" sweep), then support depth ascending (a cell whose below-neighbour is also in the blueprint comes after that neighbour), then class bucket (SIMPLE/INTERACT/PARTNER < SPECIAL < FLUID < DERIVED/SKIP), then a serpentine row sweep (dz ascending, dx ascending on even dz and descending on odd dz), then a total tie-break that cannot tie (positions are unique). Two relocations then run: an attachment/partner cell is emitted immediately after the cell that provides its support (a bed head after its foot, a door or tall-plant upper half after its lower half, a wall torch/sign after its wall, a chest half after its pair), and a provider is always emitted before its dependents.

WALKWAY / STANDABLE-SOURCE API (user ruling 2026-10-27): {@link #standableTop(AiBuilder.Cell)} is the pure surface test of a placed state, {@link #walkwayCell(int)} is a required cell that is a standable source surface with a clear column above, and {@link #walkwayFrontier(int,int)}, {@link #standableNeighbours(BlockPos)}, {@link #sourceFloorPositions()} let the runner grow its access by standing on / spilling over the build's own finished blocks instead of temp scaffolds.

Owner: impl-site. See analysis/schematic-20261027/DESIGN.md.

One half of a multi-part cell whose partner must be handled with it (bed foot/head, door halves). Derived/world state only (redstone lit/powered): never a placement request of its own. Cannot be reproduced in survival: reported, never placed (survival gap). Packed-delta field width; blueprint offsets are normalized to 0..4096, this also holds negatives. Radix-sort span for the order keys (normalized blueprints sit inside 0..4096). Spatial index bucket: 16^3 cells per section (DESIGN). How many {@link #pendingCount()} reads pass between two observed-fluid reconciliations. Test/headless injection; null resolves the live client world lazily. Walkway cell packed positions, ascending (read-only shared view for the hot lanes). Walkway cell indices ordered by sweep rank (spill-fill order). Incremental spill frontier: pending walkway cells adjacent to an already placed cell. Position-sorted view of the cells, for O(log n) "is this position a required cell?". cell index by sweep rank, and rank by cell index. Section key ({@link BlockPos#asLong(int,int,int)} of section coords) -> cell indices. Captured flowing fluid cells: required, never clicked, reconciled from the world. Human-readable reasons for {@link #markFailed(int,String)}; only failed cells appear. Lowest sweep rank that is still pending; only ever advances except when a cell is requeued. src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiBuildWal.notes:
Local stance movement for the build engine: a bounded walkable-cell BFS (never the 65k-node A*), converted into {@link autismclient.ai.engine.AiPathfinder.Movement} steps that the existing {@link autismclient.ai.engine.AiMovementExecutor} executes with real keys, jumps, drops and the single per-tick aim step. Distances are lane-sized (<= 24 blocks); anything unreachable is reported so the runner can choose another stance or insert one scaffold step rather than flooding a search.

The walker also owns the walking-placement hook wiring: the runner installs {@link #walkingWork(java.util.function.Function, Runnable)} before a lane, and the executor fires it once per walking tick, which is the "place while moving" lane.

Move legality: a stance cell must have a solid, non-hazardous floor and two passable, safe cells above it. Flat steps are {@code WALK}; a rise of at most vanilla's 0.6 step height is {@code STEP_UP_1}; a full one-block rise is proven with {@link AiJumpSolver} and emitted as {@code JUMP_UP_1} (an unproven rise makes the route unreachable, never a hopeful jump); a one-block drop is {@code DESCEND_1}. The executor re-validates every move live and can itself refuse one - a stall then ends the leg with the executor's own reason instead of looping. No move ever carries a dig or a bridge, and the required-cell set is installed through {@link AiMovementExecutor#keepIntact} so no route clears a build block as a soft blocker.

Owner: impl-place. See analysis/schematic-20261027/DESIGN.md.

A local route was built and walking started (or the body already stands there). Already standing in the target stance. No walkable route within the bounded search: the caller must pick another stance or scaffold. A stance cell is standable: a solid floor below, feet and head passable, no hazard. Bounded local BFS constants. Base wall-clock guard for one lane; the limit scales with the route length (reviewer W7). Ticks allowed per planned move on top of the base (jumps/steps are expensive on awkward geometry). A one-block drop is the deepest local step; anything deeper is the runner's problem. Plans a local route to {@code feet} over standable cells (walk, step-up-1, drop-1, sprint where flat) and starts it. {@code protect} positions are never broken or built over.

OBSERVABILITY ONLY: a re-issued target while a leg runs still restarts the leg (no behavioural debounce - Lead ruling, the runner's own target stability owns that), but every re-issue is counted and a bounded navigation-debug line records it so the runner-side re-issue loop is provable in logs.

Ticks the movement executor (movement only; the caller places from its own tick). Why the current leg failed, empty otherwise. Walking-placement hook: look provider (aim point or null) and end-of-tick click callback. BFS over stance cells through {@code stepAllowed}, keeping the parent of each discovered cell so the route can be reconstructed. Bounded by node count and Manhattan distance from the start; returns the ordered route including both ends, or null when the target is not reachable within the bounds. One local edge: adjacent stance cells, step-up-1 (proved) or drop-1. How high the body must step to enter {@code to} from {@code from}: the obstacle's collision top above the current feet. A full block in front is 1.0 (needs a jump); a slab/stairs 0.5 (vanilla auto-step). Converts the stance route into executor movements. Flat steps are WALK, <= 0.6 rises are STEP_UP_1, a full rise needs a proved JUMP_UP_1 plan and a one-block fall is DESCEND_1. Null when a step cannot be expressed safely (the caller falls back or reports unreachable). Bounded debug trace for an unreachable/failed lane: the runner logs its generic reason, this one says why. Bounded decision trace for target re-issues (Lead ruling: trace only, do not debounce yet). Every line carries both counters, so a per-tick re-issue loop reads directly as replans climbing with moving=true and sameTarget=true, and a target alternation reads as moving=true with sameTarget=false. The body is swimming, under water, or standing/sinking in fluid: no walking leg survives that.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiBurrow.j.notes:
game:burrow - the night backstop. Digs straight down DEPTH blocks into a classified-safe column (never into lava, water, an open drop, or a mobbed cave), caps the shaft with a solid block, hides until dawn (day time < 1000) or the deadline, then digs back out. When the column is unsafe it first tries a nearby safe shaft, then towers TOWER blocks up into a closed shelter and digs down at dawn. The model may call it at dusk itself - game:sleep with a bed is always better - but the host's dusk guard parks it when the model left the bot idle and bedless at dusk.
The op's own timeoutSeconds default and clamp ceiling (the dispatcher default sits at 900).
Shaft depth below the trigger feet the dig-down aims for.
Tower height for the unsafe-column fallback.
Ticks an open shaft cell may fail to swallow the player before the dig-down is abandoned.
One shaft cell below the dig-down: what the burrow may do with it (pure, headless-tested).
DIG: solid and breakable. OPEN: air with a safe floor within 3 and no lava below (step in). STOP: unloaded, any fluid, unbreakable, or an open/unsafe drop - the tower fallback's trigger.
The cap goes two above the feet, leaving the normal two-cell standing interior clear.
Dawn in the vanilla day cycle: the burrow exits once the clock wraps past midnight into its first 1000 ticks.
Full floor, feet/head walls and roof: a roof alone leaves the spider's melee line of sight open.
Ordinary adjacent placements, reusing observed terrain; the last wall also supports the roof beam.
Residual burning behind confirmed cover is not evidence that the cover has opened.
At most three supported steps away, without guessing an unloaded height or travelling across a gap.
Whether a shelter can be built at all from what the player carries. A run before its first cobblestone holds nothing but tools and food, and every shelter attempt then ends "insufficient spare stock for a closed tower shelter" - a failure the FOOD phase does not count, so a night at the wrong moment produced twenty identical failures a second and ended a campaign without a single counted failure. Callers that are choosing to shelter (rather than answering a mob) ask this first; digging into the ground stays available on its own, which is why this only asks for a few blocks.
Centering travels into the shelter's own cell; bounded, see {@code cap}.
Dig one classified cell per engine leg until DEPTH below the trigger feet; unsafe columns fall back to the tower.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiChatMode.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiChatMode.notes:
The assistant's continuing-conversation lane: a bounded, rate-limited responder that watches player chat and answers through its OWN provider request, on its OWN thread, while the main objective keeps moving. It never owns movement, rotation, GUI or a game operation, so a long {@code game:goto}/{@code game:mine} or a model round trip cannot stall the conversation, and a chat reply cannot cancel the body's work.

The lane is deliberately a small state machine (not an AiOperation): it survives the main run finishing, never emits {@code finish}, and is stopped by the user, {@code chat_keep stop}, a world/session change, or a lost connection. All scheduling and filtering is pure and testable; only {@link Host} and {@link Brain} touch the client/network.

Client-facing seam. Implementations may be called from the lane thread. Newest-first ledger snapshot. Queue one public chat line on the client thread; never a command. A queued host must recheck this at delivery, after stop/reconfigure/session switches. Reply to a private/team line without exposing it in public chat (production uses /msg). Merge the lane status into HOST STATE / UI state. Null/ inactive removes it. The lane became active. The lane ended; reason is user-facing. Account the provider usage to the session. One model answer plus the usage it cost. The only model boundary. Tests supply a deterministic fake; production uses {@link ProviderBrain}. Lines whose request failed: kept apart from new traffic so a retry loses neither side. Starts watching from the current ledger revision; existing lines become context, never triggers. A line sent through chat_send: suppress its server echo exactly like the lane's own replies. Updates persona/filters/limits without dropping the conversation history or rate state. One client tick. Cheap when no chat arrived; never blocks on the network. Stops the lane and closes the provider request in flight. Idempotent. Caller holds the lane lock. Reconfiguration must not lose an otherwise eligible question. A server echo of our own reply is not a new message, even when it loses the sender. Production brain: the same provider/settings as the assistant, pinned for the lane, with a small output budget and low effort so chat stays responsive beside a running objective.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiChatPoli.notes:
Pure rules for the assistant's continuing-conversation lane. Nothing here touches the client, a provider or the game: the same helpers decide what counts as a player message, whether a chat objective is a continuing conversation, how a model answer is turned into one safe chat line, and how the prompts are worded. {@link AiChatMode} owns the state machine and threading.

Server chat is untrusted input. The reply prompt therefore gives the model no tools and explicitly tells it that incoming lines are data, never instructions.

A burst cannot hold a reply back forever: answer once the oldest pending line is this old. One verified player line. Revisions come from {@link AiChatLedger}; text is already bounded. One lane's configuration. All limits are clamped here, so no caller (tool JSON, the .ai command, or auto-start) can create an unbounded reply loop. Backward-compatible default: private/team messages stay out unless explicitly opted in. Tool/command arguments; a blank instruction block is allowed for status/stop actions. Revisions at or below the baseline are history, never a trigger for this lane's first reply. A ledger entry worth showing to the model, or null. Player and disguised chat are the default sources; system chat is accepted only when it carries a player-name prefix (some servers route player chat through system messages) or when the caller explicitly opted in. Context-only admission: no audience or mention gate, still rejects self lines and commands. Vanilla player chat carries its own "<Name> " display prefix; the prompt already has the sender. The player name carried by an entry: an explicit sender, else the vanilla " " prefix. Turns "… <[VIP] Steve>" or a chat-type name into a player name. Chat packet senders are now resolved from the player UUID; this remains the fallback for disguised/system chat and for transcript entries recorded before that fix. Whole-word, case-insensitive name match: "Alex" matches "Alex?" but not "Alexandra". "keep chatting with people", "respond to chat", "talk to players", "stay in chat". "stop chatting", "end the conversation", "that's enough chat". A combined request must reach the objective planner instead of disappearing into chat controls. Names a chat objective explicitly targets. "with people/players/everyone" is deliberately generic (an empty filter); "with Steve" narrows the lane to Steve. The chat brain's system prompt. It is small and stable; the conversation rides in the user message. The model has no tools, so a successful prompt injection can only produce text. The conversation the brain sees: bounded recent history plus the new batch. One reply line, made safe for {@code Connection.sendChat}. Blank means send nothing. The model's explicit "do not speak" answer. Only the standalone token counts. Debounce for the current batch: a direct mention gets an answer sooner. Rolling-window and minimum-gap gate. {@code replyTimes} is oldest first. Collapses a raw chat line for matching and display; never used to execute anything.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiChop.jav.notes:
game:chop. The felling itself is the shared gather process (engine AiBlockMine: one route for the whole job, the tree being felled finished before the next, leaves cut when in the way, drops picked up with digging allowed). What stays here is the pure vein model the tests pin: block matching, flood fill, bottom-up order, reachable-first picking, standing candidates and the work queue.
Standing columns tried for the ground approach, relative to the target block.
Horizontal neighbor offsets used to find standable supports (e.g. leaves) beside the vein.
Block matching: a namespaced registry id ({@code minecraft:oak_log}) matches exactly; a bare word matches its exact path or the {@code _word} suffix family, so the default {@code "log"} matches every {@code *_log} block. The single implementation lives in {@code AiMine}.
Connected vein by breadth-first flood fill over 26-direction adjacency, capped at {@code cap} blocks. Only positions satisfying {@code matches} are visited, so disconnected veins are never merged; diagonally touching blocks join the same vein.
Felling order: ascending y, then nearest-first horizontally from the reference, with a full deterministic tie-break.
Reachable-first: the first directly breakable block in felling (bottom-up) order, or null when nothing can be broken right now. Bottom-up stays the preference among breakable blocks, so a ground start with a reachable trunk keeps the classic bottom-up sequence.
Candidate standing positions for reaching {@code target}, nearest-first from {@code reference}: the nine ground columns beside the target (the classic ground approach; the navigator's ground-target adjustment resolves their walkable level), then the cells above every standable support on or horizontally beside the vein — its own logs and adjacent blocks such as leaves — wherever the floor has collision and feet/head are clear. A canopy start thus tries the canopy before the ground; a ground start keeps the ground columns first (insertion order wins distance ties).
The cell above a block is standable when the floor has collision and feet and head are clear (the navigator's walkable rule).
Drops sorted nearest-first (distance key captured at queue time), entity id breaking ties.
Terminal condition: the requested count succeeds; an emptied vein succeeds only when no block was skipped. Partial felling reports failure with its completed work preserved. Null while the operation must keep running.
FIFO work queue over the felling order with per-block failure accounting; freshly dropped items are appended at the front (nearest-first) so they are collected before felling resumes. Blocks are addressable by position, so a reachable-first pick anywhere in the order can be broken, failed and removed without disturbing the rest of the sequence.
Inserts drops ahead of all remaining blocks, preserving the given (nearest-first) order.
Remaining block positions in felling (bottom-up) order, drops excluded.
Removes the block entry at {@code pos} wherever it sits in the order; false when absent.
Records one more failure on the head block, returning its total; -1 when the head is not a block.
Records one more failure on the block at {@code pos}, returning its total; -1 when absent.
Strikes recorded against the block at {@code pos}; 0 when absent or never failed.
game:chop runs on the shared gather process (engine AiBlockMine): one persistent route for the whole job, every log family target in one goal, the tree being felled finished before the next one, leaves cut when they are in the way and the drops picked up with the same digging. Without a count it fells one tree; with one, that many logs.

The body is normalised the way a person would type it (client prefix, alias, letter case and even the leading command word are all optional), the line goes through the same parser the chat box uses, and the command's own replies come back in the result. That makes the outcome definite: a parse error FAILS with every accepted form, a red client reply FAILS with its text, anything else SUCCEEDS with the reply lines - the model never guesses syntax and never re-observes to learn what a command did.
The model's line: body by contract, with the obvious synonyms accepted instead of rejected.
The exact line handed to the parser. Pure: otherCommand answers with the registered name of a DIFFERENT client command the first word names, or null. A body that starts with the client prefix, a "." or "/", an alias, or that omits the command word altogether all resolve to the canonical "name args" line; a body that names another command is refused with a pointer to its capability.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiCollect..documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiCollect..notes:
"Get N of item X": the blocks that yield the item (an exact item form, an explicit {@link #DROP_MAP} entry for ores and crops, or a {@link #CHANCE_SOURCES} chance drop) and the item lying on the ground, gathered by the shared gather process (engine AiBlockMine) until the count is in the bag. A source no carried tool can harvest is never broken (zero drops); when that leaves nothing, the op fails with a prospect-style missing{tool:1} report naming the pickaxe to craft.

The drop mapping, target ordering, count/baseline/exact math, skip records, harvest-gate decision, missing-tool report and terminal message are pure and package-visible for headless tests. Blocks whose certain, tool-independent drop differs from their item form: the common ores (including deepslate variants, which drop the same items) and the four field crops (whose item form is their seeds or planting item, never the gathered crop). Kept deliberately small and exact — no fortune/silk-touch guesses and no loose mappings like leaves to sticks; anything not listed here is gathered through its exact item form only. Named when the tool ladder has no answer for a tier-gated block (mirrors AiProspect's fallback). A unit of gathering work: a live drop entity (entityId >= 0) or a source block position. Work queue order: drops always before blocks, nearest-first inside each kind, with a full deterministic tie-break (entity id, then coordinates). Returns a sorted copy. The item a block yields when gathered: the explicit DROP_MAP entry, else its own item form. Blocks that yield the item only SOMETIMES (vanilla loot odds): seeds are 1-in-8 from grass and ferns and nothing else in the world produces them outside a field. Collecting keeps breaking them until the count is in the bag or none are left; without this, "get seeds" had no source at all. Whether breaking this block can yield the item: its certain drop, or a chance source. Inventory target: absolute count, or count on top of the current baseline when additional. Farm semantics: a surplus succeeds unless exact was requested, then it is reported (never discarded). Appends a skip record to the reported list; false once the list is full (skipTotal still counts it). Harvest-tier gate: breaking a block the carried tools have no tier for wastes the source for zero drops, so a gated block is broken only when some hotbar OR backpack stack harvests it. The tool a tier-skipped source asks for: the cheapest ladder answer, else the prospect fallback. Prospect-style structured shortage: {toolId: 1}, reported under "missing" in the terminal data. "Get N of item X" as ONE continuous operation on the shared gather process (engine AiBlockMine): every block that yields the item and every one of the item lying around form one goal, the route digs to whichever is cheapest (drops included: nothing is abandoned for want of a walkable route), and the count in the bag ends it. A source no carried tool can harvest is left standing (breaking it wastes the block for zero drops); when that leaves nothing the op fails with the prospect-style missing{tool:1} report naming the pickaxe to craft. Hotbar AND backpack: the digger can swap a backpack tool in, so the gate scans all 36 slots.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiCombat.j.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiCombat.j.notes:
game:fight - an autonomous melee combat executor. The model names a target ("zombie", an entity id, or "hostiles") and a stop condition; everything inside a fight is handled here at tick rate, because a model in the loop cannot hit an attack-cooldown window.

What the executor owns: target selection and re-selection as things die, weapon choice, the approach (delegated to the engine's travel primitive so it paths around terrain rather than walking into a wall), a bounded pillar up to targets hovering out of melee reach (blazes) - with an honest machine-readable airborne failure when the pillar cap, the footing or the block supply cannot cover it - humanized tracking through {@link AiAim}, the vanilla attack cooldown, sprint-reset knockback, jump crits, shield raising against projectiles, creeper spacing, and the health and food thresholds that end the fight instead of dying in it.

What it deliberately does NOT do: heal, eat or run a survival loop. Those are separate capabilities so the model keeps the strategic decision about whether to re-engage. Attack only inside this fraction of the weapon's reach, so a lunging target stays hittable. Cooldown fraction at which a swing is worth taking; below this the hit is heavily damped. Horizontal spacing kept from a primed creeper, in blocks. Ticks the camera may spend acquiring a target before it is dropped as unhittable. Failed acquisitions in a row after which a perched or holding fight leaves the mob it cannot hit. Brief knockback is not a reason to abandon a mob and turn to the opposite side of a perch. Seconds one approach leg runs before the target is re-evaluated. A target no route reached is skipped this long (it may come down; the fight ends meanwhile). Ticks a held fight waits for a mob in sight to come a block closer before it counts as one that cannot come. Ticks into a blaze's charge from which the shield is up toward it. Vanilla (BlazeAttackGoal) charges for 60 ticks, then fires three fireballs six ticks apart; a raised shield blocks five ticks after the key goes down. A fireball hit costs a little through diamond armour and then burns: one health a second for five seconds, armour or not (a spawner fight went from 17 to dead mostly on fire). Ticks before a due shot that the shield goes up: its five-tick startup, the tick or two the client sees a draw later than the server started it, and a margin (at six a skeleton three blocks off still landed both arrows of a fight; at nine one landed while the client already showed the shield blocking: the server counts the 5-tick delay from when ITS use began, and the client reads the hit a tick or two after the server applied it). Ticks before a projectile in flight lands inside which no swing goes out: a swing lowers the shield, and raised again it blocks five ticks later on the server, a tick or two later than the client sees. How close a mob's attack box is to the player's for it to count as striking (fought before the target). Degrees off the look within which a raised shield is taken to cover a projectile. 26.2 blocks what comes from within 90 of the head's yaw (BlocksAttacks, flat from the player to the hit's source), and the head trails the camera a little. The projectile on a hitting course that lands soonest (never the player's own), or null. Ticks until a tracked projectile lands. Where the look goes while the shield is up against what is in flight: toward {@code preferred} when a shield raised that way covers every threat due within the hold window (the soonest one at least), else the current look when it covers them, else the level yaw that covers the soonest and then the most of the rest with the least turn. Turned back to the target the tick the look covered the fireball and to the fireball the tick after, the camera flipped ninety degrees every tick under four blazes, the shield blocked neither way, and the fire burnt the player to death. Whether a shield raised along the yaw covers a projectile at its present position. Blaze id to the client tick its charge was first seen. The nearest blaze whose fireballs are due: 45+ ticks into its charge (vanilla's charged flag reads as isOnFire on the client), out of its own melee range (under two blocks it strikes instead), within 24 blocks and in sight. Null if none. Stand for {@code ticks} ticks with the shield up toward any blaze about to fire, lowered otherwise: the wait at a spawner between waves (a body standing there bare took every volley from the blazes hovering out of reach). The approach-hit-separate rhythm against a melee mob, as one radial step: -1 back away, 0 hold, +1 close in. {@code gap}: how far the player's box is outside the mob's attack box (vanilla tests boxes; below zero it can strike now). {@code slack}: how far inside the player's own reach the mob is (below zero out of reach). {@code readyIn}: ticks to the next full-strength swing. {@code chase}: blocks a tick the mob closes at. {@code kite}: a backward walk outruns it (a zombie 0.117 against 0.216); one that does not is held off with the shield between swings instead. A shooter the approach got no block closer to in this long is left to the guard's cover. An enderman farther than this has teleported off and is not chased by a guard's fight (a pearl hunt names it and does chase): an angry one teleports back to the player by itself. The End fixture's guard chased one across the island, a hundred blocks from the dragon fight. Blocks past the closest yet at which a chase in the shooter's sight is going away from it, not closing. Blocks a hold sets between a shooter and itself (a pillar top's shield is up to three high, and it strafes). Mobs a fight found no route to, until when (entity UUIDs; shared by every fight and read by the guard, which kept starting a fight on the same mob across a ravine that failed three seconds later). Whether a fight found no route to this mob a moment ago. Swimming: under water, or in water with more water under its feet. Shared by co

game:container - open a container at a position and move items by MEANING rather than by slot index. "Take all the food", "withdraw 3 iron", "deposit everything except my tools" are single calls; the executor navigates into reach, opens the block, matches slots against resolved item specs, issues one quick-move per stack, and verifies each transfer against the applied server container snapshot before moving on.

Slot-level access stays available through game:inventory_click for the cases this cannot express. This exists so the ordinary ones do not cost a dozen model turns. Ticks to wait for the server to apply one transfer before it is reported unconfirmed. Transfers issued per tick; one click per stack keeps the server's slot accounting simple. Ticks allowed for the open interaction before the operation gives up on the block. Navigation cleanup cannot erase a dig/place receipt or turn its deadline into an ordinary refusal. {@code protectedCells}: blueprint cells the approach route may never break or place into (schematic restock). Per-request totals, so a count limit never re-derives a request's id list per slot. The source slot's stack at click time; the resync is compared against it, never credited blind. Source slots whose quick-move was confirmed by the server but moved nothing (full/incompatible destination). Navigates into reach, aims at the block, and interacts until a container opens. Adopts the open menu as the transfer target and returns null, or fails when it is not a storage menu (the same whitelist AiInventoryController accepts): a furnace, anvil or crafting screen is never a transfer target. The next stack to quick-move, or null when the requested work is done. True when a full inventory can still absorb this stack into an existing partial one. Container-side contents as {slot,item,count}, player inventory excluded. The storage menus game:container and game:reconcile_inventory accept as transfer targets: chests AND BARRELS (a barrel block opens the generic 9x3 chest menu, so the ChestMenu case covers it), shulker boxes, hoppers, dispensers, droppers and crafter inputs. Package-visible for the headless menu-construction tests. Container-side slot count: the menu's slots minus the 36 player-inventory slots. One requested item family and how many of it to move; count 0 means "all of it". One queued quick-move; {@code request} is the index it counts against, or -1 for none.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiContext..notes:
Prompt tiers. The stable tier (core rules, capability index and contracts) is byte-identical for a catalog revision and speedrun scoping, so providers can prefix-cache it. The objective tier (objective, user updates, plan contract, playbooks, memories) is built once per run epoch. Per-request state never enters the system prompt: it goes into the conversation as an append-only HOST STATE block, full on the first request of an epoch and every tenth one, changed keys only in between.
The system prompt of one run epoch: stable is cacheable across epochs, objective is fixed for the epoch.
Stable-only prompt (connection probe, tests).
Both tiers as one string, for providers that take a single system text.
Rough characters per token for budgets when the provider reports no usage.
Bounds on the amendments carried in the objective tier.
Memory injection bounds at epoch start.
Hard contract carried in the objective tier while a plan-mode objective researches (State.PLANNING).
Whole-word speedrun objective check: such objectives get the scoped (smaller, faster) contract context.
Contract ids fully inlined for a speedrun objective; everything else in the index stays one catalog_inspect away.
Image payload bytes are not text tokens; reserve a conservative image allowance instead.
Fast mode (AiSettings.verifyOutcomes off): the CORE sentences about fingerprints, evidence and completion proof, each swapped for the lean rule. Exact text-block matches; a test fails when a CORE edit breaks one.
FAST_EDITS targets no longer found in CORE (a CORE edit broke them); empty when fast mode is intact.
Core rules, capability families, catalog revision, index and contracts. Same bytes for the same catalog and scoping.
verify=false is fast mode: the lean CORE and contracts without fingerprints (perform takes the id alone).
The job-level operations whose whole purpose text is inlined: their arguments' valid values (game:dig's shape, game:equip's what, game:container's action, game:farm's crops, game:dimension's targets, game:fight's "hostiles", the timeouts) sit after the first sentence, and the prompt forbids looking a listed capability up. With the first sentence alone ("Crops and animals.") the model guessed values and failed its calls.
Families listed one per line in the index and inlined as full contracts; the rest collapse to a count.
Objective, bounded user updates, plan contract and vision note: the part of the objective tier that must fit.
Builds the epoch prompt. Throws when the stable tier and the objective header alone exceed maxCharacters; playbooks, the addon guide, relevant non-game contracts and memories are added only while they fit.
One compact line per memory, bounded to maxCharacters in total; payloads are clipped, never inlined whole.
Short relative age: now, 5m ago, 3h ago, 2d ago.
Per-epoch HOST STATE encoder. The first block of an epoch and every FULL_EVERY-th one carry every field and the whole observation. Blocks in between carry only fields whose value changed and only the top-level observation keys whose JSON changed, plus unchangedKeys (and removedKeys when a key disappeared); when that delta would exceed 60% of the full observation the full observation is sent instead. Output is compact JSON.
Renders this request's HOST STATE text block. catalogRevision is non-null only when the catalog changed since the epoch prompt.
Compatibility view for the qualification smoke and tests: stable + objective tiers + one full HOST STATE, in one string. Throws when the mandatory parts do not fit maxCharacters.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiCover.ja.notes:
The guard's answer to a shooter it cannot reach at once: get out of its sight. A skeleton only lets an arrow go while it sees the player's eye, walks toward a target it lost and forgets it after 60 ticks unseen (see {@link AiSight}). So: the quickest stance no shooter can see (round a corner, back into the tunnel, a niche dug into the wall, the foot of a pillar), and when there is none within reach, a block set between the eyes. Hidden, anything that walks into reach is hit from there; a shooter that comes round the cover close by ends the op so the guard fights it. Hidden for four seconds, it has forgotten the player and the job goes on.
Hidden this long, every shooter has dropped the player (vanilla: 60 ticks unseen).
Where cover is looked for around the feet: across, above, below (a pillar's foot is far down).
A shooter this close and on the player's level walked round the cover: the guard fights it.
Blocks set between the eyes before the op gives up on shields (a pillar top's shield is three high).
A plan is renewed when a seeing shooter moved this far since (its sight lines moved with it).
The reach at which a mob beside the cover is hit.
Past this stance cost ({@link AiSight#stanceCost}) a shield goes up before the walk to cover.
A creeper swells only within seven blocks of a target it sees, stops re-planning its path the moment it loses sight and walks on to where it last saw the player: the stance keeps this far from it and from that spot, and out of sight of both.
The player tick a cover op last ran on.
Whether a cover op is under way (it ran this tick or the last): moving to cover is the defence against shots.
Ticks the striker at the body could not be brought under the crosshair.
Eating while hidden, so the health it waits for can come back (healing needs food 18).
Where the eye was the last tick a creeper saw it: where that creeper is walking to.
Finish the pending placement before its owner hands the body back.
How many of the shooters see the player now.
No stance out of sight in reach: a block set on the line between the eyes, from the player's side.
Keep the top support face in view while a waterborne body builds the ray-blocking column.
Shooters close enough to hold the player as a target (its follow range and a margin).
Swing at {@code mob} when the charge is up; true while it is under the crosshair (hittable).
One step straight away from {@code mob} (camera facing it), only where six ticks of it stay on the ground.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiCraft.ja.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiCraft.ja.notes:
game:craft - one call, whole dependency chain. "Craft an iron pickaxe" plans sticks from planks from logs, opens or places the crafting table it needs, runs every step through the client's own {@link AutismCraftingHelper} (server recipe placement where the server knows the recipe, manual grid placement otherwise), and verifies the result in the inventory.

The planning half is {@link AiCraftPlanner}, which is pure and unit tested. This class is the live half: it supplies the recipe graph from the client's loaded recipe data, owns the station and the execution ticks, and turns a shortfall into a structured {@code missing} list the model can hand straight to the gathering tools instead of a bare failure.

The helper's craft call blocks (it waits on server container syncs), so it runs on a worker and the operation polls it. The client thread is never held. One serialized worker; two concurrent crafts would fight over the same container. Ticks the inventory must agree with the target before a craft is called verified. One: the worker's step only returns once the server's resyncs confirmed it, so the bag already shows it (three stood a further 100 ms per craft). Puts the carried table down beside the player (up to eight spots, then open ground). The live craft worker, so cancel() can actually interrupt its blocking wait loops. This craft set the carried table down itself; a top-level craft picks it back up when it is done. The walk to a crafting table standing near, when the bag has no wood for one of its own. A crafting table standing within the walk radius, walked to (twice at most); null when there is none. Puts a crafting table in reach, placing a carried one when none is nearby. One stonecutter step: the station is found nearby or placed from the bag, the cuttable input is quick-moved in, the recipe producing the step's output is selected with a button click, and each result is quick-moved out - every transfer against an applied container revision. Gets a stonecutter open: nearby, walked to, or placed from the bag (the AiSmelt station pattern). The nearest stonecutter block in loaded terrain within a short walk. A player-inventory slot (0-35) holding an accepted input, or -1. Player-inventory slot -> stonecutter menu slot (input 0, result 1, main 2-28, hotbar 29-37). The visible recipe index whose option display is the wanted output, or -1. The planner's view of the client's loaded recipes, memoized for the life of one plan pass. Wrapped in the shared acquireability rank (AiObtain.acquirableGraph), so a tag slot's unstocked variant resolves to a mineable drop - this graph's missing map names minecraft:cobblestone for the stone pickaxe, never the Silk-Touch dead end plain stone. A 3x3 grid a craft can reach: a table carried, one standing within the walk radius, or wood in the bag for one. Exact inventory count for one registry id. How far a craft walks to a crafting table that stands near before it needs wood for one of its own. True when a crafting table the helper would accept is already within block reach. A free, supported, reachable cell next to the player for a station block. Prefers the ring around the feet so the placed block never blocks the player's own escape upward. Table spots tried in one place before the craft moves to open ground. The nearest cell within {@code radius} a player can stand in with at least two free, supported cells beside it at foot level (where a table goes), or null. The nearest cell the player can stand in, not its own, within {@code radius}: stepping there frees the one it stood in. Standing on leaves: a tree top, where a station spot is a leaf among leaves (see AiStationPlacer). Every acceptable station spot in preference order (stationSpot returns the first). The top face of the block under {@code cell} is the first thing a ray from the eye hits, within reach. Block form of a station id, for callers that place one.
