src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiCraftPla.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiCraftPla.notes:
Recursive crafting dependency resolution. Given "one iron pickaxe" it works out that it needs sticks, that sticks need planks, that planks need logs, and returns the craft steps in execution order plus whatever base material is still missing.

Deliberately PURE: everything is registry id strings and counts, no Minecraft types, so the whole planner is unit tested against synthetic recipe graphs. The live graph is supplied by {@link AiCraft} from the client's own loaded recipe data.

The planner never invents a route. When an ingredient has no recipe and none is in the bag it lands in {@link Plan#missing()}, which is exactly the list the model hands to the gathering tools - the plan is still returned, partially satisfied, rather than failing outright. One recipe. {@code inputs} has an entry per consumed slot; each entry lists the accepted items. {@code station} is the station block the step runs on ("" for plain crafting, which may need the 3x3 table per {@code requiresTable}; "minecraft:stonecutter" for stonecutter steps). True when this step runs on a stonecutter rather than the crafting grid. One craft to run: the recipe, and how many times to apply it. Items this step yields in total. A resolved plan. {@code steps} run in order, deepest dependency first. {@code missing} is what the player must still obtain by other means, keyed by item id. A plan is {@link #complete()} only when nothing is missing. True when the player already has everything asked for and no craft is needed. What the planner can ask about the world. Every recipe whose output is this item, cheapest first. How many of this item the player holds right now. How acquirable an unstocked item is when a slot variant must be chosen: 0 = dropped by mining a real block (the block's drop IS the item), 1 = makeable (craft/smelt recipe), 2 = no known route. Lower wins; stock then canonical order break ties. The default ranks by recipe presence alone, which is all a synthetic graph knows; the live graph overrides it with drop/smelt knowledge so a Silk-Touch-only variant (plain stone) never beats a same-tag alternative with a real route (cobblestone). The family spec covering exactly this rank-tied variant set ("log" for every log), or null when no family matches - the concrete tie-break then stands. The default knows no families; the live graph resolves them from the item vocabulary, so a nested obtain can gather whichever variant the terrain actually has instead of a canonical one that only generates two biomes over. Relative acquisition effort for a missing base item. Used only to break equal-shortfall recipe ties. Gathered from a farm animal (white wool from sheep, leather, meat): its own craft near-miss is no route. Recursion depth over the dependency chain; vanilla's deepest useful chain is far shallower. Total craft steps a single plan may contain, so a pathological graph cannot run away. Plans the crafting of {@code quantity} of {@code itemId}, consuming what the player already holds. Never throws for an unobtainable item - that item lands in {@link Plan#missing()}. Folds a step into an earlier one of the same recipe when no step between them makes something it consumes: one burst instead of two, each a server round trip (a wooden pickaxe crafted its planks twice, once for the head, once for the sticks). The earlier craft only makes more sooner, which every step after it can use. One recipe attempt that fell short, kept so the closest near-miss can be reported. Mutable resolution state: a working stock ledger over the real inventory. Satisfies {@code need} of {@code itemId}, appending craft steps. Returns how many it could not satisfy; the shortfall is also accumulated into {@code missing}. Resolves every slot of one recipe; returns how many items could not be supplied. Picks which accepted variant to spend on a slot. A variant the player already holds enough of always wins. Otherwise the best-rank tie set competes: a variant craftable from current stock stays concrete so the planner sub-crafts it; a fully unstocked tie goes out as the family spec when one covers the set exactly, so the nested obtain gathers whichever variant the terrain actually has (spruce_log, never a canonical oak_log from two biomes over); and a strict or stocked winner stays concrete (cobblestone beats stone). Cheap craftable-from-stock probe for the variant tie-break: some recipe of the variant has every input slot covered by a stocked accepted item. Count-blind on purpose - it only decides which variant is TRIED first; the resolve pass still verifies exact counts. Collapses a recipe's per-slot inputs into distinct requirements with counts. Fewest distinct requirements first, then fewest slots: the cheapest route to try first.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiCrystals.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiCrystals.notes:
game:clear_crystals - destroys the End's healing crystals, the opening move of the dragon fight. End crystals sit on bedrock atop the obsidian pillars; roughly half are caged in iron bars. Any damage pops a crystal, and the pop is a power-6 explosion, so the bow is the default and melee is only for pops that game:danger's blast pricing calls survivable point-blank.

UNCAGED crystals are shot through AiRanged's simulated-arc shooter, one shot at a time, each kill confirmed by the entity's removal and re-attempted on a miss (at most {@link #MAX_SHOTS_PER_CRYSTAL}). When the player stands too far under the pillar (the solver cannot lob steeper than 60 degrees up) or beyond arrow range, the op first walks to a firing cell at roughly pillar-height horizontal distance ({@link #shootStand}). No launchable weapon (bow/crossbow + arrows, trident, or throwables) records a no_ranged skip; once everything reachable is done the op FAILs with a missing{bow,arrow} report and code NO_RANGED - the model answers with game:obtain.

CAGED crystals cannot be shot through the bars, so the op pillars up beside the cage (engine travel with allowPillar plus backpack restock), breaks the facing bar with the verified dig path, then either punches the crystal from the tower (vanilla entity reach measures to the hitbox edge, so one bar's clearance is enough - but only when AiDanger says the blast is survivable) or, when the prediction is lethal, shoots through the broken opening instead. Getting down reuses existing machinery: an MLG water clutch when a water bucket sits in the hotbar, otherwise digging the tower back down - never a raw >3 fall.

While airborne on the tower the survival guard and the low-health abort are suppressed on purpose: a fight/flee leg up there walks the player off the edge, which is worse than the threat it answers. Everywhere else the standard guard interrupts and resumes exactly like the gathering composites. The terminal report is per-crystal {id, caged, method, result}; zero crystals observed (a fight that has not loaded in yet) SUCCEEDs with cleared:0.

Everything that does not need a live Level is a pure static seam (cage classification, target ordering, method choice, the ranged check, firing-position math, descend choice) and is headless-tested in AiCrystalsTest. The client seams never throw; all client thread. Furthest shot worth taking; beyond it the op walks to a firing cell first. The most a crystal's predicted blast may take for the sword (or a shot) to be safe from where the player stands. A flying dragon nearer than this keeps the player off the cage towers, and nearer than the abort brings it down. Horizontal clearance below which a tall pillar's crystal is not lob-able (solver caps at 60 degrees up). Arrows spent on one crystal before it is recorded a miss and skipped. Melee swings on one crystal before it is recorded failed. Ticks waited for the entity to vanish after a release/swing before it counts as a miss. Ticks the melee aim may sweep before the swing goes out anyway. Ticks the MLG walk-off may fail to get airborne before the op digs down instead. MLG clutch failures tolerated before the descend switches to digging. One loaded crystal: entity id, cell, distance at scan time and whether iron bars guard it. Both ground skips and interrupted tower climbs must report the same retry reason. A tower climb owns its safe descent; ordinary food/heal replans must wait for ground. Cover never substitutes for a fresh damage budget or a nonlethal verdict. Iron bars anywhere in the pillar-top neighborhood mark the cage (vanilla walls the cell off at +-2). Whether the crystal at the cell sits in a vanilla iron bar cage (the 5x5x5 pillar-top neighbourhood). Work order: shootable (uncaged) crystals first, nearest-first inside each kind, ids on ties. Anything AiRanged can launch that also has its ammo: bow/crossbow + arrows, trident, or throwables. How one crystal gets cleared. Caged always takes the pillar route (bars block arrows); uncaged is punched only when already inside melee reach AND the point-blank blast is survivable, otherwise shot; an uncaged crystal that can be neither punched nor shot has no route (null) and the caller records the no_ranged skip. Whether the current spot cannot produce an arc: too far out, or too far under the pillar for the 60-degree cap. The firing cell for a crystal: on the ray from the crystal through the player, at horizontal distance max(12, dy + 6) from the pillar axis - far enough that the arc never needs more than a 45-degree lob, close enough for the simulator's range. {x, z}; the caller scans the ground Y. dx/dz is the player's horizontal offset from the crystal axis. The cage side facing the player as a unit direction (dominant axis, ties to X). Down from the tower: an MLG clutch when a water bucket is in the hotbar, else dig the tower back down. The missing-items report for the no_ranged failure (mirror of AiRanged's equip shortage). Hotbar contents as registry id paths ("air" for empty slots), for the descend choice. game:clear_crystals - pop every loaded End crystal, caged or not. Tower phases, where guard actions and the health abort are more dangerous than the threats. AiObtain's guard pattern: a guard action runs to completion, then the leg restarts from scratch. The fast way down: step off away from the pillar and let the water clutch catch the fall. The reliable way down: break the tower block underfoot, one cell per leg. The crystal is gone: record it and, on the tower, get down before the next target. Same accounting for a crystal that vanished while the tower was still being climbed. A skip recorded from the tower: same accounting, but the way down comes first. Everything observed is spent: roll the skip reasons up into one actionable failure. The 5x5x5 pillar-top neighborhood; vanilla cages wall the crystal off two cells out. Vanilla reach measures eye-to-hitbox-edge, so beside-the-cage cells qualify. game:danger's verdic

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDanger.j.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDanger.j.notes:
Danger assessment for the AI assistant: what around the player is about to hurt, how much, and when. Pricing goes through the same vanilla-parity blast engine AutoTotem gates on ({@link AutismExplosionDamage}: exact exposure/falloff curve, difficulty, shield, armour, resistance, protection estimate), so the numbers here agree with the module's own thresholds. AutoTotem answers "must a totem be in hand RIGHT NOW"; this answers the LLM-facing "which sources, how much each, and is the worst case lethal".

Totals semantics (AutoTotem parity). {@code totalPredicted} is the WORST single explosion plus the fall damage, never the sum of explosions: the server resolves every blast in the same tick against one position, and stacking them double-counts the window.

etaTicks. 0..N ticks for timed sources (TNT fuse, swelling creeper, incoming fireball), -1 for trigger-driven ones (crystals, beds, anchors, TNT minecarts — they wait for someone to set them off, so no honest countdown exists).

Fireballs (verified against the decompiled 26.2 sources). Ghast {@code LargeFireball} explodes with the ghast's {@code explosionPower}, default 1 (Ghast.java:47,:372); the field is NBT-only, not client-synced, so the vanilla default 1 is assumed. Wither skulls explode with power 1 (WitherSkull.java:97). Blaze {@code SmallFireball} does NOT explode (SmallFireball.java: direct-hit 5 fire damage + ignite only), so it is not a blast source and is skipped. Impact positions come from {@link AiProjectiles}' straight-line prediction (gravity 0 for {@code AbstractHurtingProjectile}) — AiProjectiles owns when it hits, AiDanger owns how much.

Cost. Runs at observation cadence, not per tick, and a 2-client-tick memo (same staleness budget as AutoTotemModule's entity memo) lets repeated observations and the threat monitor share one assessment. The fall simulation only runs when fallDistance > 3 or vertical velocity is below -0.08.

Everything that does not need a live Level is a pure static seam (power table, dimension rules, landing multipliers, ETA curves, totals, JSON shaping, lethal verdicts) and is headless-tested in AiDangerTest. The client seams never throw; everything runs client-thread. One priced danger source: what it is, where it lands, how much it hurts and when. The full picture: every priced source, the worst of them, the fall projection, the player's protection state, and the two lethal verdicts against {@code totalPredicted}. {@code voidFall} marks a descent that crosses below the dimension's void floor - lethal by void damage, which bypasses totems, so both verdicts are forced rather than priced. The two lethal verdicts, re-exposed as a value so tests can stub the evaluator. The lethal gate, abstracted so the passthrough is headless-testable. Fall sim gate (vertical velocity, blocks/tick) and vanilla slow-falling gravity cap. Vanilla creeper fuse (Creeper.maxSwell default, 26.2 Creeper.java:55). Vanilla air drag (AutoTotemModule:116-119 BASE_* constants, the non-elytra branches). Sorted 10-block sphere offsets for the bed/anchor scan (AutoTotem's SPHERE_OFFSETS shape). The whole explosion power table in one seam, keyed by source kind. Vanilla references: EndCrystal 6, bed/respawn anchor 5 ({@link AutismExplosionDamage} constants), PrimedTnt {@code explosionPower} default 4 (PrimedTnt.java:58), TNT minecart 4 + min(horizontal speed, 5) * 1.5 (AutoTotemModule:1251-1256), creeper radius 3, doubled when powered (Creeper.java:56,:230-233), ghast LargeFireball / wither skull 1, everything else 0. Beds explode only where BED_RULE == BedRule.EXPLODES (nether, end). Anchors explode only where they do not work (overworld, end) AND hold a charge. Vanilla landing-block fall multiplier (AutoTotemModule:1374-1382), keyed by the block's registry id path (no namespace). Null/empty is the no-support-inside-the-horizon case. TNT fuse in ticks is the ETA (clamped: the fuse counter runs slightly negative at detonation). Creeper swelling 0..1 to ticks remaining (swell 0 ~ a full 30-tick fuse, swell 1 ~ now). One vanilla free-fall tick on vertical motion: gravity (slow-falling caps the decrement at 0.01 while descending), then air drag — FallingPlayerSim.calculateFreeFallTick's order. The worst single explosion in the list (0 when empty). Explosions max, they never sum. total = max(explosions) + fallDamage (AutoTotemModule:1198-1202 semantics). Lethal verdicts for a total, through whatever evaluator the caller supplies. {@link #verdicts(float, LethalEvaluator)} with the void-fall override: void damage is in BYPASSES_INVULNERABILITY, so a totem never pops for it and both verdicts force true. The report window: at most cap (clamped to {@link #MAX_REPORT_SOURCES}) sources, timed sources first ascending by eta, trigger-driven (eta -1) last, damage descending inside ties. The sources array exactly as the report emits it. The full assessment; EMPTY on any failure or when no living player is connected. The bounded JSON report shared by the observation block and game:danger. game:danger — immediate observe op, no side effects. The memoized snapshot: repeated callers inside two client ticks share one computation. A death-protection-component item (AutoTotemModule:555-557). Live explosive entities, priced at their own blast power and origin (AutoTotemModule:1242-1265). Beds and charged respawn anchors inside a 10-block sphere, where the dimension makes them explosive (AutoTotemModule:1267-1298). Only the HEAD half of a bed is priced (both halves are the same bed), and the exploding block(s) are excluded from exposure so the blast is not shielded by the block that consumes itself. Ghast/wither fireballs from AiProjectiles' scan, priced at the predicted impact position. AiProjectiles owns if/when it hits (straight-line, gravity 0 for hurting projectiles); this owns how much the blast hurts there. Blaze SmallFireballs have power 0 (no explosion) and drop out at the power table. The simplified FallingPlay

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDeathLog.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDeathLog.notes:
Where the player died and what they were carrying.

Recovery after death is only possible if something wrote the coordinates down BEFORE the respawn moved the player and cleared the inventory. Nothing did, so a death used to mean the run silently lost every tool it had spent minutes making. This records the one snapshot that makes {@code game:recover} possible, at the tick the death is first noticed.

Dropped items despawn after five minutes, so the record carries its own age and the recovery operation reports the remaining window rather than walking to an empty grave. Vanilla item despawn time. One death: where, when, in which world, and what was on the player. Milliseconds left before the drops despawn; zero once the window has passed. Snapshots the death. Safe to call repeatedly while the death screen is up - only the first call for a given death wins, because the inventory is cleared as the respawn completes. The most recent recorded death, or null when the player has not died this session. Marks the recorded death as dealt with so a later recover call reports honestly. Clears the record; used when a new world makes the old coordinates meaningless. The record as tool-result data, or an explicit absent marker.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDimensio.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDimensio.notes:
game:dimension - travelling between worlds as one call.

{@code enter} takes a dimension id, finds a portal of the right kind, walks into it and waits for the dimension actually to change - the whole point of this operation, because a portal is asynchronous and a model polling for the change burns a round trip per second. When no nether portal is nearby and {@code build} is set, it constructs the ten-block obsidian frame itself and lights it. Arrival is verified, not assumed: landing in a wall or in lava reports UNCERTAIN with the hazard named, and a nether arrival without any gold armor carries a piglin warning in the result data.

{@code find} is the read-only half: every portal block in loaded terrain with its distance, so the model can decide between walking to one and building a new one. Ticks spent standing in a portal before it is reported as not transporting. Ticks the loading handshake may take after the dimension id changes. Search radius in loaded terrain for an existing portal. Heights of the interior's bottom over the feet a build site is tried at, in order. The last frame a build began, in this world: one cut short is finished there, never begun again elsewhere. The last portal this op built and lit (the entry walks back to it from out of the portal search's reach). Portal sites a frame placement failed at, in the scoped world and dimension (see {@link #scopeFrame}). Obsidian standing in the last frame begun (0 with none, unloaded, or lit already). The frame's and interior's cells, packed. Blocks a portal site may be dug out of when none is clear, and the digs that may fail. Ticks one frame block may take to place before the build is abandoned. Ticks between portal searches; the search volume is far too large to run every tick. Obsidian blocks in a minimal corner-less nether portal frame. The gold armor pieces that keep piglins neutral (PiglinAi.isWearingGold's set). Any gold armor piece among the four armor slots (registry ids), the piglin neutrality check. Child identity and actual receipts survive cleanup at every portal boundary. AiPlacer's pending flag must be sampled before cancel nulls its target. Only applied server evidence resolves a dispatched lighting use; predicted fire does not. Dimension id to the portal block that leads there. Origins whose frame a placement already failed at: never chosen again in this world. Kept per operation, the campaign's next attempt (a new operation) picked the same site, and three identical failures in fifteen seconds ended a run holding its ten obsidian. A standing cell in front of or behind the portal's plane, level with the lowest portal block of the column {@code portal} is in, floor under it and room for the body; nearest the player, null if none. Escape local terrain without excavating or bridging through the observed portal. The hazard a portal can leave the player standing in, named for the report; null when safe. The piglin warning for a nether arrival: vanilla piglins aggro on sight unless any gold armor piece is worn. A warning, never a block - entering unarmored is legal. Picks a site and queues the ten frame cells. Returns a terminal result on refusal. Places the queued frame cells one at a time, then lights the portal. A site whose frame cells and interior are all free, with solid ground beneath. Frame cells of the site that already hold obsidian. A frame begun is finished whoever stands in it (the body steps out before a cell is placed) and whatever natural block fell into its interior (dug out first): read with the body as a block, the frame the run had built was "not clear" from inside it, and the next attempt mined ten more obsidian for a new one. Air or another replaceable block, no fluid (the player's box may be in it). What vanilla's portal shape takes for an interior cell: air, fire or portal, nothing else. Grass, a flower or a snow layer is "replaceable" for a placement but keeps the portal from forming, and the flint and steel's fire cannot go into it either (a frame on grassland was complete, twice, and never lit). A natural block the pickaxe takes and nothing flows into once it is gone. The site round the player with the fewest blocks to dig (at most MAX_SITE_DIGS), top-down; null if none. Digs the queued cells one at a time; null once the queue is empty. A standable cell next to the site and outside its frame and interior, nearest the player. The free neighbour of a frame cell, outside the frame and the interior, with a face of its own: below first. Some solid face beside the cell to click against. The body stands in a cell the frame needs: it walks to a stand outside the site first. The walk to a jamb's stance ended in the empty corner under it, the corner was dropped as "not replaceable" with the body in it, and the jamb had no face left to click ("no reachable support face" on the portal home's first jamb). The frame's, interior's and corners' cells, packed: no approach stance stands in one. A stance in front of the frame or behind it, beside the interior's foot, from where the floor's top is in view. Frame cells holding no obsidian once the list is done (a placement the server undid, a guard fight between). The ten obsidian cells of a minimal portal frame, given the bottom-left interior floor cell and the axis the portal faces along. Corners are omitted - vanilla does not need them - so this is the cheapest frame that lights. The frame's four corners, which a portal does not need: throwaway supports for the jambs and the lintel. The cells that must already be solid for the frame to be placeable: one block under each obsidian floor cell, so the floor has a face to place against. Deliberately disjoint from {@link #framePositions} and {@link #interiorPositions} - those must all be FREE. The six interior air cells the portal fills. Accepts "nether", "the_nether" and "minecraft:the_nether" as the same place.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDirectOp.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDirectOp.notes:
Direct user-command runner for game:/client: capabilities (the .tools surface) - a standalone single-op owner that needs no AI assistant module, session, or model. Ops are built by the SAME factories the LLM perform path dispatches through ({@link AiTools#directOperation}, which also serves AiTools.start); fingerprint gating stays an LLM-path concern and is skipped here. The op is created and ticked in the shared pre-movement input phase ({@link AiClientTick}), and start/progress/terminal results go to chat through the mod's prefixed, tone-colored messaging. One op at a time.

Safety parity with the AI path, kept lightweight: cancel on player death (respawning leaves the op cancelled), cancel on world change/disconnect for ops that started inside a world (dimension-travel ops in {@link #DIMENSION_TRAVEL_OPS} excepted - the crossing is their job, so their world reference re-bases instead), and cancel on the AI emergency key (F10 default - polled from the window handle exactly like AiService's handler, so it works even while a screen has focus). Stop is idempotent; engine ops release their keys in cancel(), and {@code AiMovementExecutor.release()} runs as a backstop.

Pause suspends ticking without cancelling: held movement/attack inputs are released while suspended, but op-internal deadlines keep running (a long pause surfaces as a timeout on resume). Reflex/combat ops in {@link #PAUSE_AS_STOP} cannot safely suspend - pause stops them. Ops that treat pause as stop: combat and reflex clutches hold live aim/timing state. Ops whose contract can include crossing dimensions: game:dimension is the travel itself, and a game:plan may hold a game:dimension leg. The world-change cancel must not kill these mid-portal - the supervisor re-bases its world reference and the op's own settle logic reports the arrival. Everything else keeps the cancel. The tradeoff, accepted deliberately: a plan that experiences an EXTERNAL world change (kick/rejoin) also keeps running; its steps still cancel themselves on a null level/player and re-verify their own preconditions. True when a world change should re-base rather than cancel the op with this capability id. One in-flight operation plus everything its release needs. Client-thread confined. The live capability snapshot (refreshed on the client thread; the refresh is revision-cheap). Capabilities the direct runner can dispatch (module:/command:/macro:/menu: have their own surfaces). Bare names resolve against game: then client:; explicit namespaces pass through; null when unknown. One-line contract summary for chat listings (delegates to the dispatcher's renderer). Validates and starts one capability, reporting the start to chat. Throws IllegalArgumentException (bad id/args) or IllegalStateException (busy/occupied controls) with user-presentable messages; the command handler prints them. Injects the user's direct-runner defaults at op creation; the LLM path never reads these. Sets a default only when the caller didn't and the capability's schema declares the field. Idempotent cancel of the running op (if any); reports either way so keybinds stay quiet-safe. Suspend ticking without cancelling; reflex/combat ops stop instead (documented in help). Compact status for .tools status: op id, elapsed, pause state and the latest progress. How the last operation ended (null before the first): the fixtures read a .tools run's outcome here. Explicit stops, death and world loss must replace any old receipt before cancelling pending transactions. The structured failure line: tone + [AiFailure code] + message (+ suggestions in verbose). A .tools operation is driving the body's keys and hands (Freecam then only watches). Releases the op's controls and lease; cancel=true also cancels the op itself. Hands movement keys back to the human; attack/use too when the op owned INPUT (AiService's rule). The vanilla schematics folder game:build's schematic arg loads from (<gamedir>/schematics). Swaps and persists the direct-runner settings (from the settings screen's draft). The shared AI settings: live from the service when it exists (so ops read the same copy the assistant uses), otherwise the persisted file. Never instantiates the service. Writes one AiSettings field through the live service when present (copy-save-swap, no connection test), or straight to settings.json otherwise - one setting, one storage location. The .tools invocation with the user's live command prefix (for chat hints). How much result data each verbosity prints on a terminal success line.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDodge.ja.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDodge.ja.notes:
Predictive defense with legal input: ghast returns move onto a common attack/intercept ray, lead the moving shooter and observe server redirection and target death separately. An unsafe or unavailable kill solution still permits an immediate defensive bat, else a shield or checked escape. Blaze small fireballs are never redirected. Every exit releases the movement, shield and attack inputs.
Deflect window: reflect fireballs arriving within 1.2s while close enough to swing in time.
Escape burst: hold a dodge direction for up to ~12 ticks, re-aiming every 3.
Ticks a raised shield needs before it blocks (the shield's blocks_attacks block delay, 0.25 s).
A projectile on a hitting course that the guard should answer now: any within the dodge horizon, but an arrow at a body on the move only at low health (on easy a skeleton's arrow at a moving body mostly misses, and stopping to block every one cost the route its pace). A projectile the player shot is never one.
Fireball close and soon enough that pressing attack now connects before impact.
Only changed ownership or reversed live flight proves a deflection; disappearance may be an impact.
The ballistics dodge direction with terrain folded in: probe the footing the sprint would cross before committing, try the opposite side when the preferred one runs off a ledge or into lava, and return null when neither side is walkable (stand ground).
Every cell the escape burst would occupy, checked like a combat strafe.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDragon.j.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDragon.j.notes:
The native End boss controller: observed fountain geometry, synced phase and head-part timing, conservative bed self-damage and actual solid cover, then crystal/melee/bow fallback. Every bed attempt observes removal and dragon health changes; unsafe or ineffective attempts retire the plan. Attacks obey effective weapon range/charge, and ranged attacks stop on the arrow-immune perch. Defeat requires fresh kill or central exit evidence after disappearance. No fixed bed count promises a kill; the enclosing AiEndRun verifies exit travel separately.
Six bounded child slots; cancellation cannot erase an unacknowledged interaction or its last receipt.
Bed placement radius from the fountain axis: hugging the rim, inside the perched blast.
How far out a bed may go when the sitting dragon's wing push covers every stance that reaches the rim (the head is 6.5 out).
Stands round an armed bed as {cells behind the foot, cells to the side}: straight behind first, all within clicking reach.
Stand radius from the fountain axis when meleeing the perched head.
Health kept after a bed blast priced at 8 or more. Half a point under 12: natural regeneration sits at 19.8-19.9 for seconds, a reserve of 12 needed exactly 20, and the fight handed back to heal seventy-five times at full health.
Hold radius from the fountain axis while waiting out the circling phases (at 8 a landing dragon passed over the spot).
Head-to-bed distances that open the detonation window: point-blank always, sitting wider.
Extra margin kept outside every breath-cloud radius.
Seconds the dragon may be gone before the kill counts as unverifiable.
Longest single melee engagement per perch before re-planning.
Room a melee stand keeps from the sitting dragon's wing push (the step-out fires at 0.6).
Consecutive failed bow legs before the bow is written off for the fight.
Under this health the fight hands back to its owner to heal (eat, a hole in the end stone) before the next perch.
Cells behind the bed's foot, along its axis, where the detonating body stands; the cover block goes one cell nearer.
Where the dragon is relative to the fountain, as far as the fight plan cares.
Perch classification from the synced phase name (the EnderDragonPhase constant names; the client mirrors the phase through entity data). The sitting phases and the final landing are the attack window, the landing approach is the pre-arm window, takeoff and everything else is flying, and the dying animation is hands-off.
Fallback when the phase read fails: over the fountain and slow means perched.
The one decision per re-plan. Crystals outrank everything (the dragon heals until they pop); an armed bed is either clicked (window) or held; beds beat melee in a perch window because the one-cycle is faster; the bow only works off-perch; anything else waits at the fountain.
When an armed bed may be clicked: the head practically on top of it always counts (the landing glide puts it there before the sitting phases do); otherwise only while perched (landing or sitting) with the head over the fountain.
A cell on the ray from (fx, fz) through the player, {@code radius} blocks out - the shared geometry for the bed cell (hugging the fountain), the stand-off (back along the same ray) and the melee/hold cells. A player exactly on the axis defaults to +X. {x, z}; the caller scans the ground Y.
The bed cell for a fountain at (fx, fz): on the player's side, hugging the rim.
The stand-off cell for an armed bed: back along the player's ray at click distance.
Every lingering cloud near the player (the dragon's breath, a witch's potion) as {x, z, radius}, level with the feet.
Whether the player stands in (or at the margin of) a lingering cloud.
Out of the clouds: the nearest standable cell within eight blocks clear of every cloud and its margin, walked to (null when there is none). The dragon's breath is magic: four health a touch through any armour, and a bow phase that stood in it took twelve in five seconds.
Out of the clouds to a cell {@code extra} blocks clear of every cloud's margin: a cell just at the margin was reached, the cloud grew or the body stopped a hair short, and the step-out fired again every tick from the same spot.
A spot is breathable when it lies outside every cloud's radius plus the margin. Clouds are {x, z, radius}.
{@link #cloudFree} with {@code extra} blocks more room round every cloud.
The nearest spot on a growing 8-point ring that is out of every cloud, or the original when nothing is.
Entry preflight: beds alone are the one-cycle plan, a bow/crossbow with arrows is the chip plan.
Every vanilla bed item (and block) id ends in _bed; suffix matching needs no tag lookup.
The entry-shortage report: either a bed or a working bow answers it (game:obtain).
The entity vanishing alone never proves the kill; the stat delta or the active exit portal does.
game:dragon_fight - loop beds/melee/bow around the perch cycle until the dragon is dead.
The melee step's stand by the head, and what its leg is for: 0 none, 1 the walk in, 2 out of the flame.
Defeat needs the observed dragon's zero health or its active central exit; stale lifetime stats are insufficient.
A sidestep out of the dragon's charge: while it charges ({@code DragonChargePlayerPhase}, a straight flight at the spot it picked) and its line ahead passes within nine blocks of the player, the player steps ten blocks to the side of that line onto safe footing.
Out of the sitting dragon's push and strike zones ({@link AiDragonZones}), whatever else was running.
AiObtain's guard pattern: a guard action runs to completion, then the leg restarts from scratch.
On fire or standing in it: water from a bucket at the feet (and back into the bucket), else a step out of the fire.
The same interrupt shape for fireballs: dodge to completion, then re-plan from scratch.
Local, guarded and bounded; shortage never converts a healing cage into a completed target.
One block on the ground between the feet and the bed: it takes the blast's rays to

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDragonZo.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiDragonZo.notes:
Where the dragon's body hurts (26.2 {@code EnderDragon.aiStep}). Every tick its two wing boxes, grown 4 sideways and 2 up and down and moved 2 down, push each living thing inside away from the body centre by 4 / distance squared (sitting or not, so a few ticks in one throw the player off the island: "doomed to fall by Ender Dragon" at 17.9 health beside the perched dragon), and the head and neck boxes grown 1 strike for 10. The wings sit 4.5 to each side of the body, so the push covers a 21 by 12 block area round the dragon; the head is 6.5 in front of it, one below the body while it sits. In front of a sitting dragon nothing reaches past about 8 blocks: that is where the bed fight stands.
Room kept from a push zone by routes and stands: the dragon turns while it sits, and a throw is lethal.
Room kept from a strike zone: a strike is a hit (10, about 3 through diamond on easy), not a throw.
A route cell inside a zone: about twenty blocks of walking round it.
The push zones (wings) and strike zones (head, neck) of the dragons near the player.
Whether a box meets a push zone grown by the margin, or a strike zone grown by at most {@link #STRIKE_MARGIN}.
The push zone of one wing part box.
The strike zone of the head or neck part box.
Every zone of every live dragon within 128 blocks, read from the client's part boxes; empty with no dragon.
The box a player standing in the cell takes up.
The box a player standing at (x, feetY, z) takes up.
The sitting (or landing) dragon, or null.
Whether a dragon is sitting on the fountain (or landing on it): the zones then stand still and are worth walking round.
The way a sitting dragon's head points, level and of length one (body to head); null with no sitting dragon.
The head part of a sitting dragon, or null.
Where a sitting dragon breathes ({@code DragonSittingFlamingPhase}): a cloud of radius 5 on the ground 2.5 past the head along its facing, ten seconds each, up to four times a perch. {x, z, radius}, or null with no sitting dragon. Predicted before it appears: a stand behind a bed in front of the head was inside it every time.
A stand clear of the push and strike zones, the predicted breath (a block of room) and the lying clouds.
Off a pillar out of a cloud: in a cloud with no free cell round it (the top of a crystal's pillar is all inside a dragon fireball's cloud) and a water bucket in the bag, walk off away from the cloud with the water clutch armed. The player stood on a pillar top after a cage and the clouds took it from 16 to dead. Null when it does not apply.
The route price: a cell whose standing box meets a zone (with its margin) costs {@link #SURCHARGE}. NONE without a dragon.
Out of the zones: the nearest standable cell within ten blocks whose box clears every zone by two blocks, walked to (null when the player is clear or no such cell exists).
{@link #leave} to a cell clear of every zone by {@code clearance} blocks.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiEnchant..documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiEnchant..notes:
Enchanting table observation (game:enchant_table) and the game:enchant click operation. Verified against the 26.2 merged sources: EnchantmentMenu exposes the three options via the synced arrays costs[3] (required XP level), enchantClue[3] and levelClue[3] (holder-id + level of ONE hinted enchantment); slot 0 is the item input, slot 1 the lapis slot. clickMenuButton consumes buttonId + 1 lapis and buttonId + 1 XP levels (Player.onEnchantmentPerformed) and requires experienceLevel >= max(buttonId + 1, costs[buttonId]). The click itself is a menu BUTTON (MultiPlayerGameMode.handleInventoryButtonClick), not a slot click; the client has no prediction for it, so an observed slot-0 change is always server-applied (stamped by AiServerEvidence). Item/lapis INSERTION is deliberately not part of the op: the model places both via game:inventory_click first; the op only verifies affordability and clicks once. Never auto-retries.
Per-option JSON from the synced clue arrays. Pure seam: clueEnchantment is the resolved clue id (null when the registry is unavailable, e.g. headless); safe for headless tests.
Exact deficit message, or null when the option click is affordable. Pure seam.
OBSERVE: the currently open enchanting table. Client-authoritative menu data; nothing untrusted.
ACTION: click one enchant option once, then wait for the server-applied slot change.
Clue ids are holder ids in the dynamic ENCHANTMENT registry; the client holds the same registry the server used. Degrades to null (raw id reported) when the registry is unavailable.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiEndPorta.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiEndPorta.notes:
Vanilla's twelve inward-facing frame cells and nine portal cells, verified in loaded terrain.
Filled-frame geometry alone cannot acknowledge a newly sent one-Eye interaction.
A point of {@code frame} the ray from {@code eye} meets first, within {@code reach}: the top face's grid, then the side faces. An eye goes in from any face; aimed only at the top's middle, a frame behind the platform's stair was "obstructed" from every stance and the same click failed for minutes. Null when none is seen.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiEndRun.j.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiEndRun.j.notes:
game:end_run - the speedrun's End: from the arrival platform to the main island (legit bridging only over the void, no jump over a drop that hurts), the dragon fight (game:dragon_fight with the beds carried, melee on the perch and the bow while it circles), then the exit portal at the fountain. Done when the body is back in the overworld with the dragon dead: the exit portal, never the death alone, ends the game.
The fight starts within this many blocks of the fountain (x 0, z 0).
Health the fight starts from (and comes back to between perches): a bed's blast and the dragon's charge each take a few.
How far from the fountain the run heals: past the perch, its breath and the bed fire.
The ring a heal spot is looked for in, blocks from the fountain: past the breath (about 16), inside the island.
Fire (or soul fire) in any cell the body's box touches.
Water poured at the feet puts a burning body out at once (eight seconds of burning is eight health, armour or not), then goes back into the bucket. Null without a water bucket, or where water cannot stand (the Nether).
The nearest cell within two blocks with floor, room for the body and no fire, or null.
The nearest cell within two blocks with floor, room for the body and no fire, walked to; null when there is none.
The fire at the body put out by hand, one block a tick: fire breaks in one hit. With no free cell within two blocks (a hole a blaze's fireball lit) nothing else was done, and a Nether fixture burnt to death in place over thirty seconds.
Keys straight at the portal block's centre for up to three seconds: the body drops into it. Routes stop beside a portal (portal cells are priced as a hazard), so a walk "arrived" or found "no route" beside it again and again. Done when the dimension changes or the credits show.
The heal spot in use, and spots whose hole failed.
Keys straight at the portal block's centre for up to three seconds: the body drops into it.
Under the fight's health: eat while the bar is short of full (vanilla heals fast only at a full bar), then a sealed hole in the end stone until healed - the dragon cannot break end stone, endermen cannot stand in a one-wide hole.
The health the next fight starts at: FIGHT_HEALTH, or a bed's full reserve after a fight handed back for it.
Where to heal: {@link #HEAL_MIN}-{@link #HEAL_MAX} blocks from the fountain (out of the breath, inside the island), end stone four deep under it for the hole, and every column within three blocks within two of its level (no edge to be knocked over). The nearest to the player; null when none is loaded.
The topmost block with collision in the column (open sky above it), or null over the void or unloaded.
An exit portal block at the fountain, once the dragon's death opened it.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiEntityQu.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiEntityQu.notes:
game:entities — parameterized entity query, ONE call, one pass, no world mutation. The query filters every loaded entity by range (sphere radius OR per-axis box), an optional type spec (registry id or case-insensitive substring of the entity type id) and an optional category, and returns the matches sorted by distance, capped at limit.

Classification and entry shaping are pure static seams ({@link Facts}, {@link #categoryOf}, {@link #entry}), headless-tested; the runtime half only extracts facts from live entities.

Category rules (precedence order, first match wins): {@code boss} = ender dragon, wither, elder guardian (a short documented list); {@code hostile} = {@link Enemy}; {@code villager} = {@link AbstractVillager}; {@code player} = {@link Player} (the local player included); {@code item} = {@link ItemEntity}; {@code projectile} = {@link Projectile}; {@code vehicle} = {@link VehicleEntity} (boats), {@link AbstractMinecart} or {@link PlayerRideable}; {@code passive} = any other living entity; everything else is {@code other} (returned under the default {@code all} filter only). The documented boss list: classified by entity-type id, deliberately short. The entity facts classification consumes, extracted at runtime (instanceof/registry reads). First-match precedence: boss > hostile > villager > player > item > projectile > vehicle > passive > other. Registry id or case-insensitive substring of the entity type id. One result entry; {@code health} null outside living entities, equipment omitted when empty. The one-shot query: a single pass over loaded entities; never mutates the world. Fact extraction shared with AiGameState's observation enrichment (cheap, per entity). Brief equipment ids for mobs/players: mainhand, offhand, then armor; empty slots omitted. Eye-ray approximation: the eye-to-entity ray is block-free (eye height, bbox center otherwise).

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiEquip.ja.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiEquip.ja.notes:
game:equip - "hold the right thing" and "wear the best thing", without slot arithmetic.

Armour is direct inventory logic, NOT a module window: the ranking model is the exact one the AutoArmor module uses (factored out into AutismArmorEvaluation, damage-reduction maths and enchantment weighting included), and the pieces move with verified player-inventory clicks - one click per server-confirmed inventory revision, the AiSmelt click-confirmation pattern - so the module's enabled state is never touched. The user's own AutoArmor preferences (prefer elytra, allow cursed, the save-armour durability floor, the hotbar-swap toggles) are READ from the module's settings and honored; nothing is written back.

Hand equipment is direct: the best weapon by attack damage, the best tool for a named block, or a specific item spec, moved into the hotbar with one swap when it is in the backpack. Ticks a single armour click may await its applied server inventory revision. Ticks the whole armour equip may take. InventoryMenu (window 0) menu-slot id for each worn armor piece. Stable layout: 5=head..8=feet. The hand argument: main (default) or offhand, anything else rejected. Pure for headless tests. Offhand path: moves the spec'd item into the offhand with one swap-with-offhand click and verifies it against the applied server inventory revision before reporting (the AiSmelt click-confirmation pattern). Selects an already-identified inventory slot; used by the weapon and tool paths. A backpack slot is swapped into the hotbar first (the contract's "moved into the hotbar with one swap"). Wears the best available armour with the op's own verified clicks: re-rank the live inventory every tick (the AutismArmorEvaluation model the AutoArmor module shares), and for the first slot whose best piece is not already worn, issue the one window-0 click that advances toward it, then await the applied server inventory revision before the next. The module's enabled state is never touched; its preference settings are read, not written.

The optional prefer spec (golden_chestplate, or a trailing-* family like golden_*) promotes matching pieces to slot winners ahead of damage reduction - gold for piglin neutrality; a spec matching nothing, carried or worn, fails naming itself. The first slot (head to feet) whose best-ranked piece is not the worn one. The elytra to wear for the chest slot, preferring a worn one, then hotbar, then inventory. The candidate's window-0 menu slot; -1 aborts the move (should not happen live). The per-slot candidate lists restricted to pieces matching the prefer spec; empty when the spec matches nothing carried or worn. Package-visible for headless tests. Package-visible for headless tests. src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiEventLog.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiEventLog.notes:
The AI's event feed: a bounded ring of things that happened around the player, so a model can catch up with {@code game:events since=} instead of inferring changes from raw observation deltas. Feed points are cheap and aggregated by design: damage, death, respawn and dimension changes from the service tick, hostile targeting polled every 5 ticks (diff-based), inventory diffs aggregated every 20 ticks, and the operate() lifecycle. Nothing allocates per tick except those windows.

Events are {@code {seq, tick, kind, data}} with a monotonic seq; the ring caps at {@link #CAP} and every eviction is counted, so a slow reader sees exactly what it missed via the {@code dropped} field of each page. One event: a monotonic sequence number, the client tick, the kind, and its data. Client-tick clock for event stamps. Events newer than {@code since} (the caller's last seen seq; 0 = everything retained). Events evicted since the caller's cursor: the ring's evicted seqs are always 1..dropped, so the count lost between the cursor and the oldest retained event is exactly this. Events newer than the cursor of the last game:events read (the observation's nudge). Serializes a page of events plus the cursor and eviction accounting. The game:events query: a since-cursor, a limit, and an optional comma kind filter.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiFarm.jav.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiFarm.jav.notes:
game:farm - crops and animals.

{@code harvest} is a first-class executor op, NOT a module driver: it never touches the AutoFarm module's enabled state or settings (the module stays a user-facing feature; a user's own enabled AutoFarm is paused by the operation dispatcher like any conflicting module). The op scans loaded terrain budgeted across ticks for the requested crop (name the crop block or the item it yields), walks between plants with ordinary engine legs (walk-only options: no dig, pillar, bridge or parkour - and the engine never tramples farmland, so fields are crossed without damage), harvests each mature plant with the verified block adapter, replants from inventory, and sweeps the drops it produces with inventory-delta accounting. A replant's server confirmation polls in the background once its click has landed, so the op is already walking to (or breaking) the next plant instead of idling on the verification window.

The crop table is exactly the documented one (and the module's, AutismFarmBlocks): the farmland crops (wheat, carrots, potatoes, beetroots at max age), nether wart (harvested at age 3 and replanted on soul sand - replant is deliberately ON by default for autonomy; classic bots default it off), cocoa (harvested at age 2 and replanted on the same jungle-log face), sweet berry bush (right-click harvest - vanilla keeps the bush), melon and pumpkin (the fruit is broken, the stem survives), and the column crops sugar cane, cactus and bamboo (only the segment ABOVE the base is broken, so the base regrows). Anything else fails with the supported list. Replanting only happens while the matching seed item is in inventory, and planting consumes one seed item where vanilla does (wheat replants wheat seeds; carrots, potatoes, nether wart and cocoa replant themselves; melon, pumpkin, the column crops and the berry bush never need one). Optional {@code bonemeal:true} applies bonemeal from inventory to vanilla-valid growing targets (a BonemealableBlock below its age max - never nether wart or the column crops) between harvest passes.

{@code breed} feeds a pair of nearby animals their breeding food until the requested number of feeds land, which is how a sustainable food supply actually gets built. Both actions report what they did rather than assuming it worked: harvested and replanted counts, drops observed, and the skipped list (unreachable or unreplantable targets with reasons).

The crop seams (maturity ladder, bonemeal validity, harvest kind, the column-crop break cell and the replant-seed table) are pure and package-visible for headless tests. Ticks between feeding two animals, so the pair is fed rather than one animal twice. Ticks the camera may spend acquiring an animal before it is skipped. How far an animal may be and still count as part of this pen. Crop block to the item it yields, for the crops whose drop is not the block's own item. Item to the crop block that grows it, the reverse lookup for "farm me some carrots". Crop block to the inventory item that replants it, for the crops replanted after the break. Carrots, potatoes, nether wart and cocoa replant from the crop item itself (planting consumes one of the yielded items, exactly like vanilla); wheat and beetroots consume their seeds item. Melon, pumpkin, the column crops and the berry bush are absent: the stem, the base and the bush survive the harvest, so there is nothing to put back. Animal type to the items it will breed with. How one crop comes off the plant; per-block class, pure for headless tests. Resolves a crop spec to the block that grows. Accepts the crop block, the item it yields, or a bare name, so "carrots", "carrot" and "minecraft:carrots" all mean the same field. The crop's harvest mechanics by block identity, pure. The item that replants the crop, or null when the plant survives the harvest on its own. The growth stage of a crop state, or -1 when it carries no age ladder. The ladder rule is the AutoFarm module's: any integer property literally named "age" is the growth stage (every vanilla crop ladder uses that name; "stage" belongs to saplings, which no crop carries). The top of the crop's age ladder, or -1 when it has none (melon, pumpkin). Grown-ready, the module's age-ladder verdict: at the top of the ladder. A crop with no age property (melon, pumpkin) has no "not grown" state and always reads mature. Vanilla's isValidBonemealTarget for the crop table: a BonemealableBlock below its age max. Nether wart and the column crops do not implement BonemealableBlock (26.2 jar) and never qualify; melon and pumpkin have no age ladder and are never growing targets either. The column-crop break cell: sugar cane, cactus and bamboo regrow from their base, so the harvest breaks ONLY the segment directly above it (everything higher pops with it). Null when the column is just the base - a lone base segment is the plant itself, never a target. The direction a cocoa pod's FACING points: toward the jungle log it hangs on (canSurvive). Per-tick scan budget: cells visited, plus a hard nano-clock ceiling (AiMine's scanSlice discipline). Vertical half-band scanned around the start position; fields stay well inside it. Ticks with no harvest progress and no workable target before the op gives up (60s). Ticks before a drained field is re-scanned for regrowth around the live position. Standing columns tried for each approach, relative to the work cell (AiCollect's shape). One unit of farm work: a plant to harvest, a cell to replant, a crop to feed, a drop to sweep. Harvest ONE crop with the executor's own hands: scan, walk, break/interact, replant, sweep. cropBlock is what grows; cropItem is what lands in the bag. The public arg contract is the historic one (count, additional, exact, bonemeal, timeoutSeconds); nothing here enables, configures or restores any module. src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiFarmBuil.notes:
game:farm action build (user ruling 2026-10-06: "build me a carrot farm" must just work on the built-in AI). A field that uses the least water that keeps every plot wet: one source per 9x9 (vanilla hydrates 4 blocks each way), under a waterlogged slab so nobody falls in. No fence (user ruling, same day). The engine never lands a jump on farmland. Water comes from an infinite source within 35 s of travel; with none that close the farm digs its own 2x2 infinite pool beside it from two bucketfuls.

Phases: seeds and hoe, the site (flattest open ground near the player), slabs and dirt, buckets, clearing, the foundation (dirt where the ground dips or cannot be tilled), the pool, the water under each slab, then the field tilled and sown on the move ({@link AiFieldWork}: hoe in the main hand, seeds in the offhand), and a verification. One source keeps farmland wet 4 blocks out each way (FarmlandBlock.isNearWater). User ruling 2026-10-06: an infinite source this far in travel time is used; farther, the farm builds its own. Sprinting round what is in the way covers about 4.3 blocks of straight line a second. The most a column may be cut or filled; anything steeper is the wrong place for a field. Seeds gathered when the bag has too few: enough to start, the field fills as it is harvested. Seeds no wild plant drops: only a village's fields (or a rare zombie) have them. The field for a plot count, or exact sides when given. Up to 80 plots one source in the middle of the smallest rectangle (sides 3..9) that holds them; above that whole 9x9 tiles, one source each. The middle of every 9-long stretch on each axis: every cell is within 4 of one. Whether every plot of the layout is within the hydration reach of a source. A source that refills when a bucket takes it (vanilla FlowingFluid.getNewLiquid): two source neighbours on its level and a solid block or another source under it. Rivers, lakes and oceans pass; a lone puddle does not. Travel seconds to a point this far away in a straight line. A ring side and how to walk along and out of it. A cell along the gate side (a from the side's start) and o blocks out from the ring (0 = the ring row). The open cell just outside the gate, where the walk out ends. The two pool cells a bucket goes into: diagonal, so the other two become sources by themselves. The cells around the pool on its level that must hold the water in (the ring row included). Everything the farm owns, ground level and up: never a dirt source, never dug by a route. What one column of the search area looks like from the top: its ground and what stands on it. The cheapest site within the search area: fewest blocks cut and filled, no trees, no lava, nothing a player built, near the player. columns(x, z) reads the precomputed column; null when nowhere fits. The ring side facing the player: the gate is there, so the walk in and out is the short one. The wood the fence, gate and slabs are made of: what the bag holds most of, else the nearest tree's, else oak. The species of a log, wood or planks item id ("minecraft:spruce_log" -> spruce); null for anything else. Where the farm was asked for: the site is chosen around here even after a walk for seeds or wood. The leg running is a material refill for the phase, not the phase's own work: the phase runs again after it. A finished leg moves the phase on; a failed one ends the farm, except where a retry is cheap and safe. Everything above the field's level in the footprint, top down: plants, snow, the bumps of a slope. Dirt where the field's floor does not hold: dips under the field, the ring around it, the floor under each source, and the pool's walls and floor. Only cells that are open now (air, plants, fluid). A dirt cell when this one is open; below the field level only under something that must stand on it. Tills left in every hoe of the bag. Fill one bucket at the nearest reachable source of these: the approach, then the bucket on its source ray. Cells a route may not dig: the field's ground, its ring and the pool. Any slab in the bag (each takes water in), or null. "Missing material: minecraft:dirt" from the builder -> minecraft:dirt; null for any other failure.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiFarmPlan.notes:
game:farm action plant: turns plain ground into a sown field in one call. Nothing else covered it, so a live "build a wheat farm" run spent its whole budget clicking single blocks. Picks tillable ground (grass, dirt, path) nearest a water source so the farmland stays hydrated (water within 4 blocks, at the farmland's level or one above). When the only water is frozen it breaks one ice block to open a source. Per cell it clears the cover (snow layer, grass, flowers), then tills and sows on the move (AiFieldWork: hoe in the main hand, seeds in the offhand, one click a tick). "go to 100 64 -200", "walk 20 blocks north", "run forward 15", "goto home" need no model turn at all: every one is exactly one game:goto call, and a model turn costs seconds to tens of seconds of provider latency per round. When an objective parses here the service performs the goto itself and reports the engine's verdict; anything with more meaning than a destination ("go to the nearest village", "come back when done") falls through to the model.

Tilling, sowing and harvesting on the move. Normal construction holds the hoe in the main hand and seeds in the offhand; nether wart uses soul sand and needs no hoe. Local replants and server-applied automatic replants are reconciled per cell.

The fast harvest of a farmland field (wheat, carrots, potatoes, beetroots): the field's box walked line by line, every ripe crop in reach broken with one click and sown again from the offhand on the next tick, the drops picked up by walking over them. src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiFill.jav.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiFill.jav.notes:
game:fill / game:replace — region block operations on the builder's per-cell machinery.

game:fill fills an axis-aligned box (or a shaped selection of it) with one block: already-correct cells are pre-skipped, materials are preflighted against the remainder (missing map before anything is placed), and the cells run through {@link AiBuilder#build(Blueprint, boolean, int)} bottom-up so supports exist. The shape argument picks the mask: box (solid), shell (all six faces, the hollow alias), walls (the four vertical sides), sphere/hsphere (the inscribed ellipsoid / its surface) and cylinder/hcylinder (a tube along axis x|y|z, default y / its wall). The masks are pure predicates over the box, headless-tested by counts on small radii.

game:replace first digs the matching cells with the excavation rules (verified dig, {@link ToolUpkeep} swap-or-fail with reason {@code TOOL_WORN}, lava-adjacent cells left standing), then places the replacement blueprint the same way. A dig-failed cell simply fails its placement later and is reported in failed[].

game:copy snapshots the live block states of a box (id + every block-state property) into a named clipboard ({@link AiClipboard}); game:paste builds a clipboard back through the same machinery, with the rotation/mirror transform, an optional air pass (air cells dig their live occupants through the replace leg's verified dig instead of being dropped) and the builder's failed[] semantics.

game:region transforms a region without recomputing corners: a box expands/contracts/shifts its corners (vertical movement clamps at the world's buildable span, reported as {@code clamped:true}), with {@code store:"name"} snapshotting the NEW box's live blocks into a clipboard exactly like game:copy; a stored clipboard's cells transform instead - expand EXTRUDES the face slab (the outermost layer's cells replicate outward), contract trims the outer layers, and the transformed clipboard is persisted under the same name. A clipboard's shift is refused: game:paste re-anchors at the minimum corner, so moving where a clipboard lands is the paste origin's job.

Cell geometry (order, shell test, shape masks), the replace matcher and the region transforms are pure seams, headless-tested in AiBuilderTest. Box args in the game:mine_area convention: first corner x,y,z plus second corner OR extents. A cell lies on the shell when it touches any of the box's six faces. Pure. The shape masks, all pure predicates over the box: box (every cell), shell (the six faces), walls (the four vertical sides, top and bottom open), sphere (the ellipsoid inscribed in the box), hsphere (its surface: an in-sphere cell with at least one of its six neighbors outside), cylinder (a tube along axis x|y|z, the inscribed ellipse per cross-section) and hcylinder (its wall: the perimeter of each cross-section, no caps). The ellipsoid inscribed in the box, tested in box-normalized coordinates (half-integer centers handled exactly). The tube along axis: the inscribed ellipse in the two non-axis dimensions, every axis cell included. The tube's wall: a tube cell with at least one in-plane neighbor outside (open tube, no caps). The fill order for a region: bottom layer first (supports exist), nearest-first per layer. Pure. The shaped fill order: bottom layer first (supports exist), nearest-first per layer. Pure. The replace matcher: "any" is any non-air block; a spec matches a registry id exactly or the _family suffix (the AiMine block-matching rule). Pure. game:fill: fill the box (or a shaped selection of it) with one block, bottom-up. game:copy: snapshot the live block states of the box into a named clipboard. Every cell is stored relative to the box's minimum corner with its full block-state property set, air included (air cells only act on paste when air:true). Read-only on the world; the result is the stored cell count. The live snapshot leg shared by game:copy and game:region's store: every cell of the box, relative to its minimum corner, with the block id and full block-state property set. The box must be fully loaded/observed; reaching into unloaded terrain fails naming the count. game:paste: build a named clipboard at an origin (default: the player's feet) through the builder machinery. rotation/mirror transform the cells at load and the result re-anchors at its minimum corner. air:false (default) drops the clipboard's air cells so existing blocks are kept; air:true routes the air cells whose live block is not air through the replace leg's verified dig first, so the clipboard's air really clears. Materials are preflighted with the missing map before anything is placed. A named region direction as a unit step (north -z, up +y); null when unknown. A transformed box plus whether a clamp fired (world height bounds, or contract's minimum extent). The box transform, pure (headless-tested): expand moves the face on the step's side outward, contract pulls it inward (never past the opposite face - a box keeps at least one cell per axis), shift translates the whole box. Vertical movement clamps silently into the world's buildable span [minY, maxY] and is reported through the clamped flag; horizontal movement is unbounded. A transformed clipboard cell set plus whether a clamp fired (contract's minimum extent). The clipboard transform, pure (headless-tested): expand EXTRUDES the face slab on the step's side (the outermost layer's cells replicate outward, amount times), contract drops the outermost layers on that side (always keeping at least one, clamped reported). The result re-anchors at its minimum corner through {@link AiBuilder#normalize}, exactly like the paste load does, so expanding on a negative side moves where the original content lands at paste. Whether the cell sits on the extruded face: the outermost plane on the step's side. Whether the cell sits inside the outer {@code layers} layers on the step's side (contract drops those). src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiFish.jav.notes:
game:fish - run the client's own AutoFish for a bounded window and stop on a real goal.

Fishing is already implemented, tuned and sound-driven in the AutoFish module; reimplementing a bobber watcher here would be a worse copy of it. This is a deliberate exception to the AI's no-module-toggling rule (farm and armour run their own executors): bite detection IS the mod's flagship module, and unlike walking a field or clicking an inventory there is no cheap verified client-side substitute for its sound heuristics. This operation owns only what the module does not: holding a rod, a stop condition the model can state in items, a durability guard so the rod is not fished to death, and restoring the module's previous enabled state on every exit.

Fishing is also the cheapest renewable food in the game and needs no terrain, which makes it the reliable answer to "the guard says we are starving with no food". Ticks with no inventory change before the operation reports that nothing is biting. Remaining durability at which the rod is retired rather than broken. Free inventory slots below which fishing stops, because further catches would be lost. Everything the vanilla fish loot table can yield, for the default "any catch" goal. Progress toward the goal: a named item, or any catch when none was named. Total of every item the fish loot table can produce, for the unnamed-goal case.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiFollow.j.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiFollow.j.notes:
game:follow — tail one observed entity at a fixed distance. The target is an explicit {@code entityId} or the nearest entity matching a {@code type} spec ({@link AiCombat#resolveTypes} semantics: a registry id, a comma-separated list, or "hostiles"). Engine legs are re-issued toward the entity's CURRENT position whenever it moved 3+ blocks from the leg destination or the leg outlives 4s (the AiCombat approach cadence); inside the follow distance the op simply stands and watches.

Following is open-ended: without {@code timeoutSeconds} the op SUCCEEDs once it has held the follow distance continuously for 3s; with one it returns TIMED_OUT reporting the live distance. It FAILs when the target dies, unloads or disappears, reporting the last observed position. Seconds one engine leg runs before the followed position is re-evaluated. Re-issue a leg once the target moved this far from the leg's destination (squared). Open-ended follows succeed after this many continuous ticks inside the follow distance. The tracked entity: the explicit id, else the nearest type match (empty type set = hostiles). A FAILED result carrying a machine-readable code, with the same cleanup as done().

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiForage.j.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiForage.j.notes:
The End kit, picked up on the way: the dragon fight needs beds (the perch one-cycle) or a bow with arrows (the crystals, then the perch), and the speedrun gets them from what it passes - no detour of its own. Asked between the steps of an overworld trip, it returns the most useful short errand in sight, or null: a bed block (a village's), a sheep for wool, then for the bow a spider's string, a skeleton's arrows or a chicken's feathers. Whatever the bag can turn into a bed, a bow or arrows is crafted first.
Beds the one-cycle wants; past this the bow is not foraged for. A bed blast takes about thirty from the perched dragon's two hundred (the End fixture: six beds took it to fifteen), so seven leave little for the sword.
Whether the fight has a plan: enough beds, or a bow with arrows.
The least the dragon fight can be won with: four beds (a perch's one-cycle with the head strikes), or a bow with a dozen arrows for the uncaged crystals. With neither, every fight failed "No ranged weapon or arrows for the remaining uncaged crystals" three times in a second and the End phase ended.
Food items carried under which the animals in sight are hunted on the way (a long walk burns a lot of hunger).
One recipe-confirmed cooking prerequisite or batch; callers re-read safe nutrition after every result.
The next errand within {@code range}, or null when there is none worth it.
Water sources nearer than this many blocks are worth the detour for the bucket.
One more water bucket filled from the nearest surface source within range, while fewer than {@code want} are held.
One kill of the nearest {@code type}, then its drops picked up (the spec names what matters; all drops near are taken).
A pearl hunt from safe ground: the enderman is looked in the eye until it turns on the player (its synced creepy flag), then met where the player stands (a hold: never chased). Off safe ground for half a second ends it. Walked to, the hunts in a warped forest were called off "where a knock would not land" one after the other, and a fixture went home with none; in the overworld's caves the old hunt lost the enderman ("no matching live target") before it came near.
Ground within six under every column within three of the spot, and no lava: a knock there lands on ground, not over a ledge or in a lava sea.
Feet in a hole: solid on all four sides at the feet's level and under them, no lava round it. A knock cannot move the body there (the walls stop it across, and a lift of half a block keeps it under the rim), so the hole is safe ground whatever drops lie round it.
Where a one-deep fighting hole can be dug under the feet: the block under them breaks to a cell with solid sides and a floor, and no lava or water round it.
A pearl from the nearest enderman: provoked from safe ground when one is in sight (it comes to the player), else the plain hunt that walks to it.
The provoke only (stare from safe ground, then hold); null with no enderman in sight or no safe ground underfoot.
Footing a provoke may hold on (the player stands still, an enderman's knock is under half a block): ground within four under the feet and each of the eight cells round them, and no lava within eight under any of them. The safe arena's three blocks round and six down held almost nowhere in a warped forest, so nearly every hunt walked after its enderman.
