src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGameOper.notes:
Puts a carried block down on free ground beside the player, through the crafting's own spot finder. Asked to "put it next to me", the model guessed support coordinates twice and both walks failed "no route".
Immediate terminal result carrying a machine-readable failure code.
Humanized aim step toward a world point, for the ops that own a whole operation's camera. Callers hold one {@link autismclient.ai.engine.AiAim} and step it once per tick; the ray check that gates the actual click comes from {@code AiAim.rayBlock}, never from the goal.
One-tick aim, kept ONLY for the reflex clutches (MLG water/cobweb, fireball dodge) where the look and the click are the same tick by necessity - a multi-tick sweep there would simply miss the window and the player would take the fall. Everything that has more than one tick uses {@link #look(autismclient.ai.engine.AiAim, Vec3)} instead.
One OUTLINE ray from the eye to a point, or null on a miss.
Ticks a sweep may spend reaching a target before the target counts as unreachable.
The newest server system/action-bar message recorded after the given revision, or null.
Click actions parse case-insensitively; anything else fails naming every valid action.
game:harvest_wheat keeps its wheat-shaped contract; the generic path supplies its own crop.
Harvesting for ONE crop through the AI's own executor (AiFarm.harvest): the engine walks, the verified block adapter breaks/interacts/places, replanting and drop sweeps are the op's own. Nothing here enables, configures or restores the AutoFarm module - the module stays a user-facing feature, and a user's own enabled copy is paused by the operation dispatcher like any conflicting module. cropBlock is what grows; cropItem is what lands in the bag. bonemeal:true feeds vanilla-valid growing targets between harvest passes.
Internal seam on an interaction op: true once its click has actually been sent and only the observed-outcome confirmation (the stable-tick window behind an applied server revision) remains. Lets a caller overlap that confirmation with its next unit of work instead of idling.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGameplay.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGameplay.notes:
Tick-driven gameplay adapters. Dispatches are never treated as proof of inventory or server effects.
game:collect_drops: every matching item on the ground is a goal of the shared gather process, so a drop in a pocket, behind a block or up on a ledge is dug or climbed to instead of given up after one failed walk; the vanilla pickup box (not the item's exact cell) is the arrival.
One bounded tidy admission; unknown clicks are retained and never retried as a capacity failure.
The registry ids a pickup spec stands for: itself when it names an item, else every item of its family.
Ticks a predicted container click must stand before it counts as accepted: a server that refuses one corrects it within a round trip, so one and a half round trips (the server's own latency reading) and two ticks, at least three and at most ten.
Collect resumes committed heat and valid loaded fuel; bag stock matters only after an observed dry slot.
The committed fuel ran out of the bag: another held fuel takes over instead of the whole smelt failing.
Smelting uses an already-open furnace and observes each transfer before proceeding.
Load and leave: done once the input is in and it burns (the ladder smelts in the background).
The fuel was picked automatically, not requested: another held fuel may take over when it runs out.
A held fuel for what is left of the job: the committed kind first, else any other.
The confirmation half of a dispatched click: an eject lands empty, a load lands non-empty, output lands in the bag.
game:find: one read-only search for a block over OBSERVED terrain (a cell- and time-budgeted live scan of loaded chunks) plus REMEMBERED terrain (the per-world chunk memory's notable table), merged nearest-first with per-result cache provenance. Nothing is mutated.
The survey's block ids as Block objects (ids resolved once, not per cell); unknown ids fail naming them.
Bounded discovery of requested block identities in loaded terrain, spread across ticks.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGameStat.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGameStat.notes:
{@code value} to 1/{@code scale}.
Whole-inventory counts (armor and offhand included) keyed by the server-evidence inventory revision. count() runs several times per op tick (AiCollect progress, AiObtain verification, AiInventoryController.end, AiMine deltas) and every call re-walked all slots re-stringifying every item id; one rebuild per server-applied inventory change now serves any number of item ids from a single map. The revision only moves when the server applies an update (AiServerEvidence: predicted local mutations do not advance it), so a mismatch means the bag changed; the player identity covers the respawn window before the first sync packet lands. Client-thread only, like AiServerEvidence itself.
Count across the 36 main+hotbar slots only. Station menus (smithing, anvil, brewing, furnace) can only move items from those slots, so their availability checks must not credit armor or the offhand - an item that is worn or held off-hand cannot be loaded into a station.
Time-of-day band in the vanilla 24000-tick day: AiSleep's 12542-23460 night, sunset and sunrise as transition bands around it, day otherwise. Pure.
Compact effect line: "minecraft:speed II (0:12)" - id, amplifier+1 (roman), remaining m:ss.
Remaining effect duration as m:ss; infinite effects report "inf".
Small roman numerals for effect levels (I..X); larger levels fall back to the plain int.
Compact evidence variant: verification-relevant state stays, bulky ambient arrays become counts.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGatherFi.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGatherFi.notes:
The gathering gauntlet (-Dautism.ai.gather=true, isolated qualification instance only), the parkour gauntlet's twin for the jobs: felling a small forest, the first wooden and stone pickaxes from an empty bag, iron buried fifteen blocks down, drops in a pocket and behind a wall, and ore under sand. Each lane is built on a cleared island in the sky and run through the real operations; the harness measures what a player notices: wall time, logs per minute, trees left half-felled for another one, idle ticks, drops left lying and the time to each tool. The report lands in gather-fixtures.json, one "[AI gather]" line per lane; tools/gather_test.py runs it and prints the table.
One fixed sky island, rebuilt for every lane so prior runs cannot enter the source search.
Forest lane: every log cell's tree, the tree last cut from, and cuts that left a tree for another one.
Shooter lanes: the lowest health, ticks a skeleton that has the player as its target sees it, the longest such run.
One job: what to build around the island origin, what to hand the player, what to run and what passing means.
Shooter bookkeeping: health, and every tick a skeleton holding the player as its target can see the player's eye.
No skeleton left alive on the lane's island (the real world's cave skeletons far below do not count).
A job under the survival guard, the way the tech tree runs one: the guard's op runs to its end first, then the job starts over (a fresh instance, as the ladder restarts an interrupted step).
A wall two high round the island's edge: knockback in a fight threw mobs and the player off it into the void (a fence there wedged the player in its cell after a knockback, which the planner read as stuck in solid blocks).
A persistent creeper, at normal difficulty.
A persistent zombie with a helmet (the sky islands are in the sun), at normal difficulty.
A persistent skeleton with a bow and a helmet (so the sun does not burn it), at normal difficulty.
{@code pinned}: no walking (it still turns, draws and shoots), so the unreachable one stays unreachable.
Forest bookkeeping: a log gone from tree B while tree A (the one being cut) still stands counts a switch.
Submit the actual user's wording through the local assistant and its supervisors.
Carrots in the bag when the last assistant request went out (a farm sows exactly these).
Real recipes, server transfers and normal 200-tick cooking, with no provider involved.
Real held mining, exact harvesting tools, early target choices and the rendered task lifecycle.
Set only the initial real camera; all subsequent turns come from the production mining hand.
Every item lying on or around the island, whatever its age: drops of an earlier run load with their chunk after the island is rebuilt, and a farm lane counts the carrots it sowed (a stray carrot picked up would read as a trample).
The farm on the island: 80 farmland plots (nothing trampled back to dirt), exactly the carrots the bag held planted (a trampled crop drops its carrot and gets sown again: more crops than carrots means a trample), one waterlogged slab over the source, no fence (user ruling), and (with pool) a 2x2 of still water beside it.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGhastRef.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGhastRef.notes:
Moves to a common attack/return ray; a reflected fireball follows the look, never its shooter.
Null yields immediately to the ordinary emergency shield/dodge. No unreachable swing loop.
A defensive bat cannot silently turn into a shot at a different living entity along an older facing.
Aim through the pick box, preferring an upward exit; never knowingly detonate a bat against nearby terrain.
Legal defensive directions do not depend on knowing or hitting a shooter. Physical range is checked separately.
Search return direction AND attack ray together, using the ghast's box instead of insisting on its centre.
Solve the reflected speed curve against a moving target centre, then verify swept box intersection.
Re-prove the trajectory of the facing already published to the server, before dispatching an attack.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGoal.jav.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGoal.jav.notes:
The run's general goal for the status banner and the assistant's activity row: "Getting blaze rods", "Finding a fortress", "Getting iron" - never the step under way ("Breaking Nether Gold Ore", "Closing on the blaze (8m)"), which changed several times a second. Controllers publish every tick at a depth (the speedrun 0, its stage or tool ladder 1). The banner's title is the shallowest objective, its activity the deepest goal, and a different goal is shown only once it has held {@link #HOLD_NANOS}: a dodge, a short guard fight or one leg of a walk never flips it. The detailed messages still go to the logs, the trace and the live-task pulse.
A publication older than this is gone (its owner stopped ticking).
How long a new goal must hold before it replaces the one shown.
Publish (every tick) a goal for {@code owner}; a blank goal keeps the owner's last one.
The goal shown now (objective as title, goal as activity, a short counter as detail), or EMPTY.
The assistant's activity row: the goal with its counter while one is shown, else {@code fallback}.
Pure, for tests: the text shown, switched only once a different one has held {@code hold}.
The speedrun phase's goal.
The tool ladder's goal for one of its step keys ("ore:minecraft:raw_iron" -> "Getting iron"), or "" to keep the last.
"minecraft:raw_iron" -> "iron", "minecraft:diamond" -> "diamonds", "minecraft:cobblestone" -> "stone".
The Nether expedition's goal for its leg label, else its step's; "" keeps the last (gear fixes, short errands).

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGuard.ja.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGuard.ja.notes:
Staying alive while doing something else.

A job-level operation runs for minutes. Over that span a bot will starve, get shot in the back and fill its inventory, and none of those need a model round trip to fix - they need a reaction this tick. The long composites consult this guard before each tick of their own work: it returns an operation to run FIRST, or null when everything is fine.

The escalation order is the one that actually keeps a player alive: fight what is hitting you, run when you cannot win, eat before you starve. Anything genuinely strategic - no food at all, no weapon, a hazard with no escape - is deliberately NOT handled here. Those return null with a {@link #concern} the caller reports, so the decision stays with the model.

Every decision is pure given a {@link Vitals} snapshot, so the whole policy is unit tested; only the snapshot and the operation construction touch the live client. Health at or below which the guard fights back instead of working through the damage. Health at or below which the guard stops fighting and runs. Food at or below which the guard eats; below 7 the player also stops regenerating and sprinting. Food level the guard eats up to once it starts. Hostiles this close count as engaged rather than ambient. Ticks after taking a hit that the player still counts as under attack. An angered enderman counts this much further out: it closes distance by teleporting. An angry enderman counts only this close (the old 24 stays with the legacy controller): it teleports to the player by itself, and one counted at 24 blocks started fights that chased it across the End while the dragon flew. Last client tick hurtTime was observed nonzero; hurtTime alone decays in ~10 ticks. A ranged attacker (skeleton, pillager, witch...) shooting from this far counts as engaged while the player takes hits. Ranged attackers the last {@link #vitals} counted beyond the melee radius (the fight then reaches that far). Every hostile counted by the last vitals() is a zombie of some kind (no bow, no climber, no creeper). Every hostile but the shooters counted by the last vitals() is a zombie, and there is one at least. The melee mobs counted include one diamond armour does not make safe on the ground (a brute, a hoglin...). A ground walker that cannot climb a one-wide pillar and whose attack box ends below a player standing three up: the perch's mobs. Zombies (zombified piglins, husks, drowned), piglins without a crossbow, brutes, hoglins, zoglins and wither skeletons (2.4 tall). A melee mob whose hits diamond armour does not make small: brutes, hoglins, zoglins, wither skeletons. A creeper in sight within ten blocks at the last vitals(), and how far the nearest one was. When the guard last avoided a creeper (flee or hide), the last minute's: three make it a fight. Closer than this a creeper is run from, never dug from: a shaft takes seconds, and it walked up to one being dug. A skeleton among the hostiles counted by the last vitals(). What the last vitals() counted, by kind (for the guard's log line). Until when a job's own guard is running (see {@link #selfGuarding}). When the last guard fight ended without winning; the guard runs instead for a while. A job that runs this guard itself says so every tick: the host's threat supervisor then leaves it alone. Its interrupt cancelled the tech tree mid-step (losing the furnace running in the background), and three of them in a minute paused the whole task with a skeleton still shooting - the player stood still until it died. When a guard flee last found nowhere to go; the guard hides in the ground instead for a while. The last guard op handed out was a hideout. The guard op just ended without success: a hideout is not tried again for a while. Four or more blocks of the world over the player's head: a cave or a mine, where running only finds walls. A guard fight ended without winning (the target out of reach): the next threats are run from, not fought, for a while. The nearest shooter the last vitals() counted, and whether a straight charge reaches it. When a cover op last found no cover; the older hide and flee answers run for a while. The last guard op handed out was cover from a shooter. The returned operation really is an escape, including a fight decision escalated to flee. When the guard took cover from each shooter (entity id), for the hunt after the second time. Across this, a charge at a shooter takes more arrows than cover does. A shooter worth charging: close, on the player's level, not one the last fight found no route to, and a straight walkable line to it (open feet and head, a floor, no fluid, steps of one). Anything else is hidden from: a chase that dug through the rock toward a skeleton nine blocks away stood in its sight for forty seconds. What the guard may do. Callers narrow it; a gathering job wants all of it. tidy throws junk out of a full bag (never tools, food, valuables or the ids in keep, which is what the job itself is collecting). No running: where a flee cannot get away (the End's endermen teleport after the runner and killed it). No fighting: for jobs where swinging at something would ruin the work in progress. The items the job is gathering: a tidy never throws them away. Everything the policy decides from, snapshotted so the decision itself stays pure. {@code worstToolUses} is the remaining durability of the most worn tool in the hotbar, or {@link Integer#MAX_VALUE} when nothing there is damageable. Convenience for callers and tests that do not care about tool wear. Remaining uses at which a tool is worth replacing before it breaks in the middle of a job. What the guard decided to do this tick. A decision plus the human-readable reason, which the caller surfaces in its progress. The policy, as pure logic. Order matters and is the point: something actively hitting the player outranks hunger, and running outranks fighting once health is low enough that losing the fight is likely. Too many to fight: three

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGuardLay.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiGuardLay.notes:
The survival guard as a layer any multi-step job puts in front of its legs (the ladder's own guard handling, shared): every tick it asks AiGuard whether to fight, flee, eat or hide; an action it starts runs to completion and the interrupted leg is cancelled, so the job restarts it from the observed state. Used by the speedrun's stages, whose travels and waits have no guard of their own (a fortress walk met blazes and ghasts unanswered).
A water-bucket douse for a burning body with no fire block to punch (a bed blast ignites the player).
When a step out of a fire last failed: the fire is punched out for a while instead.
The body's last ten positions, for its motion.
Whether a guard action owns the controls now.
Ticks the guard. Returns a running result when the guard owns this tick (the caller returns it), else null. A guard that steps in cancels the running leg through {@code cancelLeg} - only when that leg can be interrupted.
Preserve the failing survival action instead of describing every uncertain result as an emergency.
Capture pending effects before cleanup; a deadline or achieved kill count cannot acknowledge them.
The answer to lava, air and fire alone, the layer's own order, for jobs whose guard only knows mobs (the kit ladder, the Nether entry); null when none of them applies. A walk to a lava pool touched the lava, and the player burnt ten seconds holding a water bucket.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiHazardEs.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiHazardEs.notes: Bounded native survival reflex, also available while the assistant is between productive operations.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiHistory..documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiHistory..notes:
Wire-history rules shared by transcript replay and compaction. Replay (a new epoch under a new system prompt) strips Anthropic thinking blocks, whose signatures bind the old prompt, and repairs tool rounds a pause or a crash left open, so every call has a result and no result is orphaned. Other providers' reasoning fields stay untouched.
Copy of an Anthropic assistant message without thinking/redacted_thinking blocks (the same instance when there are none).
A stored transcript made safe to send under a new system prompt: deep copies, thinking stripped (Anthropic), tool rounds repaired.
One tool call in an assistant message: wire id (Gemini: position), tool name, and a digest label.
Every assistant tool call gets a result right after it; results without a matching call are removed.
Anthropic rejects empty text blocks; a stream can leave one behind.
Outcome of a keep-tail cut: the kept tail (starts with an assistant message, or is empty), the dropped head, and its digest.
Keep-tail compaction: keeps the newest complete rounds (an assistant message plus everything up to the next one) whose characters fit keepChars, so a tool call is never separated from its results and the tail starts with an assistant message. When not even the last round fits, it is kept anyway if it fits hardChars, otherwise everything is dropped. Anthropic thinking is stripped from every kept message. The digest of an earlier compaction note among the dropped messages is carried over. Null when nothing can be dropped.
keepLastThinking: budget-thinking Claude models (3.7-4.5) need the thinking block of the assistant turn whose tool results continue the conversation, and they do not bind blocks to the prefix, so that one block stays.
Digest of the newest earlier compaction note among the dropped messages, so a second cut does not lose it.
The first text of a user message: string content, the first text block, or the first text part.
Host digest of dropped rounds: round and call counts, then each tool (perform by capability id) with its result statuses.
The single plain user message that replaces the dropped rounds.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiHopperCl.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiHopperCl.notes: Source-derived recognition of the finite existing-lever startup recipe, independent of file names.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiHttp.jav.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiHttp.jav.notes:
Bounded response subscriber: cancellation and response-size limits apply while the body is arriving.
Shared by model discovery and inference; credentials never appear in URLs or diagnostics.
Claude Code / Claude app sign-in tokens are subscription credentials that Anthropic only honours inside its own apps.
Accept a base URL or a pasted API resource URL; never redirect credentials to a different host.
Redact before truncation, including a provider echo of a nonstandard credential.
Provider text that means the account is out of quota (OpenAI insufficient_quota, DashScope arrearage, Gemini free tier).
Anthropic-style "credit balance is too low" (400 or 402): the key lists models but cannot call the API.
One line per failure, the way a key checker reports it: the provider's own text (credential redacted) plus what the status means for THIS provider - invalid key, authenticated but no access, out of credit, rate limited, model not served - so the user never has to decode a raw 4xx.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiIntents..documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiIntents..notes:
The host's front desk (AiSettings.hostIntents): reads a request the way a person would and does the plain steps itself before any model turn. "get 16 oak wood and build a house" becomes game:obtain oak_log x16 run right away, and only "build a house" goes to the model, told the wood is already in the bag. Deliberately strict: a clause is claimed only when EVERY word of it is understood and its item or target resolves; the first clause it cannot read ends the prefix, and that clause with everything after it goes to the model in the user's own words. Pure apart from the injected lookups, so it is tested headless.
One host step: the clause it came from, the capability call, a line for the transcript, and what to ask first.
A detail the request left open ("build me a farm": which crop, how big); the answer fills argument key.
Steps the host runs, then what is left for the model (blank when nothing is).
World lookups the parser needs; injected so tests run without a game.
A wish for an item is a request for it: "i want a diamond pickaxe", "give me ...", "gimme ...", "can i get ..." read as "get ...". Not "i want you to ..." or "i need to ...", which the lead words strip before their own verb.
A question that is a polite request ("can you get me a diamond pickaxe?"), not one for the model.
An amount followed by whitespace (so "acacia" never reads as "a" + "cacia"); groups 1..4, see amount().
Amounts a person gives without a number: the host picks the default for the item.
Bulk materials where "get wood" means a working amount, not one.
An item named alone, with an amount at most (same groups as a verb pattern).
Words that only end the previous step ("... and stop", "then wait there"): nothing to do.
The whole game: "beat the game", "speedrun", "kill the ender dragon".
"fill it with water", "fill a bucket", "get some water": a water bucket.
"put it next to me", "place the furnace here", "set a chest down": a carried block put down beside the player.
"cook the meat", "cook it": whatever raw food the bag holds by then, all of it (counted when the step runs).
The meat a food animal drops, for "kill a cow and cook the meat": the kill is a hunt that picks the meat up.
Splits the request and claims the leading clauses it fully understands. Never throws.
"make a furnace and put it next to me": "it" is the step before's item.
A smelt with no amount of its own makes what the step before it fetched: "get 10 sand and make glass" is ten glass. The bulk default made sixteen and dug six more sand for them.
Whether the clause names an amount (a number, or a number word).
A kill of food animals that a later step cooks or eats becomes a hunt for their meat (game:obtain: the fight, then the drops picked up). A bare fight left the beef on the ground, and the cooking step hunted another cow for its input.
File names retain case and spaces; contents are never interpreted as objectives.
One clause to one host step, or null when any part of it is not understood.
The item words with the fillers a person adds ("of", "some", "from nearby trees"), and wood named as logs.
A spec game:obtain takes: a family ("log") or one exact id; null when nothing resolves.
The single item id the words name, or null (unknown, or a family with several members).
The one vanilla item id within a typo of the words ("dimond pikaxe" is the diamond pickaxe): one edit for a name of five letters or more, two from ten, and never when two ids are that near. Null otherwise.
Levenshtein distance, cut off above {@code cap} (returns cap + 1 there).

Each value is a list of specs resolved recursively, so an alias can be a tag, a list of exact ids, or another alias. Tags carry datapack content; the explicit lists exist only where no vanilla tag groups what a player would actually mean by the word. Specs handled by a live predicate instead of a fixed id list. Resolve memo. src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiMlg.java.notes:
The human no-fall clutch (game:mlg): saves a damaging fall with legit inputs only. Packet no-fall is a detectable cheat and is never used here - the op does what a skilled player does: place water at the landing point in the last ticks before impact (MLG water bucket), place a cobweb there (the web catches at any depth), or steer with vanilla air control onto a soft landing block (hay/slime/honey/bed/powder snow) next to the natural landing cell.

Method selection. {@code method} = water|cobweb|auto (default auto). Auto prefers a water bucket from the hotbar, then a cobweb, then a redirect to a soft block within {@link #REDIRECT_RADIUS} blocks of the natural landing cell, else fails "No clutch item in hotbar". An explicit method requires its item and fails naming it. In ultrawarm dimensions water evaporates on placement, so auto skips the bucket and an explicit water request fails with the dimension reason.

Fall forecast. Replicated from AiDanger's simplified FallingPlayerSim - same vanilla drag/gravity constants (AutoTotemModule:116-119 via {@link AiDanger#HORIZONTAL_AIR_DRAG}/ {@link AiDanger#VERTICAL_AIR_DRAG}), the same {@code freeFallMotionY} tick, the same swept {@code level.findSupportingBlock} collision test and 20-tick horizon - reusing AiDanger's package-visible pure pieces so the two never drift; only the private sweep loop is replicated. The forecast recomputes EVERY tick because the player (or knockback) can steer. Predicted damage is raw vanilla {@code calculateFallDamage} at the landing block's multiplier (AiDanger.landingMultiplier table: water/cobweb/powder snow 0, hay/honey 0.2, slime 0 unless sneaking, beds 0.5) - pre-mitigation, an overestimate, i.e. safe. game:danger's mitigated figure stays the authority for how much the fall would hurt; this op owns saving it.

Placement. Cobweb goes through {@link AutismFaceScan#best} exactly like AiTelly (proven support/face/hit, instant rotation from the candidate's emitted rotation, one vanilla {@code useItemOn}); on no candidate it falls back to a synthetic top-face hit - late is better than never, vanilla decides. A water bucket is NOT a BlockItem, so it cannot use the face-scan placement predicate: it is aimed at the support's top face and emptied with {@code gameMode.useItem}, whose own POV raycast places the source exactly like a human's right-click. Placement fires when the forecast says landing is within the method's window (water {@value #WATER_WINDOW_TICKS} ticks - earlier spreads water and can fail in 1-deep holes, widened by half the measured connection RTT so the server-side placement still lands in time; cobweb {@value #COBWEB_WINDOW_TICKS} - the web catches at any depth) and re-fires every tick until the block is observed client-side. The verified block adapter (AiGameOperations.block, server block-revision) is deliberately NOT used: the landing arrives within the window, long before any revision round-trip. A descent that crosses below the void floor has no landing at all, so the op fails fast instead of riding the fall to the timeout.

Terminal. Landing in water/web/soft block with at most 0.5 fall damage applied (the health delta measured across {@value #SETTLE_TICKS} settle ticks after touchdown) SUCCEEDs with {method, landing, damageBefore (predicted), damageAfter (actual)}. A natural soft landing (multiplier ≤ 0.2) or a predicted-harmless fall SUCCEEDs immediately without placing. Landing with no placement placed FAILs "Clutch missed". With collect (default true) a landed water clutch re-collects the source with the emptied bucket (≤3 attempts), surfacing first when submerged on low air ({@link #collectSafe}) and reporting unableToCollectSafely instead of ever leaving the player drowning. timeoutSeconds (default 10, clamp 1..30) bounds the whole op; cancel releases movement keys (engine release discipline) and restores the hotbar slot. Health ≤ 4 does NOT abort - this op IS the save.

Everything that does not need a live Level is a pure static seam (method selection, window predicate, multiplier/soft-landing reuse, redirect choice, collect safety, hotbar lookup) and is headless-tested in AiMlgTest. Client seams never throw past the op boundary; all client thread. One fall forecast: the support block found by the sweep, its registry id, the vanilla landing multiplier, the predicted raw fall damage, ticks until touchdown (-1 when no support lies inside the horizon; damage is then a lower bound at multiplier 1.0), and whether the descent crosses below the void floor - a fall with no landing at all. Placement windows in ticks before touchdown: water late so it cannot spread away, cobweb earlier because the web catches at any depth. Horizontal reach of vanilla air control over the window; a soft block beyond it cannot be steered to. Minimum air supply (300 max, drowning at 0) for collecting while submerged; below it the op surfaces first. Post-touchdown ticks the applied damage is measured over (server health arrives a tick late). Ticks the op waits for a fall to actually begin when called pre-emptively on solid ground. Ticks spent swimming up before giving up on a safe collection. Fall damage at or below this counts as a saved landing (half a heart is vanilla's smallest unit). Soft blocks landed IN (feet cell is the block itself); all others are landed ON (feet above). The method for the requested mode and hotbar contents (registry id paths, "air" for empty slots). Auto: water bucket beats cobweb beats redirect; a redirect is only possible when the caller already found a soft landing block. Null = nothing can save the fall. First hotbar slot (0..8) holding the item, -1 when absent. Ticks before touchdown at which the method may place; redirect never places (0). {@link #windowTicks(String)} widened for the measured connection latency. src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiNetherEn.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiNetherEn.notes:
game:nether_entry - THE overworld phase of a speedrun as ONE tool call: from a fresh survival spawn to standing in the Nether with zero model rounds in between. The tools do the work; the model only decides to call it. Existing verified ops run as nested legs behind seven phases, each SKIPPED when its outputs already exist:

VILLAGE-FIRST: when a village is planned (villageX/villageZ args, else the nearest game:oracle structure:village prediction within {@link #VILLAGE_RANGE} blocks), the VILLAGE phase runs BEFORE the opening - the speedrunner's route, because the opening's wood/tool chains then execute in the village's friendly biome (trees, animals, flat ground) instead of the spawn's. The overland trip rides the engine at up to {@link #VILLAGE_LEG}s; an unreachable village is recorded and the run falls back to spawn order (villageDone, never looped). At the village: game:container loot the chests, break the hay bales, take up to beds (default 2) beds with the verified break op; skipped cleanly when nothing is predicted nearby or beds are already held. OPENING then locates the nearest log within 96 blocks (game:find), travels to it when it is out of the local scan, then fells with game:chop at radius 64 - the real need is 3 logs (table, wooden pick, sticks), padded to 5, and 4 lets the run continue on sparse spawns. Then game:obtain wooden_pickaxe and stone_pickaxe (obtain plans the whole chain incl. the crafting table), plus a stone axe/sword only when the cobble is already in the bag. FOOD runs only when the food level is low or fewer than {@link #FOOD_ITEMS_MIN} food items are carried: one bounded game:obtain food hunt, never a farm detour, and a failed hunt does not fail the run. IRON_FIRE obtains minIron (default 4) iron_ingot through the prospect/smelting chain, obtains flint from gravel, and crafts the bucket and flint_and_steel - its legs ride the deep {@link #IRON_LEG}s budget (uncapped). LAVA asks game:oracle for observed lava, falling back to travelling toward a structure:ruined_portal prediction, then goes there. PORTAL runs game:portal_cast: its preflight missing{} is answered entry by entry (water/lava bucket fills, dirt via game:collect, anything else via game:obtain) and the cast re-issued, at most {@link #MAX_PORTAL_ATTEMPTS} attempts. ENTER is game:dimension action enter the_nether; SUCCEED reports {phases, inventory, netherPosition} and emits the nether_entered split.

Between phases and between nested legs the survival guard (eat/fight/flee) runs exactly like AiObtain's: a guard action completes before the work resumes and the interrupted leg restarts from scratch - every leg used here is restartable by construction (obtain rechecks counts, chop rescans, portal_cast skips finished cells). One interpretation on top: a guard EAT that cannot act (nothing edible in inventory, or a container/screen the eat op refuses) is INFORMATION, not an action - it never cancels the running leg (finishing the loot/gather is how the bot gets the food); the concern rides the survival report as suppressedEat instead. At the dusk window the RUNNING leg is cancelled the same way and the night action runs to dawn: game:sleep with a carried bed (which also sets the respawn point), game:burrow without one. A failed night action retries after a short cooldown (the guard owns the gap) instead of giving up, so the bot never grinds through the night unprotected; a successful night never fires twice the same night. Every nested leg is capped at min(configured budget, LEG_HARD_CAP) - the uncapped set rides legCapUncapped instead: iron_fire's obtains/crafts (deep badlands prospecting), the village overland travel, portal_cast's re-issue loop, the night legs (dawn-bounded) and the final dimension enter. Health <= 4 aborts FAILED LOW_HEALTH like the neighbors; legs the dispatch funnel would mark recovery-allowed (game:sleep) get the same lowHealthRecovery wrap here, so the exception machinery covers them.

Restartability is the design's spine: every phase's completion predicate reads LIVE inventory or world state (tools in the bag, beds held, iron and lighter present, lava within cast range, a lit portal within enter range), so re-issuing the op after a death or interruption resumes from what exists instead of redoing finished work. And a phase FAILURE no longer ends the run on its own: the op retries it internally (attempts reported as {attempts:N}) when the cause is transient - timeouts, unreachable targets, interruptions - with escalation instead of blind repetition: the opening pages the next located wood sites, obtain legs get a 1.5x budget on the final attempt, the food hunt fires once more, lava rescans after travelling. Permanent preconditions (missing materials) still bubble to the model immediately with the missing map. Failure is honest: FAILED carries {phase, reason, missing{}} when a phase exhausts its alternatives, and no failing leg is ever looped - the optional phases (food, village) record their failure and the run continues, the rest end it. Every phase report carries the nested legs' terminal accounts verbatim (id, status, message and parsed result data - obtain's attempts, craft's missing map, chop's skipped blocks) under legs[], so a failure is diagnosable from the outside rather than flattened to one string. src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiObtain.j.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiObtain.j.notes:
game:obtain - "get me N of X", whatever that takes. This is the composite the whole tool layer exists to make possible: the model states a goal in items, and the executor picks and runs the route - already in the bag, craft it, smelt it, mine it, chop it, pick it up, or go kill the thing that drops it - recursing into whatever the chosen route is missing.

Strategies are tried in ascending real cost (inventory, craft, smelt, gather, mine, prospect, hunt) and each one that fails is recorded and not retried, so the operation always terminates with either the items or a precise account of which routes were tried and why each failed. Every leg is an existing verified operation; this class owns only the choice between them and the recursion.

Recursion is bounded by depth and by a visited set, so obtaining iron cannot end up obtaining iron. When the chain bottoms out the model gets the exact base material that is unobtainable, which is a decision it can act on rather than a dead end. Dependency recursion depth. Iron pickaxe -> sticks -> planks -> logs is three. Extra passes a strategy gets when its leg ended short but brought the count up (each pass must gain again): a big quantity wears out pickaxe after pickaxe, and the second worn tool used to spend MINE/GATHER for good. Default search radius handed to the gathering legs. Acquisition routes in ascending real cost. TOOL comes first because it is a PRECONDITION, not an alternative: mining an ore the player has no tier for destroys the block and yields nothing, so the pickaxe is obtained before the trip rather than after the wasted one. MINE is the buried-commons route: a short staircase down plus game:mine's tunnelling, far cheaper than PROSPECT's seed prediction, which stays last of the gathering routes because it is only worth it when the resource is not lying around already. A hunt walks to its animal first when the nearest one is past the fight's own reach. The live target: the original spec until a family fallback swaps in the family. The target count when the running leg started, and the extra passes each strategy has had for its progress. Runs the survival guard. Returns a RUNNING result while a guard action is in flight, or null when the objective may proceed. The current leg is cancelled, not suspended - cancelling releases its keys, which a suspended travel leg would not do, so it would keep walking while the guard is trying to eat. A fresh leg starts after the guard. The cheapest strategy not yet spent that could plausibly work right now. The tool that must exist before any source block for this target can be harvested, or null when the player inventory already covers them. Only reported once: a tool already being obtained higher in the chain is in the visiting set. Starts the leg for a strategy, or null when it turns out not to apply after all. The hunt, after a search when no source animal is loaded. Wood for a sword without a trip: logs or planks held, or a tree within 32 blocks. The fight (walked to first when the nearest mob is far) and the pickup of its drops. The fight, after a wooden sword when there is none and wood is at hand where the animals are. Punched, a sheep runs at sprint speed after every one-point hit: eight punches and a chase each, two minutes for a bed's wool. A wooden sword kills in two, from the tree the bed's planks need anyway. The first still-missing base material this chain has not already tried to obtain. A hunt is only half the route: the kills leave the items on the ground. After the fight leg, one collect-drops leg per matched variant (the game:collect_drops machinery) turns the kill count into inventory - hunt-only items like ender pearls have no source blocks, so without this leg the HUNT strategy could never deliver. The nearest live mob of the types within range in the loaded world, or null. A craft that died only for the 3x3 grid recurses into the table it named (2x2-craftable, no station) and then retries the same craft once. null when the detour does not apply: not a CRAFT leg, the detour already taken, depth-capped, the table already being obtained upstream, or the failure named no table. The retry needs no bookkeeping of its own: CRAFT is only marked spent when a leg fails WITHOUT the detour firing. The bulk-buried source block this target can be dug out through, or null. The buried-commons leg: staircase down ADAPTIVELY - one bounded step at a time, re-probing the scan band from the live position after every landing and stopping as soon as the source is in range (the old fixed single descent stranded the band over deep badlands terracotta) - then game:mine tunnels to the source and extracts it to count. Each step gets a bounded slice of the remaining time, the extraction gets everything that remains, and a step that keeps failing cedes to whatever the band holds from here. A source still out of band at the depth cap fails with the depth reached. Travel carries the engine's dig-safety rules; tool death is AiMine's own ToolUpkeep (backpack swap, hands only for hand-droppable blocks, else TOOL_WORN + missing{pickaxe:1}), which the obtain ladder re-tools and retries once. One gather job for the whole target family (engine AiBlockMine): every harvestable source block and every target item on the ground in one goal, finished by the count in the bag. Any log, not the one variant a scan guessed was nearest; null when no source can be harvested. The source block inside the vertical scan band around the live position (AiTerrain's 24-block cap mirrors AiMine's SCAN_VERTICAL_BAND). Target variants that some loaded recipe can produce. Which items HAVE a recipe never changes while one operation runs, so this is resolved once - {@link #choose} asks on every tick and a per-tick walk of the recipe graph is exactly the work to avoid. Oracle queries: answering "where is the nearest X" with information no observed snapshot carries. Ore and structure answers come from seed-simulated vanilla world generation and are always reported as PREDICTED (confirm by observation); fluid, block, village and threat answers are palette-gated or entity scans over loaded terrain and are reported as OBSERVED. Every query is a bounded op (60s deadline, at most 8 chunks scanned per tick; structure location runs on a daemon worker) and never mutates world, engine or module state.

Normalizes the query argument. Precedence: fixed subjects (lava, water, village, threats), then {@code structure} / {@code structure:<id>}, then the {@code ancient_debris} alias and ore kind names, then direct structure names/aliases (bare or minecraft:-prefixed), then registry block ids (namespace optional, must exist). Anything else is rejected. Collisions: bare {@code village} always stays the loaded-chunk palette subject — seed-located villages are {@code structure:village}; no structure name collides with an ore kind or a real block id.
{@code structure:<id>} form: the only way to reach names shadowed by fixed subjects (structure:village).
Structure lookup by bare name or minecraft:-prefixed id, case-insensitive. Null when unknown.
Every locateable vanilla 26.2 structure, grouped the way the vanilla structure tags group them (village/shipwreck/ocean_ruin/ruined_portal/mineshaft tags verified against the 26.2 datapack). The dimension set is the fast pre-dispatch gate; the authoritative check at locate time is the dimension's own {@code getPlacementsForStructure}.
Copy sorted nearest-first by squared distance; ties keep input order.
Chunk square around the center chunk, nearest-first on the chunk grid, deterministic on ties.
Seed precedence: the explicit argument wins, then the singleplayer world, then the stored per-scope value.
The palette bit of the village entry in ModuleStorageStructures.ALL, resolved once by setting id.
Whole locate on the worker: context (cached per seed+dimension), holder resolution, candidate scan.
Small per-op cache. The OreSim engine's own context cache is private; this one never touches it.
Mirrors vanilla {@code ChunkGenerator.findNearestMapStructure} minus the ServerLevel storage scan (there is no saved chunk data on the client): concentric-ring placements check ring positions nearest-first, random-spread placements walk sector rings 0..25, and every candidate passes the same frequency-restriction + {@code findValidGenerationPoint} check {@code StructureCheck.checkStart} runs.
The first wanted structure with a valid generation point at the candidate chunk, like vanilla's per-chunk loop.
Biome ring-sample granularity: one quart-position sample per 64-block cell.
Whole locate on the worker: context (cached per seed+dimension), then the 64-block ring sample.
Resolves a biome spec (registry id with or without namespace, or a case-insensitive substring) against the available biome ids: exact id first, then a bare-path id, then substring matches (a unique match wins, an exact path among several wins, otherwise the ambiguity is reported with its candidates; nothing at all raises near-miss suggestions, the AiItems.resolve pattern). Pure: the id set is the only input.
Expanding Chebyshev rings of cells around the center cell, nearest ring first, deterministic inside a ring, every cell exactly once. Pure: no Minecraft construction.
Palette gate per section (maybeHas) before any 4096-block walk, same pattern as ModuleBlockEsp.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiPlan.jav.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiPlan.jav.notes:
game:plan - run a whole sequence of gameplay steps in ONE call.

This is the round-trip killer. "Get wood, make a table, make a pickaxe, mine stone, make a furnace" is five model turns as separate performs and one turn as a plan. Steps declare what they depend on, the executor orders them, and a step whose dependency failed is skipped rather than run against a precondition that never happened.

Only {@code game:} capabilities are callable from a plan. Modules, macros and commands change client configuration and stay on the direct perform path where the model sees each one.

The survival guard runs between steps, so a long plan eats and defends itself instead of starving halfway through. The result always reports every step's final state, including the ones never reached, so a partial plan is legible rather than a single failure message. Steps a single plan may contain. Beyond this a plan is really several objectives. Survival between steps; a guard action never interrupts a step already in flight. Parses and validates the declared steps, rejecting anything a plan may not call. A step as an object. A string is the .tools shorthand ("craft crafting_table 1", "mine iron_ore 10", "goto 100 64 -200"), mapped through the same parser the command uses; models write plans that way. The same AiSchemas gate a direct perform applies, run per step at parse time so a bad field is rejected with the step id named before anything executes - not discovered mid-plan after the earlier steps have already changed the world.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiPlanRunn.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiPlanRunn.notes:
Ordering and bookkeeping for a multi-step plan. Pure by construction - ids, dependencies and statuses, no Minecraft - so the whole ordering, cycle detection, skip-cascade and failure policy are unit tested. {@link AiPlan} supplies the live execution.

The reason this exists separately: a plan that silently reorders itself, or runs a step whose dependency failed, is far worse than one that refuses to start. Every refusal here names the exact step and reason. What to do when a step fails. Stop the whole plan at the first failure. The default: later steps usually assumed it worked. Skip the failed step's dependents and keep running everything independent of it. Run the step once more before treating it as failed. One planned step: a capability call plus the step ids it must run after. Mutable per-step progress. Validates and topologically orders the steps. Raises on a duplicate id, an unknown dependency or a cycle, naming the offending step - a plan is only worth running if its shape is sound before anything is executed. The next step to run, or null when none is runnable right now.

The dead-dependency sweep is a COMPLETE forward pass before any step is chosen, not a side effect of walking to the next runnable one. Doing it lazily would leave a step whose dependency already failed sitting at PENDING in the final report - indistinguishable from one the plan simply ran out of time for, which is exactly the distinction the report exists to make. The plan list is in topological order, so one pass cascades the whole chain. True once no step can still run, whatever the reason. Applies a terminal step outcome. Returns true when the plan should stop immediately, which is the STOP policy's whole job; RETRY puts the step back to PENDING for exactly one more go. Only a plain failure reaches this: UNCERTAIN goes through {@link #applyUncertain} and is never re-run. Applies an UNCERTAIN outcome: terminal and never retried - the step's effects may already be applied, so re-running it could double-apply a non-idempotent action. It lands on FAILED so the dependency skip-cascade treats it exactly like a failure. Counts by state, for the plan's result summary. The capability ids a plan may call: native gameplay only, never modules or commands. Step ids that were never reached, for an honest partial report. Ids of steps that completed, so a caller can resume a plan without redoing work.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiPortalCa.notes:
game:portal_cast - the no-diamond nether portal: a cornerless 4x5 obsidian frame cast IN PLACE at a lava pool, then lit, with nothing but buckets and throwaway blocks. This is the speedrunner's answer when there is no diamond pickaxe to mine obsidian and game:dimension build:true (which consumes 10 obsidian items) cannot run.

Casting mechanics. Water poured so it flows onto a lava SOURCE turns the source into obsidian; flowing lava would only make cobblestone, so a frame cell that is not a source is waited on, never poured over. The frame stands with its floor row at the pool's surface: floor cells are cast straight out of the pool (water only), while wall and lintel cells above lava level each get one pool-lava pour first (the lava bucket refills at the pool between cells - the site census checks the pool has enough sources up front), then the same water pour converts them. Water is never consumed: it is poured into the air cell directly above the target and re-scooped once the obsidian is verified, so a single water bucket casts the whole frame. Throwaway mold blocks dam the pour cell wherever water could spread onto pool lava outside the frame, and give the bucket a face to click where no natural support exists (a bucket empties at the cell the crosshair ray's hit face points into, so there must BE a face). Every frame cell must read minecraft:obsidian with a fresh server block-revision before the op moves on; a pour that creates obsidian OUTSIDE the frame stops the op and names the cell; lava is only ever poured into a planned frame cell, never dumped.

Lighting. flint_and_steel first, else a fire_charge (both clicked at the floor under the doorway, exactly like game:dimension's build path), else the last-resort fire spread: a flammable block placed in the doorway with a pool-lava pour beside it ignites the interior, and the burning wood clears itself out of the frame.

Preflight. FAILs fast naming what is missing in missing{} (the game:obtain shape): a water bucket (or an empty bucket while a water source is within 32 blocks), a lava bucket or a spare empty bucket when the frame needs wall pours, throwaway blocks (dirt/cobblestone family), and a lighter. In the nether water evaporates, so the op refuses there outright. Survival interrupts (flee/eat via AiGuard, health <= 4 abort) match the long gathering ops. All geometry (cast order, dam and pour-face planning, refill choice, lighter choice, preflight math) is pure and headless-tested in AiPortalCastTest. Nearest-pool scan radius when no x,y,z is given, and the lava census radius around the anchor. Natural blocks a cast may dig out of one frame site, the rounds of it, and the digs that may fail. The wider stance ring a cast walk falls back to: from feet two above to one below, the eye stays within 3.9 of the cell. Whether the lava search counts a site the cast must dig first as castable. Off: in caves the dug sites went on to fail at their molds (nothing to place against, faces out of view) and lava scoops, four pools in a row, while the obsidian build that follows such a refusal worked. Pool source cells kept for refills and the site search (nearest-first to the anchor). Throwaway mold/dam blocks the preflight asks for; a typical site places well under ten. Ticks the camera may spend finding a pour face before the attempt counts as failed. Ticks a finished pour may take to show in the cell. Ticks the obsidian conversion may lag the water pour. Direct-lighter clicks and the fire-spread wait (random-tick driven, hence the long leash). Re-aims per pour before the cell is reported. Mold/dam material families, cheapest first; the first id held is what gets placed. Doorway fuel for the fire-spread lighting fallback (slow-burning, so the fire has time to take). The simplified cell read the cast planner works over; flowing fluids and full blocks both map to SOLID. What one frame cell needs; SKIP already reads obsidian. Where one pour's click lands: the support block and its face toward the pour cell; mold is the throwaway block to place at the support first (null when the support already exists). One frame cell's cast: the pour target, the water cell above it, its dam cells and the pour face. The whole plan; blocked is set (with reason) instead when a frame cell cannot be cast. The live level read the planner works over (see the op's own kindAt, the same rules). Whether some 4x5 frame site at the pool round {@code anchor} plans, read from the loaded terrain the way the op's own site search reads it: the frame needs four cells of open air over the pool's surface and one more to pour the lintel's water into, which the caves at the lava level rarely have. The lava search asks this before walking to a pool: a seed walked to three such pools in a row, a minute each, and every cast failed at the site search. The engine's dig-safety rule (AiPathfinder digSafe): lava on any side, below included, or water above or beside. The frame cells in cast order: bottom-up (floor row, jamb levels, lintel), deterministic within a level. Frame plus interior cells: molds and dams must never occupy either (the interior must stay air). The pour plan for one candidate site. Floor cells sitting in the pool are WATER_OVER_LAVA; anything not already lava is LAVA_THEN_WATER (one pool source each, counted in lavaNeeded). A frame cell that is neither obsidian, a lava source, water nor air blocks the plan at that cell - the site picker simply moves to the next candidate. The cells water poured at {@code waterCell} could spread into and reach pool lava (directly, or by flowing down onto it): each is dammed with one throwaway block so the pour converts exactly its target. Reserved cells are never dammed; a site needing one there is simply not picked. The face a bucket pour into {@code pourCell} is clicked against: the natural support below when there is one, an already-planned dam when it neighbours the cell, else a fresh mold on the out-of-fram

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiPrinter..notes:
The schematic printer: builds a survival blueprint with what the bag holds, placing every block it can reach each tick (standing or walking) and walking only to where the next work is, over the build's own blocks.

Order comes from rules, not from a list: the lowest open cells nearest the body go first, a cell waits for the cell under it, nothing rises two layers above an open neighbour, fluids wait to be held in, a machine is placed so nothing fires. When nothing in reach can be placed it plans a route to a stance that can place the best open work; that route steps on the schematic's blocks and, where it must build its own way, uses the schematic's own blocks for its pillars and bridges. Temporary dirt is the last resort and is taken down before the build reports.

It never stalls silently: a run with no placement, interaction or teardown for {@code autism.ai.printer.stallTicks} ticks (beyond the time its current route needs), or a stance reached again and again without work, ends the run with a diagnostic of what it was trying and why each candidate was refused. Ticks with no progress before the run is declared stalled (on top of what a running route is given). Open cells the target pick takes per plan. Rays and placer solves one plan may spend proving stances. Reach a stance is proven with, short of the hand's: the body stops a little off the stance's centre. What the build order's own stance for a target is worth over any other that also places it. One layer up is worth this many blocks of walking when picking targets. Orders worked out again from the world as it stands, and when the last one began. Ticks the next cell in the order has been left without being done. The running route: its targets, when it started, what it is expected to take. Ticks a walk spent waiting on its route's search, separate from movement execution. Stance cells no walk reached from where the body was (cleared as the build moves on). Targets whose failed walk was granted the watchdog's grace since the build last moved. The box of the last site a printer worked (its margin round it), and when (nanoTime). {@code pos} lies by a site a printer worked within the last ten minutes. The service's dusk burrow digs a capped hole where the body stands, and the body stands on or beside the build when it ends. The build's poured pools no body gets out of ({@link AiPrinterGoal#traps}), read every second. Temporary blocks the teardown still has to take down that some stance reaches, as of its last choice. No pool is barred: none is known, or the teardown is down to its last blocks (nothing to walk to after them). The old executor has yielded at its safe boundary; target conversion cannot keep the client in one long tick. Ticks by what the build did with them (the first words of each tick's status): where the time of a build goes. Route placements use the schematic's own block where the cell is part of the build, else dirt (recorded). Keep native reads here: the route worker receives only the approved position snapshot. Reads back the cells around the body every tick, and a slice of the whole site. Anything that changed the world toward the blueprint is progress. The progress tick the watchdog last saw, and when it changed. Failed walks that taught the order new stances to leave since the build last moved, and how many may earn time. Ends the run when nothing has moved toward the blueprint for too long, with what it was doing and why. Why the open cells nearest the body cannot go in now, counted by reason. A route that does not reach its goal and ends in water: never walked. Twice a teardown walk with no way to its stance took its partial route down into a pool walled in by the machine, and no route got out of it again. How far off a scaffold block of the walks' own may be for a walk to go and take it down (the rest of one just gone for: further). Scaffold blocks a walk went for, with the tick of the last walk and the walks so far: a few walks each, far apart (the walks build their pillars at the same spots again, and one walk a spot left them standing). A scaffold block of the walks' own a little out of reach is gone to now: the walk that built it (a pillar up onto a roof) went on to its work, the body never stood in reach of it again, and once the build closed over the ground there was no way back down to it. No temporary block is placed on the way. Ticks a walk to a scaffold block may take. Tidy walks in a row with no way that pause the tidying, and for how long. Moves a walk to a scaffold block may plan. The scaffold block a tidy walk takes down now, the feet it was proven from, and whether they lean (crouched). Steps onto the proven feet and takes the scaffold block down, crouched where the stance leans: the hand's own takedown let go of the sneak the step held, the eye rose a third of a block and the block was out of reach. Lets go of the movement keys, the sneak too unless the body overhangs an edge: let go there, a body leaning out over an edge drifted off and fell. Ticks a tidy walk's takedown may take, the step onto its stance included. A stance a scaffold block is taken down from: the walk's goal cell and the exact feet there (off an edge, crouched). Stances in reach of the scaffold block at {@code target}, nearest the body first, each proven by a ray from its own eye. A stance may lean out over its floor's edge, crouched, as the build's own stances do: the top of a pillar left beside a roof is in reach only from the roof's very edge. The eye sees a face of {@code target}, and its ray to it misses {@code pillar} (a block still to be put there). The body stands on an edge with its middle over a hole (a temporary block under it just came down): before any walk it steps back, crouched, onto the column that holds it. A walk planned from the hole's own cell dropped the body three blocks into a pocket of the build with its first step. True while it steps. Temporary blocks standing, and the cell each was placed for. Temporary blocks placed and taken down (the report). The printer's build order. Every cell's possible clicks are listed first, each with what it needs: the block it is clicked on and the block the body stands on (both built before it), and the blueprint cells its body and its ray pass through (built after it). Then the finished build is taken apart in a search: a cell may be taken away (built last) when one of its clicks works in what still stands and the open space a body can reach, never leaving another cell with no click at all, the cell with the fewest clicks left first, backtracking out of dead ends. Reversed, the cells taken away are the build order, and each cell's click tells which later cells must wait for it.

Clicks are judged by vanilla's own placement rules against the planned world ({@link AiPrinterWorld}): the placer's prediction for the look, clicked face and point, the shapes the ray passes. A stance may stand on a temporary block outside the blueprint (the route builds it) when no real floor serves. Space around the build a body may stand in. Reach a click is proven with, short of the hand's: the body stops a little off a stance's centre. Clicks kept per cell, the cheapest first. Optional developer-requested search limit; ordinary builds retain their search across slices. Development check: every kept count against a fresh one. Optional explicit search-work allowance, disabled by default. Preparation never spends it. An explicit allowance for this order, when requested through the developer setting. Cells with this many live clicks or fewer press for themselves and for what they stand on and are clicked on. One click for a cell: what it is clicked on and stood on (built before it), what must be empty (built after). The body stands on a temporary block. The click is made on a temporary block outside the blueprint (placed before, taken down after). An order worked out again lists a cell's clicks anew only where they could have changed: per cell, the blueprint cells whose state or place in the order the listing read; unchanged, with the terrain round the build unchanged too, the earlier order's clicks are the same clicks. The world outside the blueprint the clicks were listed against: block state ids by grid cell. Lists clicks with {@code old}'s where nothing they were read from has changed. The earlier order's position of each cell it proved a click for (-1 none): the first attempt follows it. Worked out again from scratch, an order that had found the last trapdoor of a bubble-column room its one place lost it again. The restart the hint was worked out for (-1: the last order's, for the first start only). The earlier order's clicks of cell c still hold. A stage yields between bounded batches even on the largest schematic. Per cell and click: how many of the click's body cells are shut off from the open space (with {@link #deadDeps}, {@link #viable} is kept up to date move by move instead of counted afresh for every cell at every node). Per grid cell: the (cell, click) pairs whose body stands in it. The open space the counts were last brought up to. Per empty cell: (dependent cell, recipe) pairs, grouped by dependent cell in prepareSearch. Build position of each cell (0 first), -1 for cells left to the printer (fluids, partners, built). The cells each cell must wait for: its stance or ray needs it empty until they stand. Cells with no proven click in the order (the printer finds one when their turn comes). The stance each cell's chosen click was proven from (feet), or null. The temporary block each cell's chosen click is made on ({@link #NO_TEMP} for none). Ground under the site taken as dug: two cells beside a bottom-layer part that is placed looking up (an observer facing up), so a stance below the ground can click it. The walk there digs them, the pillar out fills them again. A part whose own facing comes from a look up: an observer facing up, a piston, dispenser or crafter facing down. The printer's own temporary blocks standing now: they come down, so the order reads their cells as open. src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiPrinterS.notes:
One schematic build for the printer: every cell with what makes it, its live status, a position index, and the rules that decide whether a cell may be placed now. Everything here is the client thread's.

The rules are what keep the build reachable and quiet: a cell waits for the blueprint cell under it (nothing is covered while it is still to be placed), no cell goes two or three layers above a cell still pending beside it (a cell at the bottom of a pit is out of reach), a fluid waits for every blueprint cell its flow would reach, a piston or TNT is never placed where it is powered, an observer waits for the cell it watches and a part an observer drives waits for that observer's view to be finished. What makes a cell. One block-item click, then any interactions its state asks for (open, delay, layers, waterlogged...). Made by another cell: a bed's head by its foot, an upper half by its lower half. Never clicked itself. A water or lava source, poured from a bucket once its flow is held in. Flowing water or lava: what the sources make; never placed, only waited for. Farmland or a path: dirt, then the hoe or the shovel on its top. A potted plant: the pot, then the plant. A filled cauldron: the cauldron, then the bucket. A composter with a level: the composter, then pumpkin pie. The cells as the audit wants them. The cells as built: a captured on-lever goes in off and is switched last. Immutable routing candidates: avoid rescanning every structural cube for every new walk. Cells lost after being finished (a fixture loss): counted for the diagnostics. The planner's build position of each cell (-1: left to the printer), and the cells each must wait for. Per cell, the cells the order's rules put before it (the plan's), or null. Potential influence whose bounded trace could not be resolved; kept separate from physical order edges. For a cell to place, the cell still open whose last possible click it would close (-1 for none); null when unset. Falling cells of a flow still to be shaped: no source pours whose water reaches one (their blocks go in first). The shaping blocks themselves (the block under a falling column and the ways out it shuts): they stand through the pour. The temporary block the plan proved each cell's click on ({@code AiPrinterPlan.NO_TEMP} for none). Per cell, the feet its click was planned from (null: no plan, or no stance). The item that starts a cell (the block, the bucket, the dirt under farmland, the pot, the cauldron). Reads one cell back from the world: DONE when it is exactly what the build wants now, PLACED when the right block stands and only interactions remain, else PENDING. A FAILED cell stays failed until {@link #retry} reopens it. Returns true when a finished cell was lost. The right block stands and every property that differs is one an interaction sets (or a chest still unpaired). A property's value as vanilla writes it ("single", not the enum's name). A chest half standing single whose only difference is its pairing: the partner's placement finishes it. The second chest half completes the first half's pairing; it cannot wait for that pairing to finish first. The right block stands and still wants its water: the bucket goes in next. Places a failed cell back in the queue (a later pass, or relaxed rules). How far the ordering rules are relaxed: 0 strict, 1 no layer-depth rule, 2 no column rule, 3 no soft redstone holds. Why cell {@code i} may not be started now, or null when it may (the item and the click are the placer's). The pathfinder proves the click support in its planned world, including preceding bridge placements. A neighbour stands that a click for this cell may be made on (and the cell's state allows that side). Hung from the block above (lanterns, ceiling attachments): its support is the cell over it. The redstone rules: a piston placed powered extends, TNT placed powered goes off; an observer placed before the cell it watches fires when that cell is built; a part an observer drives waits for the observer's view; an unlit torch waits for its block's power. The last three are relaxed when nothing else can move. The cells whose change sets off the observer at {@code observerAt} (facing {@code facing}): what it watches and that cell's neighbours (not the observer itself, nor below), and when what it watches is an observer too, what that one watches, along the chain. A sticky piston waited only for its observer's own view; the observer it watched fired when the next one up the chain was placed, and the piston moved an observer out of the build. Per observer cell: 0 not yet read, 1 its pulse reaches nothing that answers, 2 it does. Observer cell i pulses into something that answers: the block behind it reacts, or conducts into a neighbour that does. When nothing answers, it need not wait for the cell it watches: an observer facing up over a cauldron was held after the block it watches, and with it a dropper, a hopper and a comparator in a loop no order could untie. What the build will hold at {@code p}: the blueprint's block, else the ground as it stands. Moves, fires, toggles or passes a pulse on (a lamp, a rail's light or a hopper's lock only changes how it shows). Cell c's block can only be placed against its neighbour in direction {@code d} (on a floor, from a ceiling, one wall). Cells no temporary block may go into: what an observer watches, and every cell beside a part a block update sets off (a piston, a dispenser, a door...). With {@code redstone}, also the cells beside the circuit's wires, torches and gates, through which an update or a block's power reaches the parts. A teardown pillared up beside a machine and its sticky pistons fired. {@link #VIEWS} is only what the observers watch. {@link #quietCells} levels. A part a pulse sets off and leaves changed. game:obtain for anything behind the pickaxe ladder, with no model: "get me a diamond pickaxe" from an empty bag. One recursive obtain cannot do it (its depth stops around the stone pickaxe, nothing made a furnace, and ores out of sight were only found through the world seed), so the ladder runs as separate, restartable stages that re-read the live bag before every step: 
 wooden pickaxe -> stone pickaxe -> raw iron (carrying a crafting table, a furnace and fuel) -> iron ingots -> iron pickaxe -> diamonds, or whatever base material the target still needs -> the target itself
Ores come from loaded terrain first (game:mine), then from their richest depth (a staircase down), then from branch tunnels. A full bag is tidied between steps (tools, food, valuables and the ladder's own materials stay), the survival guard eats, fights or flees between legs, and a failed step is retried before the whole thing gives up with the step that could not be done. The stone tools include an axe for fighting, wood and table recovery. The wooden pick mines only enough stone for the stone pick; that faster pick mines the axe and furnace materials. An ore: the block family game:mine takes, the item it drops, the depth it is richest at, the pickaxe it needs, drops per block, and whether it only exists in the Nether. Smelted base materials and the ore drop each comes from. Whether a base material has to come from the Nether (so everything else is gathered first, at home). Overworld materials before Nether ones: the trip through the portal is one way as far as the ladder knows. Netherite gear is a smithing upgrade: diamond gear, an ingot and a template that only bastion chests hold. The materials the ladder produces itself; the craft planner treats them as leaves (their block and nugget recipes hidden). The night the ladder already handled, shared by every ladder run: a step resumed after an interrupt must not burrow twice. The pickaxe a base material must be mined with (smelted ones through their ore). A material-only job stops carrying a craft kit after its final tool is ready. The pickaxe item that opens a tier. The tier a pickaxe item gives (a golden one mines what a wooden one does). The next pickaxe the ladder should make on the way to `needed`, or null when `have` already mines it. How many blocks of an ore to mine for `drops` items. Whether the staged ladder should run: the target needs a material only a stone pickaxe or better mines.
