src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiProjecti.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiProjecti.notes:
Projectile awareness: scans live projectile entities and predicts their closest approach to the player with vanilla per-class ballistics. Gravity values and air drag are verified against the decompiled 26.2 sources: AbstractArrow 0.05, AbstractThrownPotion 0.05, ThrownExperienceBottle 0.07, ThrowableProjectile 0.03 (snowballs/eggs/ender pearls), LlamaSpit 0.06, all with air drag 0.99; AbstractHurtingProjectile (ghast/blaze/dragon fireballs, wither skulls, wind charges) flies straight with no gravity. ShulkerBullet homes on its target (gravity 0.04 only while targetless) and is approximated as straight-line, so its prediction degrades to the current velocity vector. Live predictions sweep the moving body and terrain; terrain impacts retain blast/cloud danger. Point-model helpers are pure; live body prediction also reads current client collision/fluid observations.
One predicted projectile: identity, observed state and the simulated outcome.
Simulated trajectory outcome: clearance to the player capsule and when it occurs.
Air drag for ballistic classes (AbstractArrow.getAirDrag / ThrowableProjectile.getAirDrag).
What a fireball keeps of its speed each tick out of water (AbstractHurtingProjectile.getInertia).
Projectile hitbox margin (0.3) + player half-width (0.6): clearance is measured around the eye point.
Threat zone: predicted clearance at or below this, with impact inside this horizon.
Same-tick scan memo. scan runs every client tick from AiService's threat check, the observation builder and the dodge op, and each call re-simulates every projectile's trajectory (up to 100 steps each); one scan per tick serves all three. The window is one tick, not AiDanger's two: projectile positions and velocities change every tick, so a wider window would have the dodge op acting on last tick's trajectories. The player identity guards the respawn swap. Client-thread only (the same confinement AiDanger's memo documents), so no synchronization.
Projectiles within 32 blocks of the player with their predicted approach; never throws.
Segment sweeps prevent fast arrows passing between samples or low arrows passing under an eye-point model.
Distance along the entire flight segment, including a near miss between its endpoints.
Simulates the trajectory in tick steps (at most 100) with vanilla arrow ordering (move, air drag, gravity; gravity 0 means straight-line with no drag) and returns the minimum clearance to the target eye point and when it occurs. Clearance subtracts HIT_MARGIN, so <= 0 is a predicted hit. Null when the projectile is already past / moving away, or still approaching at the horizon because its closest point lies beyond maxSeconds.
{@link #closestApproach(Vec3, Vec3, double, Vec3, double)} for a flight that gains {@code accel} along its heading every tick and keeps {@link #HURTING_INERTIA} of the sum, before the move (26.2 AbstractHurtingProjectile.applyInertia: blaze and ghast fireballs, 0.1). {@code accel} 0 is the old straight or ballistic flight.
Imminent danger: impact predicted inside the threat zone within the dodge horizon.
The "now missing" evaluation: no tracked projectile is an imminent threat any more.
Unit horizontal dodge direction: perpendicular to the projectile's horizontal velocity, on the side escapeSide picks. A vertical or stationary projectile (falling arrow, hovering shulker bullet) is dodged by stepping horizontally away from it; directly overhead falls back to a fixed direction.
Picks the dodge side perpendicular to the projectile's horizontal velocity by re-simulating the approach against the player shifted to each side (sprint ~5.6 blocks/second for the available time, capped at 2 blocks). +1 / -1 select sideVector's two directions. An exactly symmetric head-on path resolves deterministically away from the path's closest point.
Unit horizontal perpendicular to the projectile velocity; side +1 rotates (x,z) to (z,-x).

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiProspect.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiProspect.notes:
game:prospect - get a buried resource that is NOT in loaded terrain yet.

This is the difference between a bot that can pick up cobblestone and one that can finish a progression. game:collect and game:mine both only see what is already loaded, so "get three diamonds" from the surface fails on them by construction. This operation asks the seed-simulating oracle where the ore actually generates, walks there with digging enabled so the engine tunnels down to it, and then extracts with the ordinary verified mining loop.

Tool tier is checked BEFORE anything is dug: a block the player cannot harvest is reported as a missing tool with the exact item needed, which game:obtain turns into "craft that pickaxe first" rather than a wasted trip underground.

Oracle positions are PREDICTIONS. Each one is treated as a place to go and look, never as proof; the extraction phase re-scans real loaded terrain there, and a prediction that turns out to be wrong simply advances to the next candidate.

Ore families only: the bulk-buried commons (stone, dirt, gravel, ...) are not ore-kind and have no oracle entry by design - game:obtain's MINE strategy digs those without a prediction. Candidate sites taken from one oracle answer. Blocks around a site the extraction phase re-scans in real terrain. Arrival radius at a predicted site; the vein is scanned from there. A site that yields nothing after this many ticks of extraction is abandoned. Item to the oracle ore family that generates it. argumentsError != null means the raw arguments were malformed; arguments is then an empty object.
A tool call whose streamed JSON has closed; index is the provider stream index (Reply call order is ascending index).
Token usage of one request: uncached input, cache reads, cache writes, output (thinking included).

tokens is the total processed by the request (usage total, or the provider's bare total when it sent only that).
Beta that allows thinking.block_binding; only api.anthropic.com gets it.
An objective tier this short is not worth its own cache breakpoint.
Side-effect-free retry budget per request (lost streams only retry when no tool deltas arrived): long autonomous runs must survive multi-minute provider wobbles.
OpenAI on /v1/responses instead of /chat/completions (current models take function tools with reasoning only there).
OpenAI's own host speaks /v1/responses; a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint keeps /chat/completions until it says otherwise.
Per-request knobs from the live settings: effort and output tokens. The connection (provider, endpoint, model, key) stays pinned.
Sets the effort for the next request (a stored EFFORTS level; mapped to the provider's nearest).
The level actually sent for this provider and model.
Appends a user note to the trailing user message (after any tool results), or as a new user message; never two user messages in a row.
toolChoice: null = provider default; "required" = must call a tool; "none" = must not call. DeepSeek thinking rejects non-auto values, so it is left unset there; Anthropic drops "required" whenever thinking is on (current models reject forced tool use) and the caller verifies the call happened.
The two system tiers as text blocks, each with a 1h breakpoint; a tiny objective tier rides without its own marker.
The chat-format history as /v1/responses input items; history and transcripts keep the chat format. Reasoning is not replayed (the chat path never sent it back either), and no item ids are sent, so no call waits on a missing reasoning item.
The block-binding safety net needs a beta header that only the first-party Claude API accepts.
anthropic-beta header value for this body, or null; block_binding is never sent without it.
True when a provider error or stop reason says the prompt no longer fits the context window.
Stream died or ended before any completion marker; retryable only while no content was received yet.
onCallReady fires exactly once per tool call, the moment its streamed JSON closes, tagged with the provider stream index. OpenAI-compatible: when an event's tool-call deltas no longer touch that index (a new call's first delta closes the previous one), when non-tool text or finish_reason ends the tool sequence, or at stream end; Anthropic: at content_block_stop; Gemini: as each functionCall part arrives. Every call in the returned Reply was emitted exactly once: Reply.calls() is the emitted set, ordered by ascending stream index.
OpenAI /v1/responses stream, folded into the chat-format wire message and Reply the chat path produces. A function_call is emitted once, at its output_item.done (which carries the complete arguments), tagged with its output index.
Responses API: input_tokens includes input_tokens_details.cached_tokens; output_tokens includes reasoning.
Anthropic: message_start carries the input side, message_delta the cumulative output (and on newer APIs cumulative input too).
OpenAI, DashScope, Moonshot: prompt_tokens includes cached_tokens (prompt_tokens_details or top level); DeepSeek splits hit/miss.
Gemini: promptTokenCount includes cachedContentTokenCount; output is candidates + thoughts. Every chunk repeats the running totals.
Emits a finalized call exactly once per stream index; the 33rd distinct call rejects the response like the final count check.

A block whose arguments never streamed is NOT settled here - a proxy re-chunking the stream could deliver them in a later event, and settling early would emit a call with empty arguments. Blank blocks close at finish_reason or stream end.
Attaches the accumulated partial_json input (empty object plus error excerpt when malformed) and builds the call; raw == null means no input deltas arrived.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiRanged.j.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiRanged.j.notes:
game:shoot - bows, crossbows and thrown projectiles, aimed properly.

An arrow does not travel in a straight line, so a bot that points at a target and releases misses everything beyond about ten blocks. The pitch here is solved by SIMULATING the shot with the client's own {@link TrajectorySim} - the same physics the trajectory overlay draws - and searching for the launch angle whose arc actually reaches the target. That makes the aim exact rather than approximate, and it stays correct for crossbows, tridents and thrown potions because the simulator already knows their different gravity and drag.

Ranged attack is what makes ghasts, skeletons on towers and anything across a gap killable at all, and it is the safe answer when the melee guard would rather run. Pitch candidates tried when solving the arc, from a flat shot to a steep lob. Coarse then fine search steps, in degrees. Ticks the simulator flies a shot before giving up on it. Ticks a bow is held to reach full power; vanilla full pull is 20. Ticks the sweep may spend on an arc before the shot is abandoned. How far a target may be and still be worth shooting. A target moving more than this (squared, blocks a tick) is led. An arrow's mean speed over a shot's first thirty blocks, blocks a tick (3 at the bow, drag 0.99). Bow: hold the use key while the aim settles, release at full pull on a solved arc. Crossbow: charge once, then a single click fires the loaded bolt. Anything thrown in one click: snowballs, eggs, tridents, potions. Holds a ranged weapon, reporting exactly what is missing when there is none. The launch rotation whose simulated arc actually hits the target, or null when none does. A coarse sweep finds the bracket and a fine sweep lands inside the hitbox; the simulator is the client's own, so the answer matches what the server will fly. Whether the entity is one of the target's parts (the dragon's head, body, wings, tail). The target's motion over the last tick (positions, not the synced velocity: the dragon's is not synced). True for anything this operation knows how to launch. Ender pearls are deliberately excluded: thrown at a target they teleport the PLAYER into it, and nothing in the spec can ask for that.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiRaycast..documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiRaycast..notes:
game:raycast — ONE call eye-ray query, no world mutation. The ray leaves the player's eyes in the requested direction (toward x,y,z, or yaw/pitch, or the current look when neither is given) and reports the nearer of the block hit (ClipContext OUTLINE, fluids opt-in) and the entity hit (nearest pick-radius-inflated AABB clip along the ray, the crosshair rule).

Result shaping ({@link #blockHit}, {@link #entityHit}, {@link #miss}) is a pure static seam, headless-tested; the runtime half only resolves the direction and clips. The one-shot cast: completes immediately, never mutates the world. Pure result shaping: a block hit with id, block-state properties and both light channels. Pure result shaping: an entity hit with id and type. Pure result shaping: nothing hit within maxDistance (pos is the ray end).

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiRecover..documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiRecover..notes:
game:recover - go back to where you died and pick your things up.

Dying is not an edge case for an autonomous run, it is a routine event, and without this the run silently loses every tool it spent minutes making. The death position comes from {@link AiDeathLog}, which snapshots it at the tick the death is noticed - before the respawn moves the player and clears the inventory.

The five-minute despawn window is reported honestly rather than treated as absolute: item despawn timers only run while the chunk is loaded, so when the window has closed but the grave chunk is not loaded the trip proceeds with a warning instead of being refused. The trip itself routes through {@link AiTravelFar}, because a grave beyond loaded terrain is exactly the common case and local navigation cannot get there. Recovery always reports what was actually picked up against what was carried, so a partial recovery is visible rather than assumed. Radius around the grave that drops are swept from. Ticks spent standing on the grave collecting before the sweep is called done. Arrival radius at the grave. What the inventory gained since the operation started. Read-only view of the recorded death, for the model to decide whether a trip is worth it. The grave position, for callers that route there themselves.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiRedstone.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiRedstone.notes:
game:redstone - read and drive redstone components.

{@code inspect} reports the powered state, the signal strength and the interesting block-state properties of every redstone component in a radius: levers, buttons, pressure plates, doors, trapdoors, fence gates, repeaters, comparators, dispensers, droppers, hoppers, observers, pistons, wire, torches and lamps. That is the observation a model needs to reason about a circuit it did not build.

{@code toggle} and {@code set} drive one component and VERIFY the resulting state rather than trusting the click - a lever that was already on and a lever that did not respond look identical otherwise. {@code set} is idempotent by construction: it does nothing when the component is already in the requested state, which is what makes it safe inside a plan that may be retried. Radius for the inspect scan, in blocks. Components reported per inspect. Ticks the sweep may spend before the component is reported unreachable. Ticks to wait for the block state to change after the click. Block-state properties worth reporting; each is what a circuit actually turns on. The property a toggle flips, in precedence order: a door is OPEN, a lever is POWERED. Every redstone-relevant block within radius, with its live state. One component: id, position, live power and the block-state properties worth reading. The strongest redstone signal this block emits to any neighbour, or -1 when it emits none. The boolean property a toggle would flip, or null when the block has none. True when a block is worth reporting in a redstone inspection.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiRide.jav.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiRide.jav.notes:
game:ride - mount, steer and dismount vehicles.

A boat is the fastest overworld travel there is and the only sane way to cross an ocean; a minecart is how a mineshaft gets used. Neither is reachable through the pathfinder, which plans on foot, so this is the seam that makes them usable at all.

{@code mount} finds or places a vehicle and gets in, verifying with the actual vehicle attachment rather than the click. {@code travel} then steers a mounted boat toward a destination using the same humanized aim as everything else - a boat goes where it is pointed. {@code dismount} gets out and confirms it. Radius searched for an existing vehicle. Ticks the mount interaction may run before the vehicle is reported unusable. Arrival distance at a boat destination; a boat cannot stop on a coordinate. Ticks without progress before a boat journey is reported stuck. Steers a mounted boat toward the destination; a boat goes where it is pointed. Vanilla dismounts put the player on the vehicle's cell or a horizontal neighbour; getting out is refused unless at least one of those cells is solid ground with no lava (a strider over a lava lake is the case this exists for). Boats, minecarts and saddled animals are the things worth getting into.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiRunResou.notes:
The survival route's observed resource ledger, shared by the assistant and built-in controllers. Inventory, equipment and offhand are counted once; the cursor is reported separately as in transit. Expected loot is never available stock. Eyes protect both sides of their recipe, including already crafted eyes, and optional building/discarding cannot spend a live run's obligations.
Food the run wants before it goes deep, in nutrition points (a cooked steak is 8, cooked chicken 6). These were 96 and 80 - five to nine cooked meals - and that gate ended live campaigns that had every tool they needed: a run with the whole iron kit in ten minutes hunted animals for five minutes on a seed whose spawn area was empty, took a creeper's blast to 1.9 health, could not shelter (water in the burrow), and was then stopped by "Food preparation could not secure the 96 nutrition required for the remaining kit work" with ELEVEN food items in the bag. A run needs enough to cross the lava level and the Nether, not a banquet: the expedition reserve is a little over four meals, and the entry reserve the same, which every observed seed reaches from the animals near spawn.
Powder-side supply, in individual eyes, without rounding a lone powder up to a whole rod.
The netherite piece that does a diamond piece's job better ("minecraft:diamond_helmet" -> netherite_helmet), or null. The kit names diamond gear because that is what a run makes; netherite the player already has is never traded down.
{@link #usable(String, int)} counting netherite pieces toward their diamond counterparts.
Safe carried nutrition; raw meat is only credited after its real cooking output arrives.
Hunt quotas include cookable meat, but harmful incidental drops cannot finish a supply trip.
A bounded preparation gate. Deficits are actionable facts, never a timeout-based waiver.
Called by the campaign every tick, before nested controllers borrow the input owner.

The live task's trace is reachable through {@link #current()}; every emission is a no-op when no task has opened one, and trace I/O failures never break the run being traced.
A timed milestone inside a run (nether entered, end entered, dragon dead); scored straight from the trace.
Opens the trace for a freshly submitted objective, replacing any previous one. Pure path work; no I/O here.
Detaches the live trace (test seam); emissions after this are no-ops.
No-op-safe split emission for code without a trace reference.
Gameplay facts are queued through the existing storage worker, keeping disk I/O out of combat ticks.

One compact JSONL line: ts (epoch ms), elapsedMs since task start, the event kind, then the payload fields.
Roll the file over to .1 before a line when appending it would push a non-empty file past the cap.
The newest n lines across the rollover and the live file (the live file flushes per line).

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiScaffold.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiScaffold.notes:
game:scaffold — continuous scaffolding: bridge legs laid by the engine's bridger ({@link AiBridger} through {@link AiBridgeDriver}, the one goto's bridge moves and game:telly use: telly where a jump fits, legit walking backward otherwise, real clicks on the face the crosshair meets), a vertical tower, or a scripted leg list mixing both. A bridge leg runs along the cardinal nearest its yaw; follow:true takes the look the op started with. The lava rule mirrors the planner: a support whose fall column holds lava is never placed.

Pure seams (Plan.parse, quantizeYaw) carry no Minecraft references so AiScaffoldWalkTest exercises them headless. One scripted leg: a bridge leg along a yaw, or a vertical tower leg. blocks is the leg's placement target. Validated run(...) arguments: exactly one of a fixed direction, follow:true, tower:true, or a legs array. The 8-wind compass bucket of a Minecraft yaw (0,45,...,315): the follow leg's pivot key. The hop cadence's secure window, identical to game:telly's: hops only over placed cells. The dead-end proof: the player is clearly PAST the fill column's near plane and it still will not solve. The solve zone for a rim/side face starts AT the plane and reaches ~0.3 past it, so failing at +0.35 fired before the creep ever arrived (proven in-game). A tower click is legal only once the feet clear the takeoff cell (vanilla hitbox rule). follow: the look the op started with (the bridger owns the camera from then on). The active bridge leg's lane. Anti-freeze: the op must never ride its deadline while wedged (tower legs count the rise). The lava rule, mirroring the planner's fall-consequence check: 3 down from the support. Face-scan solve, instant aim at the proven rotation and one vanilla useItemOn. Bridge leg: one straight lane of leg.blocks cells along the cardinal nearest the leg's yaw, laid by the bridger. Tower leg: jump in place, clicking the just-vacated feet cell under us at rise window.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSchemas..notes:

Works on a copy; the model's own call object (part of the wire history) is never touched.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSchemati.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSchemati.notes:
Schematic ingestion: reads a schematic file from /schematics and decodes it into the {@link AiBuilder} blueprint model (block id + properties map per cell). The decoders are pure NBT -> cell-list seams, headless-tested with programmatically built fixtures.

Supported formats:

  • Sponge .schem v1/v2/v3 (gzip NBT: Width/Height/Length shorts, a Palette compound mapping "minecraft:xxx[prop=val,...]" state strings to indices, a BlockData varint array, optional Offset int[3] - v2 also honors the Metadata WEOffsetX/Y/Z triple). Version 3 uses the Schematic wrapper and Blocks compound with its Data varint array.
  • MCEdit legacy .schematic (gzip NBT: Blocks byte[] + optional AddBlocks nibble array for the high id bits, Data byte[] of legacy metadata). Numeric legacy ids go through the mapping table ({@link #legacyBlock}); ids with no mapping are collected and reported - the load fails listing count and ids unless skipUnknown:true, which treats them as air.
  • Litematic .litematic v1-v7: every entry of the Regions compound is decoded (Position/Size offsets - negative sizes normalized -, the BlockStatePalette list and the BlockStates packed long array) and merged into one blueprint. Legacy palette states use vanilla flattening and versioned block-state fixes before registry validation.

Air cells are never part of the blueprint (the builder places blocks, it does not clear) and are counted in airCells. The decoded cells keep their source offsets; {@link #load} applies the rotation/mirror transform and then anchors the blueprint at its minimum corner via {@link AiBuilder#normalize}, so the schematic's minimum corner lands on the requested origin. Compressed file size ceiling: schematic NBT is attacker-controlled input. Independent of the much smaller clipboard budget; includes ignored entity/inventory NBT. Preview/import decode ceiling. A captured base with its terrain (17071.schem: 124 x 77 x 141, 369336 blocks) is a real schematic; the ceiling only stops a hostile file from asking for gigabytes of cells. Preview/import only: larger than the bounded file-build footprint. A file may span a 64-chunk strip without widening inline, clipboard or repeat offsets. Keep dense X/Z column bookkeeping within the previously accepted 257-by-257 square. The decode output: cells with source offsets applied, plus bookkeeping for the report. Saved rail vehicles retain their positions; native item placement must later verify its own fresh entity. A saved item frame (or glow item frame): the cell it hangs in, the face it looks out of (its support is the block behind), what it holds (null: empty, an item stack compound already brought up to this game's data version), the item's rotation and the flags survival cannot set (invisible, fixed). The printer hangs and fills it at the end. Frames turned and mirrored with the cells, counted from the transformed blueprint's minimum corner. The entities a schematic carries (mobs, item frames, armor stands), counted by id: the builder places none of them. A legacy-id mapping result: the modern block id plus the block-state properties the legacy data value implies. The folder schematic names resolve against: /schematics. Schematic names are plain file names: no path separators, no traversal. Resolves a name against the schematics dir: an already-suffixed name is tried as-is, otherwise the extensions in order (.schem, .schematic, .litematic). A missing file fails listing what was tried. Loads a schematic file into a blueprint anchored at {@code origin}: decode by extension, apply the rotation/mirror transform, then shift so the minimum corner sits at the origin and validate the schematic cell cap and bounded file-build dimensions. A loaded blueprint and its signs' front text, keyed by the blueprint's own (dx, dy, dz) packed as a BlockPos. The execution entry shared by live builds and qualification; preview/import limits stay separate. Source-only bounds check, also used before the placement wizard starts execution. Reads bounded gzip/raw NBT and recognizes known schematic structures. A Sponge/Litematica block-state string "minecraft:oak_stairs[facing=north,half=bottom]" into the block id plus validated cell properties (the same definition validation inline blueprints get - an unknown block, property or value fails the load, never a mid-build surprise). The decoder's conversion of one raw "id[k=v,...]" palette state saved at {@code dataVersion}. Convert once per palette entry, never per block, then retain strict registry validation. Legacy palettes use vanilla's flattening map before the normal versioned state fixes. File palettes describe concrete native states: omitted properties retain their native defaults, not wildcards. A sign's front lines, newline-joined, or null for any other block entity or a blank sign. Text is a JSON string before 1.21.5, a string or component tag after it, and Text1..Text4 before 1.20; the player types the plain words. The decoded sign text keyed by the blueprint's own coordinates after the same mirror, rotation and anchoring at the minimum corner {@link #load} applies to the cells. Upgrade only saved item stacks; the storage slot is container metadata, not part of the item codec. Rotate positions around block centers, then use exactly the blocks' normalization origin. Legacy stair data: two facing bits (0 east, 1 west, 2 south, 3 north), bit 4 = upside down. Legacy "horizontal" order (getHorizontal): 0 south, 1 west, 2 north, 3 east - pumpkins, beds, fence gates, diodes, cocoa... Legacy door data: 0 east, 1 south, 2 west, 3 north. Legacy trapdoor data: 0 north, 1 south, 2 west, 3 east. Legacy anvil data: 0 west, 1 north, 2 east, 3 south (the anvil's own rotated order). Legacy side-attachment data (chest, furnace, ladder...): 2 north, 3 south, 4 west, 5 east; out-of-range data clamps to north. Legacy full facing (pistons, droppers, end rods): 0 down, 1 up, 2 north, 3 south, 4 west, 5 east. The legacy nu

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSchemati.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSchemati.notes:
Survival construction of cells made by an interaction rather than one BlockItem click.
Exhausting a proof budget is uncertainty, never permission to breach a finished structure.
A bed is placed as a pair; closing either half's ceiling first can remove its final click access.
Native survival rules evaluated against one hypothetical block edit, without changing the world.
A source neighbour that must be finished before installing its dependent attachment.
A repair shaft must be clearable all the way down before committing to its first floor removal.
A floor needed by a source door, plant or other dependent block is permanent construction.
The shaft may contain air gaps: each floor removal proves its real landing before digging.
Expose a neighboring floor block's side without leaving its support.
A reversible, connected stair outside the source footprint, usable in both directions.
Completed upper floors do not need a rebuilt access route when only lower cells remain.
Where the stairs turn after tread {@code at}: the cell beyond that tread against the new direction, else null.
Why a source poured at target would spill now, or null when it is held in. The flow is followed as far as it can run (down, and up to seven cells sideways from where it last fell) through the blueprint's own fluid cells and every cell it can enter now (open air, or a block water washes away); a cell on that way the blueprint fills with a solid block must stand first. Checked only beside the source, 19449's channel ran past the unbuilt end of its wall and washed away the redstone behind it. Open cells outside the blueprint are what the schematic itself has there.
A natural block standing where the schematic has air (user ruling 2026-10-06: a build on real terrain must come out as the schematic): soil, stone, sand, gravel, ores, trees, plants, snow and ice. Never a fluid (nothing to break) and never anything with a block entity or made by a player.
Opening this cell lets no fluid into the build: no lava beside it, no water above or beside it.
Every cell inside the schematic's box that the schematic leaves empty but natural terrain fills, top down. A plant's upper half over a blueprint plant is the plant, never terrain.

AI-facing server intelligence: the plugin scanner (driven by {@link AutismServerInfoOverlay}'s probe pump) and the DupeDB radar ({@link AutismDupeRadar}) as bounded operations. Entry points run on the client thread (AiTools hops through AiService.operate); the mapping/validation helpers are pure and headless-testable. Scan/radar results are observed evidence about the server, never proof of exploitability.
Mirror of the overlay's private SAVED_PLUGIN_CACHE_MAX_AGE_MS (two months).
One normalized per-plugin view of a {@link AutismConfig.PluginScanCacheEntry}: display name plus its per-key maps resolved.
Builds normalized per-plugin views from raw {@link AutismConfig.PluginScanCacheEntry} fields. The cache's per-plugin maps may be keyed by display name or canonical key, so lookups mirror the overlay's listForPluginKey canonical-key fallback. Commands are capped at maxCommands per entry.
Mirrors the overlay's radarPluginSnapshots feature filter: these evidence kinds are features, not plugins.
Mirrors the overlay's radarPluginSnapshots confidence gate (EXACT/STRONG only; labels accepted too).
The radar-candidate subset of a scan: strong-confidence, non-feature plugins, sorted by display name. One deliberate approximation: the overlay also drops rows whose PluginResultKind is FEATURE (a private command-label table); that kind is not persisted in the cache, so only the persisted evidence/confidence signals are reproduced here.
Label form matching the overlay's confidenceLabel (what RadarPluginSnapshot.confidence expects).
Serializes scan entries under a total character budget; flags truncation instead of exceeding it.
Bounded (<=150s) plugin scan of the current multiplayer server. Reuses the overlay's own driver: autoProbeOnSpawn() is cache-aware (a saved scan younger than two months is reused) and the module tick pumps tickBackground() whenever a scan is in progress, so this operation only triggers and observes — it never pumps the scanner itself. Terminal when the config cache entry for this address is present and the scan revision is stable; TIMED_OUT returns whatever the cache holds.
Immediate read of the cached plugin scan for the addressed/current/last server. Never triggers a scan.
Bounded (<=60s) DupeDB radar check for the current server. Preconditions are clean IllegalArgumentExceptions: multiplayer server, a cached plugin scan (run client:plugin_scan first), and an existing DupeDB login (interactive OAuth only, via the server info overlay — never attempted here).

CHATTING: the continuing-conversation lane is alive (optionally after its objective ended).

Lava in the cells a rise of 0.6 would bring the body into.

Shared by the assistant and the .tools runner, so neither ever drops a jump the other would have finished.
A predicted hit worth releasing the controls for: the worst non-fall source, lethal even through a totem. A fall is never one.
Cooldown after a threat-escalation pause before an unattended task auto-resumes.

Post-respawn stabilize decision: a bounded flee reflex only for a same-dimension respawn into nearby hostiles, with the death-pause resume flow live (a manual stop clears it first), and never in plan mode.

The reflex's "worth standing ground" weapon bar by registry id: a sword or axe of stone tier or better (never wooden/golden).
The dusk trigger window in the vanilla day cycle (mobs spawn ~13188).

A fall that will hurt (four points or more), with something to clutch it with, in a dimension where the clutch works.

True while a gameplay operation owns the client controls (the direct runner checks this before macros).

Dimension the death-stop fired in; the post-respawn stabilize reflex only runs when the respawn lands in the same one.

Threat-cancel timestamps within the escalation window (client-tick confined).
Event-feed state: hostile diff set, the 20-tick inventory snapshot, and the alive transition.
True while the background conversation lane is answering players.
One-line chat status for the UI/status command.
Full bounded status for chat_keep/.ai chat/UI.
Immediate operation evidence for qualification; the user-facing task snapshot is sampled.
Last tick result, including its terminal counters; callers must scope it to their own operation/session.

Evidence id of the current user statement (backs USER memories), or null before the

Out-of-the-box defaults per provider: model ID and output-token ceiling. Advanced settings can override both.

Stored effort for unknown or missing values.

Anthropic takes all four (adaptive: output_config.effort, older models: a thinking budget), OpenAI low/medium/high, DeepSeek and Moonshot low/high/max, DashScope all four as thinking budgets, Gemini 3 low/medium/high levels, Gemini 2.x all four as budgets. Empty when the model has no reasoning control at all.

Unknown aliases retain the provider's default reasoning behavior.
Claude generation as major.minor (4.5, 5.0), or -1 when the id carries no recognisable version.

Budget-style thinking tokens for an effort level, clamped so at least 1024 output tokens stay for the reply; 0 = too small to think.
A stock (blank or default) model follows the provider's defaults on a provider switch.
A stock (blank or some provider's default) endpoint follows the provider on a provider switch.
Copy switched to another provider; stock model/endpoint/output/vision follow the new provider, custom values stay.

The API provider below is kept for switching back. Fresh installs and saved settings with no key start here (see load).
Reasoning effort, one of EFFORTS (default high); providers map it onto their nearest supported level.
"Stop on input": the player's own keys, mouse turns, clicks or hotbar scroll pause a running operation. Off by default (user ruling 2026-09-30): the AI keeps going through any human input, alt-tabbing back in included, and keeps the camera; the stop key ends it.
Detectable movement features are opt-in; the default posture is legit human methods only.
Combat aim rides the silent-rotation holder (packets) at its lowest rung instead of the real camera.
Automatically rebase and resume objectives after a live world/session change (kick, rejoin, world switch).
Plan mode: a new objective first researches read-only and writes a plan; execution starts only after the user approves it.
Strict mode: the host checks fingerprints, evidence and every completion before accepting it. Off by default: the model performs by id, finishes freely and never has to prove an outcome. Latched per run.
"Use built-in when possible": plain steps of a request ("get me a diamond pickaxe", "craft a pickaxe", "eat") run on the client at once, with no API request, and only the rest goes to the model, told what is already done. On by default.
The assistant window stays on the HUD after the menu closes (the toolbar pushpin). Off by default.
Read-only world plans, shared by Built-In, API and .tools operations.
The chat models each provider account listed on its last scan (provider name -> ids): fills the model dropdown before the next scan and when offline.
True when a sealed or external key exists for the id; never decrypts or returns it.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiShield.j.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiShield.j.notes:
A block set on the line between a shooter's eye and the player's: the quickest cover there is when the stance out of sight is far (a pillar top) or the way to it passes mobs. Shared by the cover op and by the fight's perch, which shields the skeleton off while it fights the zombies below.
How far below a cell on the line its footing may be built (beside a pillar top with a zombie at its foot: four).
Shield cells are set within this of the eye (the block reach, a margin off).
The next block to set: of the cells on the line from the eye to the shooter's eye (outside the player's own two cells, within reach), the one whose column down to a face to click is shortest; that column's lowest open cell is set first and the rest follow on the next calls. Null when no cell on the line can be reached, footed, or is free of mobs (a zombie at the pillar's foot stands in the nearest column).
The block behind a one-wide perch, on the side away from the shooter, at foot level (or its footing first): an arrow knocks the body away from the shooter, off the column and down among the zombies below. Null when that side is already walled or nothing there can be footed.
Replaceable air, plants or water with nothing standing in it; a solid shield displaces the water.
A swimming body must still be able to stand when the new shield displaces its water.
The cheapest throwaway building block held (the ladder's reserves left alone), or null.
A hostile that is not a shooter within {@code radius}: the walk to cover would meet it.
A live hostile shooter that sees the player's eye from beyond {@code beyond} and within its follow range, or null. Its synced aggressive flag can drop between shots; that never makes an exposed pillar safe or cancels its shield.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSleep.ja.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSleep.ja.notes:
game:sleep - skip the night and set the spawn point.

Night is when an autonomous run dies. Sleeping removes that entire risk window in one call and moves the respawn point to where the work is, which is what makes a death recoverable at all. The operation finds a bed in loaded terrain or places a carried one, walks to it, uses it, waits out the sleep, and reports the resulting day time.

The refusals are the informative part: the server tells the client exactly why a bed was rejected (monsters nearby, not night, obstructed) as a system message, and that line is captured from the chat ledger and passed straight back rather than guessed at. When the bed CAN be used is the dimension's own BED_RULE - exploding dimensions are refused up front, and a daytime thunderstorm is accepted because vanilla accepts it. Radius searched in loaded terrain for an existing bed. Ticks the use interaction may run before the bed is reported unusable. Ticks a placement may take before it is abandoned. Ticks asleep before the wake is considered finished even without a time change. Ticks between bed searches; the search volume is too large to walk every tick. Day time at which the world counts as night, in the vanilla 24000-tick day. Any bed colour in the inventory; the model should not have to name one. Time of day in the vanilla 24000-tick cycle. True while beds accept a player, which is the only definition of night that matters here. Vanilla's own "may sleep now" rule, straight from the dimension's BED_RULE: dark enough outside, which covers night AND a daytime thunderstorm (Level.isDarkOutside stays true through one) plus any custom-dimension rule, instead of a hard-coded time window. The server's own bed-refusal line, captured from the chat ledger: vanilla sends the reason (monsters nearby, not night, obstructed) as a system message on the rejected click, and the ledger records system messages. The newest matching entry since the click wins; empty when nothing was observed.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSmelt.ja.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSmelt.ja.notes:
game:smelt - name the OUTPUT and a count; everything else is worked out. The cooking recipe comes from the client's loaded recipe data (so datapack and modded smelts are covered), the input is whichever accepted variant is in the bag, the fuel is chosen automatically, and the station is found nearby, walked to, or placed from inventory when one is carried.

The loading loop itself is the existing verified furnace adapter: this operation resolves the arguments and owns the station, then runs that adapter as a nested leg rather than duplicating its slot accounting and server-confirmation rules. Ticks the open interaction may run before the station is reported unusable. Ticks a placement may run before the station attempt is abandoned. Ticks between station searches; an 18k-block volume must not be walked every tick. Fuel fetches one smelt makes when its own fuel choice runs out short of the target. A furnace load that stopped for want of fuel (none held, or only the run's / the kit's reserve). Vanilla's actual block interaction, including a furnace opened by hand; never guesses among nearby stations. Explicit open-container tool uses the same productive scheduler and transfer adapter. Fuels that are far more useful as themselves than as heat. Damageable items are excluded separately - every tool and weapon in the game is damageable. A station that would not open once: make our own instead of failing the leg (see ensureStation). The fuel was picked here, not requested: when it runs out, more is fetched (fetchFuel) instead of failing. Coal from ore in sight when it can be mined, else planks on top of the replacement kit's wood. Gets a station of the right kind open: nearby, walked to, or placed from the bag. The nearest matching station block in loaded terrain within a short walk. Keep the original target and station while committed contents continue cooking. Fuel for {@code items} cooked in a furnace (coal from ore in sight, else planks above the kit), then the smelt itself. The resolved smelt: what goes in, what burns, what cooks it, and what comes out. Keep the committed load's identity; only an observed dry furnace may request another held fuel. Works out the recipe, the input variant to spend and the fuel to burn. Explicit {@code input} or {@code fuel} arguments override the automatic choice; everything else comes from the loaded cooking recipes and the current inventory. Candidate plans are tried best-station-first (standing nearby beats in the bag, which beats nothing), so the operation never commits to a furnace recipe when only the blast-furnace variant is actually usable. Station availability: standing nearby beats one in the bag, which beats one we cannot place. A station block of this id in loaded terrain within the same short walk the op searches. Preparation must recognize the same recipe-compatible stations that resolution can actually use. The accepted input variant the player actually holds, or the explicitly requested one. Picks a fuel from the inventory: junk first (saplings, bamboo, spare sticks), then real fuel (coal, charcoal, rods, buckets), and wood last - planks only above the replacement kit's wood (AiRestock.woodReserve), logs only when nothing else burns (a log burns no longer than one plank and crafts four; the obtain turns logs into planks first). Wood is what every new pickaxe, stick and crafting table is made of: burnt ahead of coal, it left the AI with a broken pickaxe and nothing to make another. Within a tier the winner is the smallest per-item burn whose held total still covers the whole job, so a lava bucket is never committed to a two-item smelt; when nothing covers the job the richest fuel of the earliest tier that has any takes it as far as it goes. Never the smelting input, never a tool, never furniture worth keeping. How many of this fuel the choice above may burn: the bag less the run's reserve, wood above the kit, sticks above two. Sticks a fuel choice leaves for a pickaxe's handle. 0 junk (saplings, bamboo, sticks), 1 real fuel, 2 planks, 3 logs: the order a fuel is burnt in. A family must pick a variant that covers the load, rather than its first non-empty stack. Near-worthless burnables spent before real fuel: spare sticks, any sapling, bamboo. (Planks are wood: see chooseFuel.) The cooking recipes the client knows for an output, as tool-result data.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSmith.ja.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSmith.ja.notes:
game:smith - smithing-table work as one verified transaction: upgrade (netherite template + diamond gear + netherite ingot) or trim (armor trim + armor piece + trim material). The station is found nearby, walked to, or placed from the bag (the AiSmelt station pattern); the three inputs go into their exact slots with verified clicks and the result is quick-moved out against an applied container revision.

The combo is validated upfront ({@link #comboError}): a wrong template, addition or base fails at parse time with the reason, never as a server rejection surprise. A shortfall of any input fails with the missing map. Ticks the open interaction may run before the station is reported unusable. Ticks the result extraction may wait for its applied server confirmation. Diamond-tier gear eligible for a netherite upgrade. Vanilla armor-trim materials. The open menu id whose slots were verified empty, so foreign contents are never consumed. Inventory count of the result item when its take was dispatched. Chosen stack note for ambiguous same-id picks (result data). Each of the three inputs must be in the menu already or still in the reachable bag. PICKUP-places one unit of the item from the bag into the exact slot, verified client-side. First bag slot with the item id; the plain-only pass keeps named/enchanted gear out of material roles. Records an ambiguous same-id pick so the result data says exactly which stack was consumed. Player-inventory slot -> smithing menu slot (table 0-3, main 4-30, hotbar 31-39). Gets a smithing table open: nearby, walked to, or placed from the bag (AiSmelt's station pattern). The nearest smithing table block in loaded terrain within a short walk. A FAILED result carrying a machine-readable code, with the same cleanup as done(). Upfront combination validation: null when the combo is sane, else the plain reason it cannot work (wrong template, wrong addition, or a base the mode does not apply to). Pure. Any armor piece a trim applies to.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSpeedrun.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSpeedrun.notes:
game:speedrun - the built-in speedrun: a fresh survival world to the Ender Dragon's death and the exit portal, with no model and no seed knowledge (AiOracle refuses every seed prediction while it runs: it plays as on a server whose seed nobody knows, from the blocks and mobs it has seen). Every time a step ends it reads the observed state - dimension, the bag, the worn gear - and starts the first phase not yet satisfied, so an interrupted run picks up where the world is.

Overworld gear (the user's route, src/Minecraft-26.2-Speedrun.md): wood, food, then the required iron bootstrap when moderate food can cover useful preparation before the full expedition reserve. The diamond ladder (AiProgression with a kit) makes the diamond pickaxe plus the diamond axe, shovel, helmet, chestplate and leggings, golden boots, three buckets (two for water, one for lava), a shield and a flint and steel - its ore trips cover the whole kit, so the iron trip mines every ingot and the diamond trip all 27 diamonds. Then the armour goes on and the Nether entry (AiNetherEntry: lava from observed terrain, the lava-cast portal, through it). The Nether, the stronghold and the End follow. The overworld gear besides the diamond pickaxe (the ladder's target), by item and count. Logs for the whole overworld kit: the ladder's tools and tables, the shield's planks, the axe's sticks. Sixteen, not the thirteen a plan counts: the ladder sets down a table at each crafting site and one to carry (six on one run), and the shield came four planks short at y -44 - a climb of a hundred blocks for one log. An enderman in sight this far off is a pearl chance: looked in the eye, it comes to the player. A step failing this soon after its start counts as "at once" (see the stuck rule in the leg handling). Planks the kit's crafts take besides the ladder's own: the shield's six and the diamond axe's and shovel's four sticks. Food items carried before the ladder goes underground; under it the run hunts first. What the first food trip hunts for, before the kit. What a food trip hunts for, its legs out from where it began, and how long it may take. A campaign food trip is NOT given fewer legs. Three was tried (to cut the ten-to-twelve-minute wander a sparse seed produces) and it made the first FOOD phase fail outright on a seed with no animals near spawn: three short legs found nothing, the trip reported no food, three identical step failures ended the run inside two minutes. Food the run does not find is a dead campaign; food found slowly is a slow one, and the phase's own deadline already bounds it. Cooking prerequisites and batches share the current trip's deadline, with a finite retry budget. Only required iron gear belongs to the bootstrap; diamonds retain their separate expedition gate. Only required iron gear belongs to the bootstrap; diamonds retain their separate expedition gate. A resumed equipped kit can still have a station item on the ground from its last acknowledged break. Held hay is converted through recipes; this count never authorizes a wheat or food search. Deep diamond acquisition needs the expedition reserve; later equipment repairs need a travel reserve. A known shortage requests only its missing pearls; already crafted Eyes remain available supply. Optional food exploration arrives on observed ground, so the route prices any climb out of a gully. Bounded nearby-column scan; an unavailable destination falls back toward the known frontier. Under this, with nothing hostile near, a step that can stop does, and the run heals first. An enderman this near on the overworld (armour on, pearls short) is hunted for its pearl. Blaze rods and ender pearls the Nether brings back: sixteen powder (the guide's eight rods) for fourteen eyes plus a spare, twelve frames and two throws' worth of shatter. Nutrition the kit work starts on when the food trips could not reach the full preparation goal. A phase that fails this many times ends the run with its reason; the same failure three times ends it sooner. A retry is worth it when it differs (the Nether entry's lava pool with no route is skipped by the next try, so three tries at three pools are progress, not a loop). How many times a phase may answer "I cannot tell what happened" before the campaign gives up. UNCERTAIN is a request for fresh observation, not a failure: an interrupted transfer, a furnace that timed out mid-batch, a click whose acknowledgement was never seen. Every one of those used to end the whole run on the spot - a fresh campaign died after five minutes with "FOOD: cook: Smelting target not reached; pending changes need observation before restarting work", six cooked porkchops in the bag and the furnace still burning - even though the campaign's own design re-derives the next step from observed state every time a step ends. It still cannot retry forever: this budget, and the phase's own failure budget, end it. Counts one "the world does not say what happened" for {@code phase} and answers whether the campaign may observe again. A burst inside {@link #UNCERTAIN_BURST_NANOS} is ONE occurrence: an interrupted portal-frame placement reported the same pending acknowledgement three times in sixteen seconds and ended a live campaign at eighteen minutes - the budget is for distinct doubts, not for the retry loop's own cadence. Pure, for tests. Repeats inside one burst window that count as a further occurrence: a stronghold step answering "uncertain" in the same tick it started reported 578 times in two minutes, and the one-look burst rule let it go on for good. Fresh observations granted to each phase after a child could not establish what happened. When each phase last spent one: a burst inside UNCERTAIN_BURST_NANOS is one occurrence. The day (overworld clock / 24000) whose night shelter failed: not tried again that night. The last ticks' body state, logged when a fall passes six blocks: which keys walked it off, and from where. Every health drop with its cause, and the hu

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSpeedrun.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSpeedrun.notes:
Development fixtures for the speedrun's later stages (qualification instances only, flag autism.ai.speedrun.stage): the overworld kit is given and worn, and the player is put where the stage begins - the Nether beside a lit portal at an arbitrary spot (nether), the overworld spawn with rods and pearls (stronghold), the End's obsidian platform (end). These are setup commands for testing a stage quickly; the AI never reads them, and whole runs start from a fresh world.
Into the Nether over the overworld spawn (x and z divided by eight), beside a lit portal on a safe floor.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiStationP.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiStationP.notes:
Puts a station (crafting table, furnace, stonecutter) down beside the player: the nearest usable spot within two blocks, up to {@link AiCraft#MAX_TABLE_SPOTS} of them, then one walk to open ground and a fresh try there. On a tree top, a ledge or in a one-wide tunnel the first spot alone failed and the whole craft or smelt failed with it.
Ticks one spot gets before the next is tried.
No horizontal exit has room for the body. Pure, also used by the sealed-shaft regression.
Clear a leaf wall above a proved short landing instead of chopping the trunk to get below it.
Walled in (a pit, a one-block hole) with no spot and nowhere to step: dig out the wall block beside the feet that has a floor under it, and the cell it leaves is the spot. Never an ore, a station or anything with fluid next to it.
Clear the upper wall before its foot cell, so the new station's support face is visible from the shaft.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiStrongho.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiStrongho.notes:
Observed stronghold navigation: associated Eye flights, lateral ray baselines and uncertainty, real pickup accounting and a protected twelve-Eye activation reserve. Loaded inward-facing frame rings and every insertion are verified before the nine-cell portal can be entered. Preparation expiration reports deficits; it never waives the health, food, equipment, water or dragon-fallback gate. World/connection changes stop stale navigation. AiStrongholdSearch keeps a bounded observed route graph near an Eye lead when the portal room is not loaded.
The End kit's errands rest this long after four failures in a row.
Endermen within this are hunted for pearls on the way.
A bounded preparation budget; expiration reports deficits and never waives the entry gate.
How long the room hunts endermen round it when the eyes are short of the empty frames.
Pitches tried in turn for a throw with nothing in the crosshair.
One sent use, retained until an applied server spend or a post-ack full snapshot resolves it.
Eligible dark time accumulates across dawns; daylight cannot reset a bounded pearl hunt.
A parent stop cannot erase an unacknowledged Eye or a child receipt during cleanup.
The current child's identity owns its receipt; arrival and cleanup cannot acknowledge its pending changes.
When this world's End kit search began and round what (kept across restarts: each restart searched eight minutes more).
The bearing (unit x/z) and where it was read; null before the first throw.
A throw in flight: the eye entity watched, its first position, ticks since the click.
The point an eye is clicked on: the frame's top face.
From {@code eye} some point of the frame is in reach and the first block its ray meets (an eye goes in by any face).
The nearest standing cell whose eye sees {@code frame}'s top: on the platform beside the ring, or on the frames. From the room's floor two below the platform every click met another frame's side, the same insertion failed 1700 times in two minutes, and the run never moved.
A cell on the platform just outside a frame block next to a portal block, level with the portal, with a floor and room for the body: the nearest to the player. Null when none.
The portal block across the frame from the stance.
The open sky over the feet's column is at most {@code blocks} above them.
Look up a little (no block in the crosshair: the click must throw, not insert or place) and use the eye.
The eye flies about three more seconds, then drops as an item or shatters: collect it when it lands near.
Open sky over some cell within {@code radius} at the feet's level (the body is out from under a cap or a roof).

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiStrongho.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiStrongho.notes:
Bounded local structure exploration from an uncertain Eye lead, using only loaded floors and legal route excavation.
A campaign's successive bounded searches continue from observed frontiers, not from scratch.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSurvival.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiSurvival.notes:
Survival self-maintenance: eating to a food-level target and fleeing observed hostile mobs. Eating drives the real use input (composing with combat modules that stand down while the player is using an item) and restores the previous hotbar slot and key state on every exit. Fleeing delegates movement to the engine in short local legs, inheriting its low-health abort. Each leg re-reads the hostiles before continuing, and cannot take a long detour through a cave. A failed leg rotates through alternate bearings and distances rather than giving up, every candidate is hazard-filtered (loaded, no lava, no drop over three - the combat strafe's footing rules), and a live projectile threat switches the escape to short zigzag hops because a straight line is trivial to lead. Bearings are ranked against every observed hostile along the escape distance, including mobs outside the alarm radius; the engine's SAFEST route still checks terrain and prices the actual path past those threats.
A meal must yield before a nearby hunter's delayed aggression flag arrives. Neutrals still need engagement evidence.
Preserve crowd/health tactics, but never answer an unsafe meal with another meal.
Harmful but edible as a last resort: hunger or poison side effects, still net nutrition.
Never eaten: random untelegraphed effects (stew) or positional teleport (chorus).
Combat consumables, not hunger food: burned only when no other safe food exists.
Where the flee began and the legs walked since: boxed in, the legs go round in a few blocks.
Edible through the held-use path: nutrition (FOOD) behind a consume animation (CONSUMABLE).
Best edible inventory slot (0..35), or -1 when nothing edible exists. Any safe hotbar food beats inventory food (no swap needed); inside a region the highest nutrition+saturation wins. Tier order: ordinary safe food first, then PRECIOUS (golden apples - combat consumables, eaten only when no other safe food exists), then HARMFUL as the last resort. NEVER items are never returned.
Meat that cooks into far more food: raw porkchop is 3 hunger, cooked 8.
Routine eating waits while the only food is raw meat and food is above 6 (sprinting still works there). On the way to the furnace for "cook the meat", the guard ate the three porkchops raw at food 12, and the cooking had nothing left to cook.
Pure escape geometry: the horizontal position distance blocks away from the threat centroid, keeping the player's height. Null when there are no threats (no escape direction exists); a threat exactly under the player falls back to a fixed horizontal direction.
{@link #escapeTarget(Vec3, List, double)} with the away bearing rotated by bearingDegrees, for the alternate candidates a failed leg rotates through and the zigzag a ranged threat forces. Rotation is around Y; the sign convention does not matter because both sides are always offered.
The alternating lateral offset (degrees) of a zigzag hop against ranged attackers.
An emergency walking leg must stay local; no detour back through the cave to reach a clear distant endpoint.
Snapping a blocked bearing to the two cells beneath a boundary stance is not an escape leg.
A mined shaft has no lateral exit: build at most three steps through existing clear headroom, away from mobs below.
Risk added by approaching another mob along a bearing, plus exposure at its endpoint.
Living hostile (Enemy) entities within radius of the player position.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTaskDura.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTaskDura.notes:
Only an explicit duration in the user's own request may change a task's configured allowance: for/during raises it, an under/within-style cap sets it.
Minutes for an amount+unit pair, or NaN when the value is unusable (non-finite or over a year).

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTaskStat.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTaskStat.notes:
Presentation of a live task, independent of the number of render primitives it produces.
Show the actual current phase, without leaking route coordinates, nested receipts or planner counters.
{@link AiGoal}'s layer: above every task (100) and render layer status.
How long a different banner (outside a published goal) must hold before it is shown.
The banner as shown: a published goal as it is (it holds its own), anything else only once its title and activity have held {@link #HOLD_NANOS} ("Mining / Breaking Stone", "Breaking Dirt" and "Travelling" took turns several times a second under one mining job). The detail row follows at once.
Root tasks publish after their child work; render-layer refreshes cannot replace their status.
Banner uses five pixels of horizontal padding on each side and the shared body font for all rows.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTelly.ja.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTelly.ja.notes:
game:telly, the AI's own bridge: straight lanes of supports laid by the engine's bridger ({@link AiBridger} through {@link AiBridgeDriver}), the same one goto's bridge moves use. Telly (the default) sprint-jumps forward and flicks the real camera back to click each support under the arc; under a ceiling, without food to sprint, or in walk/sprint mode it bridges legit, walking backward and clicking each support as the eye passes the edge. Every click is a real right click on the face the crosshair meets.

Pure seams (Plan, chooseBlockSlot, fellOff) carry no Minecraft references so AiTellyTest exercises them headless. Validated bridge(...) arguments: exactly one of the x/z target column or a direction yaw. Minecraft yaw to horizontal forward vector: yaw 0 = south (+z), 90 = west (-x). Flat hotbar view for the pure slot choice. Held slot while it still holds usable construction blocks, else the first other construction slot; -1 = out of blocks. The bridge is lost when the player drops more than 2 blocks below the walk surface. The hotbar's construction view: full, non-falling, entity-free blocks. Lava within three under a support: the planner's fall rule, never bridged over. The next straight lane from where the body stands: the direction, or the target's longer axis first.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTerrain..documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTerrain..notes:
ClientLevel.hasChunk is not a reliable loaded-terrain test; explicitly avoid the empty fallback chunk.
Bounded, palette-filtered source census; never scans whole empty sections on the client tick.
A water trip compares separate shores rather than committing to one nearby buried pool.
At most one candidate per eight-block region; a dense lake cannot consume every goal.
Squared distance to the nearest of these blocks in loaded terrain, or {@link Double#MAX_VALUE} when none is within {@code radius}. Sections whose palette cannot hold any of the blocks are skipped whole, and sections are read nearest first until no closer hit is possible: the old cell-by-cell box read ran a few hundred thousand block lookups per call on the game thread.
The same, counting only the cells {@code accept} takes.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiThreats..documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiThreats..notes:
Who is coming for the player and what it is about to do, from what the client really sees: the synced aggression flag (arms or bow up, a brain's attack target), a drawn bow and how long it has been drawn, a blaze's or ghast's charge, a creeper's fuse, a mob that hit the player, and a mob closing in. A mob with none of that is left alone - a zombie wandering forty blocks off, a piglin beside golden boots, an enderman not looked at - and the job goes on (user ruling 2026-10-07: "most mobs/enemies should be left alone"). Read by the guard (what counts) and the fight (spacing, shots).
The combat profiles: each answers differently (spacing, shield, cover, bypass, never touch).
Too costly to fight on the way (a warden, an evoker, a ravager, an elder guardian): never engaged, always left.
The combat controller of before the 2026-10-07 rework (every Enemy near counted, no bypass, the old fight keys), for A/B runs of the combat gauntlet: -Dautism.ai.combat.legacy=true or the qualification flag.
Vanilla's default melee reach: the attacker's box grown this much sideways (Mob.DEFAULT_ATTACK_REACH).
How long a hit on the player, or a raised arm or bow, keeps a mob counted (ticks).
A bow drawn this long shoots within the shield's startup (vanilla shoots at 20, the shield blocks 5 ticks after).
Neutral until provoked: never attacked, never counted, unless it shows it is after the player.
A melee profile: it has to come to the player, so a body that keeps moving leaves it behind.
Blocks a tick the profile closes in at, chasing on flat ground (vanilla: zza = speed, accel speed squared, ground friction keeps 0.546): a zombie 0.117, a baby 0.26, a spider 0.2. A player walking backward makes 0.216.
The sideways growth of this mob's attack box: its weapon's attack range, else vanilla's default.
How far the player's box is outside this mob's attack box, along the nearer horizontal axis (negative: inside, it can hit now). Vanilla tests the boxes, not the centres: a diagonal stance is safer than its centre distance says.
Refreshes the per-mob evidence (once a tick; every reader calls it).
A piece of gold armour worn: piglins leave the player alone until provoked.
Whether the player's look was in this enderman's stare cone in the last two seconds.
Closing on the player for at least this many ticks running.
Whether this mob is after the player now, by its profile's evidence. Hostiles that hunt every player they see (zombies, creepers, blazes) count in sight within their hunting range once they come for it; neutrals only once they show it; a passive or unknown entity only once it hit.
Endermen already logged as angry at the player.
The last tick each enderman was inside the player's stare cone (client view).
The camera step during each enderman's last stare.
Blazes seen uncharged at least once: only their charge start was watched.
Ticks until this shooter's next shot is due, or -1 when none is coming soon: a bow drawn (vanilla lets go at 20 ticks), a crossbow loaded and raised, a blaze into its 60-tick charge, a ghast charging (10 ticks to the shot).
The shooter whose shot lands soonest within {@code within} ticks and that sees the player (a blaze under two blocks strikes instead of shooting), or null.
The horizontal look from the player toward a point, for the shield (it blocks what comes from in front).

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTickQueu.notes: Client work may run inline only inside the pre-movement phase, never merely because it is on the client thread.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTidy.jav.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTidy.jav.notes:
game:tidy - make room, by throwing away the right things.

A full inventory is not a warning, it is silent data loss: every subsequent drop a gathering job produces falls on the floor and despawns. The guard can see it coming but cannot fix it, because deciding what is worth keeping is a judgement. This operation encodes that judgement as an explicit, inspectable ranking and drops from the bottom of it.

{@code inspect} reports the ranking without touching anything, which is the safe way for a model to check what a tidy WOULD throw away before it does. Anything named in {@code keep} is never dropped whatever its rank, and equipped armour, the offhand and the held item are never candidates at all. Ticks to wait for each throw to be applied before the operation reports it unconfirmed. Keep-value ranking, high to low. The numbers are ordinal only; what matters is the ORDER, which is the actual judgement: a tool took minutes to make, food is life, ores are the point of the trip, building blocks are replaceable, and the bottom tier is what a player throws on the floor without looking. Items worth more than their stack size suggests: progression currency. Things that do a job: buckets, flint and steel, boats, beds, torches, crafting stations. The bottom tier: abundant, instantly replaceable, or actively useless. Items a run cannot do without, never thrown away whatever their generic rank: the water buckets (a fall, fire), the lava bucket and empty buckets (the portal cast), the ignition, the beds and their wool, the bow's arrows and the barter gold. Ranked as valuables: a tidy for room once threw the run's only flint and steel ahead of a cobblestone stack, and beds (unstackable, a slot each) rank as plain building blocks. Throwaway blocks kept whatever their rank: a pillar out of a hole, a bridge, the dragon fight's cover. One inventory stack with the rank the policy gives it. The whole inventory with its ranking, plus what a drop would target first. Every droppable stack, worst first. The stack a drop would take next, or null when nothing is safe to drop. The keep-value of one stack. Called only while evaluating room: retain useful tools, release proven dominated basic spares. A full solid block a pillar or bridge can use (no falling block, no block entity, no wood, nothing valuable). Player-inventory index to the slot number the open inventory menu uses.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiToolCall.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiToolCall.notes:
Pure argument handling for the .tools command surface: k=v parsing (JSON-ish primitives, arrays and objects), {@code ~} relative coordinates, positional shorthand mapping onto capability argument objects, and near-miss capability suggestions. No Minecraft references - everything here is headless-tested. Errors are deliberately explicit: every rejection carries the usage line the chat handler prints verbatim.
A resolved invocation: capability id plus its argument object.
Parses {@code k=v k=v ...} tokens into an argument object; values are JSON-ish (see parseValue).
JSON-ish value: {@code true/false}, {@code null}, integer, finite decimal, "quoted string", {@code [a,b,...]}, {@code {k:v,...}} (bare or quoted keys), else the bare token as a string.
Splits on a separator at bracket depth 0 outside quotes; keeps empty segments (callers validate).
Parses one coordinate token: {@code ~}, {@code ~3.5}, {@code ~-2} (relative to base) or absolute.
Block coordinate for schema integer fields: absolute or ~-relative, floored like waypoint coords.
Maps a positional shorthand to its capability invocation. px/py/pz are the player's feet for {@code ~} resolution (0 when no player - absolute coordinates still work). Throws IllegalArgumentException with the usage line on bad input.
goto on foot only: the same planner, destinations and jumps, with nothing broken or placed on the way. goto itself is the same wherever the player cannot build.
{@code <spec words...> [count]}: a trailing all-digit token is the count and everything before it is the spec with its words joined by '_', so "crafting table 2", "crafting_table 2" and "crafting_table" all mean what a person means by them. The count is never required.
The first {@code end} tokens as one spec ("crafting table" -> "crafting_table").
Up to max near-miss ids for an unknown input, best first: prefix matches, then substring matches, then small edit distances against the id's local part. Deterministic (score, then id) so chat output and tests are stable.
Bounded Levenshtein; returns limit+1 as soon as the distance provably exceeds limit.
