The model's tool set for one run; verify = strict outcome verification (AiSettings.verifyOutcomes), latched per run.
A VALID example value for a string field. The generic defaults are fine for coordinates and item ids, but an enum-shaped field needs a member this capability actually accepts - an example the model would be rejected for copying is worse than no example.
fromScript exempts script-bridge calls from the catalog repeat guard: a worker's auto-fingerprint inspects are process-local lookups, not model round trips.
"; did you mean ..." for an unknown capability id: the closest catalog ids, so the retry needs no search round.
Capability ids grouped by family with one-line summaries (the list_tools alias body).
The first sentence of a purpose, or the whole string when short (ellipsis past 120 chars). Also used by .tools list/schema.
Dispatcher-level default deadlines, injected only when the caller omits timeoutSeconds (explicit values always win, and the ops' own clamps still cap them). Anchored at the family defaults (navigation 300, perception 60, crafting/stations 600, combat 300, plans 7200); entries without a timeoutSeconds arg or with deliberately open-ended semantics (game:follow) are intentionally absent.
Injects the dispatcher default timeout for a capability when the caller omitted it; the args are copied, never mutated in place. Pure (headless-tested).
Constructs a native gameplay operation by capability id. This is the ONE place a game: capability is built, so the plan executor composes exactly the operations the model can perform directly - it can never reach modules, macros or commands through a plan step. Returns null for an id this dispatcher does not own.
An exact block that drops nothing without a tool nobody carries fails before the first swing: a live run mined stone bare-handed, broke 4 blocks for 0 cobblestone and blamed the terrain ("no more reachable sources").
Wraps recovery-allowlisted ops for the low-health aborts; everything else runs unwrapped.
Session-free operation construction: every game:/client: capability whose factory needs no LLM session state, shared verbatim by the perform path (start) and the direct user-command runner (AiDirectOps) so both dispatch identically. module:/command:/macro: capabilities stay session-bound (the service's change tracking and catalog), and this method rejects them with the same "Join a world" or "no adapter" errors the old monolithic start produced. observation may be null - addon providers tolerate it exactly like a service that has not observed yet.
Detectable-movement policy scan over a serialized macro; returns a clear error or null.
Launches a macro under the shared executor and watches it as an operation. Static so the direct user-command runner (AiDirectOps via directOperation) supervises macros under the exact same detectable-movement restrictions and run tracking as the LLM path.

Completions for a positional shorthand's argument string.

.tools list: the capability families that hold something callable.

Outputs of every furnace-family recipe the client knows.
Families, then every real item: obtain and collect work out the route themselves.
Block families first, then every block a survival player can break and carry.
"hostiles" plus every mob type.
The first goto word: a coordinate, a direction for the relative form, or a saved waypoint of this world.
The second goto word: a coordinate, or a distance after a direction.
key= tokens for a capability's schema; after "key=" the enum values or true/false of that key.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTrade.ja.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTrade.ja.notes:
game:trade - villager and wandering-trader commerce as whole transactions.

{@code inspect} walks to a trader, opens it and reports every offer with its cost, result, remaining uses and whether the player can currently afford it - which is the information the model actually needs to choose. {@code trade} then executes N of one offer, selected either by index from that listing or by the item it produces, verifying each result against an applied server container update before taking the next one.

Locked and out-of-stock offers are refused up front with the reason rather than clicked at, and the operation never trades more than the offer's remaining uses allow. Ticks the open interaction may run before the trader is reported unreachable. Ticks one trade waits for its applied server confirmation. Ticks after selecting an offer before the result slot is expected to be filled. How far a trader may be and still be worth walking to. Ticks a waitRestock wait may run (2.5 minutes; villagers restock about twice a day). Vanilla job-site blocks a villager's profession hangs on, for reroll break+replace. The block goes back as the SAME type or the profession never re-links. Rerolling is only possible while the trader has never been traded with (every offer unused). Pure. The result stack taken and its inventory count at click time; a trade counts only when the gain is observed. Finds a trader, walks to it and opens its trade screen. How many of this stack's item the whole player inventory holds (components must match). A free slot or a mergeable partial stack: without one the result take is refused server-side. One reroll cycle: eligibility (never traded with), break the trader's job-site block with the verified dig loop, collect the dropped block item, place the SAME block back, then close so the trade re-opens on fresh offers. Null when the cycle finished and the caller should re-resolve the offer index. The nearest job-site block within 16 blocks of the trader. A live item drop of the block item within 8 blocks of the job site. A FAILED result carrying a machine-readable code, with the same cleanup as done(). "3x minecraft:emerald", the form a model can read back without a second lookup.

Text a right-click copies for the message.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTravelFa.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiTravelFa.notes:
Long-range travel: the retired AiNavigator's coarse routing, re-seated on the engine. A trip of more than 64 blocks chains {@link AiGoto#travel} legs instead of one unbounded walk: the remembered region graph (AiService's scoped observations, {@link AiRegions#route} — computed off-thread over immutable observations, the legacy CompletableFuture pattern) supplies coarse waypoints, and a hop longer than ~40 blocks is walked as sub-legs in its direction so no leg ever outgrows the engine's 48-block search box. With no remembered route the legs simply run straight at the target (the legacy bounded planner's keep-walking-toward-the-goal behavior).

Legacy semantics kept: waypoints and a {@code groundTarget} final target get the ±24 co-target adjustment ({@link AiGoto#walkableNear}, up preferred at each distance), waypoint arrival uses the caller's radius (sub-legs a forgiving ≥4), one overall deadline bounds the whole trip (each leg gets the remaining budget), a failed leg fails the trip, health ≤4 fails inside the leg, and cancel() releases every control. Completed legs hand off in the same tick; at most four immediate transitions run per tick. The legacy coarse-routing threshold: trips longer than this chain legs (squared distance). Sub-legs of a long hop stay well inside the engine's 48-block horizontal search box. A hop lands directly once it is inside the search box with margin. Strategy-selecting variant: every chained leg is planned with the caller's cost strategy. The ~40-block sub-target toward {@code head} from the live position (player height kept).

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiWorldRea.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiWorldRea.notes:
Bounded, never-throwing readers behind the deepest observe() surface: scoreboard sidebar, tab roster plus tab header/footer, boss bars, player vitals, and item component (NBT) data. Every reader runs on the client thread inside every observation, so each one is null-safe, capped, and swallows all component/HUD failures into empty results rather than failing the whole snapshot. All server-supplied text is untrusted world data: it is carried only as JSON string values, never interpreted as markup or instructions.
Visible scoreboard sidebar rows (team prefixes baked in), capped at 15.
Tab-list roster excluding the local player, capped at 64 entries of {name, prefix}.
Server-supplied tab-list header/footer text, each bounded to 1024 chars.
Active boss bars, capped at 8 entries of {title, progress}.
Experience, air, and armor. Health/hunger are already part of the base observation.
Short per-slot component digest for observation payloads, guaranteed to serialize to at most 512 chars by progressively trimming list fields and then dropping optional detail fields.
Full bounded component dump for inspect_item, packed into pages of at most ~6000 serialized chars. Page 0 carries the identity plus as many sections as fit; long sections (enchantments, lore, attribute modifiers, container contents, book pages) flow across pages as array slices. Book page texts are bounded to 640 chars each so roughly eight land per dump page, matching the established inspect_item paging; each bookPages slice carries its bookPageOffset. Every page is tagged untrusted. Requesting a page past the end returns an identity-only page with the total page count, which signals the end of the dump.
One try/catch per component: a single broken component must not hide the rest.
Trims list fields, then drops optional detail fields, until the summary fits its budget.
Greedy top-level-field packing; array sections split element-wise across page boundaries.
Mojang-named HUD fields with no public accessor (tab header/footer, boss event map). The mod stays deobfuscated at runtime, so the names are stable; a failed lookup simply yields empty reader results. Same established pattern as AutismCraftingHelper's recipe-book field.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/AiWorldSca.notes:

Nothing here knows the seed - a fortress is found because its nether bricks loaded, a blaze spawner because its block entity came in with them. Callers bound how often they ask (a full 12-chunk scan walks every section's palette once).
Chunk offsets within the radius, nearest first.
Matching blocks in loaded chunks around the player, nearest chunks first: at most {@code perChunk} from one chunk (a fortress fills hundreds of cells per chunk; a few per chunk tell where it runs) and {@code cap} in all.
Lava sources with open air over them, nearest first, at most {@code perChunk} from one chunk. A pool's surface is what a bucket and a portal cast reach; the nearest lava of a seed-free run was a lake sealed under rock twelve blocks up, no route led there, and the run failed with 35 thousand lava sources loaded.
True when the lava source at {@code pos} has open air over it.
The nearest matching block, or null.
Monster spawners in loaded chunks whose next spawn is {@code mobId} (e.g. minecraft:blaze), nearest first.
A classic spawner's configured mob id from its client-synced spawn data, or null.
Living mobs of a type within range of the player, nearest first.
The block id of a state, for predicates over several ids.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiA.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiA.notes:
The AI's hand. Every operation that needs to face something goes through one of these instead of writing setYRot/setXRot directly. Working turns apply the intended goal in one tick: aiming must not delay a break, placement or attack. CALM retains an eased survey turn and TELLY retains the turn its placement simulation models. The movement executor presses its keys against {@link #plannedYaw} while a turn is under way, so the legs never wait on the camera, and clicks are gated on the crosshair ray ({@link #aimingAt}), not on an angular tolerance.

This drives the REAL camera, not the silent-rotation holder. The AI is the player here - it is not hiding a correction behind a camera the user is also steering - so it never enters {@link autismclient.util.AutismKillAuraRotation}'s owner ladder and can never contend with KillAura, Scaffold or the auras for that single stream.

Opt-in exception ({@code aiSilentAim} setting, captured per op at start): {@link #silent} moves the instance onto the holder instead - the AI's LOWEST ladder rung, so every module outranks the op and the visible camera stays untouched. {@link #clear()} releases the holder back to the camera sweep.

Usage per operation: one instance, {@link #lookAt} the goal whenever it moves, {@link #tick} exactly once per client tick, and gate the actual click on {@link #aimingAt} - the crosshair ray, not an angular tolerance, is what the server re-derives from the rotation in the movement packet.

The camera never rests on an enderman: vanilla aggros one whose crosshair-stare lasts about five ticks, so a goal that would stare at one the op is not aiming at is applied with a small yaw offset instead ({@link #ENDERMAN_YAW_OFFSET}). The silent holder's envelopes stay independent of the real camera's purposeful turns. Surveying and block work. The default working speed for mining, building and navigation. Walking and combat tracking. Exact in one tick: jumps and bridge lines whose physics were planned on the exact heading. The build engine's exact working turn: the REAL camera is set to the goal in one linear step (no easing, any delta up to a full 180) so a placement click is aimed on the same tick it is dispatched.

The SILENT lane keeps the humanized envelope: {@code yawCap}/{@code pitchCap} stay at 72 degrees and the stream still steps through {@link AutismKillAuraRotation}, because a 180-degree packet snap is not a legitimate client shape. An op that needs the silent lane gets the humanized turn, not this real-camera exactness - only the camera branch reaches the goal in one tick. The bridger's hand ({@link AiBridger}): an even {@link AiBridger#TURN_CAP} a tick with no easing, a 180 back to the rim face in two ticks and forward again in two, exactly the turns its rollouts planned the clicks on. Real-camera per-tick ceiling of the eased turn (180 = exact). An even turn up to the cap every tick instead of the eased half-the-rest. Angular arrival band; the ray check is the real gate, this only reports convergence. Vanilla enderman stare-aggro range (the EnderMan follow distance, in blocks). Yaw offset (degrees) applied when the goal would stare at an enderman the op is not aiming at. The last real-camera step, for diagnostics (which aim held the camera when an enderman turned). The point the goal was solved for (lookAt(Vec3)), null for a bare rotation: tells an enderman aimed at from one behind the aim. The enderman this aim may stare at on purpose (a pearl hunt's provoke); -1 for none. Lets this aim stare at the given enderman (by entity id); -1 forbids it again. Aim path: real camera (default) or the silent-rotation holder (captured at op start). Aims the eye at a world point. Recompute every tick for a moving target. A point almost straight above or below the eye keeps the current yaw and only sets the pitch: its heading is set by a few hundredths of a block of body drift and flipped half a turn every time the body crossed it (the dig-down spin). The kept look lands in the point's block, or the point is in open air (a walk look): see lookAt(Vec3). Horizontal distance under which a point counts as straight above or below the eye. Selects the silent-rotation path for this instance's remaining lifetime (op-start capture). Drops the goal; the camera stays where the last step left it. One real-camera step toward the goal, pure for tests: eased (half the remaining angle), capped per tick, exact once within {@link #LAND_DEGREES}. A 90 degree turn takes about six ticks, a 180 about nine: a quick survey turn. Working speeds use a cap of 180 to reach their chosen goal immediately. One tick's turn at a speed: the linear bridger turn, else the eased one. Within this the camera lands exactly on the goal. The yaw this tick's {@link #tick} will leave the camera at: what the movement keys press against. src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiC.notes:
Persistent simplified chunk memory for long-range pathing: each visited chunk column is remembered as a 2-bit-per-block class band ({@link #AIR}/{@link #SOLID}/{@link #WATER}/ {@link #AVOID} - AVOID covers lava and the hazard blocks) over a bounded y-range, plus a small table of "notable" block identities (ores, chests, spawners and similar finds; the 2-bit classes deliberately carry no identity, so ordinary stone and dirt are never remembered by name). The store is advisory from the ground up:
  • Feed: {@link AiPathfinder.ClientGrid} publishes every live chunk copy it makes (cheap flag classification, same budget discipline - no extra world reads beyond the notable scan of solid cells).
  • Probe fallback: a grid probing an UNLOADED chunk serves memory cells flagged {@code cached} (SOLID as an opaque full block that is always NOT_DIGGABLE - the cache is never trusted enough to dig blind -, WATER as water, AVOID as lava, AIR as air). Live terrain always wins: the copy is dropped the tick the chunk loads for real.
  • The executor never commits an irreversible move into a cached-only cell (the {@code stillValid} provisional rule); walking through cached cells is fine because a mismatch just stalls and replans against fresh data.
  • Persistence: per-world region files (32x32 chunks each, GZIP) under the mod's config dir, written on the storage thread (interval + world change, never per-tick), loaded lazily per region on first touch. In-memory LRU caps the resident chunks; region files are capped and pruned oldest-first.

The shared instance is scoped to the current world+dimension by {@link #tickWorld} (called from the client tick loop; {@link #init} supplies the storage directory once). All packing, classification, band-union and codec logic is pure and headless-tested in AiChunkMemoryTest. Tallest remembered y-band per chunk column; an over-tall union re-bases on the freshest ingest. Resident chunk bands (LRU-evicted beyond this). Notable identities kept per chunk. Region files kept per world; oldest pruned beyond this. Notable exact-match block paths; anything ending in {@code _ore} also qualifies. One find result: position, 3D distance to the query origin, and cache provenance. One remembered chunk column band: 2-bit classes over [yLo, yLo+height), plus notables. A decoded region file (the codec's read side). The engine-wide shared store (world-scoped by {@link #tickWorld}). Supplies the persistence root once (the client initializer); without it the store is memory-only. The always-on client-tick hook: re-bases the shared store when the world/dimension changes (flushing the old scope) and schedules the interval save while dirty. Cheap when nothing changed: one reference comparison and one timestamp check per tick. The memory class of one snapshot cell's flag set: hazards and lava are AVOID, water is WATER, open is AIR, else SOLID. The notable-identity rule for {@code game:find}'s cached results (block id path). The 2-bit class at a y-major cell index. Packs one fresh band from a finished snapshot copy's flags (x-major source, y-major target). Publishes one freshly copied live chunk into memory. The fresh band overlays (and re-decides) whatever the chunk held before: mined-away notables vanish, new ones appear. Bands from different visits merge; an over-tall union re-bases on the freshest band. Merges the remembered band with a fresh ingest (fresh cells win; fresh notables re-decide). The advisory probe of one cell: the remembered class as a conservative {@code cached} probe (SOLID is never diggable; AVOID reads as lava), or UNLOADED when the cell was never remembered. Triggers the lazy region load on a miss, never disk I/O inline. Builds a snapshot copy of the remembered chunk for {@link AiPathfinder.ClientGrid}'s unloaded-chunk fallback: every remembered cell flagged CACHED, dig always NOT_DIGGABLE; cells outside the remembered band stay plain unloaded. Null when the chunk is unknown. Every remembered notable cell matching {@code idMatch} within {@code radius} (3D) of the origin. Merges live and cached find results (pure, headless-tested): live wins a duplicate cell, nearest-first order, capped at {@code limit}. Posts the dirty chunks to the storage thread (merged into their region files there). Storage thread: read-modify-write each touched region file (atomic replace), then prune. Lazily loads a region file on first touch; probes miss (advisory) until it lands. Caps region files per world, oldest last-modified first. Serializes one region (32x32 chunks): GZIP container, palette-shared notable ids. Parses one region file, strictly bounded (a corrupt file fails fast and is forgotten).

The decisions a run makes, measured from the outside (live tasks only, with {@link AiMotionAudit}):
  • every block the player breaks, with the step that broke it;
  • a dig that was started and left before the block broke (a change of mind, its progress thrown away);
  • a stare: the body and camera at rest on a block that is not being broken (time spent looking at nothing useful);
  • a backtrack: the body walked 4+ blocks away from a spot and came back to it (a route it went back on);
  • a gap: more ticks from one block breaking to the next dig moving than vanilla's held floor (the 5-tick gap, the start tick, the first progress tick), with what the run did meanwhile;
  • a flip: the camera left by {@link #FLIP_OUT} degrees or more and came back within {@link #FLIP_BACK} inside {@link #FLIP_TICKS} ticks (a turn started early and taken back; the motion audit's there-and-back is the coarse 25-degree version).
One "[AI] decide" line per event and a summary per operation. Break tick, first progress tick two ticks after the gap: vanilla's floor from one held break to the next. The counts of the operation the audit last closed (read by the gauntlets' lane reports). Held mining under way: a block with progress, or vanilla's 5-tick gap counting down between blocks. A small turn taken back: see the class comment. Bridging's flicks and a cap's look up are what they are.

The best line over {@code targets} from {@code eye}: the most targets met in turn, then the least turn from the camera at ({@code yaw}, {@code pitch}), then the widest margin. Null when no face of any target is in sight and reach.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiE.notes:
game:mine_area / game:dig — excavation on the engine: clear an axis-aligned box, or dig a shaped goal (tunnel/room/staircase), using the shared break controller (best durability-guarded carried tool, vanilla dig progress, applied server-removal proof, drop sweeps with inventory-delta accounting).

Rules, shared by both ops: top-down layers so the player is never buried; air skipped for free (re-issuing is idempotent); unbreakables recorded in {@code skipped}; any cell adjacent to lava is left standing and counted in {@code skippedLava}; the block under the player's feet is never dug without a floor beneath it; cells out of reach use the shared interaction goal; cells in unloaded chunks defer to a re-sweep (a missing chunk is transient) and are only recorded unreachable after no-progress passes; a failed break defers the same way and is only recorded break_failed after its per-cell attempt cap (transient break failures are common mid-dig). When no suitable hotbar tool remains above the durability floor, a verified backpack swap rescues the job, else the op FAILs with reason {@code TOOL_WORN} and {@code missing{tool:1}} (the AiProspect shape, so game:obtain re-crafts).

All geometry (box order, tunnel slices, room anchor, staircase steps, direction parse, lava adjacency, the cell sweep) is pure and headless-tested in AiExcavateTest.

Shape staircase: a descending 1-wide 2-high stepped tunnel from the player's feet toward targetY (required), direction like tunnel. Every excavation safety rule applies; the first unsafe cell (lava-adjacent, undiggable or fluid, no footing, persistent break failure) stops the descent early and reports the reached Y instead of continuing past it.

Optional {@code backfill} (default false): cells the dig loop broke are refilled behind the player's back with throwaway hotbar blocks via {@link AiBackfill} - best-effort, one per tick, only from bounded camera-idle branches; the result counts them as {@code backfilled}. Whether a cell on the dig path may only be broken with its proper tool: ores (their drop is the point) and blocks too hard to clear by hand. Snow, dirt and plain stone are just in the way: a snowy spawn refused every staircase because a snow layer drops nothing without a shovel. Reported skip reasons (also the machine-readable strings in skipped entries). Per-tick skip-scan budget (the ClientGrid fillRequests 750µs planning-slice precedent). Exclusive camera window for the backfill drain before a success report (see finishSuccess). No-dig-progress re-sweeps before deferred (unloaded) cells are given up as unreachable (~5s at 20 tps). Total break attempts per cell before break_failed is final (each AiBreakBlock run already retries its dig twice). The dig order for a box: top layer first (the player is never buried), each layer nearest-first around the anchor at that layer's height. Pure cell geometry. The dig order for a tunnel: slice-by-slice forward from the origin (the player's feet, own column included), each slice's cross-section centered horizontally around the axis, top-down then nearest-first so the player stands in the previously dug slice. The dig order for a descending staircase (game:dig shape staircase): one 2-high column per step, head cell then feet cell, each column one lower than the last so the player can walk down and back up, ending with the feet cell of the last column at targetY. The player's own column leads (already air in practice), and the head cell digs first so the player is never buried. The feet level a partial staircase has safely reached after {@code cleared} leading columns stand open. Room extents anchored feet-level and centered horizontally: [minX, minY, minZ, maxX, maxY, maxZ]. A direction name to its unit step; null when unknown. The cardinal step nearest a yaw (0=south, 90=west, 180=north, 270=east). Lava lookup for the adjacency rule (pure seam, shared with game:replace). A cell is lava-adjacent when any of its 6 neighbors is lava; such cells are left standing. The resumable cell sweep, pure and headless-tested. Walks the dig order with a cursor; cells that probe unloaded DEFER to a later pass instead of being skipped on sight: a missing chunk is transient - the player working the box loads it, and a cell judged unreachable early routinely becomes reachable once its neighbours are dug open (the live "tunnel with backfill" failure: one cell failed the whole op while its same-chunk neighbours dug fine). {@link #retry} bounds the wait: passes that dig nothing only repeat so many times before the sweep gives up (the box is then genuinely outside the server's view distance) and hands the cells back for skip recording, so an unreachable box still fails instead of spinning to the op deadline. Armed so the first drain always retries once: a one-tick miss must never fail the op. A cell that probed unloaded: held for the next pass, not yet a skip. The cells still deferred after a refused retry (the caller records them as skips). At pass end: starts a new pass over just the deferred cells and returns true. False when nothing is deferred, or when maxDryPasses consecutive passes dug nothing (the remaining chunks are not loading; waiting longer would only burn the op deadline). Per-cell break-attempt budget, pure and headless-tested. A failed break is usually transient (aim/dig desync, or a stance that only opens once neighbours are dug - the live "tunnel with backfill" failure: one cell's break_failed killed the op while its 9 siblings dug fine), so the op defers and re-sweeps the cell. The budget is per cell because a re-attempt costs a whole approach+dig: the sweep's pass-based no-progress bound (100 cheap probe passes) would be far too slow for these expensive retries. Records a failed break on the cell: true while another attempt is allowed (defer it). game:mine_area: clear the box between the two corners (or first corner + extents). game:dig: a shaped goal - a tunnel from the player's feet, or a room anchored at

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiF.notes:
The last line against a fall nobody planned: while an AI operation drives the body, a tick whose keys would carry it off an edge into a drop that hurts (more than three blocks onto anything but water, or into water it names a trap) gets a real sneak, and vanilla's edge clamp keeps it on the block. Moves that leave the ground on purpose (jumps, walk-off descends, bridge runs, pillars, climbs) prove their own landings and are left alone, and so is any tick that jumps.

What it caught (schematic build, 2026-10-06): a body still carrying a telly bridge's speed when the keys went up, a slide during a replan, a step off a slab: thirteen falls, 1 to 13 damage each, every one from an edge the route never meant to leave. Ticks simulated ahead: the sneak must be down before the tick the box would leave the edge (it acts a tick late). Vanilla's fall damage starts past three blocks of fall distance. Moves whose ground ticks walk off an edge on purpose: a jump's run-up (the press comes a tick or two later) and a descend's walk-off. A rise (jump-up, step-up, dug ascend, pillar) only ever leaves the ground with the jump key, which the guard never touches: a dug rise whose body slid off the tower's edge mid-dig fell five blocks while it was still on this list. An AI operation is driving the body this tick (travel, a build, a break): the guard is armed. The executor's move under way this tick. A telly bridge run leaves the ground on purpose (its sprint jumps are rollout-proven); a legit one walks backward and is clamped like a walk. The caller walks off this tick on purpose, with a water clutch armed (a crystal tower's way down, a pillar top out of a dragon's cloud): the guard lets this tick and the next go. Held at the edge, the crystal run's step-off failed, and it went on to the next cage across the air at the tower's height. Water the caller knows no body gets out of (a schematic's pool walled in by a rim too high to climb out over): a fall into it counts as one that hurts. Refreshed while the caller drives the body. A stalled teardown walk let go of the sneak while the body still slid at a temporary block's edge, and it dropped three blocks into 16773's roof pool, with the last temporary blocks out of reach for good. The guard held the body at an edge this tick or the last (a walk that keeps pushing there would jump off next). Ticks the guard held the body at an edge since the game started (fixtures report it). Input hook, after SafeWalk: only ever adds sneak. Whether the input hook would add Sneak to these keys while an AI operation drives the body (the edge rule only; the End's void and magma rules are separate). Movement planners that never want the guard to take over their walk reject such keys, and the headless simulator applies the same rule to stay in step with the game. These keys (and then none) carry the body off its footing into a fall that hurts or ends in lava. These keys (jump on the first tick only, then the keys let go) carry the body more than 64 blocks below where it stands within 90 ticks: in the End, the void (a crystal tower's clutch descent drops 45 at most). A ladder, vine or scaffolding at the feet or the head catches the body (vanilla's onClimbable).

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiG.notes:

The engine plans async off-thread and walks, sprints, jumps, descends (soft landings priced in), digs tunnels, pillars and bridges as a single continuous movement list; the client thread only executes it. Segment boundaries are spliced with zero idle ticks (the next segment is planned as soon as the current one starts), and a stalled movement escalates replan → blacklist → FAILED. The replan carries the never-loop guardrail: the stalled move's TYPE is withheld from the new plan (a sprint-tier exclusion degrades to its walking tier), a second consecutive stall on the same type and target cell fails honestly, and real progress re-enables every excluded type.

Also the reusable delegation seam: {@link #travel(BlockPos, double, boolean, boolean, boolean, int)} is the engine travel primitive other ops (game:mine, future chop/collect approaches) compose. A momentary click ray while passing a stance is not a stable handoff to the builder. How many travels in a row (within 30 s of each other) found no route at all from this very cell. The shared prefix of the wedged-start failure text (AiSeek/AiMine match on it). Recovery edits obey the same placement authorization and protected cells as planned scaffolding. Called only for a grounded, collision-free body; an empty centre can still overhang its support. Ordinary rim walk-offs keep their route; only a tall shape needs early centring. The legacy navigator's co-target adjustment for ground targets: when the target cell itself is not walkable, the nearest walkable cell within {@code range} — LATERAL neighbours at the target's own level first (a face-level stance with line of sight, e.g. in front of an ore wall), then up/down scanning outward with up preferred at each distance (a spot under a tree or inside a build column resolves to its standing surface). Returns {@code target} unchanged when it is walkable or nothing nearby is. Live walkability of one cell through the engine's own probe + walkable rule. The stabilization steering scan, pure for tests: the nearest breathable cell (per the caller's predicate) within ~2 blocks horizontally and -1..+2 vertically of the feet cell, or null. A drowning or lava-swimming player steers toward it instead of treading in place under a ceiling. The game:goto operation factory: parses args and delegates to {@link #travel}. The movement knobs a goto call may set on top of the capability flags; every default is the fast, legal vanilla behaviour. -Dautism.ai.snapshotGrid=true brings back the copied-chunk planner view (the live one is the default). A leg whose goal got no closer in this long is going round in circles and fails (the owner moves on). A travel whose goal can move while it runs (Baritone's PathingBehavior fed by a process every tick): {@link #retarget} keeps the running path while its end is still in the new goal and replans from where the player stands otherwise, so a job that mines block after block keeps one path session instead of starting a fresh route per block. A persistent travel holds at the goal ({@link #atGoal}) instead of finishing, until the owner retargets or cancels it. When the last no-route terrain dump was written (one per ten seconds). The owner starts a new leg of its own: the moves walked before it count toward no loop. Paused: no movement keys and no path, until unpaused (the owner is breaking something in place). Held: the path runs (planned, turned to, its blocks dug) but the body does not move, until released. As {@link #holdPosition(boolean)}, but a plain walk into a cell {@code keeps} accepts still goes. The cell a move kept stalling into when this travel failed on it, or null. Shuts a cell out of this travel's plans (the owner remembers where earlier travels got stuck). Moves left on a route that reaches the goal, or -1 (partial or none). Moves left on the route being walked, partial or not, or -1 (none). A pause would take hold this tick: no move under way that must finish first (a jump, a placement in flight). The cell the route being walked ends in, or null (none). The still-solid cells the route digs in its running move and the next one. The cells the rest of the route being walked stands on. Where the camera should rest once at the path's end (given its last cell), for the last walk steps; see AiMovementExecutor. How far below the feet the owner is headed (0 when it is not going down), for the shaft cap rule; see AiMovementExecutor. Restricts tools only for source states whose drops the owner's mining task needs. The job travel: persistent, every capability on (dig, pillar, bridge, backpack restocks, parkour) and the standard tick pricing. The goal is the owner's; {@code anchor} only names the trip. {@link #session}, with movement options (the stronghold's bearing legs keep out of water when they can). Hands a travel's walk a look and a click for work on the way (the schematic printer places as it walks). A neutral mob (zombified piglin, piglin, enderman) that shows no sign of being after anyone. The destination in any of the forms a caller may give: absolute x,y,z; x,z alone (the nearest standable height near that column); dx,dy,dz offsets from the player's feet; direction plus distance (north/south/east/west, or forward/back/left/right relative to the camera yaw); a saved waypoint name; an entity id; a player name. Block offset for a direction word, pure for tests: compass words are absolute, forward/back/left/right follow the yaw (0 = south, 90 = west). Blocks worth opening on arrival (goto-and-use): storage, stations and utility menus. Pure so the set is pinned headless; everything else is just walked to. Wraps a travel op: on arrival, when the destination block is an interactable station ({@link #arrivalInteractable}), runs one verified interact leg and reports ITS outcome, so "go there and open it" is one call. Arrival at any other block reports the travel result. Engine travel primitive: autonomous continuous navigati

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiG.notes:
Global per-chunk revision counters, bumped on the client thread whenever the server applies a block change (single block or section batch) or a chunk unloads. {@link AiPathfinder.ClientGrid} snapshots record the revision at copy time and treat a chunk whose revision moved as a never-copied chunk again (drop the copy, re-queue the request, probe pending), so a mid-plan world change re-plans against fresh terrain instead of a stale snapshot.

The read side is one map lookup plus one volatile int per probe; bumps are uncontended CAS increments. {@link #reset()} runs on world change (AiService's evidence reset seam): surviving grids hold revisions that no longer match and simply re-copy.

The table is bounded to {@link #MAX_REVISIONS} counters: past the cap a bump evicts the oldest half by stamp age. That needs no positional knowledge and is safe because a missing entry reads as a changed revision, so a grid re-copies the chunk; it never sees stale data. Cap on remembered counters (package-visible for tests); a bump past it halves the table. Client thread: a server-applied block change invalidated this block's chunk. Client thread: everything this chunk held is suspect (section batch or chunk unload). The chunk's current revision; the current reset stamp for a chunk that never changed. Halves the table by stamp age. Every chunk unload used to leave a permanent entry, so a long session leaked one counter per ever-touched chunk; stamps increase globally, which makes the oldest half the stalest with no position lookups. Losing an entry only makes {@link #revision(long)} report a change, and grids answer a change by re-copying: safe. Test seam: counters currently remembered. Drops every counter (world change, tests); live grids re-copy on their next probe.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiJ.notes:
Collision-proved jump controls for approaches which cannot share the flight's heading: tunnel exits, angled single-block landings and roofed momentum run-ups. Every recorded input is an ordinary key combination and camera facing; planning and live execution replay the same vanilla physics.
Ground preparation opposes the actual incoming velocity, including a backward or sideways approach. Below a walking acceleration, release the keys so braking cannot oscillate across zero.
A complete remaining-flight proof, also used against live position/velocity before dispatching keys.
Broad fallback, used only after the cheap straight jump fails. Starts are reachable along supported ground.
Re-solve from the real body at the run-up start, retaining the planned corridor heading.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiJ.notes:
Finds a vanilla jump from one footing onto another by simulating it ({@link AiPhysics}), the way a parkour player tries a jump in their head: face the landing, run up as far as the takeoff footing allows, leave on the tick whose arc comes down on the landing's centre, and let go of forward part-way through the arc when even the earliest takeoff flies long. The landing distance grows with the run-up and shrinks with an earlier release, so both are found by bisection (a handful of arcs per candidate, not a brute-force sweep). Because the simulation runs against the real collision boxes, diagonal jumps, slab and fence landings, head hitters, drops onto lower footing and ice approaches all fall out of the same code path instead of needing their own rules. {@link #maxReach}/{@link #minReach} are the flat-world envelope the planner uses to skip hopeless candidates without simulating them. When a roof or corridor prevents a straight approach, {@link AiJumpManeuver} also proves separate run-up, head-hitter warm-up, takeoff and air-turn controls. Its longer runway and every flight tick are collision checked, then replayed against the live body's real state.

The executor reuses the same simulation live: {@link #takeoff} picks this tick's input from the player's real state (jump now, or run one more tick, with a strafe correction when the approach is off the line) and {@link #steer} does the same for the air control while the arc is in flight. Longest run-up examined inside the takeoff footing (ticks); the body leaves a one-cell footing long before. Longest run-up the live takeoff examines from wherever the player stands (ticks). Longest flight the live air control and the reach envelope examine (ticks). A planned jump never flies longer than this, and one this far below its landing is a fall. Kept shallow on purpose: the bisection reads a failed arc's distance where it was cut, and a deep cut lets a short arc drift on past the landing and read as long. A slime landing bounces and never settles inside the window, so it is never a landing. Landings whose footprint hangs over the landing cell by more than this are not landings. The planner offers a jump only when its predicted landing sits at least this far inside the cell. A touchdown this far below the landing surface is still on it (the lower step of a stair, a carpet on a slab). "Hold forward for the whole arc" as a release tick. The horizontal speed a sprinting approach carries into the takeoff cell. A solved jump: the yaw to face, how many ticks to run before pressing jump, whether to sprint, the flight tick forward is released at ({@link #HOLD} = never), and the predicted touchdown. Whether the plan leans on the speed the body brings into the takeoff cell (else it starts from a standstill). Ticks from entering the takeoff cell to touchdown (a step back for the run-up, the run-up, the press, the flight). The walk back to {@link #startX}/{@link #startZ} before the run (0 when the run starts where the body stands). The same plan translated by a cell offset (the geometry cache stores plans by their takeoff cell). The executor's takeoff decision: run this many more ticks (0 = press jump now) with this strafe, for this predicted margin. The executor's air-control decision: the forward/strafe to hold for the rest of the arc, for this predicted margin. Where an arc ended: the final state, flight ticks, whether it settled on ground, the release tick, the distance along the line, the landing margin (-1 off the landing), and whether it struck a wall or a ceiling on the way (then the landing distance no longer grows with the run-up and bisection cannot be trusted). The arc chosen for a run-up: its run ticks and the arc itself. The jump line: the origin the run-ups are measured from, the unit direction, and the distance to the landing centre. @param fromSurface the takeoff footing's top (the standing y), toSurface the landing's top @param approachSpeed the horizontal speed the body carries into the takeoff cell along the jump line (0 = standstill) @param allowSprint whether sprinting is available (food); the solver still tries the walking jump How far behind the takeoff cell's centre, straight back along the jump line, a body can stand on the takeoff's footing with some of the footing left under it (0 when there is no room). A body stands here: footing at exactly this height under its box, nothing in the box. A sprinting jump that lands safely beats a walking one; otherwise the larger landing margin wins. The run-up states under {@code run} from {@code start} (index = ticks run), ending where the footing ends or at {@code maxRun}. The arc that comes down nearest the landing's centre over the run-up ticks and the forward release: the landing distance grows with the run-up, so bisect the run-up between the shortest and the longest held arc; when even the shortest flies long, bisect the release tick of the earliest takeoff instead. About eight arcs per candidate. A held arc may be requested by bisection, the obstruction check, and the exhaustive scan. Whether the longest or the shortest held arc strikes something before it comes down. Every run-up tick (up to 16) with a few forward releases; the deepest landing wins, and a comfortable one ends the scan. Bisects the forward-release tick of a long arc until its landing sits nearest the centre; the held arc when nothing improves. Presses jump from {@code takeoff}, flies holding {@code air} until {@code coastAfter} flight ticks have passed and coasting after, and reports where the body came to rest (or fell past the landing level). Null when the press never leaves the ground (cooldown, a ceiling at the feet). How safely a touchdown stands: the footprint's margin inside the floor at the landing's level (a side whose neighbouring cell is more of that floor counts a block further). A touchdown that hangs over an edge is judged where its momentum takes it: running on along the flight's heading when the floor goes

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiL.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiL.notes:
The planner's view of the loaded world, read live from the client's chunk cache on the planner thread (Baritone's BlockStateInterface) instead of copied chunk by chunk first. The copy was the bottleneck of every route: a dig search into stone asked for chunks faster than 4 ms a tick could copy them and ran out of budget before it saw the ore.

Everything a probe needs that depends only on the block state is computed once per state and cached; break times come from a tool snapshot ({@link #tools}) and are cached per state too, so picking up an item or a new tool never throws terrain away. Section reads race the network thread exactly like Baritone's do: a torn read is a wrong cell in one plan, which the executor's per-tick revalidation catches; a null read reports the cell unloaded.

Unloaded chunks fall back to the advisory chunk memory (never diggable, like before), and the grid feeds that memory from the live chunks around the player ({@link #feedMemory}). A falling stack taller than this over a cell makes the cell undiggable (the refill loop would run on). State facts that never change for a given block state (cached globally by state id). Tool pricing for one hotbar snapshot: best break ticks per state, cached. Replaces the tool snapshot. Only a change a dig price can see (another item, enchantments, the worn floor, haste) bumps the revision and so re-prices later searches; stack counts never do. Uses the executor's source-specific drop policy when pricing route clearance. Search abort signal: moves only with the tool pricing, never with block changes (reads are live). The live block state, or null when the chunk is not loaded (or a racing read came back empty). Break ticks for a solid cell: require its harvesting tool, price it, then check fluids and falling blocks. A lit portal block beside the cell: the cell is its frame (see {@code ClientGrid.portalFrame}). Water above or on a side: the hole floods (ClientGrid.digSafe's rule; water below cannot flow up). The falling-block flag of the live cell (for moves that must not dig out from under a hanging stack). probeCell's rules, minus everything position-dependent (dig safety and pricing live in {@link #digTicks}). Same item, enchantments and worn flag in every slot: nothing a dig price reads changed. A source that defeats two travel/extract attempts is blacklisted; the op fails only when no reachable sources remain, reporting "no more reachable sources (X of Y)".

Travel and drop collection are delegated to {@link AiGoto#travel} legs — the exact seam the integration spec recommends for chop/collect approaches too.

Tool upkeep ({@link ToolUpkeep}): while a suitable hotbar tool above the durability floor exists the Digger's own selection stands; with none, ONE backpack→hotbar swap rescues the job; with no suitable tool anywhere the op FAILs with reason {@code TOOL_WORN} and {@code missing{tool:1}} instead of continuing bare-handed.

Optional {@code backfill} (default false): cells the extraction loop broke are refilled behind the player's back with throwaway hotbar blocks via {@link AiBackfill} - best-effort, one per tick, only from camera-idle branches, never slowing the job; the result counts them as {@code backfilled}. The op used to launch this only after a block was fully done and stood "Comparing source routes" for up to 3 seconds between every two breaks; called at extraction start instead, the search overlaps travel+extraction+collection and the next target is ready the tick the last drop lands. Fresh candidates only: the cell being mined was already removed when it was picked, and matchesAt re-validates the choice live at pickup anyway. Drops near the broken cell become the collection queue (AiChop's 8-block sweep). Ore against water or lava cannot be dug to without breaching it (the planner refuses fluid boundaries), so it is not a candidate at all: a live iron trip under a frozen river spent 30 s of replans on each such block before blacklisting it. Sets this tick's aim goal; the single step is taken by the extraction branch. The upkeep check for the current target (ToolUpkeep decision): while a suitable hotbar tool above the durability floor exists, the Digger's own best-tool selection stands; with none, ONE backpack→hotbar swap rescues the job; with no suitable tool anywhere, FAIL with reason TOOL_WORN and missing{tool:1} (the AiProspect shape). src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiP.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiP.notes:
The AI's own A* pathfinding engine core, implemented natively for this mod: goals as functions, movements priced in ticks, an off-thread planner over snapshot grids, zero-idle segment splicing and an escalating stall ladder (the classic block-game pathing architecture, built from scratch here).

Everything outside {@link ClientGrid} is PURE: no Minecraft construction, no world access, so the whole engine (move legality, cost model, A*, segment splicing, stall ladder, and the async two-segment overlap driver) is headless-tested in AiEngineTest against synthetic grids.

Design invariants:

  • Goals are functions ({@link Goal#isInGoal} + {@link Goal#heuristic}), never fixed cells.
  • Costs are TICKS, so walking, sprinting, sprint-jumping, digging, pillaring and bridging unify in one A*.
  • The planner runs off the client thread against a snapshot {@link Grid}; a null probe means "copy pending" and only ever defers a search round, never blocks the game.
  • Movements carry their world edits ({@link Movement#cellsToBreak}/{@link Movement#cellsToPlace}) so the executor mines/tunnels/pillars/bridges AS PART OF the movement, never as a detour.
  • Legit-only: no falls >3 unless the landing is proven soft, no step-ups above the 1.25 vanilla jump apex (full-block rise max 1.0), no teleports/clips/fly anywhere.
  • Never trample: no airborne-landing move (descends, dig-down drops, gap jumps, sprint-jumps) lands on farmland and no jump-in-place move (JUMP_UP_1, PILLAR) — nor the bunnyhop — takes off from it — vanilla {@code FarmlandBlock.fallOn} converts it to dirt past a 0.5 fallDistance. Walking and auto-stepping onto or across farmland stays legal (a same-level approach never falls further than the 1/16-block surface lip, far under the threshold).
One immutable cell snapshot. {@code breakTicks} is the best-hotbar-tool break time INCLUDING the vanilla post-break cooldown, or {@link #NOT_DIGGABLE} when the cell must never be broken (unbreakable, block entity, fluid inside, lava in any of the 6 neighbors — water adjacency stays allowed — or a falling block anywhere directly above, unless the cell itself is the top of that falling column; the dig-safety rules are folded in by whoever builds the probe). {@code door} marks a closed wooden door or fence gate: collision-closed, but enterable via the DOOR interact move (open doors probe plain passable and walk like air). {@code slabStair}/{@code farmland} carry the block identity the landing rules need: gap jumps never take off from slabs or stairs (full footing only), never take off from farmland for ANY jump (JUMP_UP_1 and PILLAR land back on the takeoff cell) and never land on farmland (every airborne landing past the 0.5 fallDistance threshold tramples it to dirt — descends, dig-down drops, parkour). {@code ice} marks the slippery ice family (ice/packed/blue/frosted): never a parkour landing either, because an ice touchdown out-slides the two proven overshoot cells. {@code soulSand} marks soul sand, the 0.4-speed floor: the flat travel family pays the crawl multiplier and the bunnyhop takeoff is refused. {@code cached} marks a probe served from the chunk memory (AiChunkMemory) rather than live or freshly copied terrain: the planner may route through it, but the executor's revalidation treats the cell as provisional and never commits an irreversible move into it. No portal (the common case). Compatibility: no thorns (sweet berry bushes were a hazard before they became a priced passage). The four immutable cached-memory probes (never trust the cache enough to dig blind). A plain full block (top 1.0 = 16 sixteenths) with the given best-tool break time. A closed wooden door or fence gate: collision-closed, but pathable via the DOOR interact move. Slab/stair block identity (parkour takeoffs require full-block footing). Farmland block identity (never an airborne landing - it tramples - and never a jump takeoff). Ice-family block identity (never a parkour landing: the slide outruns the overshoot proof). Soul-sand block identity: the 0.4-speed floor - the flat travel family pays the crawl multiplier and the bunnyhop is refused outright (a damped takeoff lands the planned arc short). Sweet berry bush at the feet: walkable at a slow, priced crawl (a heart of damage on contact), never a jump landing or a sprint. A nether portal, end portal or end gateway: stepping in leaves the dimension (priced, never forbidden: a route may end there). Served from the chunk memory: provisional until a live probe replaces it. A cobweb: open to walk into, yet it arrests a fall (landing multiplier 0) with no fluid or hazard, which no other block does. A body touching one moves a quarter of its input a tick across and a twentieth up or down, its speed dropped every tick (WebBlock): no jump gets through and a fall through one sinks for seconds. What hurts (or sends off) a body whose box merely touches it: fire, a wither rose, powder snow, a berry bush, lava, a portal, and a cactus's side (the one hazardous floor 15/16 tall; magma and a campfire only hurt what stands on them). A honey block (the one 15/16-high floor that softens a fall to a fifth): x0.4 speed and half a jump on it. A slime block (the one full-cube floor that takes the whole fall): walking on it drags, landing on it bounces. How much slower than plain ground walking over this floor is (soul sand and honey x0.4, slime's drag). Cell source for the planner. Contract: returns the probe, or null when the cell's chunk copy is still pending (planner defers; the caller's client thread fills requests in time-boxed slices). Synthetic grids never return null. Never called from the game thread by the engine. Changes invalidate in-flight calculations; immutable fixture grids keep zero. The cell's collision shape id ({@link AiShapes}) for the physics simulator, or {@link AiShapes#PENDING} while the cell's copy is still being made. src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiP.notes:
A vanilla-accurate player movement simulator, pure and headless-tested, so the planner can try a jump before the player does and the executor can steer by prediction. One {@link #step} is one client tick of {@code LivingEntity.aiStep} + {@code travel} + {@code Entity.move} for a walking or airborne player: input impulse (x0.98, x0.3 sneaking) rotated by the yaw and scaled by the friction-influenced ground speed (0.1 x 0.216/friction^3, x1.3 sprinting) or the air speed (0.02, 0.026 sprinting); the jump (0.42 up, +0.2 forward when sprinting, ten-tick cooldown); the axis-separated collision sweep with the 0.6 step-up; gravity and drag (y: -0.08 then x0.98; horizontal x0.91, x block friction on the ground); block speed factors (soul sand, honey) and the slime bounce; a cobweb's or berry bush's hold on the next move. Water, climbing and elytra are out of scope: the engine's own moves handle those.

Verified against the community-measured constants: walking 0.2158 b/t (4.317 b/s), sprinting 0.2806 b/t, jump apex 1.2522, sprint-jump reach a little over four blocks edge to edge. The body's pose when the room around it forces one (vanilla's updatePlayerPose): standing, crouching, crawling. A read-only, per-forecast view; never moves the live body or changes its keys. The collision world: the boxes a query box may hit, plus the per-block surface properties the physics reads. Effective ground movement attribute; pure fixtures retain vanilla's base speed. Every collision box intersecting the query (world coordinates). Block friction under the body (0.6 stone, 0.98 ice, 0.8 slime). The block speed factor of the block the body stands in/on (1.0 normal, 0.4 soul sand and honey). True when landing on this block bounces (slime). The share of the fall a landing on this block returns upward (1.0 slime, 0.75 bed, 0 everything else). The block jump factor of the block the body stands in/on (0.5 honey, 1.0 everything else). Climbing changes vanilla velocity; a dry-air jump proof cannot cross this feet cell. What holds a body whose move swept through {@code box} (vanilla's entityInside effects): {@link #WEB} for a cobweb, {@link #BUSH} for a sweet berry bush, 0 for nothing. A world without either answers 0 (the default). Whether {@link #stuck} can answer anything but 0 here (asked every tick first: most worlds hold nothing). Lava is traversable by the collision solver, but never by a safe movement proof. Water changes vanilla drag and gravity; dry jump proofs must not cross it. Contact or landing damage which collision geometry alone cannot represent. Damage from touching the cell at body height (fire, a berry bush, cactus), not from standing on it: magma, pointed dripstone and a shrieker hurt only underfoot. Read as a hazard beside the body, a stalagmite next to a dug step stalled the walk to the lava in a dripstone cave, again and again, until the run made no progress. Damage from standing on the cell (magma, pointed dripstone, a shrieker), read in the row under the feet. Fire there is no floor: it burns in a dip the body walks over at the level above. Read as a hazard, a fire in a one-deep dip at a diagonal's corner refused the step every tick while the planner kept choosing it, and the run was cut as a loop. An optional proof that this whole dry-flight sweep contains no relevant hazards. Swept standing body and feet with a steering margin: fluids and damaging contact. Both hazardous lava and water invalidate a flight simulated with dry-air physics. The first cell {@link #lavaBetween} objects to, as {x, y, z, 1 for a contact hazard / 0 for lava}, or null. A cell the body's box already overlaps at the start of the step: touching it again is no new harm, and refusing it kept a body standing in fire from every step out (a bed's blast lit the cell under the player, and it burnt in place). Whether the body's box at the end of the step (with the sweep's margin) still meets the cell. The holds of {@link World#stuck}: a cobweb (WebBlock: x0.25 across, x0.05 up and down) and a sweet berry bush (x0.8, x0.75). One tick of input. forward/strafe are -1..1 (strafe positive = left), yaw in degrees (0 = south, 90 = west). The body: feet position, velocity, ground contact and the jump cooldown, plus vanilla's main supporting block (the block under the feet nearest the body's position, kept from the last move; {@link #NO_SUPPORT} when unknown or in the air): friction, bounce and the slime drag are read from its column, not from the block under the centre. {@code sprintCut}: the last move hit a wall and what was left of it went more than 8 degrees off the keys' direction (or nowhere), which makes vanilla drop the sprint at the start of the next tick (no sprint speed, no sprint-jump boost that tick). {@code stuck}: the last move swept through a cobweb or a berry bush ({@link World#stuck}), so the next move is scaled by its hold and the speed is dropped (vanilla's stuckSpeedMultiplier). Immutable; step returns a new one. A body in a pose that nothing holds. The live body, including the old crouch state LocalPlayer reads before refreshing its keys. The first simulated tick retains that slowdown; subsequent ticks resolve the room's pose. The hold on a live body: a cobweb or berry bush its box is in (the end of its last move; vanilla sweeps the move). The same body at rest where it is (its pose and hold kept). A body at rest on the ground carries vanilla's resting fall velocity (gravity, then drag): that is what keeps it in ground contact every tick. One client tick. Placement forecast only: retain native crouch speed/pose, but see the fall beyond its edge stop. LocalPlayer.isHorizontalCollisionMinor, given the move as the collision left it: the body still went within 8 degrees of where the keys push (sliding along a wall at a shallow angle). Head-on (next to no movement left) is not minor. Vanilla's findSupportingBlock: of the blocks whose collision reaches the thin layer under the feet, the one whose middle is nearest the body

The support face comes from the client's own {@link AutismFaceScan} (the same solver the Scaffold uses, so partial blocks, self-occlusion and the pitch cap are all already handled), the camera gets there through {@link AiAim}'s humanized sweep, and the click only goes out on the tick the crosshair ray actually lands on the support.

One instance per placement site; {@link #begin} resets it. Every gameplay operation that has to put a block down - crafting stations, bridging, structures, portal frames - shares this instead of writing its own aim-and-click. Ticks a single placement may spend before it is abandoned to the caller's recovery. Client ticks a placed block must survive before the placement counts as confirmed. Rays one face scan may spend; the scan resumes where it stopped on the next tick. Face scans in a row that found nothing before the cell is given up. A portable container is selected by its entire stack, never merely by its colour. Combat speed for the aim: a shield block racing the next arrow. Targets a new cell. {@code item} must have a block form or the placement fails at once. One exact owned stack. Its placement is dispatched once and is never retried after uncertainty. Why the last placement failed, in a form a tool result can report verbatim. One client tick of the place attempt. Call at most once per tick. Releases the aim goal; the caller's camera is left wherever the sweep reached. Where a placement stands, for a caller that gives up on it first: clicked or not, and why the last scan found no face. Rays a one-call reachability check may spend: the whole scan at once. Whether a support face for {@code target} can be clicked from where the eye is now: one full scan, no split budget. A caller choosing among spots asks this first: tried one at a time, each impossible spot took a dozen empty scans (eight table spots in a dug hole, four and a half seconds standing still). The cobwebs and berry bushes among the cells whose shape was read (their hold, see {@link #stuck}).

The raw surface material id of a cell (the planner's slime-pad scan).

allowInventory mid-travel restock: the engine's pause-based pull from the backpack (player inventory slots 9-35) when the hotbar runs dry. Two pure decision seams choose WHAT to pull ({@link #chooseConstructionSlot} for throwaway building blocks; the tool case is ToolUpkeep's existing Swap decision) and WHERE it lands ({@link #chooseDestination}), and one tick-driven, verified state machine performs the swap: at most one container click per tick, stationary (the owning executor holds every key neutral while the machine runs), confirmed against the applied server inventory revision exactly like the AiEquip/AiSmelt click-confirmation pattern.

Discipline: at most one restock per {@link #COOLDOWN_NANOS} (the machine waits the remainder out before clicking); a refused or unconfirmed swap (non-empty cursor, revision timeout) is not replayed after sending; an up-front refusal is retried once before the machine fails (a placement that cannot happen stalls the move and escalates the replan ladder; a dig with no tool anywhere continues bare-handed).

Everything except the production {@link Slots} bridge is headless-tested (AiRestockTest): the choosers are pure functions and the machine runs on injected slot/revision/clock seams. At most one restock per two seconds (the classic allowInventory pacing). Ticks a click may stay unconfirmed before it counts as a failed swap. An up-front refusal is retried once; an unconfirmed sent swap is never replayed. Planks' worth of wood a running job has budgeted for its crafts (the tech tree's sticks, table and fuel), and until when: the engine never builds with that wood nor crafts it into building planks. Pillars of planks up a tree and bridges on the way to the ore spent the ladder's sticks, a tree trip back up from the mine every ore. Holds {@code planks} for the next few seconds; the job refreshes it every tick it runs. 0 lets go. The wood held for crafting now, in planks: a running job's budget, never less than the replacement kit's. Wood the engine may build with, in planks (a log is four): what the bag holds above the reserve. The bag's wood in planks: planks, four a log. The replacement kit, kept whatever job runs: the wood for a crafting table and a pickaxe's sticks, and the cobblestone for a stone pickaxe. Without it, pillars, bridges and furnaces spent the last planks and stone, the pickaxe broke, and the AI stood in a hole with nothing to make another one from. Creative keeps nothing (its items never run out). Planks the replacement kit keeps: sticks for one pickaxe unless two are held, a table unless one is carried. Cobblestone the replacement kit keeps (0 in creative). Stone-tool material (cobblestone, cobbled deepslate, blackstone) the job still crafts with, and until when. Stone-tool material held for crafting now: a running job's budget, never less than the replacement kit's. Keep an iron pick's last strikes for ores a stone pick cannot harvest. Stone-tool material, the kind a stone pickaxe, a sword and a furnace are made of. Stone-tool material the engine may build with: what the bag holds above the reserve. Blocks a running build still has to place, per item, and until when: pillars and bridges never take them (a schematic build put 184 of its own stone bricks into scaffolding, and a player hands over the material list's counts, not more). Holds these counts for the next few seconds; the build refreshes them while it runs. An empty map lets go. Whether a stack may be placed as a building block under the reserves: planks only above the wood reserve, stone-tool material only above the stone reserve (the stone job put the cobblestone for the pickaxe into a scaffold), a build's own material only above what the build still places. {@code survival}: a block that keeps the player alive (a hideout's cap, a shield block, a perch) may spend the replacement kit; a running job's own budget still stands. A block any bridge or pillar may spend when it takes whatever full block the hotbar holds (game:telly, game:scaffold): never logs (each is four planks of tools and tables), ores, ancient debris or storage blocks (an iron block is nine ingots), and never below the reserves ({@link #buildable}). Throwaway stock ranks first through the caller's own order. The fixed throwaway preference list, most preferred first; never valuables. Other cheap full blocks a player builds with, used after the preference list. Planks and plain terracotta rank last. Where a block item ranks as throwaway building stock, lower first, or -1 when it never is (valuables, ores, logs, anything unlisted). The placement rules (full block, not falling, no block entity) are checked apart. True for an item {@link #throwawayRank} accepts. The click + observation seam; the production bridge wraps Minecraft, tests a fake. One atomic backpack↔hotbar swap click; false when the click was refused up front. The client-observed contents of a hotbar slot (registry id match). The production machine: verified swaps through the shared inventory helper. Test seam: injected slots, revision counter and clock make the whole machine deterministic. A sent swap stays unknown even after its confirmation timeout; an upfront refusal sent nothing. Completed verified restocks since construction (the op result's {@code restocks} count). Arms one swap of {@code backpackSlot} (9-35) into {@code hotbarSlot} (0-8), expecting {@code expectedItem} (registry id) to land there. The machine waits out the remainder of the previous click's cooldown before clicking, so the pacing holds no matter how often the executor asks. Back to IDLE (op cancel/stall, or the owner consumed a terminal outcome). No control state is held. One machine step per owner tick: at most one click goes out per tick, and SUCCEEDED requires both the client-observed item in the destination slot AND an applied server inventory revision past the click. One backpack slot's restock view: registry id, stack size, and the construction rules. One hotbar slot's

The executor's scaffold ledger: every bridge/pillar support it places is recorded here, so a later op can remove the litter instead of letting yesterday's scaffolding block today's stances and routes (the fill-class live failures: corner cells whose placement rays die on a leftover support outside the work volume). Intentional placements (blueprints, backfill, the telly bridge) never register - only the executor's own throwaway supports do.

Entries carry the placed block identity: a drain digs a cell only when it still holds that exact block or its native dirt/grass/mycelium successor, so unrelated replacements are left alone. The table is bounded and evicts the oldest record past the cap; {@link #reset()} drops everything on world change. All mutators run on the client thread, like AiGridRevisions. Resident records cap; older ones are simply forgotten (their cells stay placed, harmless). Job-owned supports survive the advisory ledger's eviction and include access outside the work box. Snapshot on the client thread; ordered disk writes never delay a movement tick. Recover nearby job supports when resuming, including access outside its selected cells. A world-and-blueprint-specific journal retains access outside the footprint across resumption. Client thread: a confirmed executor support placement (bridge/pillar cell). Client thread: forget one cell (it was dug or consumed by a drain). A record dropped on the client's word (a predicted break): kept a few seconds in case the server undoes the break. Client thread, a block the server set: a scaffold whose break the client predicted and the server undid (the block comes back) is a scaffold again. Forgotten for good, it stood in the work as an orphan nothing tore down: a tower's build ended with 74 of them, and once with the body's own feet inside one ("wedged" for 300 cells). The recorded block for a cell, or null when unrecorded (drain identity check seam). Whether the live ledger or an active job scope already owns this cell. Random ticks can grow grass/mycelium on a dirt support, or shade it back into dirt. Cells recorded inside the box [min,max] (inclusive), highest first for safe pillar teardown. Records currently held (test seam). World change and tests: drop every record.

Bounded workstation scheduling; no world reads, input changes or route execution.
Include teardown even with supplied materials; already present floors cost no new support.
Select a spatial frontier from the whole bounded window, not its first 32 rows.
Bounded, resumable beam search over entire itineraries, rather than independent coverage scores. Every retained alternative pays for the return to unfinished cells. A click may not destroy the last known view of a later job.
One bounded expansion: callers retain control of their per-tick CPU budget.
before[i] contains clicks that must precede i because i would occlude them. A visibility cycle cannot be built from this stance: retain a deterministic safe subset. Native survival/support dependencies have already excluded unready jobs from available.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiS.notes:
game:surface / game:cave — seek travel ops on the engine. Both scan loaded columns in expanding rings around the player (nearest-first, budgeted per tick, own column first), then run an {@link AiGoto#travel} leg to the found cell — walk-only first, one retry with digging allowed.

game:surface seeks the nearest column whose heightmap top is walkable ground (direct sky access in the MOTION_BLOCKING sense). game:cave seeks the nearest sizeable underground air pocket: an air cell below the column top with a solid floor and a connected air volume of at least 12 cells, proven by a bounded 6-connected flood fill.

The flood fill ({@link #floodAirVolume}) is a pure static seam, headless-tested in AiSeekTest. Surface scan: heightmap reads are cheap, walkable probes only per column. Cave scan: up to SCAN_DEPTH cell probes per column. Cave scan: cells inspected below the column window top. A pocket counts as a cave at this connected air volume. The flood fill never explores past this many cells. game:surface: travel to the nearest open-sky column. game:cave: travel into the nearest sizeable underground air pocket. The shared seek skeleton: budgeted ring scan, then walk-only leg, then one dig-allowed retry. Columns a seek tries (walk, then dig) before it gives up. The seek target inside this column, or null. Whether the first try may already dig. A FAILED result carrying a machine-readable code, with the same cleanup as done(). game:surface: the nearest column whose heightmap top is walkable ground under open sky. Cover at most this far over the feet counts as shallow; its columns near the feet's level are looked for this far out. Under shallow cover (a mushroom's cap, an overhang), the columns near the feet's level come first. game:cave: the nearest underground air pocket with a solid floor and a proven >=12-cell volume. Cells at or below this y are considered (default: the player's level + 8). Expanding-ring column source: the origin column first, then 24-block annuli, nearest-first. The next column to inspect, or null when the scan is exhausted. Columns of the (radius-24, radius] annulus around the origin, nearest-first. Air test for the bounded cave flood-fill (pure seam, headless-tested in AiSeekTest). 6-connected air flood from a seed inside a bounded box, capped at {@code cap} cells. Returns the connected air count (at most cap). Pure: no Minecraft construction.
