src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiS.notes:
Interned collision shapes for the planner's terrain snapshots. A cell stores one short: 0 is empty, 1 the full cube, and every other id is a distinct list of cell-local boxes (slabs, stairs, fences, walls, trapdoors, carpets, heads, lily pads, snow layers...). The physics simulator reads the boxes back, so a planned jump is evaluated against the real footing and the real obstacles, not against a passable/solid bit. The table is global and only ever grows; the client thread interns while copying chunks, the planner thread reads. A negative id means "not known yet" and reads as the conservative full cube.
The id for these cell-local boxes; a full-table overflow falls back to the conservative full cube.
The cell-local boxes of a shape id (the full cube for unknown or pending ids).
Height of the highest box top in the cell (0 for empty).
A full-width slab of the given height in sixteenths (the shape a probe without a shape layer implies).
The shape a probe implies: unloaded reads solid, passable empty, everything else a full-width block of its top height.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiS.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiS.notes:
What a shooter can see, the way vanilla decides it. A skeleton only lets an arrow go while {@code LivingEntity.hasLineOfSight} holds (a ray from its eye to the target's eye through collision shapes, fluids ignored), and it drops a target it has not seen for 60 ticks or that is further than its 16-block follow range. So out of sight is safe, and a few seconds out of sight ends the attack.
A skeleton's follow range: further out it forgets the target.
The player's eye above its feet.
No key for the stance's own cells.
Everything that shoots or throws at the player from range.
Whether nothing solid lies on the straight line from {@code from} to {@code to}: the vanilla clip (collision shapes, fluids see-through). {@code ownA}/{@code ownB} are cells taken as open, a stance's feet and head that the route digs out before the player stands there.
The eye of a player standing on {@code feet}'s cell centre.
The points a shooter's eye covers: where it stands, and a block to either side across the line to {@code toward} (it strafes while it draws, and a cover it could see around a moment later is none).
Whether any of the shooters' eyes (their strafe points included) sees a stance eye at {@code feet}.
Stances around {@code feet} no shooter can see, nearest first: a floor with collision, feet and head open or breakable (a niche the route digs), no fluid. {@code down} reaches further below than {@code up} above: a player stuck on a pillar or a ledge gets its cover at the foot of it.
The same, keeping {@code keepAway} further than {@code distance} off every stance (a creeper and where it heads); {@code openOnly}: stances already open, reached without a single dig (a creeper outwalks a hole being dug).
A swimmer may reach cover across breathable surface water; dry players retain dry cover routes.
A rough price of a stance from the feet, for ordering: climbing costs more than walking, going down more than a step aside.
{@link #coverCost}'s price of one block dug while the body stands where the shooter sees it (a stone block is 12 ticks).
{@link #stanceCost} plus the stance's own blocks still to dig when it is level with the feet or above: a niche dug sideways into the wall keeps the body in the shooter's sight for every block of it (two stone blocks were 25 ticks in a skeleton's sight, and it hit). A hole takes the body down with its first block, so a lower stance's blocks are free.
How long a shooter that made the player take cover stays one whose sight the routes keep well out of.
The guard took cover from this shooter: its sight is priced {@link AiPathfinder.Costs#ENGAGED_SIGHT_SURCHARGE} for a while.
Whether the guard took cover from this shooter within {@link #ENGAGED_NANOS}.
Feet and head open now.
Standable after at most digging its own two cells: a solid, fluid-free floor, feet and head open or breakable.
SAFEST's shooter term: a cell whose stance eye a shooter within its follow range can see costs {@link AiPathfinder.Costs#SHOOTER_SIGHT_SURCHARGE} more, so a route stays behind rock and walls where that is about as quick. Read on the planner thread, memoized per cell.
{@link #sightField(BlockGetter, List)} with a price per shooter (one that made the guard take cover costs more).

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiS.notes:
The AI's silent-aim lane on the shared silent-rotation holder. When the {@code aiSilentAim} setting is on, combat ops feed their aim goal to {@link AutismKillAuraRotation} at the ladder's LOWEST rung ({@link AutismKillAuraRotation#PRIORITY_AI_ASSISTANT}), so every combat module outranks the assistant and always wins contention for the one humanized stream. The visible camera is never touched; the packet rewrite in {@link AutismSilentAim} and the mixins carries the rotation, and the mixin's crosshair-pick redirect makes the crosshair agree with it.

The {@code ai-assistant} module answers the ownership gate through {@link #silentCorrectionApplies(boolean, boolean, boolean)}. The lane is full-jar only by construction (the module and every op live in {@code ai/}); nothing here is lite-gated. True while an AI op is feeding the holder this engagement (its rotation may ride packets). The packet/correction gate, KillAura's exact shape: the normal path (module enabled and an op feeding) OR a live return-to-camera sweep, with Scaffold outranking us in both states. Pure and headless-testable. Whether an AI op is feeding the holder; read by the ai-assistant module's gate. Marks the op's feed state (called by AiAim's silent tick path). Releases the holder: the human wind-down sweeps the wire back to the camera instead of a one-packet snap. Scoped to the AI owner inside the holder, so calling it while a module owns the rotation is a no-op; calling it twice is safe.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiS.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiS.notes:
A walkable staircase down toward a block, dug through the engine: one step per block down, each step three high, so the way back up is a walk (a jump per step, no block placed) and the way down again is a walk too. The tech tree digs one while the furnace cooks: digging straight down and pillaring back up to the furnace built blocks that the trip down after it dug out again.

The path goes along the axis with the most distance to cover first, then the other one; once over the target it turns in a two by two spiral. A bounded eight-step look-ahead chooses a continuing direction over an immediate dead end, keeping the preferred heading whenever it has a complete safe prefix. A step never opens an earlier step's floor, a station, an unbreakable cell or a cell the caller wants kept (the ore itself: the pickaxe that mines it is still in the furnace). Directions a spiral turns through (clockwise seen from above). The feet cells of the staircase from {@code start} (not included) toward {@code target}, pure: one block down per step, ending one block above the target's level or after {@code maxSteps}. {@code blocked} names cells a step may not open; a step with no open direction ends the staircase there. {@link #steps}, and never a step whose floor is missing ({@code noFloor}: a cave under it). A step over a cave needed a block placed under it, and without one the planner found no way on: the staircase turns, or ends there. Bounded foresight: prefer a safe continuation over stepping into an immediate dead end. A short level continuation toward the ore when a cave leaves no safe descending step. Never doubles back. A descent, or a short supported approach to where that descent can safely continue. Whether a step with these feet may be dug: its three cells open no floor of the stairs and nothing blocked. The cells a staircase opens: three per step. The planner's goal for a staircase: stand on its last step, breaking only its cells and placing only on its step floors (a cave crossing gets a floor, nothing else is ever built). The steps in order, nothing else: the planner walked the grass over the staircase to the column of a later step and dug down into it from above (the dig had no face to hit and looped three times). Never straight down, never a pillar: a spiral's steps two apart share a column, and the planner dug down the overlap instead of the step between, a two-deep shaft in the stairs that the way back up had to pillar out of. A one-wide shaft straight down the column of {@code top} to feet level {@code bottomY}: the planner may only dig and enter that column, and only downward. The surface cell over a column beside {@code ore} (its four sides, the one nearest the body first) whose blocks down to the ore's level are all solid and none of them {@code blocked}: a shaft there ends with the ore beside the feet. A body in the column or its adjacent open station alcove continues at feet level. Null when no side has such a column within {@code maxDepth}. A walk to {@code top}, then the shaft straight down its column to feet level {@code bottomY}, done when {@code enough} holds. Cells a staircase must not open in the live world: stations and other block entities, unbreakable cells, fluids, and {@code keep}. Water over or beside the cell, or lava on any side (AiPathfinder's dig safety). Cells with nothing to stand on in the live world (air, a cave, fluid, a plant): no stair step goes over one. Whether a block is one of a family ("diamond_ore" matches the deepslate variant too). The nearest block of a family in loaded chunks within {@code radius} across (any height), or null. Palette-prefiltered. The block of a family a staircase from {@code from} gets to soonest: the steps it takes are the larger of the walk across (along the axes) and the drop. Only blocks at least {@code minDrop} under the feet count; null when none is loaded. {@link #nearestBelow}, only blocks {@code usable} accepts (asked only of a block that would be the best so far). The block of a family the ore job goes for first from {@code from}: the least digging ({@link AiBlockMine#oreCost}, the job's own ranking), at least {@code minDrop} under the feet, only blocks {@code usable} accepts. Stairs dug toward the nearest by distance went one way while the job, ranking by digging, went the other: the stairs were wasted. Compare a complete local batch with the access cost of collecting a partial site and its missing remainder. Bounded local count, including only harvestable/safe members; a larger distant vein is a separate trip. Digs the staircase through a persistent engine travel; done on its last step. The owner's timer usually ends it sooner (the furnace is ready): whatever was dug by then is a walkable way down. {@link #dig}, done as soon as {@code enough} holds (the stone step stops once the bag has what the tools take). {@link #dig}, after a walk over the surface to {@code approach} (the feet cell the steps start from) when it is not where the body stands. Where to start digging when the ore lies further across than down: the stairs drop one block a step, so from the body they reach the ore's level still short of it, and the way on is a tunnel across, which costs more than climbing back out and digging straight down (the iron step climbed the stone stairs just dug and sank a shaft beside them). The start is that many cells along the stairs' own course (the long axis first), on the surface. Null when the stairs from the body already end beside the ore.

The search node the player stands in, shared by the goto driver and the movement executor.

A click ray is not a stance proof: the full standing body must fit at its exact feet.
On the ground the node is the cell above the supporting surface (rounded up, so standing on a slab or bed top reads as the cell above it). One exception: the player stands on the lip of a partial block in the NEXT column (the edge of a bed or trapdoor). The rounded-up node assumes a higher body and its own floor is empty: a ceiling can make it look wedged, or an empty descent can finish repeatedly without moving. When the lower cell is open with its own floor and headroom, use that stance: the first step drops off the lip.
The open cell at {@code y} over the block under the box whose top is at the feet, nearest the centre; null if none.

Resolves an outline hit to an exact feet position on a collision surface.
Recheck stationary aim periodically and always proof-check an actual click.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiS.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiS.notes:
Sideways input (A/D) for the walk family, the way a person uses it: line the body up with a one-wide opening before reaching it, slide off a corner the hitbox caught on, and lean into a water current that carries the body off its line. Travel used to hold W and steer with the camera only, so a body sitting 0.3 off the line of a notch pressed into its edge until the stall budget ran out, and a current swept a swimmer past the one exit column every time. Pure: the executor feeds positions, the facing yaw and the live flow; tests call it headless. Sign convention is vanilla's leftImpulse: +1 = the left key, -1 = the right key, 0 = neither.
How far off the line a body may sit in a one-wide opening: half the cell minus the half-width of the hitbox, less a margin.
Off-line slack on open ground while blocked: past it the catch is the corner, not the goal.
A current weaker than this (blocks per tick) is not worth leaning into.
Ticks a blocked body that is already on its line waits before it wiggles.
Ticks per wiggle direction.
The leftward component of a horizontal vector for a body facing yawDeg (vanilla: yaw 0 faces +Z, its left is +X).
The leftward offset of the move's line from the body: the line runs through the target cell's centre along the move's own direction (dirX, dirZ, need not be unit length), so a body left of it gets a negative value (go right).
One tick's strafe. offset: lineOffset of the move. narrow: the target cell has a wall beside it (a notch, a door width gap, a one-wide shore exit). blocked: the body presses into something and barely moves. currentLeft: the water current's leftward component. blockedTicks feeds the wiggle for a body stuck while already on its line.
Whether a body counts as blocked this tick: it collided sideways and its horizontal speed is almost gone.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiS.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/AiS.notes:
Strides decided by simulation (AiPhysics, vanilla's own tick), pure: when a step up takes off, whether a hop comes down where the path allows, and which keys a fall holds. A few short flights a tick, so the decisions cost nothing.

Cells are column keys ({@link #cell}): only the x/z of the cell the body's centre comes down in. Ticks a flight may take before it counts as never coming down (a 3-block fall takes about 10). Distinguish a hazardous arc from a takeoff that merely needs a closer run-up. The column key of the cell a body centred at x/z stands in. Ticks a touchdown is followed on with the keys let go: where the body comes to rest is what counts. Whether a body that just came down stays on that floor in cells {@code allowed} takes while its speed runs out with the keys let go. A touchdown on the far edge of the last allowed cell slides off it: the landing tick alone said yes. Ticks a touchdown on the step's near edge may walk on with the run's keys before its centre is over the landing. A touchdown on the step's near edge, the centre still over the takeoff (a jump cut short by a roof, from a standstill against the face): the executor keeps the run's keys after it lands, so it counts when those keys walk the centre onto an allowed cell of the step's own floor within {@link #WALK_ON_TICKS} and it settles there. Settling with the keys let go at the touchdown itself rejected the jump a player makes up every step of a one-wide dug staircase (the camera a little off the step's heading pushes into the side wall), the move stalled, and the route was dug again beside it. Keep the route while incoming sideways speed settles, only when that coast enables a proved rise. A flight's end: where it came down (null when it did not within the limit), its ticks, and whether it struck a wall. Holds {@code keys} from {@code s} until the body is down again (the jump pressed on the first tick when {@code jump}). A body on the ground that never leaves it within the limit comes back with a null landing. A step up: the ticks until the body stands on {@code surface} in a cell {@code allowed} takes, with the run's keys held and the jump pressed after {@code delay} ticks; -1 when it never does (an arc that comes down short of the face, a landing somewhere else, or no takeoff at all). Press now when a tick later is no sooner (see {@link #takeOffNow}). The step up's takeoff, pure: press the jump this tick unless the run a tick longer stands on the step no later. A jump pressed early enough clears the face (the feet are a block up on the third tick) and keeps the run's speed; one pressed late strikes the face, stops dead and climbs on slower. One that comes down short is no takeoff at all. The keys a fall can hold: toward the heading, none, or against it (the brake). The keys a fall holds this tick: the landing each choice comes to with it held to the ground, judged against the cells the path allows. {@code far}: the path goes on past the landing the same way, so the furthest allowed landing is the best and the brake only ever goes on to keep the body inside them; else the one nearest the target's centre ({@code tx}/{@code tz}). Nothing allowed: the one nearest the target.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/Too.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/ai/engine/Too.notes:
Tool upkeep for the digging ops: the durability-guarded selection policy as ONE pure decision function, so AiMine, AiChop and AiExcavate share it exactly.

The policy: a suitable hotbar tool above the durability floor wins (the job continues unchanged); with none, ONE backpack→hotbar swap of a suitable tool rescues the job; with no suitable tool anywhere, the op fails with {@code TOOL_WORN} and a {@code missing{tool:1}} map (computed by the caller via AiItems.requiredTool, the AiProspect shape). "Suitable" for a target is computed by the caller per slot (correct-tool-for-drops, or anything when the block needs no tool); this class only ranks what it is given. The durability floor: at or below this many uses left a tool counts as worn (the AutoTool guard). One slot's upkeep state: player-inventory slot (0-8 hotbar, 9-35 backpack), the uses left (-1 for non-damageable, which never wears), and whether the slot suits the current target. The upkeep decision: keep the hotbar slot, swap the backpack slot in first, or fail. The decision over the current tool states: best suitable hotbar tool above the floor, else best suitable backpack tool above the floor, else FAIL. "Best" is the most uses left, so a nearly-new tool outranks a tired one and a damageable tool outranks the bare hand; non-damageable slots rank last but never wear out.

Reads describe the world and body as of the start of this tick; actions are applied by the environment in vanilla's order (look and keys this tick, a click judged by the server with the pose it was last sent).
Observed native container/comparator state; absent for an unknown or merely assumed future block.
Identity for native side-effect receipts; a new world cannot inherit a dispatched action.
Native prediction acknowledgement for the last non-idempotent block use, after reconciliation.
Nearby native rail vehicles; null means their loaded entity evidence is unavailable.
The item frames hanging in {@code cell}, or null while that is unknown (an unloaded chunk).
What stands in the cell and stops a block going there (a minecart, a boat, a mob), or null.
False where the client holds no chunk: never air, never support.
Exclusive top of the world.
Hands every block position whose state changed since the last call (any cause: our clicks, the server, physics). An environment that cannot track changes reports none and the core re-reads what it needs.
A changed cell and the state it had before (null: not known).
{@link #drainChanges(java.util.function.LongConsumer)} with each cell's state before the change where it is known.
Startup may consume a bounded prefix. True means no queued block observations remain.
Full chunk loads, resends and unloads, using x in the high 32 bits and z in the low 32 bits.
A bounded event queue overflowed; conservatively revisit all source chunks.
Feet, velocity, ground contact and jump delay, as {@link AiPhysics} steps them.
Collision world the body moves in (the live level or the simulator).
Current eye height above the feet (1.62 standing, 1.27 crouched).
What the server last received: feet, look and Sneak. A click is judged with these.
Cooperative planning work allowed per tick, in {@link PrintView#work()} units (world reads, a ray counting as {@link PrintView#RAY_WORK} more): about 5 to 8 ms of planning a tick. The same in every environment: a wall-clock slice made the game (a few milliseconds a frame, less under load) and the simulator (a whole tick) finish the same search on different ticks, so their builds went different ways from the first search.
Optional isolated-fixture resource supply; normal environments never delay for this provider.
Slots 0-8 hotbar, 9-35 main, 40 offhand.
False while a stack swapped into the hand has not been confirmed by the server's own inventory snapshot. The slots show the client's prediction of the swap; if the server's bag had changed (a pickup, a plugin, a lag spike), the server swapped something else into the hand and a click now places that.
Creative/instabuild: items are not consumed and blocks break instantly.
Whether this exact carried stack can recover a block in its original form.
Native flight grant and the user's movement policy, including while temporarily working on the ground.
Flight movement is currently selected and permitted; spectator is not a building mode.
Use native ground controls for work windows that flight cannot use; creative inventory rights stay unchanged.
Whether native forward sprint flight can start in the current player state.
The server's own head rotation is this look (null: it cannot be read, as on a remote server). A piston's, observer's or dispenser's facing is the head rotation, which the server takes from the body only when the player ticks.
Elapsed input time; accelerated client tick batches must not stand in for a server tick.
The game's own fall guard held the body at an edge just now (a drop it reads as one that hurts).
The core needs this item and holds none (a supplier may restock; the live game waits for the player).
Confirmed construction ownership, never a placement prediction. Live jobs persist it across interruption.
Loaded native evidence discharged a previously confirmed construction block.
The state vanilla would place at {@code at} for this click with this look and Sneak, or null when the click would place nothing there (another cell, nothing placeable). The live client evaluates it against its level; the simulator against its own.
Vanilla survival of a state at a position in the real world (supports, attachments).
The eye the server judges a click from. Native environments also retain forced poses independently of Sneak.

A finite count of complete native phases, never elapsed or planning ticks.

Recheck machine ordering after observing stock but before an inventory-changing click.

Every native slot was observed holding its maximum legal stack, with an empty cursor.

Completed capacity proofs retain the definition, never a closed native menu/player snapshot.

Additional exact material to retrieve before reopening the saved container.

Model-predictive steering: every tick each key set (eight directions or none, with or without jump and Sneak) is simulated a few ticks ahead with {@link AiPhysics} from the observed body, and the safest one that brings the feet closest to the goal is pressed. Nothing is assumed about the last tick's outcome, so a bump, a slip or a server correction is simply the next starting state.
Where the feet should go. {@code floor}: the lowest feet height the body may reach on the way (a drop's landing, or the current floor when it must not fall). {@code crouch}: Sneak is required (an edge, a crouched click). {@code stop}: arrive at rest.
Ticks a rollout still in the air at the window's end is followed until it lands.
True once the feet are inside the goal's tolerance, on the ground, and (for a stop) nearly still.
The keys for this tick, given the camera yaw this tick's movement will use.
A short work adjustment needs a single key pulse followed by braking, not seven held ticks.
Lowest cost along the simulated path, or infinity when the path drops below the floor or touches a hazard.
{@code -Dautism.ai.print.braking=false}: a stopping walk only weighs keys held for the whole window.
The keys held for {@code heldTicks} ticks (the jump only on the first), then let go with the same Sneak, or crouched ({@code crouchedCoast}: the coast of a braking walk, which arrives crouched as the creep it replaces did, the edge stop on).
Check corner samples without allocating sets for every steering candidate and predicted tick.
The cells the body's box corners are in, at its feet, middle and head.

Walking on the printer's own model: stances are cells a standing body fits in ({@link PrintView#stance}); moves are steps to the eight neighbouring columns that are flat, a step up (jump) or a safe drop. The mover executes exactly these moves, so a route found here is a route the body can walk.
Ticks per block walked, per diagonal, and the extra for a jump or each block dropped.
The stance cells reachable from a start, each with its walking cost and the stance it is reached from.
Nodes reached by riding the open schematic cell under them (jump, place it under the feet).
Rides on the way to each node.
The cells ridden (placed under the feet) on the way to {@code key}.
Stances from the start to {@code key}, start excluded.
Bounds a search may use.
Dijkstra over walk moves from the stance the body stands in. {@code maxNodes} caps the work; a capped search is marked truncated.
Ticks a ride takes (jump, place, land).
Also rides: from a stance whose own cell {@code rideable} accepts (an open schematic cube), jump and place it under the feet, arriving one higher. The structure is its own ladder.
{@code avoid}: stances a walk stalled on (not entered again).
The same native walking graph, with every neighbor cursor retained between work slices.
The caller owns geometry invalidation, as for other retained native route searches.
Cost of moving from feet height {@code h} in column (x,z) to feet {@code h2} in the neighbouring column, or NaN. Flat steps up to 0.6, jumps up to 1.25 (head room over the take-off), drops up to 3 (room over the landing).
Execution uses Sneak for the same low passage the route priced as crouched movement.
Head room a jump keeps over the landing while the body crosses its edge.
The take-off column holds the jump's rise and the swept body fits {@link #JUMP_MARGIN} over the landing.
Drops deeper than this check the cell past their landing while building (a body walking off carries on).
The cell past a drop's landing stops the body (a wall at its height) or is a floor no more than a safe drop below the take-off.
Least footing a jump or drop may land on (of the footprint's 0.36; a wall post is 0.25).
A bowl's native step-up rim can put a legal landing two integer cells above its inside floor.
The highest collision top in the feet cell within a step above the feet (the feet height when there is none).
Both columns beside a diagonal step let the body pass at height {@code y} (no corner to snag).
The stance cell a body at {@code feet} stands in: among the columns its box overlaps, a standable cell whose floor is the height the feet are really at, or a native step below it. A hopper's rim can hold the body higher than its own column's central floor; choosing an equal-height diagonal column instead can put walls across the return walk.
Walk moves the plain move model allows off a stance (stances only, a block up to three down).

Exactly the nearest eligible centers below top, ties by source index; no fixed search radius.
Retained exact best-first traversal. Rejected live candidates still consume a step, and a partly expanded leaf is finished before the queue can publish another point. Callers retain their eligibility/body policy separately from this active-index epoch.
The optional monotone clock can count native work or elapsed nanoseconds; one primitive may finish past its allowance.
Exact minimum for a nonnegative cost monotone away from zero on each signed axis. The relaxed native travel lower bound has this property; boxes only skip costs they cannot improve.

src/main/java/autismclient/ai/print/Prin.notes:
The world as the printer sees it: the environment's blocks plus an overlay of assumed changes ("if this block stood here"). It is a vanilla {@link BlockGetter}, so shapes, rays and placement checks run vanilla's own code against it. Unloaded space reads as a barrier: never air, never a floor to plan on.
Exact overlay membership: one vertical 64-cell mask per occupied column section.
The client world cannot tick during one planner call. Never retain its states across calls.
Stance heights by cell (no assumptions); cleared around every observed change.
Blocks whose uses must land on one face: an item frame hangs from it and is used through it.
Exact map equality using reusable primitive entries, without allocating one entry per block on every check.
Any block assumed (placed or taken away in thought) right now.
The same assumed blocks within {@code radius} of {@code c} (what a search that only reads there can have seen).
A fingerprint of the blocks assumed within {@code radius} of {@code c} (0 when none).
A block changed: forget the stances that read it.
A solid dry block arrived in a cell that had no shape: like {@link #changed}, but recorded as an addition (an addition can only give a click a face or a floor, it never opens a ray or a stance).
The observed revision of the last change in each 4x4x4 bucket: blocks added into empty cells ({@code bucketAdded}) and every other change ({@code bucketChanged}); with the last additions per bucket, for proofs that are brought up to date rather than redone.
A change that keeps the block, its collision and outline shapes, its fluid and its hazard (a wire's power, a lamp lit, an observer's pulse): no stance, ray or body test reads differently, so searches and proofs stay valid. Waits for new evidence still see it ({@link #anyRevision()}).
An observed distant key still matters to a native route that read that exact cell.
Every observed change, the cosmetic ones included.
Validate exact retained states through the bounded keyed observation journal. Missing history or a bulk replacement falls back to reading every retained input. Callers must separately guard unreported changes, dynamic shapes and their original outer hypotheses.
A block changed where no plan or search reads (outside the planning region): only the stance cache entries that could have read it go. Search sessions and proofs stay valid; in game the server's updates anywhere in the loaded world (fluids, leaves, other players) used to restart every access search before it could finish.
A full chunk replacement can change every read without individual block events.
The work positions of a stance ({@link PrintClicks#feetPoints}), all validated, kept while nothing they read changed: every body box and floor test of a stance in cell (x,y,z) reads the cells one round its column, from three under to three over. The kill check, the stance choice and access ask the same stances again and again (Bruta: 37% of its planning validated the same 49 positions of the same stances). Built on a stance's second request, so one asked once costs what it did. A cache hit forwards its native input cells to active proof receipts; it never substitutes the state from the cache for the caller's initial-world state.
A cache miss has a fixed eviction allowance as well as a fixed total receipt size.
Geometry does not mutate hypotheses, so its own collector needs keys rather than a full overlay snapshot.
Planning work done so far, counted in world reads (every stance, ray, collision and click test reads through here). Cooperative searches yield on this count, never on the wall clock, so the game and the headless simulator spend the same work on the same tick and make the same decisions whatever the machine's speed or load.
Click rays cast (each walks its cells' outline shapes: far dearer than a plain read).
The planning work a ray counts as beyond the reads it makes (measured: a ray costs about as much as 25 plain reads), so a slice of work takes about the same time whatever it is made of: counted as its reads alone, a slice of 28758's ray-heavy searches took seven times longer than one of Bruta's, and the game's tick rate dropped where the simulator's did not.
Reads made only for a trace are not planning work: counted, they made a traced run (game or simulator) yield on other ticks than an untraced one, and the two builds went different ways.
Live cells last read as lava. A route's lava margin looks here instead of reading the cells round every node (those reads count as planning work: 19449, with no lava at all, gave its cells up sooner while flights planned).
Exact initial-world inputs read while replaying a successful route, including cache-hit stance queries.
Reactivation requires the caller's world/policy validation before installing any child hypotheses.
One bounded dependency receipt, inactive between cooperative slices.
A cached query still supplies every dependency to an enclosing native proof.
Native animated collision inputs, separate from unloaded cells and ordinary container reads.
Called with the session's outer assumptions restored, never with a path's temporary overlay installed.
Native support rules over these exact hypotheses; unavailable environmental evidence cannot prove survival.
Nothing assumed within one block of {@code pos}: vanilla's placement answer from the live world holds there.
Blocks assumed and not forgotten (none should outlive the check that assumed them).
Reuse only geometry vanilla itself caches per state; dynamic shapes still read this exact world.
No collision box meets the box (world coordinates).
Every collision box meeting the query, for {@link AiPhysics}.
Some cell the box overlaps holds lava (up to its surface) or a hazard block.
Damage or capture the body must not enter (lava, fire, cactus, berries, webs, powder snow, magma underfoot).
Feet height of a body standing in cell (x,y,z) on the floor under its middle, or NaN. The floor is the highest collision top under the 0.6-wide

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/AirJu.notes:
Java port of AUTISM's ModuleAirJump (1:1), with all three modes: - JumpFreely: jump again in mid air any time the jump key is pressed. - DoubleJump: exactly one extra jump per ground touch; the first airborne jump consumes it. - GhostBlock: while the jump key is held, blocks below the player get a full collision shape, so you can stand on air. Vanilla's 10-tick jump delay is kept after every air jump, exactly like AUTISM, so the modes don't turn into a jetpack. Two AUTISM quirks are kept on purpose: the aiStep hook applies to EVERY LivingEntity (mobs with an active jump input air jump too), and the doubleJump flag is never reset on disable - it only re-arms on ground contact and is consumed by an airborne jump.
AUTISM's doubleJump flag: re-armed on ground, consumed by an airborne jump.
AUTISM's allowJump getter: running && (mode == JUMP_FREELY || (mode == DOUBLE_JUMP && doubleJump)).
AUTISM's aiStep hook (MixinLivingEntity.hookAirJump): air jump when the mode allows it. AUTISM does NOT scope this to the local player - any LivingEntity with an active jump input air jumps.
AUTISM's PlayerJumpEvent handler: any jump performed while airborne consumes the double jump (mode-agnostic in AUTISM, so ground jumps never count).
AUTISM's BlockShapeEvent handler for GHOST_BLOCK: full collision below the player while jumping.
Effective jump-held state for GhostBlock: the raw key state plus a short grace window, so a genuinely held key that flickers for a few ticks (keyboard ghosting, tap rhythm, focus blips) doesn't drop the platform mid-move. The window stretches with the player's speed: at high forward/fall speed the same brief gap would otherwise let you fall through before the next press lands. For an uninterrupted hold this is identical to AUTISM's raw keyJump.isDown.
Grace window scaled by the player's fastest axis of motion: ~0.3s at walking pace, ramping to ~0.9s at very high speed (speed boosts, elytra dives), so momentum can't outrun the platform.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Ancho.notes:
Places, charges and detonates respawn anchors on the silent-rotation and real-ray infrastructure. Module id, and the owner token this module holds the shared silent rotation under. Read from the ladder rather than spelled again: AutismKillAuraRotation is the only file allowed to name a rung or an owner, and the ladder drifted the last time four files kept their own copies. RespawnAnchorBlock.MAX_CHARGES, read from the block rather than restated. How many ranked cells the placement aim search may try before giving up for the tick. Ceiling on full (raycasting) damage evaluations per placement pass. Ticks of enemy travel the placement ranking prices in, and the cap on that travel in blocks. The blast lands the better part of a cycle after the cell is chosen - place, switch, charge, switch, detonate, every step floored by Step Delay - so pricing the enemy where they ARE sells every cycle to a moving target: they simply walk out between the decision and the click, and the follow-through doctrine then fires the armed anchor at nobody. Six ticks is the warm-cycle middle of that latency; the cap keeps a sprint-by reading as "ahead of them", never as "a room away" (and a teleport snap as two blocks of lead, not eight). Rays the whole tick may spend on aim. The scanner bills rays only, never candidates.

The shared value, not a local one: 48. The scanner sized it against the starvation case it names by hand - at 12, three ray-paying candidates, a caller sweeping several ranked cells spends the whole allowance inside the first and never rays the rest. Even 48 only stretches so far across a ranking, which is why the placement cursor below resumes where the rays ran out instead of restarting at the best cell. Lost charge/detonate packets use the same latency-bounded resend window as crystals. This never delays a first click or a step whose authoritative state already advanced. How long an abandoned cell is refused, so a cell we just failed on is not picked again at once. Consecutive out-of-rays deferrals one adoptable anchor is given before it is banned like any other refused cell. The placement cursor may park on a dry budget indefinitely because its walk RESUMES where it parked; the adoption park could not, because it returned before the fresh ranking ran. And a NO_BUDGET on a fresh budget is deterministic geometry, not flicker: a partially occluded anchor's face probes exhaust the whole allowance on every retry. Three strikes is long enough that a genuinely budget-crossed anchor keeps its retries, short enough that a pit-fight occluder stops starving the rest of the module well inside one ban. Placement clicks one cycle may spend on its cell. A cell the server silently reverts - a claim, a protected region - looks exactly like a lost placement tick from here, and the state-driven plan would rebuild it on every step delay. Two retries, then the cell is abandoned and banned. How long a cell that ate its whole commitment is refused. Much shorter than a cycle ban: nothing was ever built there, so the failure was the aim's or the budget's, not the cell's - but the next decision still has to try its neighbours instead of marrying the same cell. Consecutive scan refusals a held placement commitment absorbs before it is released early, with the same short ban an expiry hands out. The commitment doctrine is "deferred, never denied", but taken literally that married the module to a cell whose faces never solve - one clickable face permanently occluded, or a solve that eats the whole ray budget before the confirm - for the full pendingCommitTicks() while the cells ranked behind it were never asked a ray. Three strikes is the adoption park's own count, picked for the same reason: long enough that ordinary flicker keeps its cell, short enough that a geometrically stuck one hands its rays to its neighbours well inside one ban. Refused rankings the same target must stand through before Force Engage relaxes the placement ranking to "adjacent to the enemy, not lethal to us". Three: a damage gate that merely flickers re-passes within a tick or two of movement, so three consecutive refused rankings is already past flicker - and the old dwell of eight cost nearly half a second of dead time in exactly the flat-ground stalemate the fallback exists to break. Glowstone pieces the GLOWSTONE shield route needs on the hotbar before it may commit: ONE is placed as the shield block and ONE is consumed by the charge click. Committing with less would arm an anchor whose cover was never built. The obsidian fallback has its own recipe - one obsidian for the cover plus the charge click's one glowstone - checked beside this one in {@link #shieldMaterialsPresent}. Anchor cells the shield route runs its full verification on per tick, best-ranked first. The verification is a second damage evaluation per shield candidate, so the route is bounded separately instead of spending the main scan's whole allowance on a fallback. Shield candidates verified per anchor cell, best-aligned with the us-to-blast line first. The ring around the player yields a dozen cells at most, and its aligned front almost always holds a working one when one exists. Cached candidate sphere, rebuilt only when the radius changes. Cells refused for a while - a cycle was abandoned on them, or a committed placement expired there without ever clicking - and the client tick each refusal expires at. Client tick this module last committed the silent rotation to an anchor action. The reservation outlives the stamp by the rotation request's own lifetime (see reservesCombatTick), so a plan that flickers off for a tick does not release the tick in between. The stamp itself is gated: ticks a higher rung is aiming on - and this module is not finishing committed work on - are never claimed. A live cycle's cadence-wait ticks ARE claimed here: offence must see an unbroken fence for the whole fight, and the exact-tick activity stamp below is the one defence reads instead. This res

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/AntiH.notes:
AntiHunger module — a port of AUTISM's ModuleAntiHunger. Two mechanisms stop hunger from decreasing: NoSprint (default on): makes the server never see the player sprint. The server's sprint state is set ONLY by the ServerboundPlayerCommandPacket (START_SPRINTING) that LocalPlayer.sendIsSprintingIfNeeded emits — so we cancel that one network read and the server is never told, while the client-side sprint state (speed boost, Flight's sprint speed) is untouched. This is AUTISM's SprintEvent NETWORK branch. KeepFloating (default on): rewrites outbound move packets so onGround is false whenever the player is on the ground and not falling. The server then treats the player as airborne, which bypasses the on-ground exhaustion costs in ServerPlayer.increaseTravelMotionStats. Guard order matches AUTISM exactly: the packet rewrite is skipped while riding, breaking a block, swimming, in water or underwater. The NoSprint part is also exposed as {@code noSprintRequested()}, which Flight's own AntiHunger toggle feeds into — so the server stays sprint-blind while flying even when this module is off, and the two never double-apply (a single OR gate).
AUTISM NoSprint.running: NoSprint enabled unless swimming (and WhileSwimming is off).
Whether the server must be kept unaware of sprinting, from ANY source: the AntiHunger module's NoSprint, or Flight's own AntiHunger toggle (so the effect applies while flying even when the module is off). OR semantics — either being on applies it, both on is fine (single boolean gate).

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/AutoA.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/AutoA.notes:
Keeps the best available armor equipped by moving pieces from the hotbar or inventory onto the body.

Every move is a silent player-inventory (window 0) click, so it looks exactly like a manual click to the server. In paced mode (any Timing band above zero) moves happen inside SESSIONS: a session starts after a Reaction draw, equips EVERY slot that needs it one move per Click Delay draw - open, move, move, close, never open-close-per-piece - and ends with one container-close on the Close Delay band, with the next session spaced by the Spacing band. For the session's whole length the operation window ({@link #operationActive()}) silences movement, jumping, sneaking, camera rotation, attack, use and the combat modules, and every packet goes out at tick HEAD, before the movement packet. All four bands at zero runs the legacy every-tick path. Clicks only ever use SWAP button 0-8 / QUICK_MOVE button 0 / THROW button 0-1 (Grim's BadPacketsP valid ranges) and never change the held hotbar slot. The which-piece-is-best model itself (damage-reduction maths, enchantment weighting, durability guard, kit refinement) is shared with the AI's game:equip armor path in {@link autismclient.util.AutismArmorEvaluation}, so the module and the AI can never disagree about what "best" means.

Slots we manage, highest first. InventoryMenu (window 0) menu-slot id for each worn armor piece. Stable layout: 5=head..8=feet. The ranking model (damage reduction, enchant weighting, kit refinement) lives in AutismArmorEvaluation. Idle rescan cadence for the paced path: full re-evaluation at most this often when nothing changed. Timing bands, parsed once per string change instead of parsed per call (the band text never changes between user edits, so per-tick parsing was pure churn). Session state (paced mode): one session equips EVERY slot that needs it - open, one move per Click Delay draw, then a single close on the Close Delay band. Opening and closing per piece (helmet, close, reopen, leggings) is the shape no human produces, so it does not exist here. Earliest client tick a NEW session may start: the Spacing band's stamp. Tick a fresh session's start is held to by the Reaction band, or -1 when not holding. Runs at Minecraft.tick HEAD (via ModuleRegistry.preMovementTick), NOT at END_CLIENT_TICK: every click then precedes the movement packet, the region vanilla uses for real inventory clicks - emitting after it is Grim's Post/PacketOrderO flag shape. Never move this back. The legacy every-tick path: all four Timing bands at zero, exactly the pre-Timing behaviour. Advances a live session by one move per Click Delay draw. The window re-arms every live tick, so the whole session - moves, the close and the tail - stays silenced. When the last slot is equipped the close follows on the Close Delay band; new loot mid-close sends the session back to moving, exactly like a human spotting another piece before leaving their inventory. Ends a session. A clean end already closed in tickSession; an aborted one (a gate broke, or a totem took the wire) closes immediately - the session has been open for ticks, so that close is a human "interrupted mid-inventory", not the 0 ms open-close shape. The one move the session would do next, or null when every slot is already best. Legacy path: at most one move per tick, then the old close/recheck pacing. Issues the single window-0 click that advances this slot toward wearing {@code candidate}. Draws one wait from a Timing band, in ticks - fresh every event, so no two gaps ever match. True while any Timing band can produce a wait - all four at zero is the legacy every-tick path. The freeze tail after each click: a click-band draw, at least one tick. src/main/java/autismclient/modules/AutoF.notes:
Harvests, fertilizes, replants and tills the crops in reach of the player's own hands.

Sits at 5 on {@link AutismKillAuraRotation}'s fixed ladder, the bottom rung, below KillAura (10): a melee hit answers a deadline a farm never has, so the farm yields every tick combat wants the stream. The rung is declared once, in {@link AutismKillAuraRotation#PRIORITY_AUTO_FARM}.

There is ONE shared stream and only its owner may step it, once per client tick, so this module is registered AFTER KillAura: whichever module's preMovementTick runs first takes the step, and a later winner of the priority arbitration would own a stream that was already advanced toward the loser's goal. Ticks the hold stays off right after the walker arrives, plus a rolled 0-2 more: a human walks up, settles, THEN swings, so the first contact lands 2-4 ticks after the stop instead of on the arrival tick. There is NO other pace floor anywhere: for a held key vanilla's own cadence (an instant break per crop the crosshair touches, the native right-button repeat for seeds and hoes) IS the 1:1 human pace, and a module floor on top would only read as slower than hands. Ticks between a successful action and putting the previously held slot back. Wrapped-degree floor when asking whether the wire still carries our silent rotation. The effective tolerance is one sensitivity quantum PLUS this floor - see sameRotation for why the engine's own converged-tick jitter forces that shape. Bound memory without evicting unfinished work; a full queue pauses new harvesting. Target stickiness: how long a pinned cell may be kept while the wire-nearest pick flaps between two cells equidistant from the wire. The click itself no longer needs the pin - the ray-driven gate fires on whatever valid cell the wire crosses - but an AIM that re-solves to a different single crop every tick is the non-human camera signature the auras needed commitment for. Eight ticks is long enough to cross the cluster, short enough for a genuinely better cell to win. The leftovers sweep. A cell that failed to solve an aim, or that burned CELL_DRY_LIMIT consecutive arrived-but-refused ticks, is refused AS A PLAN for CELL_COOLDOWN_TICKS and the wire-nearest pick rotates to the class's next candidate - the rest of the field gets worked and the cell is retried once the geometry has had reason to change (the player or the walker shifted, a neighbour crop came down). The cooldown never reaches the click gate: a cooled cell the wire ray lands on validly still fires, exactly like the walk blacklist only ever steers the walk scan. 80 ticks is a four-second retry - shorter than a pass back across the field, long enough to end the re-elect-the-dead-winner loop. Two invalidations cut the wait short when the geometry the refusal proved is already gone: every accepted harvest clears cooled cells within Chebyshev 2 of the break (the occluding crop came down), and a cooled cell whose base block changed identity (farmland trampled or tilled) is dropped on read - see rememberHarvest and cellCooled. The dry meter's second tier: arrived-but-refused ticks that cool a cell when they follow an ACCEPTED action. Six refused ticks prove genuinely unsolvable geometry (an occluded face, an unservable sliver); right after an action the same refusal means something else - the goal just COMPLETED under the hold and the wire has not swung to the next cell yet - so two are enough to rotate the pick. Finished work must never sit out the six-tick dead-cell proof, and the cooldown it lands on stays plan-level steering: the click gate is free to fire the cell the moment the ray lands on it validly either way. How close to the plan's goal rotation the wire must sit before a refused tick may count against the cell: mid-travel refusals are the sweep doing its job, and the row brain's lookahead goal never lets the wire catch it while the row is firing - only an ARRIVED camera that still lands nothing proves the plan dead. "Few cells left" for every pre-staging path: a row this close to its end hands the snake's pivot goal over early (the camera swings DURING the last holds instead of parking at the clamped end point and re-converging - a beat a hand does not take), a cluster thinned to this many members blends the next patch's cells into its centroid for the same reason, and a class batch with this many workable cells left pays its hotbar flip ahead of time. Three is the span whose last holds cover the pivot/settle window. The harvest cluster: how far around the pick siblings count as the same sweep, and how many of them the aim centroid averages. Two blocks reaches across a farmland row and the ditch beside it; eight cells keeps the centroid on the near side of a big patch, so the goal stays inside the reach cull instead of pulling toward the field's middle. How many cells beyond the cluster band a nearly-finished patch folds into its centroid: enough to pull the aim toward the next patch during the last holds, few enough that the blend stays on the near side of what comes next. The row model's reach: how far around the pick the line census samples on x and z, which is also how far ahead of the wire a row end is scanned. Rows are flat farmland structures, so +-8 sees the whole row a player standing in it could be working. Fewer than three listed crops on a line through the pick is no row: scattered aim. How far ahead of the wire the sweep goal rides, in blocks: far enough that the camera keeps travelling down the row instead of parking on one crop, near enough that the pitch stays on the plants. Never past the last crop + 1. Consecutive water or lily-pad cells the row scan steps over without ending the row: a 1-2 wide channel splits a logical row into segments of the SAME row (the ray crosses water without firing); a wider gap is a new row. Lily pads ride on the water and are neither crops nor row breakers. A snake pivot anchors on a parallel row 1-3 lines over whose crops sit this close along the axis. The w

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/AutoL.notes:
Answers a server's login/register gate for the real player, the same way a Multi bot does.

The decisions live in {@link AutoLoginEngine}, which the bots run too, so both sides handle a server identically and testing one tests the other. This class is only the wiring: where the password comes from, what counts as spawned, and how a packet leaves. Never shareable. These settings hold a server password, and a share blob carries every option value verbatim, so one click would hand it to a lobby. This also refuses inbound settings, so nobody can push a crafted blob that overwrites the local password either. NETWORK THREAD. Fed straight from the connection mixin rather than {@link #onPacketReceive}, because that hook only runs once the player has spawned and a login gate is answered before then. The rendered client's side of the shared login engine.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/AutoT.notes:
Keeps a totem in the offhand. 1:1 port of AUTISM's AutoTotem (the Totem feature of its Offhand module): same health threshold logic, same in-hole Safety threshold, same predicted-damage model (entity explosions, bed/respawn-anchor explosions, fall damage), same switch modes (Smart / Switch / PickUp) with hotbar-first totem search, same switch-back of the displaced item after healing, and the same millisecond switch / switch-back delays.

On top of the port sit the five Timing bands (double sliders, one wait drawn fresh per event; all at zero keeps the port's exact instant behaviour) and a default switch mode of Switch - vanilla's own hover-F: one ContainerClick on the totem's slot with button 40 (SWAP), the exact packet AbstractContainerScreen sends when a player hovers a slot and presses F, on any hotbar or inventory slot, with no pickup anywhere. Click Delay paces the packets inside an operation, Close Delay the session close after the last click, Spacing the gap between operations, Reaction the hold before a fresh one starts (a metronome is what timing-deviation checks measure, so no two gaps ever match) and Settle the beat between the ghost inventory opening and its first click. From the first packet until the tail after the last the operation window ({@link #operationActive()}) silences movement, jumping, sneaking, camera rotation, attack, use and every combat module - no human click, placement, glance or stride ever neighbours an inventory action - and a session that clicked ends with the same container-close packet a real inventory session ends with.

Paced click operations do not run screen-less: with no screen open the module first opens an {@link autismclient.gui.AutismGhostInventoryScreen}, a real InventoryScreen the user never sees and cannot touch, because a genuinely open inventory is the session shape vanilla produces for a human (Gui.setScreen releases every key and gates keybinds for as long as it stays open, and LocalPlayer.closeContainer emits the closing packet when it goes away) - a screen-less click burst is exactly what packet-session checks (BonkAC InventoryA/G) flag. The first click waits out a fresh Settle draw after the ghost opens, the ghost stays open for the whole sequence, and the session close IS the ghost closing the human way. The Smart swap, the all-zero legacy path and foreign containers never get a ghost: their shapes are already correct. AUTISM DIRECTIONS_EXCLUDING_UP: the four horizontals plus down. Vanilla drag constants (LivingEntity travel/air + elytra branches). Sorted 10-block sphere offsets for bed/anchor scans (AUTISM getSortedSphere(10f)). How long an unfinished switch-back stays alive while its item is nowhere to be found. A Smart swap is server-side only, so the displaced item is invisible to us until the sync lands - this has to outlast that round trip while still being short enough that a dead trip does not sit on a hotbar slot for a whole fight. How long an unanswered Smart swap counts as still in flight. The latch normally clears the moment the offhand changes, one round trip after the send, so this only ever catches a swap the server did not apply. Waiting cannot delay protection: if the swap did land the server already holds the totem in the offhand and only our view of it is stale. The offhand item displaced by the last totem equip and the slot it landed in. When the last Smart swap was sent (-1 = none in flight) and what the offhand showed at that moment. State of a tick-paced switch (any Timing band above zero): the packets performSwitch would fire in one tick are spread one per drawn wait instead. SEQ_PICKUP spreads the two or three container clicks; SEQ_SMART spreads the SetCarriedItem / offhand-swap / SetCarriedItem burst. Both run from the first packet (already sent by startPacedSwitch) until the last one, paced by seqNextTick. The lone close of a hover-F session, a human beat after its single click. Earliest client tick a NEW operation may start: the jittered inter-operation spacing. Tick a fresh operation's start is held to for reaction slop, or -1 when not holding. The ghost inventory this module opened for a paced click session (null = none open), whether the live operation runs inside one, and the tick its settle hold ends. The flag survives the reference on purpose: a ghost the user or a takeover replaced mid-sequence must suppress the session close entirely, which a bare null check cannot tell apart from a session that never had a ghost. Runs at Minecraft.tick HEAD (via ModuleRegistry.preMovementTick), NOT at END_CLIENT_TICK: every packet this module sends then precedes gameMode.tick, handleKeybinds and the movement packet - the exact region vanilla uses for SetCarriedItem flushes, F-swaps and GUI clicks. Emitting after the movement packet is Grim's Post check's flag shape for held-item/dig packets, and suspicious for clicks on any order-sensitive anticheat. Never move this back to tick(). Derives every claim from live state and makes the arbiter match it exactly. The offhand is ours while a totem sits in it, while a swap we sent is still in flight, or while an item is owed back to the inventory; one slot is ours for exactly as long as that switch-back can still run. Nothing else in the module takes or drops a claim, so there is no second copy of this to drift out of step. Whether an item is still owed back to an inventory slot. This is the module's one answer to that question - the reservation, the switch-back and the dead-trip cleanup all read it. Whether the last Smart swap is still unanswered. Vanilla does not predict SWAP_ITEM_WITH_OFFHAND at all - Minecraft.handleKeybinds just sends the packet - so the local offhand keeps showing the old item for a whole round trip. Sending a second swap in that window swaps the totem straight back out server-side, which is what this stops. Hotbar first, then main inventory (AUTISM gives totems hotbar priority). 40 = already held. The slot the displaced item landed in, while i

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/AutoT.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/AutoT.notes:
Places cobwebs, lava or fire into the cells an enemy is about to occupy.

Sits at 15 on {@link AutismKillAuraRotation}'s fixed ladder: above KillAura (10) and below CrystalAura (18), AnchorAura (20), Surround (25) and BedDefender (30). The rung is declared once, in {@link AutismKillAuraRotation#PRIORITY_AUTO_TRAP}.

Above the melee aura because AUTISM requests this aim at IMPORTANT_FOR_PLAYER_LIFE and pauses combat for the placing tick - a trap that lands is worth more than one melee swing. Below the four above it because each of them answers a deadline this one does not: the bed is the loss condition, the surround ring is the difference between living and dying to the next crystal, and the two blast auras own the damage source in crystal PvP. A trap can wait a tick.

There is ONE shared stream and only its owner may step it, once per client tick, so this module has to be registered BEFORE KillAura: whichever module's preMovementTick runs first takes the step, and a later winner of the priority arbitration would own a stream that was already advanced toward the loser's goal. AUTISM's TrapPlayerSimulation constants. The FURTHEST ahead of a mover the trap is ever laid, in ticks: roughly the two to three the silent rotation needs to settle on the solved face, plus one for the packet. The landing gate this replaces (a fixed 8 ticks-to-ground) could never pass for a player already ON the ground, which is exactly the case of trapping a runner. The lead actually used scales down from here with the target's measured direction instability - see adaptiveLeadTicks - so this is the straight-runner horizon, not a fixed guess. Squared per-tick speed under which a target counts as standing still. ~0.03 b/t: only a genuinely idle player. The old 0.05 let anything under ~0.22 b/t - walking (0.215) and sneaking (0.065) included - pass as "stationary", so the trap went to their current feet and landed behind them every time. AUTISM's TrapPlanner constants. How far a mid-air trap position may be walked down to the cell under it. Covers a jump apex (~1.25 blocks) with slack; anything higher off the ground is a real fall, whose planning belongs to the simulator's landing spot, not to a snap. Vertical drag applied after gravity, vanilla LivingEntity.travel. How long the combat-timing hold may starve a ready plan before it is abandoned. Consecutive planning failures before a live plan is dropped instead of aimed at forever. Ticks a valid, moving target may fail the confidence gate before its latest lead position is accepted anyway. A strafing or jump-resetting enemy can hold the spread above the gate forever, which read as the module "thinking" and never firing; the click side still refuses any cell outside the box the target actually occupies when the ray lands, so a wrong guess costs a replan, never a misplaced web. How long the ignite half of a web combo may be chased before the combo is abandoned and the normal cooldown starts instead (no cell, no plan, target slipped the web). The lava recovery clock. A pour leaves a live source and an EMPTY bucket behind, and the rule here is that the source ALWAYS comes back: as soon as the target is on fire (the job is done), as soon as the target leaves the world (the fight is over), and in every case after {@link #LAVA_PICKUP_TICKS} whether anybody burned or not. The give-up bound is the honesty valve on "always": a source still unrecovered ten seconds after the pour - walked away from, walled off, hardened into obsidian by someone else's water - is written off as map lava instead of being chased forever, and the never-pour-twice veto lifts with it. Overworld lava creeps one block per 30 ticks, so neither the pickup delay nor a cooldown-length wait can let a reachable source get away. Human floor between two accepted placements, in milliseconds, plus a per-attempt jitter. 100 ms is the same floor the Scaffold charter uses and it is never zero - the tick rule alone would allow 20 placements a second on a Delay of 0. Ticks between a successful trap and putting the previously held slot back. Wrapped-degree tolerance when asking whether the wire still carries our silent rotation. No trap cell may land closer than 1 block to our own eye, and no target may be selected closer than 1 block either, squared for the checks. Reach is automatic (the player's own block interaction range) but has no near side: without this floor a target at point-blank can put a web or lava bucket into our own cell. One block is enough for that - the old 2-block floor also excluded every enemy standing at melee range, which is exactly where a trap is most needed. Enforced at plan time AND re-checked on the click, whose ray may legitimately land on a different cell than the one the planner solved. One simulated future for one enemy: where they land (when airborne), in how many ticks, where they are now, and where they will be one through {@link #LEAD_TICKS} ticks from now. The whole short path is kept, not just the horizon: how far ahead the trap is laid scales with how straight the target actually runs, so the shorter leads have to already exist when the planner asks for them. The integrated position {@code ticks} (clamped to 1..LEAD_TICKS) ahead of this snapshot. A trap item that is actually reachable right now. A hotbar slot of -1 means the offhand. AUTISM's BlockChangeIntent, flattened: what to place, who it is meant for, and where to look. The chosen cell is deliberately not carried - the click accepts any cell inside the target box, so remembering one would only invite a gate that refuses the cell the armed ray is actually on. A pickup plan is the exception in every field: it places nothing (it takes the module's own lava source back with the empty bucket the pour left behind), its box is the source cell itself, and its click is validated against the tracked cell, not a box. The lava source THIS module poured and still owes a bucket for. Only pours are tracked - lava is never scanned for,

Actual accepted native bursts, including manual/AutoClicker hits that deliberately skip charge.
Called after vanilla's thread guard. Only these entity-pose handlers may be cancelled.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/BedDe.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/BedDe.notes:
BedDefender builds the selected bed's shell, finishing inner layers before outer ones. Materials use a shared editable filter or independent layer lists. Auto Bed matches the explicit team/account-name colour; an unknown colour never silently selects an enemy bed. The read-only preview shows remaining cells and their intended materials, including missing inventory. Placement order preserves analytic face opportunities before a cube can hide them; exposed face windows include partial shapes, with every click confirmed against the real world and wire rotation. Clutch keeps emergency priority; a valid defence placement pauses KillAura and releases its automatic guard, then returns the hand promptly when placement stops.

Ported from AUTISM's ModuleBedDefender, which is about ninety lines of real logic and is a TARGET-SET GENERATOR ONLY: it finds a bed, grows a shell of cells around it and hands the set to the 932-line generic BlockPlacer. That engine is not ported. What a bed defence actually needs from it is an ordered list of cells, a face/support planner, a reach test, a cadence gate and one click, and every one of those is already solved in {@link SurroundModule} - this module is that module's pipeline with a different target set.

THE GEOMETRY is AUTISM's searchBedLayer and it is the whole design. Both halves of the bed seed a breadth-first walk whose direction set is {@code {away from the partner, UP, and the two horizontals perpendicular to the bed axis}}. Neither walk can step toward the partner, so the bed's own two cells are never yielded and the two seed sets are provably disjoint. The module never reads BedPart and is completely head/foot agnostic; all it needs is which way the partner lies, which is exactly what vanilla's {@link BedBlock#getConnectedDirection(BlockState)} answers.

DOWN IS IN NEITHER DIRECTION SET and stays out of both, because at maxLayers >= 2 it would grow a downward hemisphere and turn a bed shell into an excavation filler. The underside is still a real hole - BedBlock declares no canSurvive and no support-dependent updateShape in 26.2, so a bed floats and an opponent tunnelling underneath breaks it through its own cell - so the two cells directly under the halves are added by hand as layer-1 targets instead. On solid ground they are not replaceable and cost one state read each; over an open tunnel they are exactly the cells that matter, and the eye-side-of-the-plane test refuses them until the player can genuinely see in.

THE BED IS A LEGAL SUPPORT ONLY WHILE SNEAKING and that is the only route to the two cells on top of it at maxLayers 1. Vanilla's performUseItemOn computes {@code isSecondaryUseActive() && haveSomethingInOurHands} and, when it holds, skips the clicked block's use action entirely and drops straight into BlockItem.place - which is exactly how a hand puts a block on a bed. A bed click WITHOUT that carve-out runs BedBlock.useWithoutItem instead - a sleep attempt, or a 5.0-power explosion in the Nether and the End that destroys the bed we exist to protect - so the carve-out is scoped to the BED and nothing else, and no door, chest or respawn anchor becomes a support just because shift is down.

THIS MODULE PRESSES SHIFT FOR IT, which is a deliberate exception to the client-wide rule that a module never writes a movement key, granted for this one case and nothing else. It is NARROW in three ways at once and every one of them is load-bearing: only while the chosen plan's support really is the bed (see {@link #sneakForBed}), only additively - the input hook can add shift and can never take one away, so a player already crouching is untouched and there is no "previous state" to restore - and only for as long as such a plan is live, since {@link #preMovementTick()} clears the request at its head and every stand-down path leaves it cleared. The press is booked one tick AHEAD of the click by construction, which is what {@link #serverSeesSneak()} needs: the input packet carrying shift leaves on this tick's LocalPlayer.tick and the use packet the server computes suppressUsingBlock for cannot ship until the tick after. Turn the setting off and the top cells are placed off a riser instead, exactly as before.

THE BED SCAN is throttled, unlike AUTISM's. There is no BedBlockEntity in 26.2 - the bed is a plain block with no block entity at all - so a block-state sweep is the only option, and AUTISM runs a 15x15x15 cuboid of getBlockState EVERY tick with no cache and no throttle, growing to 25x25x25 at its widest settings. That is not acceptable inside the pre-movement tick, where Scaffold's planning also lives. This port caches the accepted bed, re-validates it with a single getBlockState per tick, and sweeps only when that validation fails or the rescan interval comes round. The cache doubles as the hysteresis AUTISM lacks: standing between two beds, AUTISM rebuilds the whole set from the nearest half every tick and thrashes between them as you move, finishing neither. Here the first bed is kept until it dies or leaves the scan radius.

"ALREADY PROTECTED" IS ONE TEST and it is AUTISM's: a cell counts as defended iff its current state is not replaceable. Wool counts. A sign counts. Nothing is ever compared against what you hold, no weak block is ever upgraded and nothing is ever mined - which is the correct behaviour for a module that must not break blocks.

WHAT WAS NOT PORTED is the placer's whole permission surface, because every item on it is something a hand cannot do: WallRange (through-wall reach, granted with no raytrace at all), Range as a hardcoded slider unrelated to the real attributes, ConstructFailResult (fabricate a hit vector when the verification ray misses and send it anyway), RotationMode NoRotation, the Ignore = {OpenInventory, UsingItem} opt-ins, SwingMode's swing-hiding variants and a 1-2 tick placement cooldown. Reach here is blockInteractionRange and nothing else - the attribute the server actually bounds a block in

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Chams.notes:
Chams: renders selected entities through walls, like ESP, but as the actual model. In "Colored" style the model is drawn twice - a bright colour where it's visible and a solid colour where it's hidden behind blocks (default bright green / dark red). "Texture" style draws the real model see-through with no tint. An armor toggle controls whether worn equipment gets the same treatment.

All the work is a per-entity decision computed once per frame (in {@code extractEntity}) and two extra model submissions through memoized render types, so it stays cheap even for hundreds of players. See {@code AutismChamsLivingEntityMixin} / {@code AutismChamsEquipmentLayerMixin} / {@code AutismChamsRenderTypes}.
