src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Cryst.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Cryst.notes:
Places and detonates end crystals on this client's silent-rotation and real-ray infrastructure. Module id, and the owner token this module holds the shared silent rotation under. Verified against the 26.2 jar. EndCrystalItem.useOn ignores the clicked FACE entirely: it requires the clicked block to be obsidian or bedrock, requires {@code pos.above()} to be empty, requires the box (x, y, z)-(x+1, y+2, z+1) at that cell to contain no entity, and then spawns the crystal at (x+0.5, y, z+0.5). Two consequences the port depends on: the face we send only has to be a face the ray really hit (no face substitution is ever needed), and the occupancy cell is TWO blocks tall, not one - AUTISM's 1x1x1 box under-rejects. Rays the whole placement scan may spend in one tick, across every ranked support.

The sample grid this replaced cast one ray per face sample - up to 54 per support and over 200 per tick - because it had no way to tell an impossible face from an unlucky sample. AutismFaceScan refuses the plane, the reach and the pitch cap in closed form for free, so the only rays left are the ones that can actually confirm something, and the ladder needs at most four of them per candidate.

Raised from 12, which bought at most three ray-paying candidates for a whole tick and was the reason a spot behind those three took several ticks to reach. The number itself is the shared one now: two auras on two private literals is how the budget drifts, and a client-world clip is a voxel walk over loaded chunks, well under what the exposure grid already costs. The damage contest between a crystal on an existing support and building a fresh obsidian elsewhere. The builder is consulted at all only while the place plan promises less than UPGRADE_BAR - past that the crystal is already a strong hit and the faster action wins by default. When consulted, the fresh spot must beat EVERY usable existing support (and the place plan itself) by both margins: an absolute MIN_GAIN, because the obsidian route costs two extra actions before any damage lands, and a MIN_RATIO, because "huge" is relative to what was on the table.

The margins are deliberately wide. The builder's damage promise is measured against an enemy who keeps moving: by the time the fresh support is built and carries a crystal, a knockback has usually shifted the target a block, and the support that was just used still passes every gate against the new position. Anything short of a doubling is that noise - chasing it plants a block one step closer and hands the enemy the time to wall it off, which is exactly the trade the crystal-on-existing-support route exists to refuse. How long a won place-vs-obsidian decision is HELD, in client ticks, before the contest may re-run. The decision is re-priced every tick off inputs that move with the aim itself - the place scan's face solvability is wire-referenced, its cursor parking follows the budget, and the margins straddle - so with static geometry the winner could alternate every tick. Each side resolves its hand by moving the hotbar and returning null for that tick, and the loser's switch consumes the one-change latch the winner then needs, so an alternating contest became an alternating HOTBAR in which neither side ever fired. Holding the winner for a window makes one material switch impossible within a commitment lifetime, and the committed side gets the consecutive ticks a switch-plus-converge needs to fire. The builder's window is the longer one: its route costs a hotbar switch and a full sweep before it can fire. Consecutive contest ticks an active builder ban may suppress planObsidian while no place plan forms, before the ban expires on its own (C1). The ban's re-check ({@link #builderBanned}) re-verifies only the coarse gates - it never asks whether the aim pipeline can actually solve the support's faces - so a support behind durable cover, on a reach or pitch fringe, or starved by the ray budget would otherwise hold the lock forever in static geometry: planPlace null every tick, the builder locked out, no commitment riding, and the offence producing nothing and no packets. Four is long enough that a transient aim gap (the sweep still travelling, one tick of budget starvation) never lifts a healthy ban, and short enough that a genuinely unaimable support costs the offence four ticks instead of the fight. Prime-position detection for the spam cadence, stationary path: how many consecutive ticks the place plan must keep landing on the same support area before the configured delays are bypassed, and how far the plan may drift and still count as the same spot. A stationary enemy in a hole or pit re-elects the same support every tick; a moving one re-elects a new one or none, so the streak alone is most of the detector and the radius only absorbs the one-step wobble a knockback inside the hole produces. Both parties must be under this speed (blocks per tick, squared) for the position to count as prime. Walking is ~0.21 and sprinting ~0.28, so 0.25 admits standing, shuffling and walking but never sprinting - the case the configured delays remain for. The stationary path measures the WHOLE vector, so a jumping enemy (0.42 vertical) breaks it at once; the vulnerable path applies the same threshold to the horizontal components only, because an enemy trapped above keeps being a spam target through jumps and falls, and only a horizontal escape changes that. The place plan's predicted target damage must clear Min Target Damage by at least this much for the stationary streak to grow: spamming is only worth the dropped delays while every blast is a strong hit, not merely an acceptable one. A flat bonus on the damage model's own one-heart scale, NOT a multiple: the 2x ratio this replaced put the bar at twice the setting, which a high Min Target Damage (2x of 5 = 10 hearts through real exposure) made unreachable in exactly the pit geometry the detector exists for. Offence-free ticks a warm streak survives. One, and only

AUTISM's FreeLook: while the bind is HELD the mouse steers only the camera, never the player rotation - the third-person camera orbits freely and the view snaps back on release. Defaults match AUTISM: Back perspective and no pitch limit.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Ghost.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Ghost.notes:
Client-side ghost blocks: placements only exist in the local world copy — no interaction packets are ever sent, the server never sees them, and server-side block updates for ghost positions are swallowed so they persist. Right-click with a block places a ghost, left-click a ghost removes it, and sneak + right-click keeps the real vanilla interaction as an escape hatch. Creative mode rides the shared fake-gamemode utility ({@link autismclient.util.AutismFakeGamemode}) so the creative inventory hands out local ghost items; its creative slot writes and drops are cancelled before they reach the server, and left-click removes any block locally instead of desyncing a real break. The highlight follows the ghosts, not the toggle: switching the module off leaves them standing (unless Clear On Disable), so they keep their outline until they are cleared or the world takes them back. Modelled on the GhostBlock Fabric mod, rebuilt around this client's module hooks.
The fake creative gamemode is always handed back — leaving that behind is what made a disabled module look like it was still ghost-placing in survival. Ghosts themselves only go if Clear On Disable is on; with the module off they are inert local blocks that the next server update overwrites, and they stay highlighted for as long as they are standing (see {@link #tick()}).
Ghosts outlive the toggle, so the module keeps ticking while off for as long as any are left — that tick only prunes the map, it never writes to the world.
Creative mode = a real client-side fake creative session (infinite ghost items, creative inventory, local block breaking). Survival mode = plain ghost placement from held blocks only. Re-applied from tick so join timing or a server gamemode reassert can never leave it stuck either way.
Strips the fake creative this module applied. Ownership is tracked here rather than read back off the shared snapshot: anything else touching the fake gamemode in between used to flip that check false and leave the player stuck in a creative they never asked for.
Clear keybind from the module settings: one press wipes every ghost block.
Re-applies any ghost state the server overwrote through a path we could not cancel (section/chunk updates), and re-seeds ghosts after a chunk reload. Single-block updates are cancelled outright in {@link #onPacketReceive}.
The off-state counterpart of {@link #sweepGhosts()}: a disabled module must never write to the world, so a ghost the server has taken back (single-block update, section update, chunk reload) is dropped from the map instead of re-applied. The highlight then only marks cells that really are still fake.
Placement runs through vanilla's own {@link BlockItem#place}, so doors, beds, slabs, stairs, waterlogging, block entities and placement sounds all come out exactly like a real one. Nothing is sent: the level write stays local and the held stack is handed back, because the server still owns the real item.
The clicked cell plus its six neighbours: enough to catch the second half of doors, beds and tall plants, so removing the ghost later takes the whole thing with it.
Backstop for held left-click and macro-driven breaks: same gate as the gameMode path.
Ghosts are removed (or just shielded when Click Removes is off). In Creative mode a real break would only desync against the server, so the block is taken out locally and tracked as a ghost instead — vanilla's own creative break delay paces a held click.
While the fake creative session is up, creative-inventory traffic stays strictly local: the server (or an anticheat) must never see creative slot writes, and dropping a ghost item must not drop the real item the server still has in that slot.
Middle-click. Since 26.2 pick block is entirely server-driven — {@code Minecraft.pickBlockOrEntity} only calls {@code gameMode.handlePickItemFromBlock}, which sends the packet and nothing else — so a server that still has us in survival simply refuses and the key does nothing at all. The fake creative session has to answer it itself, exactly where the packet would have left. Vanilla's creative rule: select a hotbar slot that already holds the item, otherwise put it in the held slot. The slot change rides vanilla's own carried-item sync, never a hand-rolled packet.
The server never caused our placements, so any single-block update for a ghost position is either a prediction correction or a stale resend — drop it, and take the state it carried as the new restore target since that is what is really there.
Restores every ghost block to its original state. Returns how many there were.
Inflated unit boxes for every ghost block, rebuilt only when the ghost map mutates.
GUI-usable targets keep their real right-click action; mirrored from vanilla's own interaction priorities without calling use methods (which would have client-side side effects).

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/GifMo.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/GifMo.notes:
GIF: custom animated images on capes, shields and the HUD.

The module only holds the settings; the actual rendering happens in the cape/shield/HUD render mixins, which read {@link GifState} (a plain holder). This module parses its live settings into one immutable snapshot and swaps it into that holder on every toggle and option change - see {@link ViewmodelModule} for the same pattern and why the indirection matters. Never shareable. These settings hold local file paths, and a share blob carries every option value verbatim, so one click would leak the local disk layout to a lobby. This also refuses inbound settings, so nobody can push a crafted blob that overwrites the local paths either. Pushed-state modules must republish on tick (same pattern as {@link ViewmodelModule}): a module restored as enabled from the config never gets an onEnable call at startup, and the local username only becomes knowable once the session is up. Without this the snapshot could stay EMPTY (or keep a blank selfName) forever and every cape/shield lookup would silently fall back to vanilla. Parse the live settings into one immutable snapshot and swap it into {@link GifState}. Safe to call in any state: the snapshot carries the raw enabled flag itself, so a push while disabled simply publishes an inactive snapshot (and keeps the freshly edited paths warm for the next enable). Best-effort local username: refreshed from the session when possible, otherwise the last known value. name=path entries, split like NameCensor (first '=' else first ':'), keyed by lowercase name. Slider 1-4 → canvas resolution scale; 4 (Original) is the file's own resolution.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/HoleE.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/HoleE.notes:
Draws the crystal-PvP safe spots {@link AutismHoleScanner} finds, coloured by shape so a 1x1 you can burrow into reads differently from a 2x2 that a crystal can still reach around in, and bedrock-walled 1x1s read differently again because nothing mines those out from under you.

The module owns no detection of its own: it {@link AutismHoleScanner.Subscriber subscribes} with the two scan radii and the scanner takes the max over every subscriber, so a later Surround or HoleFiller shares one region and one rebuild instead of paying for a second scan.

PURELY VISUAL. It reads block states and submits geometry; it never touches the player, the hotbar or the connection, and disabling it only stops the drawing.

FRAME BUDGET. The enabled check is the first thing the render callback does; settings resolve through a {@link ModuleRegistry#revision()}-gated snapshot rather than per frame; the hole list is the scanner's last published generation, rebuilt on the client tick in slices, never in the frame; and the whole frame is at most two {@code submitCustomGeometry} calls - one fill, one lines - no matter how many holes are drawn.

CULLING, and why some surfaces are emitted twice. {@code storageEspFillSeeThrough} has no depth test but DOES cull back faces (its pipeline never calls {@code withCull(false)}). A closed box is therefore drawn the way every other ESP box in this client is drawn - one outward winding, three visible faces - but the glowing plane is a set of open sheets that must read from above, from beside, and from inside the hole you are standing in, so each of those sheets is emitted in both windings. Exactly one winding survives the cull from any given viewpoint, so nothing blends twice. AUTISM's face and outline alphas, applied as a fraction of the alpha the user picked. House-style nudge off the real block faces; cosmetic here, since the fill has no depth test. The floor sheet sits on the top face of the floor block, so lift it clear of the terrain quad. Installs the world-render callback. Safe to call any number of times and from anywhere during client init; the module arms it on its first enable, so no wiring is required for it to work. Re-read every render-path setting only when the registry revision moves. A {@code value(id)} call is a linear scan of the settings list plus a map get plus a parse, and this module would otherwise do a dozen of them per frame. AUTISM's cull and fade in one pass; returns 0 for a hole that should not be drawn at all.

The vertical term is SIGNED on purpose. A hole ABOVE you produces a negative fraction and is then governed purely by the horizontal term, because the holes worth seeing are the ones at or below your feet. Taking the absolute value here would fade out exactly the ones you are about to drop into. Scales the colour's own alpha, so a user who dialled their colour down stays dialled down. A horizontal sheet in both windings - see the class note on culling. The four walls of the glowing plane: full colour at the floor, fully transparent at the top. The hole's outline in GlowingPlane mode: just the four edges of the floor it sits on. The canonical six outward-wound faces. This is the client's sixth copy of fillBox and it is a deliberate one, not an oversight: the shared promotion into AutismWorldGeometry is a cleanup that belongs in its own pass across all six call sites, not smuggled in under a new module. Per-vertex colour, which is what makes the glow gradient possible on the plain fill type.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/KBDis.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/KBDis.notes:
Redirects an already selected native melee hit toward a predicted ledge. TriggerBot, AutoClicker, KillAura's normal/packet paths and physical attacks all use the same game-mode attack boundary. Uses one hittable ordinary native look, with the selected full hit carried to the following input interval. The look is handed back right after the hit goes out: Grim judges a hit by the movement before and after it (current or previous look), so the turned look already covers it; holding it until the damage receipt (350-700 ms) froze KillAura after every redirect (user report 2026-11-12). An unavailable or unhittable opportunity leaves the native attack alone.
How each hit through the module ended (diagnostics): redirected, or why not.
Qualification view of the last redirect: tick, turn and what it was planned to do.
The on-target look written before the redirect: sent again right after the hit (see {@link #flanked}).
The redirect look itself does not meet the body; the looks on either side of it do. Grim judges a queued attack at the next update packet against its current OR previous look (javap of Reach 2.3.74), so with the on-target look written before the turn and sent again right after the hit, whichever pair Grim reads holds a hit, and the turn is free up to Max Turn instead of the few degrees the body covers. That corridor was the reason a hit from straight behind on a one-wide bridge never threw (user report 2026-11-12, in-game lanes).
The tick the flank look must stay written (no hand-back step before it goes out).
How far the predicted body was carried on from the last position received (diagnostics).
Which of our hits can still knock back, in send ticks (ping-proof: see {@link KBDisplacementTiming}).
When each recent redirect landed, for the array list (each one shows {@link #INFO_NANOS}).
Ticks a target's predicted server body may be ahead of the last position received.
Reach kept back when the carried hit's next distance is predicted.
Largest turn off the walking direction that still keeps forward (and so sprint) under the key correction.
Read-only qualification view: plans, their mean/slowest cost, all redirects since enabling, landed throws and steers. The array-list info is off by default and only shows ten seconds, so harnesses count from here.
The built-in W-Tap. A turn only moves the sprint (or Knockback) push, and after a damaging sprint hit the server keeps our sprint off until the next START: without a sprint reset only the first hit of a run can be redirected. One tap engine with the W-tapping module ({@link WTappingModule#active()}): while that module is on, its tapper (and settings) is the live one and this one stays idle.
KBDisplacement's tapper while it is enabled with W-Tap on, else null.
Called after native target selection. Held-slot synchronization and the full hit stay together.
Our round trip in client ticks while none of our hits has been measured yet: the tab list's latency.
{@code body}: where the target's own client starts the pushed flight; {@code shift}: from the server's body, which the push direction is taken from, to that one (added to our origin so the direction is the server's).
Where the hit finds the target. The server pushes the body it has when our attack arrives: the last position we received is already a downlink old, and our attack goes out after this movement and takes the uplink, so that body is one of our round trips (plus the carried tick and the position's age) further along. The push then reaches the target's own client a round trip of ITS later, and the flight starts where that client is. At 150-300 ms a body walking the bridge is one to two blocks further on, and the old plan, made at the last position received, threw a body that was no longer there. Carried on at the received speed, stopping at an edge rather than walking off it (KBDisplacementMath.ahead).
What the server will halve: a player's server-side motion is the server's own input-free replay, snapped back to the client's position every tick. Sideways it stays ~0; on the ground it is the resting gravity step; in the air it is gravity accumulated since the replay last met the ground, so a mid-air hit does NOT keep a jump's rise. Mobs are simulated by the server: observed motion.
A throw must still fall if the server's motion is what the client sees, or freshly landed; and it is robust when it survives the target holding forward along its look (most fighters hold W).
Last client tick each nearby player was seen on the ground (from its move packets).
The last server position received for a nearby player, when, and its speed per tick between the last two.
After all owners have had this tick's request: resume KillAura directly when it can run, otherwise complete the normal hand-back BEFORE input and physics, never at packet tail.
The ordinary forward-key band cannot cancel a 65° aim on a one-wide bridge. For the bounded aftermath of our hit, keep the camera's course with the two native bracketing keys.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/KillA.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/KillA.notes:
KillAura based on AUTISM's default combat path, adapted to this client's packet APIs. Human target acquisition uses the shortest curved move inside the rotation guards. Deliberate misses start after an actual attack on that enemy and reset after five seconds without an attack; opening attacks use the first full charge. Later attacks retain the configured miss rate and timing band. Miss intentions never block a valid hit and expire after two ticks or 150 ms. Bare modern misses preserve weapon charge; weapon restores and critical-hit waits cannot restart or hold it forever. Block Hit owns only its own defensive item use and releases it a tick before a useful attack. Confirmed equal-damage immunity keeps the guard up unless Respect CPS spends a scheduled press. Enemy facing, clear sight and the weapon's real reach plus its defensive margin decide whether to guard. Queued Real Input clicks commit hit windows, aim rhythm and follow-ups only after native attack dispatch. A refused ray or GUI-interrupted input pass cannot invent a hit or leave a pressed edge. Neither defence nor attack timing reads ping or estimated server TPS.

The old -50..25 swung on 12 or 13 only (600 or 650 ms, two in three on 12), right on FairPlay 4.0.8's sword_19 cheat set (640 +- 20 ms): 1.5 alerts a minute in its replica over re-timed live fight streams (the worst 9.8). src/main/java/autismclient/modules/LeafD.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/LeafD.notes:
Grim-only leaf dupe. Each role defaults to automatic acquisition; custom positions stay saved independently. Both target modes use the registry whitelist (diamond, netherite and all 17 shulker variants by default). A leaf must be an isolated upper small-dripleaf half.

Setup automatically selects a suitable hotbar tool, proves an accepted target look, and sends one non-instant START. Only its final accepted write arms cycles. Every cycle revalidates loaded state, outline reach and world visibility from both live and last-written server poses, yields to manual/GUI/emergency hand use, and sends reset, leaf, then STOP before vanilla's movement. Normal pacing has no ArrayList suffix. Session changes cancel pending work; a final reset is scoped to its original world and hand. Owns one activation/target/tool; old queued packets retain cancelled receipts after it ends. Read-only final-write gate: only this module's exact packet identities are subject to it.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Modul.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Modul.notes:
Mutation stamp for conditional restoration by automation; explicit same-value edits count. The configured enabled state without the early-access lock applied. Internal bookkeeping (toggle transitions, panic disable/restore) must see the truth; only feature consumers get the locked view. Silent automation ownership: runtime hooks run, while the user's configured toggle and config file stay intact. Updates the saved state from a title-screen editor without running world hooks. Registers a typed setting and returns the same instance, so a module can keep a strongly-typed handle: {@code final DoubleSetting speed = add(new DoubleSetting(...));} Hold-bind modules (e.g. FreeLook) stay enabled exactly while their keybind is physically held. Whether this module's settings may ever leave this client — matchmaking shares, and anything added later.

Override to {@code false} for a module holding a credential or anything else private: AutoLogin stores a server password, and a share blob carries every option value verbatim. This is enforced at the capture, decode and apply choke points rather than in a UI, so no screen, card action, or future share path can miss it. A module that returns {@code false} also refuses INBOUND settings, so a crafted blob cannot overwrite the local values either. Whether this module appears in the on-screen module arraylist HUD while enabled. Override to {@code false} for a module that must stay invisible when active (e.g. Fake Coords — showing its name would defeat it). AUTISM PlayerNetworkMovementTickEvent (PRE): LocalPlayer.sendPosition HEAD, before this tick's move packet. AUTISM TickPacketProcessEvent: once per frame, after inbound packets were processed. Once per frame at the end of runTick: where mouse input timed in ms is made (the next tick consumes it). AUTISM PlayerTickEvent cancel: true freezes the whole LocalPlayer tick (no physics, no movement packet). Client timer multiplier contributed by this module. The global timer multiplier is the product of all enabled modules' values. Return 1.0f to leave tick speed unchanged. Updates a live setting without writing the config during continuous UI input. Updates an offline setting without writing the config during continuous UI input. An external write made by an offline (title-screen) change: a setting it updates in turn goes the same way. Writes a setting another one is only a view of, the same way (live or offline) as the write under way. Optional storage override for a setting whose lifetime is not the active client profile. Returning a non-null value makes {@link #value(String)} and the typed setting API read that value directly. The default keeps every existing module setting in {@link AutismConfig.ModuleState} unchanged. Counterpart to {@link #externalSettingValue(String)}. Return true only when the value was handled by the external store; false preserves normal profile-config persistence.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/NameT.notes: Floating name/info labels above entities (a screen-space nametag ESP). Tags players and optionally mobs and dropped items; player text always comes from the account profile, preserving server name colors but stripping ranks, suffixes, and custom fonts. Health, distance, equipment and enchantments remain independently configurable, with independent distance, enchantment and background colors (including opacity); the health readout tints itself by HP, from green at full to a bright red near death (never a dark, hard-to-read red). Font selects Onest (default) or vanilla; Pill Background defaults on with antialiased edges. src/main/java/autismclient/modules/NoCli.notes:
Java port of AUTISM's ModuleNoClip (1:1). Every tick the player is pushed straight through blocks: noPhysics on, fall distance cleared, and the velocity replaced by the WASD direction at the configured speed with jump/shift driving the vertical axis. Player.tick wipes noPhysics again right after, so AutismPlayerNoPhysicsMixin re-applies it (AUTISM's hookNoClip). One deliberate deviation: AUTISM only clears noPhysics on the vehicle you ride at the moment you disable, so a vehicle you dismount while NoClip is on keeps falling through the world forever. The vehicle this module forced is tracked and released instead.
AUTISM's noClipSet: the disable cleanup runs once when the module pauses mid-flight.
Set on the netty thread, consumed on the client thread.
AUTISM's tickHandler. It has to run before vanilla movement, not after it, so this is not tick().
AUTISM's hookNoClip condition (running && !paused()), read by AutismPlayerNoPhysicsMixin.
AUTISM's paused(): with OnlyInVehicle on and no vehicle, the module behaves as if it were off.
AUTISM's onDisabled.
AUTISM's withStrafe at strength 1.0 followed by the jump/shift vertical write: neither the old horizontal velocity nor the old y ever survives, so both collapse into one assignment. The vehicle branch steers by the PLAYER's input and movement yaw, not the vehicle's.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/NoRen.notes:
Suppresses rendering of a large set of world/HUD/overlay/entity elements — the full "No Render" feature set ported from Meteor Client and retargeted to this version of the game (26.2).

The module holds the settings; the actual suppression happens in the {@code AutismNoRender*} mixins. Those mixins DO NOT read this class — they read {@link NoRenderState}, a plain holder with no {@link Module} or {@code Minecraft} dependency. This module simply {@linkplain #push() pushes} its current settings into that holder every tick (and on enable/disable). This indirection is deliberate and load-bearing: some No Render mixins fire during block bootstrap, before the {@code Minecraft} instance exists, so they must never touch a {@code Module} subclass (that would statically init {@code Module.MC = Minecraft.getInstance()} too early and null it out for every module). See {@link NoRenderState}.

A few Meteor options are intentionally not ported because they hook game internals that changed too much in 26.2 to reproduce safely (chat message-signature indicator, barrier invisibility, cave-culling) or need a registry picker kind this UI doesn't have (arbitrary per-particle list — covered pragmatically by "hide all particles" + firework/eating toggles). Forced client time-of-day; VANILLA leaves the real clock alone. Ticks follow the vanilla /time presets. Forced client weather; VANILLA leaves the real weather alone. SNOW shows as snow only in cold biomes. Copy the live settings into {@link NoRenderState} (the plain holder the mixins read). Clock ticks for a time preset (tuned to the actual sun position, matching AUTISM for 26.2); CUSTOM reads the slider, VANILLA is unused.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Phase.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Phase.notes:
Java port of AUTISM's ModulePhase (1:1), with all four modes: - Clip (AUTISM Hypixel): one spoofed move packet to the centre of the block you stand in, one gravity step lower, then the module turns itself off. It lives for exactly one tick. - Intave: holding attack while looking down keeps re-sending STOP_DESTROY_BLOCK for the block below, and the raw position sinks 0.0052 per tick while the bounding box stays where it was. Sneaking adds a 0.005 micro-step in the pressed direction. - Blink: walk into the block with collisions turned off and hold every packet until the server-side block is gone, then release the backlog. The disable path flushes the inbound queue BEFORE the collisions come back, so the anticheat never sees you walking through a block that still existed. - Spider (AUTISM BlocksMC): a three-tick hop ladder (0.42 / 0.33 / 0.25) with the collision shapes at and above your feet emptied, plus a 0.179 strafe while sneaking. Every AUTISM {@code tickHandler} body is on {@link #preMovementTick()} (Minecraft.tick HEAD): Clip in particular needs its spoofed packet to go out before vanilla's own sendPosition for the same tick. Per-mode enter/exit runs on module toggle and on a mode switch while enabled, exactly like AUTISM's ModeValueGroup.
AUTISM's BlockShapeEvent handlers, called from the three collision hooks.
The shape mode drops first, so a mode's own disable() sees real collisions while it flushes.
AUTISM's Entity.doesCollideAt: the player's box moved to {@code pos}, tested against real block shapes.
AUTISM's Mode contract: enter/exit plus the handlers a mode may install.
Short arraylist suffix after the mode name. Empty for a mode with nothing to say.
AUTISM PhaseHypixel: one block-centre move packet a gravity step lower, then the module is done.
AUTISM PhaseIntave: fake a finished block break below you every tick while attack is held and you look down, sinking the position past the floor. Only works on 1.8.x servers.
The mode is silent until both inputs are held, so the arraylist names the missing one.
The micro-step does move the bounding box, so this one is a real setPos.
AUTISM PhaseBlink: with collisions off you walk into the block; once the box really overlaps we start holding packets, and we keep holding until the held positions no longer collide (the server told us the block is gone). At the tick budget the backlog is released and the cycle restarts, the way the Blink module's Auto Reset works.
A phase that never reaches WALKING is not working, so it gives up instead of holding forever.
Non-null means "turn the module off on the next safe frame", and carries the reason.
Set at the tick budget: release the backlog and start over on the next safe frame.
AUTISM's PlayerNetworkMovementTickEvent PRE: the phased-in position, before the move packet goes out.
AUTISM freezes the player tick forever once the budget is spent, and its counter can never advance again, so you stay frozen until you toggle the module off by hand. This recycles instead. The tick keeps being cancelled until the recycle lands on the next packet-process frame, so no tick ever runs against the emptied shapes with a stale backlog behind it.
The Blink module's Auto Reset, applied to this mode: release the backlog and go back to WAITING so the next collision opens a fresh hold. Mirrors {@link #disable()} except the policy stays registered. Returning to WAITING makes the policy vote FLUSH, which is what lets the manager release the outgoing queue; the explicit request only covers the frame ordering.
AUTISM's BlinkPacketEvent handler. The six clientbound carve-outs are how the client gets to SEE the block disappear, so without them the walking exit could never fire.
AUTISM PhaseBlocksMC: a three-tick hop while the shapes at and above your feet are emptied.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/PingS.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/PingS.notes:
Spoofs your ping while enabled by holding the server's keep-alive and answering it late, so the server measures your real round-trip plus the configured delay. Modelled on AUTISM's PingSpoof (see {@link PingSpoofController}). The delay is additive — it raises your ping; it cannot lower it.

The base toggle only fools the server's measured ping. "Real: Incoming" / "Real: Outgoing" make the client actually behave as if it had the latency by also holding received / sent packets, each independently toggleable (both on = full round-trip lag).

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/SafeW.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/SafeW.notes:
SafeWalk — a real sneak at ledges, gated on looking down.

Built on the same principle as the Grim scaffold's edge guard: the sneak rides the REAL input record, so the server (and any movement simulation on it) applies the identical edge clamp and slowdown on its side. Nothing is spoofed and no {@code isStayingOnGroundSurface} override is forced — that variant clamps the client at edges while the server sees no sneak state at all, and the resulting divergence is precisely what a simulation check flags.

Three knobs, all of them about when it is allowed to fire rather than how it moves:

  • Look Down — minimum downward pitch. Walking along a ledge looking at the horizon leaves the sneak off; the moment you look down at the drop it engages. 0 means any downward look qualifies.
  • Edge Distance — how far ahead the drop is probed, along actual travel (or the camera when standing still).
  • Hold Time — once engaged the sneak is held for a random duration inside this band. A ledge probe flickers on and off as you walk, and releasing on the exact tick the probe clears produces a machine-perfect stutter; a randomized minimum hold turns that into a human-looking crouch. The hold re-arms with a fresh roll while the ledge is still there, so safety is never traded for it.

Stands down entirely while Scaffold is enabled: Scaffold runs its own edge sneak with a placement cadence and a full-speed escape, and a second opinion on the same key would only bleed its bridging speed. How far below the probed foot position counts as "nothing there". A step-up ledge is not a drop. Horizontal shrink on the probe box, so brushing a wall corner does not read as solid footing. Floor on the probe distance, because below it the guard cannot physically win the race.

The probe looks {@code edge-distance} ahead along travel and the sneak it asks for only takes effect on the NEXT tick. A grounded walk covers 0.116 blocks per tick and a sprint more, so any probe shorter than one tick of travel can read solid footing on the tick before the foot is already past the lip - the sneak then engages behind the player and the clamp has nothing left to clamp. Reported at 0.05-0.10: falls; 0.15 and up: none. One tick of travel is the hard lower bound and 0.15 is the first step above it. Probe distance actually used. Clamped at the read so a config saved under an older, lower minimum cannot resurrect the fall. Consecutive clear probes before the sneak is allowed to drop.

The ledge probe flickers as the footprint slides over a rim, and releasing on the first clear tick turns that flicker into a crouch toggle every other tick. That is the one thing a hand cannot produce, and it is the whole difference from Scaffold's sneak, which rides the 7-tick placement cadence and so can never toggle faster than that. Both take the identical input path (one mixin, one Input record), so the delivery was never the problem - the RATE was. Holding through a short clear run is strictly MORE sneak, so no safety is traded away. Input hook, chained after Scaffold and KillAura. Only ever ADDS sneak — a player already crouching, or another module that wants it, is never overridden. True while the sneak should be held this tick, advancing the randomized hold timer. Once engaged, ride out a short run of clear probes rather than dropping on the first one. True when there is nothing to stand on {@code distance} blocks ahead. Probes along real travel when moving so a strafe or a diagonal is guarded the same as a straight walk, and falls back to the camera when standing still (which is also the only case where the look direction is the honest intent). Scaffold's own edge sneak is cadence-aware; two modules pressing the same key would only fight.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Scaff.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Scaff.notes:
AUTISM Normal Scaffold profiles with this client's real-click hotbar routing. Eagle shares Telly's cardinal placement/acknowledgement/landing planner, retains the rearward look between placements, and caps mouse steps at 18 degrees. Its Jump toggle defaults on; off suppresses takeoff and physical Space. Both routes brake with movement keys, never automatic sneak, and Eagle never hands a blocked jump to Legit's sneaking controller. Telly stops accelerating when movement keys are released, retains placement ownership through interrupted landings, and hands blocked jump routes to the Legit controller until they clear. Telly never adds sneak: only the player's physical Shift key can crouch its owned input. Allow Diagonal hands diagonal travel to rate-unlimited Legit while keeping Telly or Eagle selected; cardinal travel resumes Telly from settled footing, never by interrupting an airborne arc. Humanization samples a 0-100% smoothness band independently for the rear and return sweeps, using the combat hand's curved minimum-jerk movement; zero turns immediately. Turn Delay's ceiling reserves time for the slowest end of the band. Imperfection may add up to two tops behind the body during the same rear sweep, only on confirmed support with spare look/use intervals; it never raises the landing plan. At 200% each flat jump plans two distinct tops, reserves both look/use pairs before takeoff and shortens its arc. A short hop may stack its second top once behind the body. Held Space prioritizes climbing; actual reach, body clearance and catch checks still apply. Emergency catches may use a visible adjacent wall/support for the actual landing footprint. And the cap on the tick we actually CLICK. Vulcan's Scaffold check measures the rotation delta of the placing tick, not of every tick, so the free sweep above may keep its 20 while the click waits for a step under this. A global 10 is what the 00:19 trace blamed for leaving the validation ray 4 cm above the block through the ticks the chain had to place on; this splits the two so neither problem comes back. 13:06 emitted -19.95, -17.40, +19.95 and -11.70 on four consecutive ticks and placed on the last of them. Ticks of travel a candidate cell must stay clear of the body for. See grimCellClearOfBody. Ticks of travel the airborne chain may look ahead when asking whether the eye is on a face's outward side. Planning only - the click gate still rays the real eye - so this buys the aim its approach instead of starting it the tick the plane is crossed. Minimum horizontal speed that counts as travelling (edge prediction, void-ahead tests). Lane error the strafe fallback tolerates before it engages. With the posture lined up on the course the walk is already straight, so this only has to catch a real disturbance - a jump, a knockback, a corner. Holding it wide is what keeps A/D silent on a straight run. The Legit corrector's ENGAGE threshold. It is a hysteresis latch, not a deadband: nothing happens until the drift is worth one weave, and then the correction holds its side until the player is back on the line.

A plain deadband here is a limit cycle and 12:14 rode it for the whole capture. One strafe tick builds ~0.06/tick of lateral speed, so the 4-tick velocity lead swings the PREDICTED error by +-0.24 - more than twice the 0.10 band the first version used. It therefore reversed on the prediction while the real offset was still large: t213 +0.245 pressing A, t215 +0.373 flipping to D, t219 +0.089, t220 +0.091 flipping back to A. A strafe key change every 2-4 ticks for hundreds of ticks, which is exactly what the user called out as inhuman.

0.28 was where the offset starts to cost real footing (grimFootingOverlap measures the box against the one-wide bridge, so 0.30 off centre reads ovl 0.50 instead of 0.60). That was the right number while half the lane readings were fabricated - see buildMovementLine, whose fallback anchor was algebraically the player's own position, so the corrector could not tell a centred run from an 0.23 offset. With the anchor honest, the real steady offset on a bridge is ~0.23 and sat permanently under 0.28: the module would have measured it correctly and still never acted. 0.15 is under that, so a persistent lean now draws one short tap.

It cannot move alone. The corrector only ever changes WHICH KEY is pressed, and the emitted strafe does not flip until {@link #GRIM_INPUT_OCTANT_BOUNDARY_DEGREES}, so the engage point and {@link #GRIM_LANE_INPUT_LOOKAHEAD_LEGIT} are one tuning pair - lowering this without lowering that asks for 19 degrees and flips nothing at all. The position band the correction is finished inside. The hard cap on how long one correction may hold, whatever the position says.

Position alone is not a release: the player reaches the band still carrying the ~0.078 per tick of lateral speed the correction built, and coasts straight through. 13:39 t048-t055 held D for seven consecutive ticks and turned an 0.079 error into 0.381 on the FAR side, and lane= never settled for the rest of the 700-tick capture.

It is also what keeps a diagonal diagonal. A saturated correction asks 38 degrees against 45-degree octants, so it selects the ADJACENT octant - which on a diagonal lane is a cardinal one, i.e. one motion axis removed outright. 13:38 t088-t095 held D for eight ticks and watched vz decay 0.007 -> 0.000: the SE walk flattened to straight east, the placement chain and the real path diverged, and the run fell.

Round 10 took it from 3 to 2, and the number is set by the deadband, not by taste. The emitted octant is 45 degrees off the lane, so a held tick is ~0.08 of lateral travel and the coast after release adds ~1.2 more ticks of it. Three ticks is ~0.30 plus ~0.08 = an arrival 0.23 past centre against a {@link #GRIM_LANE_CORRECT_ENGAGE} of 0.15 - outside the band and immediately eligible to re-engage the other way, which is a limit cycle by construction. Two ticks lands at ~0.12 and stops. The predictive

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Surro.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Surro.notes:
Surround - fills the cells around your feet so a crystal cannot be placed next to you.

Ported from AUTISM's ModuleSurround, which is a target-set generator plus a set of self-disable guards; the placement itself lives in its 932-line generic BlockPlacer. That engine is not ported. What a surround actually needs from it is small: an ordered list of cells, a cadence gate and one click, all of which live here. The face and support planning does not - that is {@link AutismFaceScan}, shared with BedDefender, CrystalAura and AnchorAura, which is what gives this module real sub-box rects, partial faces and edges rather than a face-centre of the shape's bounding union.

THE TARGET SET is AUTISM's, rebuilt from the live bounding box every tick. The feet layer is the cell the feet are IN - AUTISM ceils minY, which is off by one on anything partial, so standing on a snow layer or a slab built the whole ring a block too high - the feet columns are the hole, and every neighbour of those columns in DOWN/WEST/EAST/NORTH/SOUTH is a target. UP is never targeted and the feet columns themselves are never targeted - that would be a burrow. WHICH columns is the Ring setting: the player's own by default, or AUTISM's every-column-the-box-touches. AUTISM can afford the latter because it snaps the player onto the block centre on enable; this port does not move the player, so an off-centre stop under that setting grows the ring to six or eight cells whose far arm sits a whole block further out.

ORDER IS DELIBERATE, unlike AUTISM's, which inserts a HashSet into a linked map and therefore places in BlockPos hash order. The horizontal ring goes first because it is what stops a crystal landing beside you, then the Down cell, then the protection layer. Within each group a cell WE placed and something broke jumps the queue - that is this port's answer to AUTISM's Instant feature, which fires a real useItemOn from the netty thread off an incoming block-update packet. That is neither thread-safe against the client world nor tick-aligned, and an off-tick interaction packet is a Grim Post violation on its own. Rebuilding the set every tick already re-queues a broken cell within one tick; ordering it first is the whole benefit without the flag.

WITHIN the ring the order is the Aim Speed setting's: AUTISM's WEST/EAST/NORTH/SOUTH at speed 1, and a cycle rotated onto the nearest cell above that. The stream converges and holds between placements, so every transition pays the ease-in ramp from a dead stop and AUTISM's order spends 450 degrees of yaw on four cells where 270 would do. That, and not the per-tick step cap, is where a surround's wall clock actually goes.

THE CLICK is the direct path - vanilla's own {@code MultiPlayerGameMode.useItemOn} with a hit vector we computed - not the genuine-input path Scaffold uses. That choice is forced and deliberate: the input path makes vanilla consume {@code Minecraft.hitResult}, which is computed from the CAMERA, and this module aims silently. Scaffold can use it only because it owns a mixin that substitutes hitResult at handleKeybinds HEAD and a claim inside startUseItem. The direct path still runs vanilla's real interaction method, so the packet, the block-prediction sequence and the ACK reconciliation are all genuine; what it does not produce is a mouse click edge. For a burst of four to twelve placements that is the right trade.

THE CADENCE IS THE ROTATION. There is no place-delay setting and no millisecond floor: a click fires on the first client tick on which the wire gate already passes, and the only remaining limit is one interaction per client tick, which is vanilla's. The interval is therefore the convergence time, which the accel, ease and peak spans re-roll on every turn, so the placement stream carries real variance instead of a synthetic jitter on top of a flat number. A faster Aim Speed is now a faster ring, which under the old clock it was not.

Everything the anticheat judges is taken from the WIRE, not from this tick's aim. The use packet leaves at tick head, before this tick's movement packet, so the server replays it against the last rotation that actually reached the connection. The gate therefore casts its ray from the REAL eye along {@link AutismServerRotationView#snapshot()} and refuses unless that ray lands on the intended support and face. On a tick that fires, the silent aim's goal becomes that same wire rotation, so the movement packet emitted later in the tick carries the rotation the click was validated with - Intave's InteractionRaytrace reads the click against the NEXT movement packet's pitch. That guarantee holds only while this module owns the shared rotation stream, so losing the arbitration to BedDefender means no click on that tick rather than a click under its aim.

Where Surround sits on {@link AutismKillAuraRotation}'s fixed ladder: 25, below BedDefender (30) and above AnchorAura (20), CrystalAura (18), AutoTrap (15) and KillAura (10). The rung itself is declared once, in {@link AutismKillAuraRotation#PRIORITY_SURROUND}; this module declares none of its own.

Above CrystalAura because the ring is self-preservation and the crystal is offence. A ring that fails to close is death; a crystal aim dragged onto a block face costs one crystal that can be re-placed on the next tick. The ring also has a hard deadline - it has to close before the opponent's crystal lands - and its goal is a static world point, where the crystal aura recomputes its goal from live state every tick anyway. That deadline argument covers everything below this rung and not just the crystal aura: melee tracking and trap placement both recompute from live state and so lose nothing by yielding for the two or three ticks one placement takes. Below BedDefender because losing the bed is the terminal loss condition - the ring buys time, the bed is the game.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Teams.notes:
Teams (friends) module: a manual friends list plus automatic teammate detection inspired by AUTISM's ModuleTeams. Visual modules (ESP, Tracers, Nametags) still show friends by default but tinted with a configurable color (light blue); combat modules (AimAssist, KillAura, TriggerBot) ignore friends unless explicitly allowed here. Default visual tint for friends: light blue (aqua), ESP-family alpha. How long a live Multi bot name list is reused before it is rebuilt. After a player (re)spawns its teammate signs come late: the server sends the helmet, and on some servers the team color, a few seconds after the body. A teammate already known in this world keeps counting for that long. Players seen as teammates in this world, by UUID: a respawn makes a new entity of the same player. Press the configured Quick Add key on a player to toggle them as a friend (edge-triggered). Adds a friend by name, or reports the name already exists. Returns false when it was already there. Removes a friend by name. Returns false when no matching friend existed. Clears the whole friend list. Returns false when there was nothing to clear. Current friend names as stored (original casing), for command tab completion. Manual friend, one of my own Multi bots, or an automatically detected teammate; false while disabled. Combat gate: friends are excluded unless the matching toggle explicitly allows them. {@code option} is one of "aimassist", "killaura", "triggerbot". Whether a visual module (esp / tracers / nametags) should draw friends at all. The configured friends tint for ESP / Tracers / Nametags (light blue by default). A player in the running Multi batch is one of mine, so it counts as a teammate without being typed into the friends list. Deliberately live-sessions-only: a name from a saved profile that is not connected belongs to whoever is wearing it right now. Bot names on a short timer rather than on a revision: a session's username resolves asynchronously after it connects, so a structural revision would happily keep an unresolved batch cached. Half a second is imperceptible when a bot joins and costs one list pass. Automatic teammate detection with AUTISM's ModuleTeams defaults: scoreboard team (vanilla isAlliedTo), tab-list name color equality, and dyed helmet color equality.

A player once seen as a teammate is remembered for the rest of this world. A respawned teammate is a new entity with no helmet yet (and on some servers no team color yet), which used to read as an enemy for the few seconds before its equipment arrived: KillAura went for them. Only contrary evidence forgets one: their own explicit name color or dyed helmet differing from ours, and never while either side has just spawned. Account-name run only: rank colors are not team evidence. The tab entry often outlives a respawn. Fresh from a spawn or a respawn, or watching as a spectator (a dead teammate): its signs are not in yet.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/Trigg.notes:
Presses attack when the crosshair is on a configured entity, the way a player would. The server's combat is told apart live: attack speed 20+ is a 1.8 (no cooldown) fight, played with the clicking technique; anything else is the modern charge game, one timed swing per charge, unless Respect Cooldown is off. Runs once per frame, in ms; presses are real mouse edges the next tick consumes. Opening attacks require the entity under the crosshair and skip timing noise at full charge. Grazes and pre-reach swings resume after a real attack, resetting after five seconds of inactivity. The direct pick is refreshed through vanilla at current positions and with the held item's range. A legal target leaving next tick may take a >90% charged hit before its timing offset expires.
User ruling 2026-10-11 (later same day): the reaction is OFF by default in both combat modes.
How far past reach 1.8 swings start, blocks: rolled once per target; 0.0 turns it off.
Back on the same target this soon after the crosshair slipped off: no fresh reaction.
Our press never became a swing (vanilla refused it): the window opens again after this.
A hit throws the timing off this much, half the time.
The boundary bands waver like a hand's: re-judged every 80-160 ms.
A 1.8 fight keeps its rhythm between hits (user ruling 2026-10-21: TriggerBot's clicks must never flag). Clicking only while the crosshair touched the target broke a 13 CPS hand into bursts of two or three with half-second gaps, which FairPlay 4.0.8's click models (10_15_st) read as an autoclicker; a player keeps clicking through the fight, and the clicks that leave the box swing at the air. So once a real hit opened the fight, the engine keeps running while the target stays this close (reach plus Pre-Reach plus the slack) and within this many degrees of the crosshair. Those clicks only ever swing at nothing: never on a block (that would start digging it) or another entity.
A double tap's holds (both presses): short enough for the second to follow a tick after the hit.
The engaged fight's presses: only while the crosshair rests on nothing (see {@link #ENGAGE_DEGREES}). On a block or another entity the click is let go of, never sent late (ClickKeyOutput.press says why).
The tick in whose frames the double tap's second press goes out (it swings on the next one).
The tick our double tap went out: the window its restart opens takes the charge floor (see startWindow).
The target of the fight under way while the crosshair is off it (see {@link #ENGAGE_DEGREES}): the last one, still a legal target, really hit within the last five seconds, close, and roughly in view.
How far the crosshair points off the box, degrees (0 on it): the angle to its centre less its angular radius.
A crosshair-driven click is only legitimate while the camera owns the packets: while a silent rotation rides them the pick comes from the wire, so an attack would be validated against a rotation the crosshair never showed. Never during a Fast EXP hold (the wire is its locked pitch) or beside a totem operation (the swap owns the hand).
The matched entity under the crosshair, else one the crosshair just grazes past the box edge (a real miss swing outside the +0.05 attack-required box; players swing there all the time, a trigger that only fires pixel-perfect has an impossible on-box rate), else on a 1.8 server one a little past reach (the poke as they close in; a bot's move on a modern server, so never there). The last two only while the crosshair rests on nothing: the swing goes to whatever it rests on, and a block there would be punched (in creative, broken) and another entity hit. They also require a real attack on this enemy within the last five seconds: the opening press always needs a direct entity pick.
Nearest matched living entity the camera ray meets within {@code distance}, box grown by {@code grow}.
One press per charge, timed on the charge the crosshair shows (see {@link SwingTiming}).
The Pre-Reach band is rolled once per target: one habit per opponent, never a flicker tick to tick.
Real ms per game tick (server tick rate, client timer).
True once per damage event.
The reaction on a new target, biased by this install's hand and the turn to see it.

src/main/java/autismclient/modules/World.notes:
World: render tweaks for the world. Its Block Tint feature multiplies block textures toward a chosen color by a chosen strength — black at 50% is the classic "darker blocks" look (the default), but any tint color works. A list of blocks acts as a blacklist (spared) or whitelist (only these) via the Mode setting; the default is an empty blacklist, so every solid block is tinted. Fluids (water, lava) render on a separate path and are never touched.

The tint is applied at chunk-mesh build time (baked into the vertex colors by the vanilla {@code ModelBlockRenderer} mixin, Fabric API Indigo's {@code AltModelBlockRendererImpl} mixin (the path chunk meshing actually takes without Sodium whenever Fabric API is installed), and the Sodium block-render mixin via {@link ModuleRenderUtil#worldDarkenTint}), so it costs nothing per frame. Any change that affects the baked color triggers a chunk rebuild here. Copy the live Block Highlight settings into the renderer that draws it.

src/main/java/autismclient/util/macro/Cu.notes:
Fill and submit a server custom screen (dialog), including configuration-phase login/register screens.

Deliberately simple: you give the values that go into the text fields (in order — the first value fills the first field, the second the second, and so on; a single value fills every field, which covers password + confirm) and the text of the button to press afterwards (for example {@code Register}). Everything else is figured out from the live screen.

How long the same skip reason stays quiet, so a fast loop cannot bury the screen in identical toasts. Values typed into the screen's text fields, in order. One value fills all fields (password + confirm). The button to press after filling: its visible text (e.g. "Register"), an action id, or "#index". Blank = auto. A custom screen that could not be answered SKIPS this step; it never ends the run.

It is a wait like any other — Wait For GUI times out and moves on too — and ending the run meant a macro set to loop forever quit for good the first time a screen was slow, missing, or answered by hand. The macro still finishes on its own if this happened to be the last step and there is no loop.

A looping macro would otherwise toast the same failure every pass — several a second with a short timeout.

src/main/java/autismclient/util/macro/Fp.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/util/macro/Fp.notes:
Caps the client's max FPS, ending on one of three conditions chosen by {@link #endMode}:
  • {@link EndMode#TIMEOUT} — the cap lasts for a fixed window set in milliseconds, or in ticks (50 ms each) when {@link #useTicks} is on. {@link #continueNextActions} decides whether the macro blocks here for the window or runs on while the cap expires in the background.
  • {@link EndMode#STEPS} — the cap turns on and the macro continues immediately; it stays on for the next {@link #stepCount} action rows (the impacted span shown in the editor) and is removed once execution leaves that span. Lifetime is owned by the macro executor, not a timer.
  • {@link EndMode#END} — like STEPS but the span runs to the last row of the macro; the cap is removed when the macro finishes (or loops back past this action).
  • {@link #maxFps} is a hard cap, minimum {@code 0}. A value of {@code 0} truly freezes rendering (zero frames presented) — but only meaningful in {@link EndMode#TIMEOUT}; the step-bounded modes clamp it up so an unbounded freeze can never deadlock the macro that has to clear it (see {@link FpsLimitController#applyUntilCleared(int)}).

The actual throttling is performed on the render thread via {@link FpsLimitController} and the framerate mixins; every override path is bounded (timer, step span, or macro lifetime) so it always reverts on its own.

How the FPS cap decides when to switch off. Number of following rows the cap stays on for in {@link EndMode#STEPS} (always {@code >= 1}). Window length in milliseconds, derived from whichever unit is selected (TIMEOUT mode only).

src/main/java/autismclient/util/macro/HC.notes:
Horizontal clip. HClip can only move HORIZONTALLY through clear air — it can never slide through a solid block. Vertical hops, on the other hand, teleport straight through blocks (the vclip primitive). So the way around an obstacle is: vclip up or down to a layer where the horizontal path is clear, hclip across it, then vclip back to the target height. The planner below does exactly that (see {@link #planRoute}).
Find the nearest height (up or down — whichever is closer) where a full clear horizontal corridor runs from the start's XZ to the target's XZ. Route: vclip to that layer, hclip across it, vclip back down/up to land at (or nearest clear to) the original height.
Walk toward the target one clear run at a time. Slide as far as the corridor is clear at the current height; when blocked, vclip to the nearest height that lets us keep going, and continue. Handles rooms where the clear layer changes along the way, and very large spaces (one big clear run per hop).
The height nearest {@code preferredY} at {@code (x, z)} where the player fits. Landing does NOT need solid ground below — it just returns to (or as close as possible to) the height the clip started at. Null if the whole column at (x, z) is solid within range (then the route simply ends at the escape layer).
The farthest point toward {@code target}'s XZ, at {@code from}'s height, that stays clear the whole way.

The ordered click actions the item editor offers, for the action dropdown.
Current action's index within {@link #itemClickActions()} - the dropdown's selected index.
How many button options the current action exposes (SWAP 9, PICKUP 3, QUICK_MOVE 2, else 1).
Button option labels for the current action (L/R/M, H1..H9, ...), for the button dropdown.
A single resolved entry ready to click. {@code cursorTarget != null} marks a cursor PICKUP_ALL (no fixed slot); otherwise {@code slot} is the resolved handler slot. {@code count} is the repeat.
Resolve every entry to a concrete click target, exactly as {@link #execute(Minecraft)} would, but without performing anything. Shared by the immediate (burst) path and the paced (delayed) plan so the two can never drift. Must be called on the client thread (reads the live container).
Perform one resolved entry in full (its whole repeat count), as the immediate burst path does.
Build the full ordered list of individual click operations, one {@link Runnable} per single click, for the executor's paced (delayed) path. Resolution happens now (call on the client thread); each returned op performs exactly one click when run on the client thread. A DROP_STACK entry stays a single op (it's one whole-stack throw); everything else expands to {@code count} single ops so the delay falls between every click — including across entries.

src/main/java/autismclient/util/macro/Jo.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/util/macro/Jo.notes:
Join: get into a server and carry on with the macro once in, at its own "Continue When" timing (the join macro's timings, default Playable; it never follows the Join Macro setting). A blank server means the last server joined.

A Join ahead keeps a macro running through a disconnect, so "Disconnect, wait 2 s, LAN step, Join" is one macro: the steps in between run on the menus and the Join brings it back in. Already on that server, a Join just waits for the timing (put a Disconnect before it to relog); on another server or in a singleplayer world it leaves first. Refused or kicked while joining, it retries until the timeout, and the timeout only counts time spent getting in: a server prompt (resource pack, rules) waiting on the player pauses it. Cancel on the connecting screen stops the macro. "Continue When" of a new Join. Bukkit refuses a second login from one address inside 4 s ("Connection throttled"). Leaving a singleplayer world saves it first; a big world can take a while. A connection that closed without an error screen counts as failed after this long. One Join at a time: two macros joining different servers would keep cancelling each other. Run by MacroExecutor on the macro thread (it blocks until in, or failed). True if an enabled Join is at or after {@code from}, or anywhere when the macro loops. Whether a run keeps going when the world goes away. A kick, a lost connection or the macro's own Disconnect keeps a run that will Join again; the player quitting (pause menu, death screen) never gets overridden by a rejoin. Everything else follows "stop macro on leave". Same server: host compared without case, the port defaulting to 25565. The server this Join goes to, as typed, or the last server; blank when there is none. The join timing this action continues at; anything unknown (the old "same as the join macro") is the default. Gets into the target server and waits for the join timing. {@code status} receives short progress lines for the progress bar. False when it could not get in (no or bad server, refused until the timeout, cancelled): the macro stops. Interrupted = the macro was stopped. After a Disconnect with a Join ahead: waits until the world is really gone, so the steps after it run on the menus. Bounded - a kick that never comes just lets the macro go on (its Join leaves anyway). One Join, from wherever the client is to "in the target server at the timing". One tick of getting in; null = keep going. In the target server's world; vanilla keeps the joined server's data through a transfer. Records the reason of an error screen once, and spaces the next try after it. The server list entry when there is one, so its resource pack choice applies. Cancel on the connect screen returns to the server list, never to a stack of error screens. Leaves the current server or world; true once fully out. One connection attempt: ours, or one already underway that goes to the same server. The connection is up but a server prompt (resource pack, rules) is waiting on the player. What the connect screen's Cancel button does. Client thread.

src/main/java/autismclient/util/macro/Ma.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/util/macro/Ma.notes:
A reusable, arbitrarily-nested boolean condition shared by {@link IfAction} and {@link FlowAction}.

A node is either a GROUP ({@link Combine#ALL ALL}/{@link Combine#ANY ANY} of its children, each child a full nested condition) or a LEAF (a single check). Any node may be negated. Leaf evaluation delegates to the existing synchronous checks ({@link AssertAction#passes}, {@link WaitInventoryPredicateAction#matches}, {@link WaitDurabilityAction#matches}, {@link WaitFreeSlotsAction#matches}, {@link WaitEntityTargetAction#matches}) plus a new {@link Kind#VARIABLE} comparison, so it "works with every condition" without re-implementing any.

Variable templates ({@code {name}}) in operands resolve through {@link MacroVariables}, which is already bound to the running macro's variable context on the executor thread.

A root group containing a single ALWAYS leaf — the default "always true" condition. The single editable leaf if this condition is "simple" — a lone leaf, or a non-negated group with exactly one leaf child. Returns {@code null} for genuinely nested/compound conditions (which the flat single-leaf editor can't represent and must be preserved as-is). Write the representative leaf's fields as flat tag keys for the action editor. Deserialize a condition for an action that supports both the nested tag and the flat editor view. The nested {@code condition} tag is canonical. When that nested condition is "simple" (a single leaf) and flat keys are present, the flat keys win (they carry the editor's latest single-leaf edits). Genuinely nested/compound conditions are preserved as-is — the flat editor can't represent them, so its (inert) keys are ignored, preventing data loss. Rebuild a single-leaf condition (root ALL group + one leaf) from flat editor keys. True if this condition is unconditionally true (so callers can skip evaluating it).

src/main/java/autismclient/util/macro/SP.documentationSource: feature-owned JavaDoc; execution schema is read from the runtime registry
src/main/java/autismclient/util/macro/SP.notes:
Spoofs your ping by adding latency, ending on one of three conditions chosen by {@link #endMode}. Modelled on AUTISM's PingSpoof: incoming keep-alives are held and answered {@link #pingDelayMs} ms late, so the server measures your real round-trip plus that delay (see {@link PingSpoofController}).

{@link #realIncoming} / {@link #realOutgoing} optionally make the client actually behave as if it had the latency by also holding the packets it receives / sends — independently toggleable.

  • {@link EndMode#TIMEOUT} — the spoof lasts for a fixed window set in milliseconds, or in ticks (50 ms each) when {@link #useTicks} is on. {@link #continueNextActions} decides whether the macro blocks here for the window or runs on while the spoof expires in the background.
  • {@link EndMode#STEPS} — the spoof turns on and the macro continues immediately; it stays on for the next {@link #stepCount} action rows (the impacted span shown in the editor) and is removed once execution leaves that span. Lifetime is owned by the macro executor, not a timer.
  • {@link EndMode#END} — like STEPS but the span runs to the last row of the macro; the spoof is removed when the macro finishes (or loops back past this action).

Every override path is bounded (timer, step span, or macro lifetime), so the spoof always reverts on its own. Mirrors {@link FpsAction}'s shape.

How the ping spoof decides when to switch off. Number of following rows the spoof stays on for in {@link EndMode#STEPS} (always {@code >= 1}). Window length in milliseconds, derived from whichever unit is selected (TIMEOUT mode only).
